source_records.title: The role of accounting in the informal economy
source_records.abstract: Using novel survey data from 1426 firms in Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador, we examine the voluntary adoption of accounting systems by microenterprises operating in the informal economy and its association with access to credit and business growth. Despite the absence of regulatory mandates, 44 percent of informal microbusinesses maintain systematic financial records, with roughly three-quarters of those using notebooks and one-quarter using digital records. Accounting quality is closely linked to the owner’s startup motivation, financial stake, and management capabilities. Informal firms that rely on larger suppliers, extend customer installment credit, engage in marketing promotions, or employ more formal organizational structures are also more likely to adopt structured recordkeeping systems, highlighting accounting’s role as a managerial tool rather than as a compliance function or as a precursor to entering the formal economy. Informal firms that maintain notebooks separating business and personal accounts are significantly more likely to apply for and obtain bank loans. Our inferences for access to credit also extend to microenterprises in the Dominican Republic. In addition, accounting quality appears to support lender due diligence even among informal firms, particularly when lenders are more sophisticated. Using a broader measure of credit market status, we find that accounting quality rises monotonically across credit tiers. Finally, we find that entrepreneurs with higher-quality accounting systems are more likely to plan for business expansion. By illuminating the motivations behind accounting choices in low-enforcement settings, this study deepens our understanding of the foundational role accounting plays in early-stage business development in emerging markets.

The role of accounting in the informal economy☆

•
Cost–benefit drives formalization and accounting decisions of microenterprises.
•
Owners with personal capital at stake voluntarily adopt higher-quality accounting.
•
Personal motivation, management skills, and customer relations also play a role.
•
Accounting quality improves credit access for informal microenterprises.
•
Informal firms with better records are 9% more likely to apply and 14% to obtain loans.

Using novel survey data from 1426 firms in Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador, we examine the voluntary adoption of accounting systems by microenterprises operating in the informal economy and its association with access to credit and business growth. Despite the absence of regulatory mandates, 44 percent of informal microbusinesses maintain systematic financial records, with roughly three-quarters of those using notebooks and one-quarter using digital records. Accounting quality is closely linked to the owner’s startup motivation, financial stake, and management capabilities. Informal firms that rely on larger suppliers, extend customer installment credit, engage in marketing promotions, or employ more formal organizational structures are also more likely to adopt structured recordkeeping systems, highlighting accounting’s role as a managerial tool rather than as a compliance function or as a precursor to entering the formal economy. Informal firms that maintain notebooks separating business and personal accounts are significantly more likely to apply for and obtain bank loans. Our inferences for access to credit also extend to microenterprises in the Dominican Republic. In addition, accounting quality appears to support lender due diligence even among informal firms, particularly when lenders are more sophisticated. Using a broader measure of credit market status, we find that accounting quality rises monotonically across credit tiers. Finally, we find that entrepreneurs with higher-quality accounting systems are more likely to plan for business expansion. By illuminating the motivations behind accounting choices in low-enforcement settings, this study deepens our understanding of the foundational role accounting plays in early-stage business development in emerging markets.

By illuminating the motivations behind accounting choices in low-enforcement settings, this study deepens our understanding of the foundational role accounting plays in early-stage business development in emerging markets.JEL classificationG21; M13; M4; O17KeywordsInformal economy; Developing economies; Microenterprises; Recordkeeping; Accounting quality; Financial inclusion; Access to creditIntroductionThis study examines the relationship between voluntary accounting practices and the informal economy in developing countries, where firms largely operate outside tax and business registrations, and beyond government enforcement (Ulyssea, 2020). We focus on informal microenterprises, defined as those that are not registered with the national tax authority, that are not in compliance with business registration requirements (ILO, 2020), and that employ fewer than ten persons (see European Union, ILO, IDB). Using cross-sectional data from a 2019 survey by the International Labour Organization (ILO) on 1426 microenterprises in Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador, we document the economic trade-offs associated with recordkeeping practices in informal firms and how these practices relate to access to credit and business growth.1Despite accounting for approximately 30 percent of global GDP and 50 percent of employment, the informal economy, where micro and small enterprises are dominant, remains underexplored in the accounting literature (ILO, 2020, Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2024, Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2025). Their business practices are typically rudimentary (Buehn and Schneider, 2012, Halvorson-Quevedo, 1991, IFC, 2010, Ulyssea, 2020) and their financial transactions are often governed by social capital and trust-based relationships (Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2024, Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2025).Prior research on private firms shows that even absent public disclosure mandates, their accounting choices are typically shaped by tax rules, loan covenants, and statutory reporting thresholds (e.g., Bernard and Sutherland, 2025, Allee and Yohn, 2009, Ball, 2024, Beuselinck et al., 2023, Lisowsky and Minnis, 2020, Minnis, 2011). In contrast, entrepreneurs in the informal economy face no such mandates, so even maintaining rudimentary records reflects a direct cost-benefit trade-off. The contrast between formal and informal firms in our data underscores this point: nearly all formal microenterprises maintain systematic, often digitized records, whereas informal firms display wide heterogeneity.2 The informal economy thus provides a distinctive lens through which to observe the foundational, emergent role of accounting, which is not readily visible in more developed and institutionally mature markets (Ball, 2024, Ball, 2025b).3Our survey-based measures capture both whether systematic records are kept and gradations in their level of sophistication, providing direct descriptive evidence on accounting adoption in the informal sector absent regulatory mandates. We first focus on a binary outcome, the voluntary decision of informal microbusinesses to adopt a systematic recordkeeping system (Systematic Recordkeeping). We later exploit the survey’s granularity to develop a four-level ordinal measure of Accounting Quality: (1) No systematic recordkeeping; (2) Commingled NB, where business and personal financial records are combined in a single physical, paper-based notebook; (3) Separate NB, where business records are maintained separately in a dedicated, paper-based notebook; and (4) Digitized, representing a more sophisticated accounting system (see Fig. 1). A distinctive feature of our setting is the commingled category (Jayachandran, 2020) because most microenterprise training programs emphasize separating business and personal finances (Dyer et al., 2016, McKenzie and Woodruff, 2014). While such separation may facilitate business sustainability and serve as a behavioral commitment device (Drexler et al., 2014), whether it has real effects is an open question.In our sample of informal firms, 44 percent maintain systematic records, with nearly three-quarters relying on a paper-based notebook. Notably, more than one-quarter of these notebook users do not separate business and personal finances. In our setting, there is no separation of ownership and control, which implies that accounting system choices are less likely to reflect classic agency conflicts. Instead, these choices primarily reflect entrepreneurs’ trade-offs between the costs and benefits of systematic recordkeeping. Using a reduced-form probit (ordered probit) model, we examine the association between Systematic Recordkeeping (Accounting Quality) and the determinants that shape these trade-offs.We find that entrepreneurs with stronger business orientation (Calderon et al., 2017), but not those motivated by family considerations, and those with greater managerial human capital (Bloom et al., 2010, Bloom et al., 2013, Bloom and Van Reenen, 2007, Karlan and Valdivia, 2011) are more likely to adopt systematic recordkeeping. Entrepreneurs who view their own equity capital or banks as desirable funding sources or who are saving toward a future capital infusion are more likely to have systematic financial records (Cassar, 2009, Dupas and Robinson, 2013). The observed association between accounting choices and owner characteristics provides novel descriptive evidence that broadens our understanding of the role of accounting in evolving business organizations (Sunder, 1997).Among operational factors, firms that extend installment credit or engage in marketing promotion activities are more likely to rely on systematic financial records, with accounting plausibly serving as a managerial tool for customer acquisition and retention. Consistent with the informational demands of supply-chain relationships, informal firms that rely on large suppliers are more likely to have systematic records. Reflecting the level of informality in organizational design (Brickley et al., 2003), businesses that rely more heavily on family members or temporary workers tend to use more rudimentary records, whereas those with more full-time employees opt for higher-quality accounting.Turning to Accounting Quality, we report the marginal effects from the ordered probit model for each outcome category. We find that these marginal effects indicate a shift in probability away from no systematic financial records toward higher-quality systems, with commingled notebooks playing only a limited role. For example, at the margin, firms that extend installment credit are 33 percentage points less likely to have no systematic records, and about 16 percentage points more likely to adopt either separate notebooks or digitized systems, relative to firms that do not extend installment credit. Robustness analyses show that accounting choices are not associated with anticipated formalization and are not merely proxies for general business sophistication. Taken together, our results align with historical evidence that merchants and money changers created accounting systems to support the efficient management of their businesses rather than as a compliance mechanism (Ball, 2025b, Basu et al., 2009).We next examine the role of accounting in microenterprises’ access to credit, a key indicator of financial development (Guiso et al., 2004). Prior research highlights the importance of social capital and trust in facilitating supplier credit in informal economies (Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2024). By contrast, we find that firms that prefer bank financing are more likely to maintain systematic financial records, raising the empirical question of whether accounting quality is associated with access to bank credit in the informal economy. For this analysis, we use the microenterprises in the formal economy as a comparison group (footnote 2).Roughly 40 percent of the microenterprises in our sample have ever applied for a bank loan, with 34 percent of informal firms and 52 percent of formal firms doing so. Among applicants, 77 percent of informal firms and 93 percent of formal firms reported receiving the loan. To model both the decision to apply and the likelihood of approval, we estimate separate Heckman selection models for informal firms and for the benchmark sample of formal firms. Our specifications include controls for collateral, contracting reputation, customer and supplier credits, and business age (Berger and Udell, 1995, Petersen and Rajan, 1994, Banerjee et al., 2017).For informal firms, only the coefficient on notebooks with separate accounts (Separate NB) is statistically significant for both loan applications and approvals, suggesting that separating business and personal financial records may be particularly relevant for credit access. For formal firms, digitized records are associated with a higher likelihood of loan applications and approvals, consistent with lenders placing greater weight on more sophisticated accounting systems. We draw similar inferences when using a broader measure of credit market status beyond mere access to bank loans, and these patterns remain robust to copula-based selection models that relax the joint normality assumption. Taken together, the results point to a positive relationship between accounting quality and credit access among microenterprises.4 However, we acknowledge that our cross-sectional data limit our ability to make causal inferences about the relationships we observe.To mitigate concerns about generalizability, we replicate our findings from the credit access analysis using data from a similar ILO survey in the Dominican Republic (DR) conducted in 2023. The results also highlight the role of social capital (Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2024): small banks appear less likely to demand systematic financial records when providing small loans to informal firms, consistent with trust-based lending. For large loan requests, systematic recordkeeping is common regardless of bank type, suggesting that traditional financial due diligence becomes more important when financial stakes are larger.Lastly, using the CA sample and controlling for the entrepreneur’s human capital, firm size, and country/sector fixed effects, we find that firms with higher-quality accounting systems are more likely to report business expansion plans, particularly along the extensive margin. We also find that higher-quality accounting is associated with greater productivity (monthly sales per employee) among informal firms. Taken together, these findings shed light on the managerial role of accounting in informal firms (Datar et al., 2009).Because accounting evolves in parallel with broader institutional transformations, establishing causation in this setting is inherently difficult and may be unproductive in assessing its social value (Ball, 2024, Ball, 2025a, Ball, 2025b). Using rich survey data from Central America, we provide descriptive evidence on the role of accounting outside the shadow of regulatory mandates, where adoption reflects a direct cost-benefit trade-off. fields.authors: Marcela Aguilar a, Gary Lind b, K. Ramesh c
fields.abstract: Using novel survey data from 1426 firms in Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador, we examine the voluntary adoption of accounting systems by microenterprises operating in the informal economy and its association with access to credit and business growth. Despite the absence of regulatory mandates, 44 percent of informal microbusinesses maintain systematic financial records, with roughly three-quarters of those using notebooks and one-quarter using digital records. Accounting quality is closely linked to the owner’s startup motivation, financial stake, and management capabilities. Informal firms that rely on larger suppliers, extend customer installment credit, engage in marketing promotions, or employ more formal organizational structures are also more likely to adopt structured recordkeeping systems, highlighting accounting’s role as a managerial tool rather than as a compliance function or as a precursor to entering the formal economy. Informal firms that maintain notebooks separating business and personal accounts are significantly more likely to apply for and obtain bank loans. Our inferences for access to credit also extend to microenterprises in the Dominican Republic. In addition, accounting quality appears to support lender due diligence even among informal firms, particularly when lenders are more sophisticated. Using a broader measure of credit market status, we find that accounting quality rises monotonically across credit tiers. Finally, we find that entrepreneurs with higher-quality accounting systems are more likely to plan for business expansion. By illuminating the motivations behind accounting choices in low-enforcement settings, this study deepens our understanding of the foundational role accounting plays in early-stage business development in emerging markets.

•

•

Using novel survey data from 1426 firms in Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador, we examine the voluntary adoption of accounting systems by microenterprises operating in the informal economy and its association with access to credit and business growth. Despite the absence of regulatory mandates, 44 percent of informal microbusinesses maintain systematic financial records, with roughly three-quarters of those using notebooks and one-quarter using digital records. Accounting quality is closely linked to the owner’s startup motivation, financial stake, and management capabilities. Informal firms that rely on larger suppliers, extend customer installment credit, engage in marketing promotions, or employ more formal organizational structures are also more likely to adopt structured recordkeeping systems, highlighting accounting’s role as a managerial tool rather than as a compliance function or as a precursor to entering the formal economy. Informal firms that maintain notebooks separating business and personal accounts are significantly more likely to apply for and obtain bank loans. Our inferences for access to credit also extend to microenterprises in the Dominican Republic. In addition, accounting quality appears to support lender due diligence even among informal firms, particularly when lenders are more sophisticated. Using a broader measure of credit market status, we find that accounting quality rises monotonically across credit tiers. Finally, we find that entrepreneurs with higher-quality accounting systems are more likely to plan for business expansion. By illuminating the motivations behind accounting choices in low-enforcement settings, this study deepens our understanding of the foundational role accounting plays in early-stage business development in emerging markets.

By illuminating the motivations behind accounting choices in low-enforcement settings, this study deepens our understanding of the foundational role accounting plays in early-stage business development in emerging markets.JEL classificationG21; M13; M4; O17KeywordsInformal economy; Developing economies; Microenterprises; Recordkeeping; Accounting quality; Financial inclusion; Access to creditIntroductionThis study examines the relationship between voluntary accounting practices and the informal economy in developing countries, where firms largely operate outside tax and business registrations, and beyond government enforcement (Ulyssea, 2020). We focus on informal microenterprises, defined as those that are not registered with the national tax authority, that are not in compliance with business registration requirements (ILO, 2020), and that employ fewer than ten persons (see European Union, ILO, IDB). Using cross-sectional data from a 2019 survey by the International Labour Organization (ILO) on 1426 microenterprises in Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador, we document the economic trade-offs associated with recordkeeping practices in informal firms and how these practices relate to access to credit and business growth.1Despite accounting for approximately 30 percent of global GDP and 50 percent of employment, the informal economy, where micro and small enterprises are dominant, remains underexplored in the accounting literature (ILO, 2020, Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2024, Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2025). Their business practices are typically rudimentary (Buehn and Schneider, 2012, Halvorson-Quevedo, 1991, IFC, 2010, Ulyssea, 2020) and their financial transactions are often governed by social capital and trust-based relationships (Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2024, Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2025).Prior research on private firms shows that even absent public disclosure mandates, their accounting choices are typically shaped by tax rules, loan covenants, and statutory reporting thresholds (e.g., Bernard and Sutherland, 2025, Allee and Yohn, 2009, Ball, 2024, Beuselinck et al., 2023, Lisowsky and Minnis, 2020, Minnis, 2011). In contrast, entrepreneurs in the informal economy face no such mandates, so even maintaining rudimentary records reflects a direct cost-benefit trade-off. The contrast between formal and informal firms in our data underscores this point: nearly all formal microenterprises maintain systematic, often digitized records, whereas informal firms display wide heterogeneity.2 The informal economy thus provides a distinctive lens through which to observe the foundational, emergent role of accounting, which is not readily visible in more developed and institutionally mature markets (Ball, 2024, Ball, 2025b).3Our survey-based measures capture both whether systematic records are kept and gradations in their level of sophistication, providing direct descriptive evidence on accounting adoption in the informal sector absent regulatory mandates. We first focus on a binary outcome, the voluntary decision of informal microbusinesses to adopt a systematic recordkeeping system (Systematic Recordkeeping). We later exploit the survey’s granularity to develop a four-level ordinal measure of Accounting Quality: (1) No systematic recordkeeping; (2) Commingled NB, where business and personal financial records are combined in a single physical, paper-based notebook; (3) Separate NB, where business records are maintained separately in a dedicated, paper-based notebook; and (4) Digitized, representing a more sophisticated accounting system (see Fig. 1). A distinctive feature of our setting is the commingled category (Jayachandran, 2020) because most microenterprise training programs emphasize separating business and personal finances (Dyer et al., 2016, McKenzie and Woodruff, 2014). While such separation may facilitate business sustainability and serve as a behavioral commitment device (Drexler et al., 2014), whether it has real effects is an open question.In our sample of informal firms, 44 percent maintain systematic records, with nearly three-quarters relying on a paper-based notebook. Notably, more than one-quarter of these notebook users do not separate business and personal finances. In our setting, there is no separation of ownership and control, which implies that accounting system choices are less likely to reflect classic agency conflicts. Instead, these choices primarily reflect entrepreneurs’ trade-offs between the costs and benefits of systematic recordkeeping. Using a reduced-form probit (ordered probit) model, we examine the association between Systematic Recordkeeping (Accounting Quality) and the determinants that shape these trade-offs.We find that entrepreneurs with stronger business orientation (Calderon et al., 2017), but not those motivated by family considerations, and those with greater managerial human capital (Bloom et al., 2010, Bloom et al., 2013, Bloom and Van Reenen, 2007, Karlan and Valdivia, 2011) are more likely to adopt systematic recordkeeping. Entrepreneurs who view their own equity capital or banks as desirable funding sources or who are saving toward a future capital infusion are more likely to have systematic financial records (Cassar, 2009, Dupas and Robinson, 2013). The observed association between accounting choices and owner characteristics provides novel descriptive evidence that broadens our understanding of the role of accounting in evolving business organizations (Sunder, 1997).Among operational factors, firms that extend installment credit or engage in marketing promotion activities are more likely to rely on systematic financial records, with accounting plausibly serving as a managerial tool for customer acquisition and retention. Consistent with the informational demands of supply-chain relationships, informal firms that rely on large suppliers are more likely to have systematic records. Reflecting the level of informality in organizational design (Brickley et al., 2003), businesses that rely more heavily on family members or temporary workers tend to use more rudimentary records, whereas those with more full-time employees opt for higher-quality accounting.Turning to Accounting Quality, we report the marginal effects from the ordered probit model for each outcome category. We find that these marginal effects indicate a shift in probability away from no systematic financial records toward higher-quality systems, with commingled notebooks playing only a limited role. For example, at the margin, firms that extend installment credit are 33 percentage points less likely to have no systematic records, and about 16 percentage points more likely to adopt either separate notebooks or digitized systems, relative to firms that do not extend installment credit. Robustness analyses show that accounting choices are not associated with anticipated formalization and are not merely proxies for general business sophistication. Taken together, our results align with historical evidence that merchants and money changers created accounting systems to support the efficient management of their businesses rather than as a compliance mechanism (Ball, 2025b, Basu et al., 2009).We next examine the role of accounting in microenterprises’ access to credit, a key indicator of financial development (Guiso et al., 2004). Prior research highlights the importance of social capital and trust in facilitating supplier credit in informal economies (Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2024). By contrast, we find that firms that prefer bank financing are more likely to maintain systematic financial records, raising the empirical question of whether accounting quality is associated with access to bank credit in the informal economy. For this analysis, we use the microenterprises in the formal economy as a comparison group (footnote 2).Roughly 40 percent of the microenterprises in our sample have ever applied for a bank loan, with 34 percent of informal firms and 52 percent of formal firms doing so. Among applicants, 77 percent of informal firms and 93 percent of formal firms reported receiving the loan. To model both the decision to apply and the likelihood of approval, we estimate separate Heckman selection models for informal firms and for the benchmark sample of formal firms. Our specifications include controls for collateral, contracting reputation, customer and supplier credits, and business age (Berger and Udell, 1995, Petersen and Rajan, 1994, Banerjee et al., 2017).For informal firms, only the coefficient on notebooks with separate accounts (Separate NB) is statistically significant for both loan applications and approvals, suggesting that separating business and personal financial records may be particularly relevant for credit access. For formal firms, digitized records are associated with a higher likelihood of loan applications and approvals, consistent with lenders placing greater weight on more sophisticated accounting systems. We draw similar inferences when using a broader measure of credit market status beyond mere access to bank loans, and these patterns remain robust to copula-based selection models that relax the joint normality assumption. Taken together, the results point to a positive relationship between accounting quality and credit access among microenterprises.4 However, we acknowledge that our cross-sectional data limit our ability to make causal inferences about the relationships we observe.To mitigate concerns about generalizability, we replicate our findings from the credit access analysis using data from a similar ILO survey in the Dominican Republic (DR) conducted in 2023. The results also highlight the role of social capital (Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2024): small banks appear less likely to demand systematic financial records when providing small loans to informal firms, consistent with trust-based lending. For large loan requests, systematic recordkeeping is common regardless of bank type, suggesting that traditional financial due diligence becomes more important when financial stakes are larger.Lastly, using the CA sample and controlling for the entrepreneur’s human capital, firm size, and country/sector fixed effects, we find that firms with higher-quality accounting systems are more likely to report business expansion plans, particularly along the extensive margin. We also find that higher-quality accounting is associated with greater productivity (monthly sales per employee) among informal firms. Taken together, these findings shed light on the managerial role of accounting in informal firms (Datar et al., 2009).Because accounting evolves in parallel with broader institutional transformations, establishing causation in this setting is inherently difficult and may be unproductive in assessing its social value (Ball, 2024, Ball, 2025a, Ball, 2025b). Using rich survey data from Central America, we provide descriptive evidence on the role of accounting outside the shadow of regulatory mandates, where adoption reflects a direct cost-benefit trade-off. This unique setting allows us to observe accounting in its foundational role as a managerial tool rather than as a compliance mechanism.5The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 examines when and why informal firms voluntarily keep systematic accounting records. Next, Section 3 explores how accounting quality relates to access to credit. Finally, Section 4 examines how accounting quality is associated with managerial decisions regarding microenterprise growth plans and productivity. proposed.abstract:
•
Cost–benefit drives formalization and accounting decisions of microenterprises.
•
Owners with personal capital at stake voluntarily adopt higher-quality accounting.
•
Personal motivation, management skills, and customer relations also play a role.
•
Accounting quality improves credit access for informal microenterprises.

Informal firms with better records are 9% more likely to apply and 14% to obtain loans.

fields.authors: Marcela Aguilar a, Gary Lind b, K. Ramesh c
fields.abstract: Using novel survey data from 1426 firms in Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador, we examine the voluntary adoption of accounting systems by microenterprises operating in the informal economy and its association with access to credit and business growth. Despite the absence of regulatory mandates, 44 percent of informal microbusinesses maintain systematic financial records, with roughly three-quarters of those using notebooks and one-quarter using digital records. Accounting quality is closely linked to the owner’s startup motivation, financial stake, and management capabilities. Informal firms that rely on larger suppliers, extend customer installment credit, engage in marketing promotions, or employ more formal organizational structures are also more likely to adopt structured recordkeeping systems, highlighting accounting’s role as a managerial tool rather than as a compliance function or as a precursor to entering the formal economy. Informal firms that maintain notebooks separating business and personal accounts are significantly more likely to apply for and obtain bank loans. Our inferences for access to credit also extend to microenterprises in the Dominican Republic. In addition, accounting quality appears to support lender due diligence even among informal firms, particularly when lenders are more sophisticated. Using a broader measure of credit market status, we find that accounting quality rises monotonically across credit tiers. Finally, we find that entrepreneurs with higher-quality accounting systems are more likely to plan for business expansion. By illuminating the motivations behind accounting choices in low-enforcement settings, this study deepens our understanding of the foundational role accounting plays in early-stage business development in emerging markets.

Informal firms that maintain notebooks separating business and personal accounts are significantly more likely to apply for and obtain bank loans. Our inferences for access to credit also extend to microenterprises in the Dominican Republic. In addition, accounting quality appears to support lender due diligence even among informal firms, particularly when lenders are more sophisticated. Using a broader measure of credit market status, we find that accounting quality rises monotonically across credit tiers. Finally, we find that entrepreneurs with higher-quality accounting systems are more likely to plan for business expansion. By illuminating the motivations behind accounting choices in low-enforcement settings, this study deepens our understanding of the foundational role accounting plays in early-stage business development in emerging markets.

Knowledge is power: A field experiment in the Chinese and US stock markets

This study examines the causal effect of financial knowledge on stock pricing efficiency. Leveraging a specially designed investor education website, we conduct a field experiment, sharing insights on the pricing of accounting accruals with investors across China and the US on social media. We find that the treatment stocks experience a reduction in accrual mispricing relative to the control stocks. This effect is particularly pronounced when knowledge that enhances the conceptual understanding of accruals is paired with knowledge that aids in the quantitative application of accruals. Furthermore, the treatment effect is strengthened among stocks with investors who engage more deeply with the educational content yet possess lower financial sophistication.

Furthermore, the treatment effect is strengthened among stocks with investors who engage more deeply with the educational content yet possess lower financial sophistication.KeywordsFinancial knowledge; Accrual mispricing; Investor education; Field experiment; Social mediaJEL classificationG14; G41; G53; C93IntroductionHaving knowledge of financial concepts and skills is crucial for making sound financial decisions. Research indicates that financial knowledge influences individuals’ financial behavior in various aspects, such as market participation and asset allocation.1 Given that financial behavior drives asset prices, it is surprising that the literature does not directly assess the effects of financial knowledge on asset prices. This study aims to fill this gap by examining whether financial knowledge affects asset pricing. Education can empower investors with the knowledge and skills needed to process and interpret public information (e.g., corporate disclosures). This, in turn, supplies the market with more informed investors, improving the efficiency of stock prices.This topic poses both conceptual and empirical challenges. First, in perfect market conditions, where investors possess comprehensive knowledge and the full capacity to process information, additional education should not influence their decisions and, consequently, stock prices (Simon, 1987). Although, in reality, investors have imperfect knowledge and limited cognitive resources (Simon, 1955; Kahneman and Tversky, 1973), education may still prove ineffective if investors lack motivation and the requisite expertise to comprehend the educational materials (Piaget, 2003; Fernandes et al., 2014), or cannot apply their newfound knowledge to real-world decisions (Merkoulova and Veld, 2022).2Empirically, it is hard to establish a causal link between financial knowledge and asset pricing. One primary hurdle is the potential endogeneity between financial knowledge and stock prices (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014; Bianchi, 2018). For instance, financial knowledge and market outcomes can be simultaneously shaped by less observable factors such as individuals’ time preferences and wealth endowment (Jappelli and Padula, 2013; Meier and Sprenger, 2013). Moreover, there is a possibility of a feedback loop: when investors gain experience and learn from past stock prices, their financial knowledge deepens, which in turn could influence prices.To tackle these challenges and investigate our research question, we conduct a field experiment that involves educating investors about accounting accruals, a concrete type of financial knowledge. Accruals represent the difference between a firm's reported earnings and its underlying cash flows, reflecting the firm's estimates of future benefits and obligations. In essence, the accrual component of earnings is less persistent than the cash flow component in predicting future earnings. However, numerous studies show that, due to cognitive limitations, investors often overlook the transient nature of accruals and overprice stocks with high accruals, a phenomenon known as the “accrual anomaly” (or “accrual mispricing”) (Sloan, 1996; Xie, 2001; Richardson et al., 2005; Chan et al., 2006; Allen et al., 2013). Our study investigates whether investor education can address the anomaly.We choose to focus on accruals for three reasons. First, the literature identifies accrual mispricing as one of the most pervasive and robust financial anomalies (Fama and French, 2008; Hirshleifer et al., 2012; Avramov et al., 2013). While extensive efforts are made to explain this phenomenon (Mashruwala et al., 2006; Khan, 2008), the mechanisms underlying accrual mispricing remain unclear (Richardson et al., 2010). Second, unlike basic financial concepts such as compounding, inflation, interest rates, and diversification (Van Rooij et al., 2011; Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014), accruals represent a more intricate concept. Gaining proficiency in this area can notably enhance an individual's financial acumen (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014). Third, given that grasping the economic implications of accruals demands a sophisticated cognitive aptitude (Collins et al., 2003), accruals present an ideal base to test the efficacy of investor education.We implement randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to examine whether providing accrual knowledge to investors reduces accrual mispricing. Our experiment has two distinctive features. First, we convey this specialized knowledge to investors via social media platforms. Evidence indicates that social media, serving as vital conduits of information for investors, play a significant role in influencing investor behaviors and stock market outcomes (Miller and Skinner, 2015). A testament to this is the stock price rebound for GameStop and AMC in January 2021, highlighting the growing sway of social media in the investment community.3Second, we conduct the experiment to across firms listed in both the Chinese and US markets. Nobel laureate Abhijit Banerjee posits that “a very simple approach to generalization … is to implement the same concept in multiple locations to build confidence in its impact” (Banerjee, 2020, p.1938). As the leading developed market, the US operates under rigorous securities regulations and features significant participation of institutional investors. Conversely, China, while being the world's largest emerging market and second-largest stock market by capitalization, has a more relaxed regulatory environment and tends to be dominated by retail investors (Titman et al., 2022). Given the large institutional differences between the two countries, any consistent findings from our study would support the generalizability of our conclusion.Our experiment ran from January to December 2020, covering all publicly listed firms in China and the US. We develop two distinct educational modules on the concepts and pricing implications of accruals. The first module offers a conceptual introduction of accruals, detailing their definition, properties, and implications for future earnings (conceptual knowledge). The second module introduces methodologies for estimating accruals, detailing specific models, key variables, data sources, and tools (methodological knowledge). The materials are made available in Chinese and English for the respective markets.We disseminate these materials using social media platforms in each country, namely Weibo, Xueqiu, and Guba EastMoney in China and Twitter and StockTwits in the US. Over a 19-day window around firms’ earnings announcement (EA) days in 2020, we share the two sets of knowledge, along with the upcoming EA news, on the designated tag pages for the treatment group of stocks. For a subset of stocks, only the conceptual knowledge and EA news are shared. Each of these posts contains a hyperlink to a custom webpage we built for the relevant stock, ensuring easy access to the complete educational materials.We create a control group of stocks by merely sharing the upcoming EA news as a placebo. In theory, any observed difference in accrual pricing between the treatment and control groups should reflect the effect of accrual education. For a robustness check, we establish an alternative benchmark by creating a comparison group of stocks for which we did not share any information. Our final dataset comprises 2284 stocks from the Chinese market and 2387 stocks from the US market. Our educational materials garnered a total of 26,834,089 views in China and 3,397,437 views in the US, tallied one day after posting on platforms that provide such data. Diagnostic tests confirm no significant differences in firm characteristics between the treatment and control groups, and the stock price movements prior to the experiment are parallel across groups.In line with prior studies (Sloan, 1996; Xie, 2001), high-accrual stocks in the control group earn positive abnormal returns around the EAs that subsequently reverse over the following year. The evidence confirms the presence of accrual mispricing in our setting and echoes recent findings that the anomaly persists when measured with true release dates and as-filed data (Du et al., 2023; Bowles et al., 2024).Next, we examine whether accrual education reduces this mispricing, which can be broken down into two components: overvaluation of accruals during EAs and subsequent price correction in the post-EA phase. First, using a difference-in-differences (DID) analysis, we find that EA returns for high-accrual stocks are lower in the treatment group than in the control group across both markets, suggesting that the education treatment results in a price discount for high-accrual stocks at the announcement. When separating the treatments, we find that the effect is driven by the treatment of combined conceptual and methodological knowledge; the conceptual-only treatment has the expected sign but lacks statistical significance. Formal tests confirm that the difference between the two treatments is significant, suggesting that adding methodological knowledge to the conceptual content is crucial for an effective intervention.Second, we examine whether our treatments mitigate the subsequent price reversal. Using the same DID framework, we find that treatment stocks indeed exhibit a smaller reversal than control stocks in both markets. For an average treatment stock, a one-standard-deviation increase in accruals improves the post-EA return by approximately 4.2% in China and 3.9% in the US relative to control stocks. As with the announcement-period results, this effect is concentrated in the group that received both conceptual and methodological knowledge: the negative relation between accruals and post-EA returns is essentially eliminated in this combined treatment group, whereas in the conceptual-only group the relation also improves but remains statistically insignificant. Together, the evidence indicates that the education treatment is effective in mitigating accrual mispricing and highlights the vital role of practical, methodological tools in this process.We obtain similar results when using unexpected discretionary accruals (see Balsam et al., 2002) and when using the comparison group as the benchmark in the DID analysis. A placebo test based on historical accruals yields no treatment effects, suggesting that our results are falsifiable. Additionally, we find that the treatment effects are more pronounced when the investors engage more with the educational materials (e.g., increased reading, comments, retweets, likes, and saves on our posts, as well as more clicks on the hyperlinks within the posts).Further analysis of the treatment effects indicates that these effects likely arise from addressing financial knowledge gaps among unsophisticated investors. First, the treatment effects are concentrated on stocks dominated by retail investors. Second, the education treatments reduce order imbalance (i.e., excessive purchases) for retail investors in stocks with high accruals on the EA day, but no similar pattern emerges for institutional investors. Third, the treatment effects are more pronounced in firms located in regions with low financial literacy.Lastly, we conduct tests to address alternative explanations. First, no education effect is found when comparing the control and comparison groups, negating the impact of treatment salience. Second, the education effect is evident only for positive accruals, aligning with our education's focus on high accrual implications and refuting the notion that our exercises merely amplify attention to accruals. Third, the education effect persists one year after the experiment, with no new messages posted, suggesting that our treatment effect is not fear-induced. Fourth, the effect remains pronounced in stocks with high trading turnover, implying a limited impact from the spillover effect due to common ownership between the treatment and control stocks. Finally, our results stay robust after accounting for the fixed effect of industry × EA months and excluding EAs during the pandemic peak, indicating minimal distortion from the COVID-19 outbreak.Our study makes several contributions. First, it adds to the literature on the effects of financial knowledge in financial markets. Existing studies mainly focus on the effects of financial knowledge on individuals’ financial decisions and behaviors (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014). To the best of our knowledge, ours is the first work to directly test the influence of financial knowledge on asset pricing.Second, our study extends research that examines financial anomalies and pricing efficiency. McLean and Pontiff (2016) posit that the academic discovery of financial anomalies can enhance market efficiency by enabling investors to pinpoint arbitrage opportunities. Our research underscores that not only is the discovery of such knowledge vital, but its dissemination and the education of investors regarding it are also crucial for improving market efficiency.Third, previous studies on accrual anomaly rest on explanations such as risk (Khan, 2008; Chichernea et al., 2015), transaction costs (Collins et al., 2003; Mashruwala et al., 2006), limited attention (Hirshleifer et al., 2011; Miao et al., 2016), and insufficient supplementary accounting information (Louis et al., 2008; Miao et al., 2016). We extend this body of literature by demonstrating a new explanation, namely investors’ limited understanding of accounting accruals. This perspective also sheds light on the understanding of other price anomalies.Lastly, our research carries policy implications. Individuals in many developed and developing countries have low levels of financial literacy (Van Rooij et al., 2011; Merkoulova and Veld, 2022). Although many financial education programs have been introduced worldwide to rectify this problem (Kaiser et al., 2022), their efficacy remains debatable (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014). Our findings underscore the potential of social media platforms as tools for investor education. Furthermore, our results highlight the importance of integrating methodological applications with conceptual explanations in financial education. This insight holds considerable relevance for the design and execution of financial education programs.Organizational accessGet full-text access by signing in with your organisationAccess through your organizationOther access optionsPurchase PDFNeed help with access?Section snippetsRelated literature“Financial knowledge,” or “financial literacy,” refers to people's ability to process economic information and make informed financial decisions (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014). proposed.title: Knowledge is power: A field experiment in the Chinese and US stock markets
proposed.abstract: This study examines the causal effect of financial knowledge on stock pricing efficiency. Leveraging a specially designed investor education website, we conduct a field experiment, sharing insights on the pricing of accounting accruals with investors across China and the US on social media. We find that the treatment stocks experience a reduction in accrual mispricing relative to the control stocks. This effect is particularly pronounced when knowledge that enhances the conceptual understanding of accruals is paired with knowledge that aids in the quantitative application of accruals. Furthermore, the treatment effect is strengthened among stocks with investors who engage more deeply with the educational content yet possess lower financial sophistication.

blocks.text: Knowledge is power: A field experiment in the Chinese and US stock markets
Knowledge is power: A field experiment in the Chinese and US stock markets
Knowledge is power: A field experiment in the Chinese and US stock markets

This study examines the causal effect of financial knowledge on stock pricing efficiency. Leveraging a specially designed investor education website, we conduct a field experiment, sharing insights on the pricing of accounting accruals with investors across China and the US on social media. We find that the treatment stocks experience a reduction in accrual mispricing relative to the control stocks. This effect is particularly pronounced when knowledge that enhances the conceptual understanding of accruals is paired with knowledge that aids in the quantitative application of accruals. Furthermore, the treatment effect is strengthened among stocks with investors who engage more deeply with the educational content yet possess lower financial sophistication.

Furthermore, the treatment effect is strengthened among stocks with investors who engage more deeply with the educational content yet possess lower financial sophistication.KeywordsFinancial knowledge; Accrual mispricing; Investor education; Field experiment; Social mediaJEL classificationG14; G41; G53; C93IntroductionHaving knowledge of financial concepts and skills is crucial for making sound financial decisions. Research indicates that financial knowledge influences individuals’ financial behavior in various aspects, such as market participation and asset allocation.1 Given that financial behavior drives asset prices, it is surprising that the literature does not directly assess the effects of financial knowledge on asset prices. This study aims to fill this gap by examining whether financial knowledge affects asset pricing. Education can empower investors with the knowledge and skills needed to process and interpret public information (e.g., corporate disclosures). This, in turn, supplies the market with more informed investors, improving the efficiency of stock prices.This topic poses both conceptual and empirical challenges. First, in perfect market conditions, where investors possess comprehensive knowledge and the full capacity to process information, additional education should not influence their decisions and, consequently, stock prices (Simon, 1987). Although, in reality, investors have imperfect knowledge and limited cognitive resources (Simon, 1955; Kahneman and Tversky, 1973), education may still prove ineffective if investors lack motivation and the requisite expertise to comprehend the educational materials (Piaget, 2003; Fernandes et al., 2014), or cannot apply their newfound knowledge to real-world decisions (Merkoulova and Veld, 2022).2Empirically, it is hard to establish a causal link between financial knowledge and asset pricing. One primary hurdle is the potential endogeneity between financial knowledge and stock prices (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014; Bianchi, 2018). For instance, financial knowledge and market outcomes can be simultaneously shaped by less observable factors such as individuals’ time preferences and wealth endowment (Jappelli and Padula, 2013; Meier and Sprenger, 2013). Moreover, there is a possibility of a feedback loop: when investors gain experience and learn from past stock prices, their financial knowledge deepens, which in turn could influence prices.To tackle these challenges and investigate our research question, we conduct a field experiment that involves educating investors about accounting accruals, a concrete type of financial knowledge. Accruals represent the difference between a firm's reported earnings and its underlying cash flows, reflecting the firm's estimates of future benefits and obligations. In essence, the accrual component of earnings is less persistent than the cash flow component in predicting future earnings. However, numerous studies show that, due to cognitive limitations, investors often overlook the transient nature of accruals and overprice stocks with high accruals, a phenomenon known as the “accrual anomaly” (or “accrual mispricing”) (Sloan, 1996; Xie, 2001; Richardson et al., 2005; Chan et al., 2006; Allen et al., 2013). Our study investigates whether investor education can address the anomaly.We choose to focus on accruals for three reasons. First, the literature identifies accrual mispricing as one of the most pervasive and robust financial anomalies (Fama and French, 2008; Hirshleifer et al., 2012; Avramov et al., 2013). While extensive efforts are made to explain this phenomenon (Mashruwala et al., 2006; Khan, 2008), the mechanisms underlying accrual mispricing remain unclear (Richardson et al., 2010). Second, unlike basic financial concepts such as compounding, inflation, interest rates, and diversification (Van Rooij et al., 2011; Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014), accruals represent a more intricate concept. Gaining proficiency in this area can notably enhance an individual's financial acumen (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014). Third, given that grasping the economic implications of accruals demands a sophisticated cognitive aptitude (Collins et al., 2003), accruals present an ideal base to test the efficacy of investor education.We implement randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to examine whether providing accrual knowledge to investors reduces accrual mispricing. Our experiment has two distinctive features. First, we convey this specialized knowledge to investors via social media platforms. Evidence indicates that social media, serving as vital conduits of information for investors, play a significant role in influencing investor behaviors and stock market outcomes (Miller and Skinner, 2015). A testament to this is the stock price rebound for GameStop and AMC in January 2021, highlighting the growing sway of social media in the investment community.3Second, we conduct the experiment to across firms listed in both the Chinese and US markets. Nobel laureate Abhijit Banerjee posits that “a very simple approach to generalization … is to implement the same concept in multiple locations to build confidence in its impact” (Banerjee, 2020, p.1938). As the leading developed market, the US operates under rigorous securities regulations and features significant participation of institutional investors. Conversely, China, while being the world's largest emerging market and second-largest stock market by capitalization, has a more relaxed regulatory environment and tends to be dominated by retail investors (Titman et al., 2022). Given the large institutional differences between the two countries, any consistent findings from our study would support the generalizability of our conclusion.Our experiment ran from January to December 2020, covering all publicly listed firms in China and the US. We develop two distinct educational modules on the concepts and pricing implications of accruals. The first module offers a conceptual introduction of accruals, detailing their definition, properties, and implications for future earnings (conceptual knowledge). The second module introduces methodologies for estimating accruals, detailing specific models, key variables, data sources, and tools (methodological knowledge). The materials are made available in Chinese and English for the respective markets.We disseminate these materials using social media platforms in each country, namely Weibo, Xueqiu, and Guba EastMoney in China and Twitter and StockTwits in the US. Over a 19-day window around firms’ earnings announcement (EA) days in 2020, we share the two sets of knowledge, along with the upcoming EA news, on the designated tag pages for the treatment group of stocks. For a subset of stocks, only the conceptual knowledge and EA news are shared. Each of these posts contains a hyperlink to a custom webpage we built for the relevant stock, ensuring easy access to the complete educational materials.We create a control group of stocks by merely sharing the upcoming EA news as a placebo. In theory, any observed difference in accrual pricing between the treatment and control groups should reflect the effect of accrual education. For a robustness check, we establish an alternative benchmark by creating a comparison group of stocks for which we did not share any information. Our final dataset comprises 2284 stocks from the Chinese market and 2387 stocks from the US market. Our educational materials garnered a total of 26,834,089 views in China and 3,397,437 views in the US, tallied one day after posting on platforms that provide such data. Diagnostic tests confirm no significant differences in firm characteristics between the treatment and control groups, and the stock price movements prior to the experiment are parallel across groups.In line with prior studies (Sloan, 1996; Xie, 2001), high-accrual stocks in the control group earn positive abnormal returns around the EAs that subsequently reverse over the following year. The evidence confirms the presence of accrual mispricing in our setting and echoes recent findings that the anomaly persists when measured with true release dates and as-filed data (Du et al., 2023; Bowles et al., 2024).Next, we examine whether accrual education reduces this mispricing, which can be broken down into two components: overvaluation of accruals during EAs and subsequent price correction in the post-EA phase. First, using a difference-in-differences (DID) analysis, we find that EA returns for high-accrual stocks are lower in the treatment group than in the control group across both markets, suggesting that the education treatment results in a price discount for high-accrual stocks at the announcement. When separating the treatments, we find that the effect is driven by the treatment of combined conceptual and methodological knowledge; the conceptual-only treatment has the expected sign but lacks statistical significance. Formal tests confirm that the difference between the two treatments is significant, suggesting that adding methodological knowledge to the conceptual content is crucial for an effective intervention.Second, we examine whether our treatments mitigate the subsequent price reversal. Using the same DID framework, we find that treatment stocks indeed exhibit a smaller reversal than control stocks in both markets. For an average treatment stock, a one-standard-deviation increase in accruals improves the post-EA return by approximately 4.2% in China and 3.9% in the US relative to control stocks. As with the announcement-period results, this effect is concentrated in the group that received both conceptual and methodological knowledge: the negative relation between accruals and post-EA returns is essentially eliminated in this combined treatment group, whereas in the conceptual-only group the relation also improves but remains statistically insignificant. Together, the evidence indicates that the education treatment is effective in mitigating accrual mispricing and highlights the vital role of practical, methodological tools in this process.We obtain similar results when using unexpected discretionary accruals (see Balsam et al., 2002) and when using the comparison group as the benchmark in the DID analysis. A placebo test based on historical accruals yields no treatment effects, suggesting that our results are falsifiable. Additionally, we find that the treatment effects are more pronounced when the investors engage more with the educational materials (e.g., increased reading, comments, retweets, likes, and saves on our posts, as well as more clicks on the hyperlinks within the posts).Further analysis of the treatment effects indicates that these effects likely arise from addressing financial knowledge gaps among unsophisticated investors. First, the treatment effects are concentrated on stocks dominated by retail investors. Second, the education treatments reduce order imbalance (i.e., excessive purchases) for retail investors in stocks with high accruals on the EA day, but no similar pattern emerges for institutional investors. Third, the treatment effects are more pronounced in firms located in regions with low financial literacy.Lastly, we conduct tests to address alternative explanations. First, no education effect is found when comparing the control and comparison groups, negating the impact of treatment salience. Second, the education effect is evident only for positive accruals, aligning with our education's focus on high accrual implications and refuting the notion that our exercises merely amplify attention to accruals. Third, the education effect persists one year after the experiment, with no new messages posted, suggesting that our treatment effect is not fear-induced. Fourth, the effect remains pronounced in stocks with high trading turnover, implying a limited impact from the spillover effect due to common ownership between the treatment and control stocks. Finally, our results stay robust after accounting for the fixed effect of industry × EA months and excluding EAs during the pandemic peak, indicating minimal distortion from the COVID-19 outbreak.Our study makes several contributions. First, it adds to the literature on the effects of financial knowledge in financial markets. Existing studies mainly focus on the effects of financial knowledge on individuals’ financial decisions and behaviors (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014). To the best of our knowledge, ours is the first work to directly test the influence of financial knowledge on asset pricing.Second, our study extends research that examines financial anomalies and pricing efficiency. McLean and Pontiff (2016) posit that the academic discovery of financial anomalies can enhance market efficiency by enabling investors to pinpoint arbitrage opportunities. Our research underscores that not only is the discovery of such knowledge vital, but its dissemination and the education of investors regarding it are also crucial for improving market efficiency.Third, previous studies on accrual anomaly rest on explanations such as risk (Khan, 2008; Chichernea et al., 2015), transaction costs (Collins et al., 2003; Mashruwala et al., 2006), limited attention (Hirshleifer et al., 2011; Miao et al., 2016), and insufficient supplementary accounting information (Louis et al., 2008; Miao et al., 2016). We extend this body of literature by demonstrating a new explanation, namely investors’ limited understanding of accounting accruals. This perspective also sheds light on the understanding of other price anomalies.Lastly, our research carries policy implications. Individuals in many developed and developing countries have low levels of financial literacy (Van Rooij et al., 2011; Merkoulova and Veld, 2022). Although many financial education programs have been introduced worldwide to rectify this problem (Kaiser et al., 2022), their efficacy remains debatable (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014). Our findings underscore the potential of social media platforms as tools for investor education. Furthermore, our results highlight the importance of integrating methodological applications with conceptual explanations in financial education. This insight holds considerable relevance for the design and execution of financial education programs.Organizational accessGet full-text access by signing in with your organisationAccess through your organizationOther access optionsPurchase PDFNeed help with access?Section snippetsRelated literature“Financial knowledge,” or “financial literacy,” refers to people's ability to process economic information and make informed financial decisions (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014). proposed.title: Knowledge is power: A field experiment in the Chinese and US stock markets
proposed.abstract: This study examines the causal effect of financial knowledge on stock pricing efficiency. Leveraging a specially designed investor education website, we conduct a field experiment, sharing insights on the pricing of accounting accruals with investors across China and the US on social media. We find that the treatment stocks experience a reduction in accrual mispricing relative to the control stocks. This effect is particularly pronounced when knowledge that enhances the conceptual understanding of accruals is paired with knowledge that aids in the quantitative application of accruals. Furthermore, the treatment effect is strengthened among stocks with investors who engage more deeply with the educational content yet possess lower financial sophistication.

Do proprietary traders provide liquidity?
Do proprietary traders provide liquidity?✰

Whether proprietary traders provide or take liquidity, and how their behavior evolves over the business cycle and across stocks, remains at the center of an ongoing debate. Using a unique dataset from the NYSE, we document that proprietary traders act as net liquidity providers, buying after price declines in a contrarian pattern. Proprietary trader liquidity provision is concentrated in large, liquid, low-volatility stocks and diminishes significantly when intermediary balance sheets are weak. Liquidity provision is stronger when price movements are plausibly not driven by information. Our findings highlight both the role and the limits of proprietary traders in supporting market liquidity across time and market segments.
