proposed.title: Private equity for pension plans? Evaluating private equity performance from an investor’s perspective
proposed.abstract: We evaluate private equity (PE) performance using investor-specific stochastic discount factors, and examine whether public pension plans could benefit from changing their allocation to PE. Plans invest in PE funds with higher than average risk-adjusted performance. This is mainly due to access to successful managers, not superior selection skill. Decomposing returns into risk-compensation and “alpha”, we find that some plans obtain higher PE returns by taking more risk without earning higher, and in some cases earning lower, risk-adjusted returns, broadly consistent with agency problems within plans.

This paper quantifies how investors’ portfolio demand responds to price changes at long horizons versus short horizons. Using investor trades – changes in portfolios – at different horizons, I first present reduced-form evidence that elasticities increase significantly over time. I then propose a dynamic demand system via a parsimonious partial-adjustment model that recovers the full term structure of elasticities while mitigating long-horizon identification challenges. The estimates imply that price impacts are three times larger at quarterly horizons than in the long-run equilibrium. The model produces a novel, stock-level measure of long-term reversal that avoids the noise of long-horizon return regressions.

The model produces a novel, stock-level measure of long-term reversal that avoids the noise of long-horizon return regressions.JEL classificationG11; G12; G23KeywordsDemand elasticities; Asset pricing; Institutional investors; Portfolio inertia; Partial adjustment; Price impact; Return reversalPrevious article in this issueNext article in this issueIntroductionThe availability of detailed data on investor portfolio holdings, and the substantial heterogeneity they reveal, has spurred growing interest in linking this data to equilibrium prices through structural models of asset demand. If the aggregate demand curve for financial securities is downward sloping, then investors’ demand shocks can have a meaningful impact on prices and portfolio holdings are informative about equilibrium asset prices. Investors’ elasticity of demand with respect to the price (henceforth elasticity) lies at the heart of linking data on investor demand to prices. If the elasticity of demand is high, then equilibrium prices do not have to move a lot in order to induce investors to rebalance their portfolios, and the price impact of demand shocks is low.While horizon dependence of demand elasticities is pervasive in economics, the recent literature on demand-based asset pricing following Koijen and Yogo (henceforth KY, 2019) has largely treated demand as static. The standard approach estimates elasticities from the cross-section of portfolio weights, abstracting from demand dynamics and horizon effects in counterfactual experiments. A natural next step in this literature is therefore to bring dynamics into demand-based asset pricing, allowing elasticities – and the equilibrium impact of demand shifts – to differ between the short and the long run. This paper addresses this gap. I first show, in reduced form, that investors become significantly more elastic over longer horizons. I then show how to structurally estimate dynamic demand curves without relying on long histories of portfolio holdings, which alleviates identification concerns. Across both approaches, I find that long-run elasticities are on average three to four times larger than their quarterly short-run counterparts. The structural estimation introduces dynamics into demand-based asset pricing in a highly parsimonious way, and allows evaluating the impact of counterfactual experiments at different horizons. Mirroring the increase in elasticities over longer horizons, the price impact of demand shifts is three to four times larger at a quarterly horizon than in the long-run equilibrium. More broadly, the dynamic demand system offers a key benefit beyond delivering price multipliers: it jointly matches both the levels and the dynamics of investor-level holdings. A central new moment revealed by the dynamic demand system is the high degree of persistence in holdings, which the model matches quantitatively and which generates equilibrium reversal in the price impact of demand shifts.Elasticities that increase over time are familiar in asset pricing, though typically framed and tested as the gradual reversal of demand-driven price impacts rather than as horizon-dependent elasticities. See Duffie (2010) for numerous empirical examples of price reversals following demand shocks. However, testing for reversal is inherently difficult, as noise and fundamental news accumulate over time, inflating standard errors and obscuring identification. Investor-level portfolio data offers a key advantage: it allows one to infer reversal from portfolio inertia rather than from noisy long-run return regressions. Even if one is skeptical about the precise structure of the demand system or the accuracy of cross-elasticity estimates, the ability to measure long-term reversal from holdings is valuable in its own right—and, as I show in applications, empirically powerful. A further benefit of investor-level analysis is its ability to construct stock-level reversal measures by combining investor-specific estimates with ownership variation, something pooled return regressions cannot directly recover.I set the stage by providing reduced-form evidence on increasing elasticities at longer horizons. I compute investors’ trades, i.e., changes in their portfolio holdings, and estimate their elasticities over increasing trading horizons in a simple difference-in-difference setting. I find that elasticities increase monotonically at longer horizons and that investors trade 3 to 4 times more elastically over the long run than in the short run. The reduced-form estimates using trades are first-difference versions of the regressions in the demand system literature that rely on portfolio holdings in levels. The status quo is to estimate elasticities via cross-sectional regressions of (log) portfolio weights onto instrumented prices.1 The cross-sectional identification from holdings does not take into account how investors trade, i.e., how they adjust their portfolios over time. The static elasticity identified from portfolio holdings in levels falls between the short and long-run elasticities identified from investors’ trades. This suggests that static estimation from levels overstates how aggressively investors rebalance their portfolios in the short run and understates their rebalancing activity in the long run. Building on the insights of Haddad et al. (2025a) and Fuchs et al. (2023) regarding the conditions under which cross-sectional regressions yield unbiased elasticities, I show that controlling for close substitutes – such as stocks with similar industry or risk exposures – has little effect on the estimated elasticities across horizons. This suggests that the average horizon-specific elasticities recovered in this paper are unlikely to be biased by omitted cross-asset spillovers.Motivated by the reduced-form evidence on increasing elasticities at longer horizons, I propose a simple dynamic extension to KY (2019) that allows for differentiating between short and long-run effects in counterfactual experiments. Portfolio inertia is a natural candidate to explain differences in short and long-run elasticities. I micro-found a partial adjustment model following Gârleanu and Pedersen (2013) in which investors gradually shift towards a target portfolio due to portfolio adjustment costs. The optimal portfolio is a weighted average of the passive buy-and-hold portfolio and the target portfolio. The weight on the passive portfolio captures inertia, i.e., persistence in investor demand. I provide an instrumental variables estimator to address the endogeneity of past portfolios and current latent demand arising from persistent demand shocks.In the dynamic demand system, long-run elasticities – and hence long-run price impacts – are not directly estimated but inferred structurally from short-run elasticities and portfolio inertia, allowing identification of the full term structure of elasticities and price impact without relying on long histories of portfolio holdings. While this requires additional structure relative to the nonparametric reduced-form approach, the partial adjustment model’s functional form fits the empirical dynamics of quantities well and delivers dynamic elasticities consistent with reduced-form estimates. The structural approach furthermore addresses a key challenge in estimating long-horizon elasticities and price impact: the absence of plausibly exogenous instruments that remain relevant over long horizons.I estimate the partial adjustment model using institutional holdings data from 1990 to 2024. In line with the reduced-form evidence, I find high inertia in institutional portfolios. The average investor’s weight on the quarterly buy-and-hold portfolio is 0.83. This implies that investors partially trade towards their long-term target allocation with a quarterly adjustment speed of 0.17. In other words, every quarter investors close the gap between their current buy-and-hold portfolio and their long-term target by 17%. Consistent with higher trading costs for bigger positions, large investors are more inert than small investors. The partial adjustment model implies that long-run elasticities are the interaction of short-run elasticities and portfolio inertia. The short and long-run elasticities implied by the model are consistent with the reduced-form estimates. Slow portfolio adjustments lead to implied long-run elasticities that considerably exceed the quarterly short-run response. The (size-weighted) average short-run elasticity across all investors is 0.28, whereas the average long-run elasticity is 1.57. There is also considerable heterogeneity in the long-run elasticity across investors. Over long horizons, large value investors are among the most important liquidity providers with a long-run elasticity of 4. All results are robust to different instruments for lagged portfolios.Elasticities that increase at longer horizons imply counterfactual price impacts that decrease over time. I illustrate this duality in a generalized dynamic demand-system setting and show that, to a first-order approximation, the equilibrium short- and long-run price effects of counterfactual demand shocks are governed by the inverse of the size-weighted average price elasticity of demand at the corresponding horizon. The speed of convergence from the short-run equilibrium to the long-run equilibrium depends on the dispersion of inertia across investors. Estimating dynamic demand curves allows the construction of dynamic counterfactual price paths that match the observed inertia in portfolio holdings. I propose a simple and efficient algorithm that numerically solves for the dynamic price path that clears the non-linear market clearing condition following counterfactual experiments. I show that the first-order approximation of price impact given by the short- and long-term multipliers closely approximates the short- and long-term equilibrium prices from the numerical solution.The difference in long-run and short-run price multipliers predicted by the model provides a novel stock-level measure of long-term reversal. Intuitively, stocks in the habitat of long-term investors with high inertia exhibit strong reversal as these investors gradually rebalance their portfolios and become more elastic over time. I provide two concrete empirical applications of the dynamic demand system and the corresponding stock-specific reversal measure.First, I show that the dynamic demand system strongly predicts which stocks exhibit greater price reversal following non-fundamental demand shocks. To ensure a true out-of-sample test, I use demand shocks that have not been used to identify the model parameters. Coval and Stafford (2007) and Lou (2012) show that flow-induced price pressure by mutual funds significantly reverts over time. I sort stocks into portfolios based on the model-based reversal measure. For low reversal stocks, flow-induced price pressure decays slowly and remains significantly positive for at least seven quarters. In contrast, for high reversal stocks, flow-induced price pressure fully reverses within three quarters.Second, the model-based reversal measure contains strong incremental information beyond traditional cross-sectional return predictors. If momentum is driven partly by non-fundamental factors, stocks with higher model-based reversal should show weaker momentum because, over time, long-term elastic investors act contrarian against the initial demand shocks. When conditioning a standard momentum strategy on model-based reversal, momentum returns vanish for high reversal stocks, while low reversal stocks yield over 3% higher annualized momentum returns. I confirm these patterns in Fama–MacBeth regressions. Conditioning on a reversal dummy doubles the coefficient on momentum for non-reversal stocks while eliminating it for reversal stocks. This underscores the incremental information embedded in investor portfolios and their rebalancing behavior more broadly.Related Literature. This paper directly relates to the recent and fast-growing literature on demand-based asset pricing initiated by KY (2019). This literature uses data on investors’ portfolio holdings for different asset classes to estimate demand curves and, via the price elasticities of demand, link them to equilibrium prices (e.g., Benetton and Compiani, 2020, Koijen and Yogo, 2020, Haddad et al., 2025b, Han et al., 2021, Koijen et al., 2021, Fang et al., 2025, Bretscher et al., 2026, Jiang et al., 2025, Darmouni et al., 2022, Tamoni et al., 2026, Jiang et al., 2024, Koijen et al., 2024, Jansen, 2024 and Jansen et al. (2024)). All of the papers mentioned above use the static demand system approach with horizon-independent demand curves to conduct counterfactual experiments. Accounting for long versus short-run elasticities can provide valuable additional insights on how the price impact of counterfactual experiments is expected to unfold over time and to what extent it reverts. Importantly, the presence of horizon effects does not invalidate existing approaches—rather, most counterfactuals or return decompositions implicitly correspond to a specific time horizon. For instance, the impact of long-run trends such as in Koijen et al. (2024) is better captured by long-run elasticities estimated from portfolio levels, while shorter-term scenarios like fire sales (Darmouni et al., 2022) may be better informed by short-run elasticities. The partial adjustment model proposed in this paper integrates easily into existing frameworks by controlling for lagged holdings and enables tailoring the elasticity to the time horizon of the counterfactual experiment. By effectively capturing static mandates that may be correlated with prices, this may furthermore sharpen the identification of existing studies. More recently, van Binsbergen et al. (2025) argue that demand elasticities in dynamic settings should be measured via transitory supply shocks that fully and predictably revert within one trading period, effectively measuring elasticities with respect to expected returns as opposed to prices. Instead, the present paper follows the extant demand-based asset pricing literature and defines elasticities that are consistent with the equilibrium price dynamics following persistent supply shocks. Prices revert in equilibrium not because the supply shock reverts but because elasticities increase over time as constraints loosen. proposed.title: Short versus long-run demand elasticities in asset pricing
proposed.abstract: This paper quantifies how investors’ portfolio demand responds to price changes at long horizons versus short horizons. Using investor trades – changes in portfolios – at different horizons, I first present reduced-form evidence that elasticities increase significantly over time. I then propose a dynamic demand system via a parsimonious partial-adjustment model that recovers the full term structure of elasticities while mitigating long-horizon identification challenges. The estimates imply that price impacts are three times larger at quarterly horizons than in the long-run equilibrium. The model produces a novel, stock-level measure of long-term reversal that avoids the noise of long-horizon return regressions.

The model produces a novel, stock-level measure of long-term reversal that avoids the noise of long-horizon return regressions.JEL classificationG11; G12; G23KeywordsDemand elasticities; Asset pricing; Institutional investors; Portfolio inertia; Partial adjustment; Price impact; Return reversalPrevious article in this issueNext article in this issueIntroductionThe availability of detailed data on investor portfolio holdings, and the substantial heterogeneity they reveal, has spurred growing interest in linking this data to equilibrium prices through structural models of asset demand. If the aggregate demand curve for financial securities is downward sloping, then investors’ demand shocks can have a meaningful impact on prices and portfolio holdings are informative about equilibrium asset prices. Investors’ elasticity of demand with respect to the price (henceforth elasticity) lies at the heart of linking data on investor demand to prices. If the elasticity of demand is high, then equilibrium prices do not have to move a lot in order to induce investors to rebalance their portfolios, and the price impact of demand shocks is low.While horizon dependence of demand elasticities is pervasive in economics, the recent literature on demand-based asset pricing following Koijen and Yogo (henceforth KY, 2019) has largely treated demand as static. The standard approach estimates elasticities from the cross-section of portfolio weights, abstracting from demand dynamics and horizon effects in counterfactual experiments. A natural next step in this literature is therefore to bring dynamics into demand-based asset pricing, allowing elasticities – and the equilibrium impact of demand shifts – to differ between the short and the long run. This paper addresses this gap. I first show, in reduced form, that investors become significantly more elastic over longer horizons. I then show how to structurally estimate dynamic demand curves without relying on long histories of portfolio holdings, which alleviates identification concerns. Across both approaches, I find that long-run elasticities are on average three to four times larger than their quarterly short-run counterparts. The structural estimation introduces dynamics into demand-based asset pricing in a highly parsimonious way, and allows evaluating the impact of counterfactual experiments at different horizons. Mirroring the increase in elasticities over longer horizons, the price impact of demand shifts is three to four times larger at a quarterly horizon than in the long-run equilibrium. More broadly, the dynamic demand system offers a key benefit beyond delivering price multipliers: it jointly matches both the levels and the dynamics of investor-level holdings. A central new moment revealed by the dynamic demand system is the high degree of persistence in holdings, which the model matches quantitatively and which generates equilibrium reversal in the price impact of demand shifts.Elasticities that increase over time are familiar in asset pricing, though typically framed and tested as the gradual reversal of demand-driven price impacts rather than as horizon-dependent elasticities. See Duffie (2010) for numerous empirical examples of price reversals following demand shocks. However, testing for reversal is inherently difficult, as noise and fundamental news accumulate over time, inflating standard errors and obscuring identification. Investor-level portfolio data offers a key advantage: it allows one to infer reversal from portfolio inertia rather than from noisy long-run return regressions. Even if one is skeptical about the precise structure of the demand system or the accuracy of cross-elasticity estimates, the ability to measure long-term reversal from holdings is valuable in its own right—and, as I show in applications, empirically powerful. A further benefit of investor-level analysis is its ability to construct stock-level reversal measures by combining investor-specific estimates with ownership variation, something pooled return regressions cannot directly recover.I set the stage by providing reduced-form evidence on increasing elasticities at longer horizons. I compute investors’ trades, i.e., changes in their portfolio holdings, and estimate their elasticities over increasing trading horizons in a simple difference-in-difference setting. I find that elasticities increase monotonically at longer horizons and that investors trade 3 to 4 times more elastically over the long run than in the short run. The reduced-form estimates using trades are first-difference versions of the regressions in the demand system literature that rely on portfolio holdings in levels. The status quo is to estimate elasticities via cross-sectional regressions of (log) portfolio weights onto instrumented prices.1 The cross-sectional identification from holdings does not take into account how investors trade, i.e., how they adjust their portfolios over time. The static elasticity identified from portfolio holdings in levels falls between the short and long-run elasticities identified from investors’ trades. This suggests that static estimation from levels overstates how aggressively investors rebalance their portfolios in the short run and understates their rebalancing activity in the long run. Building on the insights of Haddad et al. (2025a) and Fuchs et al. (2023) regarding the conditions under which cross-sectional regressions yield unbiased elasticities, I show that controlling for close substitutes – such as stocks with similar industry or risk exposures – has little effect on the estimated elasticities across horizons. This suggests that the average horizon-specific elasticities recovered in this paper are unlikely to be biased by omitted cross-asset spillovers.Motivated by the reduced-form evidence on increasing elasticities at longer horizons, I propose a simple dynamic extension to KY (2019) that allows for differentiating between short and long-run effects in counterfactual experiments. Portfolio inertia is a natural candidate to explain differences in short and long-run elasticities. I micro-found a partial adjustment model following Gârleanu and Pedersen (2013) in which investors gradually shift towards a target portfolio due to portfolio adjustment costs. The optimal portfolio is a weighted average of the passive buy-and-hold portfolio and the target portfolio. The weight on the passive portfolio captures inertia, i.e., persistence in investor demand. I provide an instrumental variables estimator to address the endogeneity of past portfolios and current latent demand arising from persistent demand shocks.In the dynamic demand system, long-run elasticities – and hence long-run price impacts – are not directly estimated but inferred structurally from short-run elasticities and portfolio inertia, allowing identification of the full term structure of elasticities and price impact without relying on long histories of portfolio holdings. While this requires additional structure relative to the nonparametric reduced-form approach, the partial adjustment model’s functional form fits the empirical dynamics of quantities well and delivers dynamic elasticities consistent with reduced-form estimates. The structural approach furthermore addresses a key challenge in estimating long-horizon elasticities and price impact: the absence of plausibly exogenous instruments that remain relevant over long horizons.I estimate the partial adjustment model using institutional holdings data from 1990 to 2024. In line with the reduced-form evidence, I find high inertia in institutional portfolios. The average investor’s weight on the quarterly buy-and-hold portfolio is 0.83. This implies that investors partially trade towards their long-term target allocation with a quarterly adjustment speed of 0.17. In other words, every quarter investors close the gap between their current buy-and-hold portfolio and their long-term target by 17%. Consistent with higher trading costs for bigger positions, large investors are more inert than small investors. The partial adjustment model implies that long-run elasticities are the interaction of short-run elasticities and portfolio inertia. The short and long-run elasticities implied by the model are consistent with the reduced-form estimates. Slow portfolio adjustments lead to implied long-run elasticities that considerably exceed the quarterly short-run response. The (size-weighted) average short-run elasticity across all investors is 0.28, whereas the average long-run elasticity is 1.57. There is also considerable heterogeneity in the long-run elasticity across investors. Over long horizons, large value investors are among the most important liquidity providers with a long-run elasticity of 4. All results are robust to different instruments for lagged portfolios.Elasticities that increase at longer horizons imply counterfactual price impacts that decrease over time. I illustrate this duality in a generalized dynamic demand-system setting and show that, to a first-order approximation, the equilibrium short- and long-run price effects of counterfactual demand shocks are governed by the inverse of the size-weighted average price elasticity of demand at the corresponding horizon. The speed of convergence from the short-run equilibrium to the long-run equilibrium depends on the dispersion of inertia across investors. Estimating dynamic demand curves allows the construction of dynamic counterfactual price paths that match the observed inertia in portfolio holdings. I propose a simple and efficient algorithm that numerically solves for the dynamic price path that clears the non-linear market clearing condition following counterfactual experiments. I show that the first-order approximation of price impact given by the short- and long-term multipliers closely approximates the short- and long-term equilibrium prices from the numerical solution.The difference in long-run and short-run price multipliers predicted by the model provides a novel stock-level measure of long-term reversal. Intuitively, stocks in the habitat of long-term investors with high inertia exhibit strong reversal as these investors gradually rebalance their portfolios and become more elastic over time. I provide two concrete empirical applications of the dynamic demand system and the corresponding stock-specific reversal measure.First, I show that the dynamic demand system strongly predicts which stocks exhibit greater price reversal following non-fundamental demand shocks. To ensure a true out-of-sample test, I use demand shocks that have not been used to identify the model parameters. Coval and Stafford (2007) and Lou (2012) show that flow-induced price pressure by mutual funds significantly reverts over time. I sort stocks into portfolios based on the model-based reversal measure. For low reversal stocks, flow-induced price pressure decays slowly and remains significantly positive for at least seven quarters. In contrast, for high reversal stocks, flow-induced price pressure fully reverses within three quarters.Second, the model-based reversal measure contains strong incremental information beyond traditional cross-sectional return predictors. If momentum is driven partly by non-fundamental factors, stocks with higher model-based reversal should show weaker momentum because, over time, long-term elastic investors act contrarian against the initial demand shocks. When conditioning a standard momentum strategy on model-based reversal, momentum returns vanish for high reversal stocks, while low reversal stocks yield over 3% higher annualized momentum returns. I confirm these patterns in Fama–MacBeth regressions. Conditioning on a reversal dummy doubles the coefficient on momentum for non-reversal stocks while eliminating it for reversal stocks. This underscores the incremental information embedded in investor portfolios and their rebalancing behavior more broadly.Related Literature. This paper directly relates to the recent and fast-growing literature on demand-based asset pricing initiated by KY (2019). This literature uses data on investors’ portfolio holdings for different asset classes to estimate demand curves and, via the price elasticities of demand, link them to equilibrium prices (e.g., Benetton and Compiani, 2020, Koijen and Yogo, 2020, Haddad et al., 2025b, Han et al., 2021, Koijen et al., 2021, Fang et al., 2025, Bretscher et al., 2026, Jiang et al., 2025, Darmouni et al., 2022, Tamoni et al., 2026, Jiang et al., 2024, Koijen et al., 2024, Jansen, 2024 and Jansen et al. (2024)). All of the papers mentioned above use the static demand system approach with horizon-independent demand curves to conduct counterfactual experiments. Accounting for long versus short-run elasticities can provide valuable additional insights on how the price impact of counterfactual experiments is expected to unfold over time and to what extent it reverts. Importantly, the presence of horizon effects does not invalidate existing approaches—rather, most counterfactuals or return decompositions implicitly correspond to a specific time horizon. For instance, the impact of long-run trends such as in Koijen et al. (2012), Coval and Stafford (2007), Lou (2012), Wardlaw (2020) and Schmickler (2020)) or dividend reinvestments (see e.g., Hartzmark and Solomon (2021) and Schmickler (2020)). This lends additional flexibility to the demand-based approach as the elasticity estimates can be ex-ante verified in a host of different settings.Finally, this paper contributes to the literature on slow-moving capital (e.g., Mitchell et al. (2007), Duffie (2010) and Bogousslavsky et al. (2021)), gradual portfolio adjustment (e.g., Froot et al. (2001), Bohn and Tesar (1996) and Bacchetta et al. proposed.title: Short versus long-run demand elasticities in asset pricing
proposed.abstract: This paper quantifies how investors’ portfolio demand responds to price changes at long horizons versus short horizons. Using investor trades – changes in portfolios – at different horizons, I first present reduced-form evidence that elasticities increase significantly over time. I then propose a dynamic demand system via a parsimonious partial-adjustment model that recovers the full term structure of elasticities while mitigating long-horizon identification challenges. The estimates imply that price impacts are three times larger at quarterly horizons than in the long-run equilibrium. The model produces a novel, stock-level measure of long-term reversal that avoids the noise of long-horizon return regressions.

source_records.abstract: Institutions facilitate short-selling by lending from their holdings, but what they hold is endogenous. This paper examines how institutional demand, driven by investment mandates (benchmarking), affects short-selling. In a model where benchmarked managers lend from their holdings, both lending supply and equilibrium price are higher for the benchmark asset, and so is shorting demand (due to inflated price). This paper examines how institutional demand, driven by investment mandates (benchmarking), affects short-selling. In a model where benchmarked managers lend from their holdings, both lending supply and equilibrium price are higher for the benchmark asset, and so is shorting demand (due to inflated price). A quasi-experiment using Russell index reconstitution shows that stocks with more benchmarked capital have greater lending supply and demand. Ultimately, such stocks are costlier to short. In theory and data, results are driven by incomplete pass-through from benchmarked capital to lending supply.JEL classificationG11; G12; G14; G15; G23KeywordsBenchmark; Lending supply; Borrowing fee; Short sales; Index effect; RussellPrevious article in this issueNext article in this issueIntroductionShort-selling is key to price discovery in financial markets. Yet, the securities lending market, in which most investors must first borrow assets to sell them short, is opaque (U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, 2021). It is still an open question what determines the cost of short-selling despite nearly six decades of academic research in this area (Seneca, 1967). At the same time, an increasing number of studies are linking asset pricing anomalies to securities with binding short-selling constraints, or those that are expensive to borrow.1The conventional view in the literature is that institutional ownership alleviates short-selling constraints by increasing the supply of lendable shares (D’Avolio, 2002 and Asquith et al., 2005). According to S&P Global (2025), short-sellers borrowed an average value of over $0.6 trillion per day in U.S. equities in 2024, where institutional investors were the primary lenders.2 Institutions, with their long-term investment horizons, are well-suited to lend their holdings and generate significant revenue by doing so.3 At the same time, institutions can only lend what they own, and hence the same asset characteristics that drive institutional demand also influence the level of supply of the asset available to short-sellers in the lending market. For instance, one can expect larger and more liquid assets, which are typically held by institutions, to have a larger lending supply. However, if institutional demand affects asset prices, for example, by inflating them, it must change the short-selling demand as well. Therefore, it is not clear ex-ante how institutional ownership should affect the cost of short-selling, that is, the borrowing fee.In this paper, I bring together the demand and supply effects of institutional ownership in the stock lending market, thereby shedding new light on the role of institutions in shaping short-selling constraints. In particular, I isolate changes in institutional holdings stemming from investment mandates and study the resulting changes in lending supply, shorting demand, and borrowing fees. Benchmarking, which involves evaluating fund manager performance against a market index (benchmark), is a key mechanism for enforcing investment mandates and has been shown to influence asset prices.4 Despite this, the potential of mandate-bound institutional investors to inflate asset prices and hence increase short-selling demand has been largely overlooked in the literature on short sales. I explicitly incorporate this channel and show, theoretically and empirically, that it is strong enough to challenge the conventional view on the role of institutions in short-selling markets.I build intuition using a tractable model with benchmarked fund managers who supply their risky holdings for lending. These managers optimally tilt their portfolios to the asset in their benchmark index, increasing both the price of the asset and its lending supply. Simple intuition suggests that a larger supply should alleviate short-selling constraints and reduce the borrowing fee (supply effect of benchmarking). However, the model shows that benchmarking may increase the fee because it inflates the asset price and hence also attracts higher shorting demand (demand effect of benchmarking). I test the model’s predictions using a quasi-experiment based on the Russell index reconstitution, in which there are shocks to how much capital is benchmarked against specific stocks. I find that the demand effect of benchmarking dominates the supply effect because it becomes costlier to short stocks that experience an increase in capital benchmarked against them due to index reconstitution. Finally, combined with my model, insights from novel regulatory filings suggest that both explicit lending limits and frictions in the lending market depress the pass-through from institutional holdings to lending supply, resulting in a weak supply effect of benchmarking.The model allows me to characterize asset prices and borrowing fees in the presence of benchmarking and securities lending. It introduces a lending market to an economy with fund managers benchmarked to a market index. Other agents include direct investors, who are net long, and hedgers, who are net short. Because fund managers’ performance is evaluated relative to the index, they always allocate a fraction of their holdings to the benchmark asset, thereby inflating its price. This results in the asset being overvalued compared to an economy without benchmarking.A unique aspect of the model is that the benchmark-induced holdings contribute to the lending supply. Fund managers can lend their risky holdings to hedgers, up to an exogenous lending limit,5 in exchange for a fee, while direct investors are not permitted to lend. The shorting demand of hedgers is upward-sloping in price so it is also higher for the benchmark asset due to its inflated price. Because both the supply and demand effects of benchmarking coexist, it is not immediately apparent how borrowing fees (short-selling costs) relate to benchmarking. By clearing the asset spot and lending markets at the same time, I demonstrate that this relationship in equilibrium depends on a simple condition related to the fund managers’ lending limit. When the managers are too constrained in lending (that is, when the lending limit is relatively tight), the demand effect prevails, resulting in a higher borrowing fee for the benchmark asset.The model features different predictions for an asset that is free to short, referred to as a general collateral asset, and an asset that is costly to short, referred to as an asset on special (or simply as a special asset). For a general collateral asset, the lending market clearing condition is slack, which means that the equilibrium lending supply is higher than the shorting demand and the borrowing fee is zero. While benchmarking increases both lending supply and shorting demand for such an asset, the borrowing fee remains unchanged. For a special asset, the lending market clearing condition binds, resulting in a strictly positive borrowing fee. Whether this fee increases or decreases with benchmarking depends on the lending limit as described above.The contribution of the paper is primarily empirical. An ideal test of the model would require variation in benchmarking that is independent of stock fundamentals. Obtaining such variation in data is challenging because index membership is typically related to factors like company size and liquidity of its shares. Additionally, as stocks in major indexes often attract more analyst coverage, index membership may be related to analyst disagreement, which the literature has associated with short-selling. I therefore turn to the following quasi-experiment.To test predictions of my model, I exploit changes in the index membership of U.S. stocks due to the reconstitution of Russell indexes. Utilizing the composition of 34 U.S. equity indexes and the assets of mutual funds and exchange-traded funds (ETFs) benchmarked against them, I construct a comprehensive measure of the amount of capital benchmarked against a stock, expressed as a fraction of its market value. This measure is called benchmarking intensity, or BMI (Pavlova and Sikorskaya, 2023). I argue that the mechanical nature of the Russell reconstitution creates a plausibly exogenous change in BMI, allowing me to test the predictions of the model.6 I first confirm that a stock’s price goes up when the stock moves down from the Russell 1000 to the Russell 2000 index (see Chang et al., 2015). Such stocks experience an average BMI increase of 8.6 percentage points (pp) because there is more capital benchmarked to the Russell 2000 index.Using comprehensive S&P Global (Markit) buyside data, I provide new insights into the securities lending market during the Russell reconstitutions. I find that both a stock’s lending supply (inventory) and shorting demand (short interest) go up with its BMI. This is true for both general collateral stocks and stocks on special, which I define empirically as those with annualized borrowing fees below and above 1%, respectively, following the literature (for example, Aggarwal et al., 2015).7 However, the pass-through to lending supply seems weak, as a dollar of new benchmarked capital translates only to around 18 cents of new lending inventory. I observe no change in borrowing fees for general collateral stocks, which is consistent with my model because the short-selling constraint does not bind for these stocks. Conversely, the fees of stocks on special increase, revealing that the demand effect of benchmarking is dominant. The magnitude is economically significant, with the borrowing fee increasing by 21 basis points (bps) for each pp increase in BMI. This means that, on average, it becomes 25% more expensive to short stocks added to the Russell 2000. Finally, using changes in BMI as an instrument for changes in institutional ownership (following Pavlova and Sikorskaya, 2023), I document that a 1 pp increase in institutional ownership leads to a 78 bps higher fee for special stocks.These findings do not depend on how borrowing fees and special status are measured. While the main analysis uses a borrower-side measure of short-selling costs, the results hold for lender-side fees and option-implied short-selling costs. Importantly, I argue that a change in BMI shifts lending supply and shorting demand curves, rather than causing a movement along the supply curve. Potential changes in analyst disagreement and borrowing risk measures do not explain my findings, as demonstrated alongside other robustness tests in Section 5.2.6. Finally, I show that, even further away from the Russell cutoff, funds mostly lend stocks within their benchmark indexes, and provide additional evidence from the Japanese equity market supporting my model.So why does the demand effect of benchmarking dominate in the Russell reconstitutions? In my model, this is primarily influenced by the lending limits that fund managers face. When these lending limits are too restrictive, managers tend to undersupply their holdings for lending. Meanwhile, shorting demand continues to rise due to the impact of benchmarking on asset prices.To explore how restrictive lending limits are in the data, I collect lending information for U.S. investment management companies from their N-PORT and N-CEN filings, which are available from 2019. I find that the regulatory portfolio-level limit, set at one-third of total fund value by the regulators in the United States, is not binding. At the same time, position-level data from major investment managers like BlackRock, Fidelity, J.P. Morgan, State Street, T. Rowe Price, and Vanguard reveal soft explicit lending limits that are often at or above 80% of how much the manager holds in a given stock (see Fig. 3).The same regulatory filings allow me to study lending around the recent Russell reconstitutions by funds benchmarked to the Russell indexes. I find that these funds often lend out over 90% of their holdings in special stocks transitioning between Russell indexes. Hence, even if the explicit position-level lending limits bind for some managers, it is unlikely that these limits are strict enough to fully explain the weak pass-through from holdings to supply. At the same time, benchmarked funds seem to entirely forgo lending many special stocks, contrary to model predictions. I show that known frictions in the lending market, such as participation constraints and search costs, cannot fully explain this sparse lending. Instead, the data suggests the presence of lending specialization, as also observed in contemporaneous N-PORT studies (Chen et al., 2024b and Dong and Zhu, 2024). Consistent with this view, I show in the appendix that many special stocks not lent at reconstitution remain not lent over the following year, even at the fund family level, with only modest and heterogeneous increases in lending activity over time.Finally, I show that limited lending has broader implications beyond its impact on borrowing fees. In my model, lending limits influence both the likelihood of an asset being classified as special (that is, how likely the lending market clearing constraint binds) and the special asset’s price sensitivity to benchmarking. As lending limits are relaxed, asset price sensitivity to benchmarking generally decreases. Without lending limits – when fund managers can lend the full value of their holdings – the model predicts that benchmarking has no effect on special asset prices. These findings underscore the significant and novel role of limited lending in designing and enforcing investment mandates, including central banks purchases and sustainable investing.Related literature. This paper is related to several strands of the literature encompassing investment mandates and index effect, theoretical and empirical work on short-selling constraints, and, in general, empirical research on investment managers and securities lending.A large body of empirical literature recognizes the importance of institutional ownership for lending markets. D’Avolio (2002) shows that the main suppliers of stock loans are institutional investors. So not surprisingly, the literature has used measures based on institutional ownership to proxy for short-selling constraints (Chen et al., 2002 and Nagel, 2005) and supply specifically (Asquith et al., 2005).8 A classical result in this literature is that institutional ownership increases lending supply, while the concentration of ownership reduces it (Prado et al., 2016). The literature has also recognized that investment restrictions influence funds’ participation in lending markets (Evans et al., 2017). I exploit exogenous changes in benchmarking-driven institutional ownership to offer a new perspective on how that ownership can impact short-selling constraints. Although benchmarking increases supply, I find that borrowing fees rise when BMI increases. I provide position-level evidence of the weak pass-through from institutional ownership to supply around index reconstitutions and link it to the prevalence of the demand effect of benchmarking. My model takes into account the price pressure induced by institutional demand, which is typically not considered in the literature.The literature suggests that passive fund ownership may influence the quality of lending supply. In independent and contemporaneous research, Beschwitz et al. (2025) examine Russell reconstitutions and argue that increased supply by passive owners reduces risks associated with stock borrowing, resulting in higher short-selling demand for all stocks.9 I test for this complementary channel using proxies suggested by the literature and find that demand and fees increase with BMI even without any observable improvements in short-selling risk measures. Specifically, in my sample of special stocks, I find no evidence of reduced borrowing fee volatility, loan utilization volatility, or failures to deliver.10 My model links changes in BMI to borrowing demand and fees without relying on the short-selling risk channel, and my findings for both special and not special stocks align closely with model predictions. My empirical tests exploit the intensity of Russell reconstitution shocks helping alleviate concerns related to the power of these tests and allowing me to study special stocks. While this group represents a small subset of stocks at any given time, over 80% of stocks in my U.S. sample become special at some point. Finally, I provide international evidence for the mechanism in the model using the central bank’s purchases of exchange-traded funds in Japan, where special stocks account for around a third of the market.This paper naturally relates to the vast literature on short-selling constraints and securities lending markets. Short-selling constraints are recognized as a limit to arbitrage,11 but they bind only for certain (special) stocks.12 Furthermore, beginning with Miller (1977) and Jarrow (1980), the literature has predominantly relied on the differences of opinion to explain the coexistence of short-sellers and investors who hold a long position in the asset, with the latter group typically supplying securities for lending. This is also true for the search-based models of the securities lending markets that endogenize the specialness of securities (see Duffie et al., 2002 and Vayanos and Weill, 2008) and the recent theoretical literature with dynamic short-selling (Atmaz et al., 2024). Securities that are subject to more disagreement are usually more special in these models. Models in Blocher et al. (2013) and Banerjee and Graveline (2013) are agnostic with respect to the trading rationale, and yet the prediction for specialness is similar. My model is first to provide a microfoundation for the effect of institutional incentives on lending supply. Furthermore, benchmarking generates short-selling demand by inflating the asset price (independent of disagreement). In contrast with the established mechanisms, its effect on asset specialness and borrowing fee is ambiguous and crucially depends on the lending limit.There is extensive theoretical literature on the asset pricing effects of benchmarking, mandates, and investor habitats. The first equilibrium model with a benchmark is offered by Brennan (1993), while (Cuoco and Kaniel, 2011), Basak and Pavlova (2013), Buffa et al., 2022, Buffa and Hodor, 2023 investigate equilibrium asset pricing effects in dynamic economies with benchmarks. Similarly, the literature considers the implications of investor styles (Barberis and Shleifer, 2003) and investment mandates in delegated asset management (for example, Binsbergen et al., 2008 and He and Xiong, 2013).13 None of these papers has examined how benchmarking or mandates affect the lending market. My model suggests that the feedback through this market has the potential to alter the effects of benchmarking on price.14Finally, this paper is related to literature quantifying the effects of index membership for financial securities. Shleifer (1986) and Harris and Gurel (1986) were first to document abnormal returns to additions to the S&P 500 index. Index effects were later found in many other markets and asset classes.15 In this strand of literature, my paper is closest to Chang et al. (2015), who document the Russell index effect, or an average price increase of stocks added to the Russell 2000 index from the Russell 1000 index, and to Pavlova and Sikorskaya (2023), who propose BMI as a measure of how much capital is benchmarked against a stock. proposed.title: Institutional investor mandates, securities lending, and short-selling constraints
proposed.abstract: Institutions facilitate short-selling by lending from their holdings, but what they hold is endogenous. This paper examines how institutional demand, driven by investment mandates (benchmarking), affects short-selling. In a model where benchmarked managers lend from their holdings, both lending supply and equilibrium price are higher for the benchmark asset, and so is shorting demand (due to inflated price). A quasi-experiment using Russell index reconstitution shows that stocks with more benchmarked capital have greater lending supply and demand. Ultimately, such stocks are costlier to short. In theory and data, results are driven by incomplete pass-through from benchmarked capital to lending supply.

In theory and data, results are driven by incomplete pass-through from benchmarked capital to lending supply.JEL classificationG11; G12; G14; G15; G23KeywordsBenchmark; Lending supply; Borrowing fee; Short sales; Index effect; RussellPrevious article in this issueNext article in this issueIntroductionShort-selling is key to price discovery in financial markets. Yet, the securities lending market, in which most investors must first borrow assets to sell them short, is opaque (U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, 2021). It is still an open question what determines the cost of short-selling despite nearly six decades of academic research in this area (Seneca, 1967). At the same time, an increasing number of studies are linking asset pricing anomalies to securities with binding short-selling constraints, or those that are expensive to borrow.1The conventional view in the literature is that institutional ownership alleviates short-selling constraints by increasing the supply of lendable shares (D’Avolio, 2002 and Asquith et al., 2005). According to S&P Global (2025), short-sellers borrowed an average value of over $0.6 trillion per day in U.S. equities in 2024, where institutional investors were the primary lenders.2 Institutions, with their long-term investment horizons, are well-suited to lend their holdings and generate significant revenue by doing so.3 At the same time, institutions can only lend what they own, and hence the same asset characteristics that drive institutional demand also influence the level of supply of the asset available to short-sellers in the lending market. For instance, one can expect larger and more liquid assets, which are typically held by institutions, to have a larger lending supply. However, if institutional demand affects asset prices, for example, by inflating them, it must change the short-selling demand as well. Therefore, it is not clear ex-ante how institutional ownership should affect the cost of short-selling, that is, the borrowing fee.In this paper, I bring together the demand and supply effects of institutional ownership in the stock lending market, thereby shedding new light on the role of institutions in shaping short-selling constraints. In particular, I isolate changes in institutional holdings stemming from investment mandates and study the resulting changes in lending supply, shorting demand, and borrowing fees. Benchmarking, which involves evaluating fund manager performance against a market index (benchmark), is a key mechanism for enforcing investment mandates and has been shown to influence asset prices.4 Despite this, the potential of mandate-bound institutional investors to inflate asset prices and hence increase short-selling demand has been largely overlooked in the literature on short sales. I explicitly incorporate this channel and show, theoretically and empirically, that it is strong enough to challenge the conventional view on the role of institutions in short-selling markets.I build intuition using a tractable model with benchmarked fund managers who supply their risky holdings for lending. These managers optimally tilt their portfolios to the asset in their benchmark index, increasing both the price of the asset and its lending supply. Simple intuition suggests that a larger supply should alleviate short-selling constraints and reduce the borrowing fee (supply effect of benchmarking). However, the model shows that benchmarking may increase the fee because it inflates the asset price and hence also attracts higher shorting demand (demand effect of benchmarking). I test the model’s predictions using a quasi-experiment based on the Russell index reconstitution, in which there are shocks to how much capital is benchmarked against specific stocks. I find that the demand effect of benchmarking dominates the supply effect because it becomes costlier to short stocks that experience an increase in capital benchmarked against them due to index reconstitution. Finally, combined with my model, insights from novel regulatory filings suggest that both explicit lending limits and frictions in the lending market depress the pass-through from institutional holdings to lending supply, resulting in a weak supply effect of benchmarking.The model allows me to characterize asset prices and borrowing fees in the presence of benchmarking and securities lending. It introduces a lending market to an economy with fund managers benchmarked to a market index. Other agents include direct investors, who are net long, and hedgers, who are net short. Because fund managers’ performance is evaluated relative to the index, they always allocate a fraction of their holdings to the benchmark asset, thereby inflating its price. This results in the asset being overvalued compared to an economy without benchmarking.A unique aspect of the model is that the benchmark-induced holdings contribute to the lending supply. Fund managers can lend their risky holdings to hedgers, up to an exogenous lending limit,5 in exchange for a fee, while direct investors are not permitted to lend. The shorting demand of hedgers is upward-sloping in price so it is also higher for the benchmark asset due to its inflated price. Because both the supply and demand effects of benchmarking coexist, it is not immediately apparent how borrowing fees (short-selling costs) relate to benchmarking. By clearing the asset spot and lending markets at the same time, I demonstrate that this relationship in equilibrium depends on a simple condition related to the fund managers’ lending limit. When the managers are too constrained in lending (that is, when the lending limit is relatively tight), the demand effect prevails, resulting in a higher borrowing fee for the benchmark asset.The model features different predictions for an asset that is free to short, referred to as a general collateral asset, and an asset that is costly to short, referred to as an asset on special (or simply as a special asset). For a general collateral asset, the lending market clearing condition is slack, which means that the equilibrium lending supply is higher than the shorting demand and the borrowing fee is zero. While benchmarking increases both lending supply and shorting demand for such an asset, the borrowing fee remains unchanged. For a special asset, the lending market clearing condition binds, resulting in a strictly positive borrowing fee. Whether this fee increases or decreases with benchmarking depends on the lending limit as described above.The contribution of the paper is primarily empirical. An ideal test of the model would require variation in benchmarking that is independent of stock fundamentals. Obtaining such variation in data is challenging because index membership is typically related to factors like company size and liquidity of its shares. Additionally, as stocks in major indexes often attract more analyst coverage, index membership may be related to analyst disagreement, which the literature has associated with short-selling. I therefore turn to the following quasi-experiment.To test predictions of my model, I exploit changes in the index membership of U.S. stocks due to the reconstitution of Russell indexes. Utilizing the composition of 34 U.S. equity indexes and the assets of mutual funds and exchange-traded funds (ETFs) benchmarked against them, I construct a comprehensive measure of the amount of capital benchmarked against a stock, expressed as a fraction of its market value. This measure is called benchmarking intensity, or BMI (Pavlova and Sikorskaya, 2023). I argue that the mechanical nature of the Russell reconstitution creates a plausibly exogenous change in BMI, allowing me to test the predictions of the model.6 I first confirm that a stock’s price goes up when the stock moves down from the Russell 1000 to the Russell 2000 index (see Chang et al., 2015). Such stocks experience an average BMI increase of 8.6 percentage points (pp) because there is more capital benchmarked to the Russell 2000 index.Using comprehensive S&P Global (Markit) buyside data, I provide new insights into the securities lending market during the Russell reconstitutions. I find that both a stock’s lending supply (inventory) and shorting demand (short interest) go up with its BMI. This is true for both general collateral stocks and stocks on special, which I define empirically as those with annualized borrowing fees below and above 1%, respectively, following the literature (for example, Aggarwal et al., 2015).7 However, the pass-through to lending supply seems weak, as a dollar of new benchmarked capital translates only to around 18 cents of new lending inventory. I observe no change in borrowing fees for general collateral stocks, which is consistent with my model because the short-selling constraint does not bind for these stocks. Conversely, the fees of stocks on special increase, revealing that the demand effect of benchmarking is dominant. The magnitude is economically significant, with the borrowing fee increasing by 21 basis points (bps) for each pp increase in BMI. This means that, on average, it becomes 25% more expensive to short stocks added to the Russell 2000. Finally, using changes in BMI as an instrument for changes in institutional ownership (following Pavlova and Sikorskaya, 2023), I document that a 1 pp increase in institutional ownership leads to a 78 bps higher fee for special stocks.These findings do not depend on how borrowing fees and special status are measured. While the main analysis uses a borrower-side measure of short-selling costs, the results hold for lender-side fees and option-implied short-selling costs. Importantly, I argue that a change in BMI shifts lending supply and shorting demand curves, rather than causing a movement along the supply curve. Potential changes in analyst disagreement and borrowing risk measures do not explain my findings, as demonstrated alongside other robustness tests in Section 5.2.6. Finally, I show that, even further away from the Russell cutoff, funds mostly lend stocks within their benchmark indexes, and provide additional evidence from the Japanese equity market supporting my model.So why does the demand effect of benchmarking dominate in the Russell reconstitutions? In my model, this is primarily influenced by the lending limits that fund managers face. When these lending limits are too restrictive, managers tend to undersupply their holdings for lending. Meanwhile, shorting demand continues to rise due to the impact of benchmarking on asset prices.To explore how restrictive lending limits are in the data, I collect lending information for U.S. investment management companies from their N-PORT and N-CEN filings, which are available from 2019. I find that the regulatory portfolio-level limit, set at one-third of total fund value by the regulators in the United States, is not binding. At the same time, position-level data from major investment managers like BlackRock, Fidelity, J.P. Morgan, State Street, T. Rowe Price, and Vanguard reveal soft explicit lending limits that are often at or above 80% of how much the manager holds in a given stock (see Fig. 3).The same regulatory filings allow me to study lending around the recent Russell reconstitutions by funds benchmarked to the Russell indexes. I find that these funds often lend out over 90% of their holdings in special stocks transitioning between Russell indexes. Hence, even if the explicit position-level lending limits bind for some managers, it is unlikely that these limits are strict enough to fully explain the weak pass-through from holdings to supply. At the same time, benchmarked funds seem to entirely forgo lending many special stocks, contrary to model predictions. I show that known frictions in the lending market, such as participation constraints and search costs, cannot fully explain this sparse lending. Instead, the data suggests the presence of lending specialization, as also observed in contemporaneous N-PORT studies (Chen et al., 2024b and Dong and Zhu, 2024). Consistent with this view, I show in the appendix that many special stocks not lent at reconstitution remain not lent over the following year, even at the fund family level, with only modest and heterogeneous increases in lending activity over time.Finally, I show that limited lending has broader implications beyond its impact on borrowing fees. In my model, lending limits influence both the likelihood of an asset being classified as special (that is, how likely the lending market clearing constraint binds) and the special asset’s price sensitivity to benchmarking. As lending limits are relaxed, asset price sensitivity to benchmarking generally decreases. Without lending limits – when fund managers can lend the full value of their holdings – the model predicts that benchmarking has no effect on special asset prices. These findings underscore the significant and novel role of limited lending in designing and enforcing investment mandates, including central banks purchases and sustainable investing.Related literature. This paper is related to several strands of the literature encompassing investment mandates and index effect, theoretical and empirical work on short-selling constraints, and, in general, empirical research on investment managers and securities lending.A large body of empirical literature recognizes the importance of institutional ownership for lending markets. D’Avolio (2002) shows that the main suppliers of stock loans are institutional investors. So not surprisingly, the literature has used measures based on institutional ownership to proxy for short-selling constraints (Chen et al., 2002 and Nagel, 2005) and supply specifically (Asquith et al., 2005).8 A classical result in this literature is that institutional ownership increases lending supply, while the concentration of ownership reduces it (Prado et al., 2016). The literature has also recognized that investment restrictions influence funds’ participation in lending markets (Evans et al., 2017). I exploit exogenous changes in benchmarking-driven institutional ownership to offer a new perspective on how that ownership can impact short-selling constraints. Although benchmarking increases supply, I find that borrowing fees rise when BMI increases. I provide position-level evidence of the weak pass-through from institutional ownership to supply around index reconstitutions and link it to the prevalence of the demand effect of benchmarking. My model takes into account the price pressure induced by institutional demand, which is typically not considered in the literature.The literature suggests that passive fund ownership may influence the quality of lending supply. In independent and contemporaneous research, Beschwitz et al. (2025) examine Russell reconstitutions and argue that increased supply by passive owners reduces risks associated with stock borrowing, resulting in higher short-selling demand for all stocks.9 I test for this complementary channel using proxies suggested by the literature and find that demand and fees increase with BMI even without any observable improvements in short-selling risk measures. Specifically, in my sample of special stocks, I find no evidence of reduced borrowing fee volatility, loan utilization volatility, or failures to deliver.10 My model links changes in BMI to borrowing demand and fees without relying on the short-selling risk channel, and my findings for both special and not special stocks align closely with model predictions. My empirical tests exploit the intensity of Russell reconstitution shocks helping alleviate concerns related to the power of these tests and allowing me to study special stocks. While this group represents a small subset of stocks at any given time, over 80% of stocks in my U.S. sample become special at some point. Finally, I provide international evidence for the mechanism in the model using the central bank’s purchases of exchange-traded funds in Japan, where special stocks account for around a third of the market.This paper naturally relates to the vast literature on short-selling constraints and securities lending markets. Short-selling constraints are recognized as a limit to arbitrage,11 but they bind only for certain (special) stocks.12 Furthermore, beginning with Miller (1977) and Jarrow (1980), the literature has predominantly relied on the differences of opinion to explain the coexistence of short-sellers and investors who hold a long position in the asset, with the latter group typically supplying securities for lending. This is also true for the search-based models of the securities lending markets that endogenize the specialness of securities (see Duffie et al., 2002 and Vayanos and Weill, 2008) and the recent theoretical literature with dynamic short-selling (Atmaz et al., 2024). Securities that are subject to more disagreement are usually more special in these models. Models in Blocher et al. (2013) and Banerjee and Graveline (2013) are agnostic with respect to the trading rationale, and yet the prediction for specialness is similar. My model is first to provide a microfoundation for the effect of institutional incentives on lending supply. Furthermore, benchmarking generates short-selling demand by inflating the asset price (independent of disagreement). In contrast with the established mechanisms, its effect on asset specialness and borrowing fee is ambiguous and crucially depends on the lending limit.There is extensive theoretical literature on the asset pricing effects of benchmarking, mandates, and investor habitats. The first equilibrium model with a benchmark is offered by Brennan (1993), while (Cuoco and Kaniel, 2011), Basak and Pavlova (2013), Buffa et al., 2022, Buffa and Hodor, 2023 investigate equilibrium asset pricing effects in dynamic economies with benchmarks. Similarly, the literature considers the implications of investor styles (Barberis and Shleifer, 2003) and investment mandates in delegated asset management (for example, Binsbergen et al., 2008 and He and Xiong, 2013).13 None of these papers has examined how benchmarking or mandates affect the lending market. My model suggests that the feedback through this market has the potential to alter the effects of benchmarking on price.14Finally, this paper is related to literature quantifying the effects of index membership for financial securities. Shleifer (1986) and Harris and Gurel (1986) were first to document abnormal returns to additions to the S&P 500 index. Index effects were later found in many other markets and asset classes.15 In this strand of literature, my paper is closest to Chang et al. (2015), who document the Russell index effect, or an average price increase of stocks added to the Russell 2000 index from the Russell 1000 index, and to Pavlova and Sikorskaya (2023), who propose BMI as a measure of how much capital is benchmarked against a stock. I show that index reconstitutions trigger large changes in both lending supply and shorting demand as well as changes in short-selling costs, which this literature typically abstracts away from.Organizational accessGet full-text access by signing in with your organisationAccess through your organizationOther access optionsPurchase PDFNeed help with access?Section snippetsThe market for lending and borrowing stockThe stock lending market plays a pivotal role by bridging the gap between short-sellers and stock owners willing to lend their shares in exchange for a fee. proposed.title: Institutional investor mandates, securities lending, and short-selling constraints
proposed.abstract: Institutions facilitate short-selling by lending from their holdings, but what they hold is endogenous. This paper examines how institutional demand, driven by investment mandates (benchmarking), affects short-selling. In a model where benchmarked managers lend from their holdings, both lending supply and equilibrium price are higher for the benchmark asset, and so is shorting demand (due to inflated price). A quasi-experiment using Russell index reconstitution shows that stocks with more benchmarked capital have greater lending supply and demand. Ultimately, such stocks are costlier to short. In theory and data, results are driven by incomplete pass-through from benchmarked capital to lending supply.

A New Keynesian model of the term structures of equity and bond returns☆

A simple production economy with nominal price rigidities explains several key asset pricing facts, including the average slopes and cyclicality of equity and interest rate term structures. Nominal rigidities amplify the procyclicality of dividends after negative productivity shocks and generate countercyclical inflation, as sluggish price adjustment leads to a gradual dividend recovery. Consequently, short-duration equities (bonds) have more (less) procyclical payoffs than their long-duration counterparts. Slow-moving consumption habits produce large, countercyclical risk prices, yielding realistic asset valuations. Extending Campbell–Cochrane preferences with both market- and home-consumption habits allows them to operate in production economies while preserving realistic macroeconomic dynamics.
