Extending Campbell–Cochrane preferences with both market- and home-consumption habits allows them to operate in production economies while preserving realistic macroeconomic dynamics.JEL classificationE32; E43; E44; G12.KeywordsEquity and bond yields; Campbell–Cochrane habits; Nominal rigidities; Macro-finance separation; New Keynesian modelPrevious article in this issueNext article in this issueIntroductionRecent evidence shows that discount rates of financial claims differ across maturities and across asset classes. In particular, the maturity structure and time variation of equity and bond risk premia contain rich information to understand investors’ marginal utility of wealth and their expectations about future macroeconomic variables. The empirical literature has documented that the returns of nominal and real bonds increase with maturity on average, while claims to short-term dividends have high average excess returns, comparable in size to the aggregate equity premium (Binsbergen et al., 2012, Binsbergen and Koijen, 2017). During stock market downturns, the slope of the term structure of equity yields decreases (Binsbergen et al., 2013), while the aggregate equity premium increases by more than short-duration equity premia (Gormsen, 2021); thus, equity yield spreads are procyclical, and equity term premia are countercyclical. Finally, at the bottom of stock market downturns, the term structures of bond yields—both real and nominal—become steeper, as they predict higher future growth and rates (an observation that goes back to at least Estrella and Hardouvelis, 1991).Our main contribution is to offer a quantitative and parsimonious general-equilibrium explanation of the macroeconomic forces that drive this set of empirical features in equity and bond markets. This paper offers a structural story that captures several of the empirical properties of equity and bond prices that so far only the reduced-form, no-arbitrage models of Lettau and Wachter (2011) and Gormsen (2021) have tried to capture. Specifically, we present a New Keynesian model with habit formation that relies on two ingredients. The first ingredient, a textbook sticky-price production economy driven by productivity shocks, provides a familiar model of output and inflation that matches standard macroeconomic data while rationalizing dividends as a levered version of consumption and the payoffs of nominal bonds. The second ingredient, slow-moving habits in consumption as in Campbell and Cochrane (1999) generate realistically large and time-varying discount rates.A key theme of our contribution is how to unite nonlinear consumption habits and a production economy without compromising the model’s ability to fit macroeconomic variables—a challenge documented by Lettau and Uhlig (2000) and Rudebusch and Swanson (2008). We avoid that difficulty by including a second habit in effective leisure, or home consumption. Intuitively, after a bad productivity shock, both market and home consumption drop close to their habit levels, with offsetting effects on the labor choice, thereby neutralizing the undesirable effect of persistent consumption habits on production. In fact, we show how one can preserve the model of quantities derived under CRRA preferences, in spite of nonlinear habits that preserve the Campbell and Cochrane (1999) pricing kernel and produce realistic asset prices. This macro-finance separation (MFS) result—whereby the states that drive variation in discount rates beyond the usual CRRA preferences do not drive consumption, hours, and inflation—implies that habits do not affect the well-known properties of quantities in the macro model. It thus extends to the habit formation setting a result analogous to that of Tallarini (2000) for Epstein–Zin preferences. MFS also implies that we can effectively inspect the mechanism by considering in isolation the role of the two ingredients.We first strip down our mechanism to the essential ingredients; we match most asset pricing facts in a simple model without capital accumulation and with only productivity shocks. Our first ingredient, the production economy with sticky prices, provides a macroeconomic model that matches the observed volatility at different horizons of the key cash flows (consumption growth, dividend growth, and inverse inflation). Thanks to MFS, the model’s quantity and inflation implications and responses to a productivity shock are standard. The central mechanism relies on nominal rigidities that produce countercyclical labor shares after a productivity shock, which imply procyclical corporate profits and countercyclical inflation. Because of this cash flow effect, dividend claims and nominal bonds pay off badly in a downturn and are therefore risky investments. Then, as more and more firms are able to adjust their prices to mark them up over marginal costs, corporate profits recover and the price level increases. Thus, the payoff of long-duration dividend strips is less procyclical and the payoff of long-duration nominal bonds is more procyclical.Our second ingredient, slow-moving external habit formation, then magnifies these cash flow risks into realistically large and countercyclical risk premia. Moreover, in the model, the discount rate also makes all long-term claims inherently risky. Specifically, during a downturn, the prices of longer-duration claims drop more than those of shorter ones. This happens because consumers in the model will get accustomed to the lower consumption level, so they are less willing to defer consumption. As a result, they demand more compensation for shifting resources into the long-term future than into the near future. Because of this habit effect, the model produces an average term structure of the equity premium that is U-shaped—with a negative slope in the short to medium run, driven by the cash flow effect, and a positive slope for longer maturities, driven by the habit effect. By the same habit effect, our model produces a positively sloped term structure of real rates, thereby avoiding a real bond premium puzzle (Backus et al., 1989), while the cyclicality of inflation implies a positive inflation risk premium at all horizons and a positively sloped nominal term structure.The nonlinear habits also generate the cyclicality of the term structures observed in the data. In bad times, dividends drop and are expected to recover, so the slope of equity yields for the observable maturities becomes more negative. Consumption also falls close to habits, which raises risk premia through the habit effect, especially at longer horizons; consequently, in the model, aggregate equity premia rise by more than short-run equity premia. At the same time, inflation is expected to increase sluggishly, and hence the slope of bond yields becomes more positive.In the background of these results, our framework preserves the main achievements of Campbell and Cochrane (1999), including a solution to the average equity premium and the risk-free rate puzzles, long-horizon predictability of excess stock returns, and the countercyclical variation of stock market returns and volatility.We then depart from MFS by extending our model to incorporate realistic capital accumulation, which is the most natural first extension of the MFS baseline and allows us to assess whether the main asset-pricing mechanism survives once realistic investment dynamics are included. We find that it preserves the desirable asset pricing implications of the baseline model, while helping match more facts about quantities. In particular, the extended model has similar implications for the average slope and cyclicality of the term structures of equity and bond returns.The choice of external habits to explain the term structure evidence may seem surprising at first, as Binsbergen et al. (2012) and Gormsen (2021) document the challenges of the habit framework in producing negative and procyclical equity yield spreads, even though they are naturally consistent with the countercyclicality of equity term premia due to the habit effect that manifests at long horizons. Those results, however, are typically derived in endowment economies with exogenous random-walk dividend streams. In fact, the endogenous mean-reverting dividend dynamics implied by our production economy avoid the counterfactual result. In particular, by using the model to make the properties of cash flows match their volatility and autocorrelation in the data, we are able to naturally generate a downward and procyclical slope at the observable end of the term structure of equity yields while preserving the property of habits that generates countercyclical equity term premia.Furthermore, the countercyclicality of equity term premia documented in Gormsen (2021), which is naturally generated in our model by the habit effect just described, challenges the use of Epstein–Zin preferences to model jointly the term structures of equities and bonds. Indeed, Gormsen shows how recent examples in Hasler and Marfè (2016) and Ai et al. (2018), who are able to generate a downward-sloping equity term structure by changing the cash flow process, display as a consequence the wrong cyclicality of the term structure of equity premia. Therefore, the use of Epstein–Zin preferences faces a tension between matching the cyclicality of equity term premia and the slope and cyclicality of equity spreads. Moreover, economies with Epstein–Zin preferences tend to produce real term structures that are downward sloping, as shown by Rudebusch and Swanson (2012) and Li and Palomino (2014), rather than upward sloping as in the data.Finally, we inspect how our quantitative results depend on the key ingredients of the baseline model—namely, the two habits and nominal price rigidities. When we deactivate the habit in effective leisure, we confirm the dramatic distortions to the model’s properties that arise when the effect of habits on the consumption–labor tradeoff is left unchecked, echoing Lettau and Uhlig (2000). As we turn off the nominal rigidities, the desirable cyclical properties of cash flows vanish—as we introduce realistic capital accumulation in the flexible-price version of the two-habit model, we even obtain counterfactually countercyclical dividends, echoing Kaltenbrunner and Lochstoer (2010). Indeed, as we increase the degree of nominal rigidity starting from the flexible-price model, the slope of the equity term structure turns negative while the bond term structure flattens, as the stronger countercyclicality of the labor share generates procyclical and mean-reverting dividends alongside countercyclical and sluggish inflation.Our paper subscribes to a recent literature that focuses on risk pricing across maturities (see, for example, Lettau and Wachter, 2007, Lettau and Wachter, 2011, Binsbergen et al., 2012, Binsbergen et al., 2013, Borovicka and Hansen, 2014, Belo et al., 2015, Hasler and Marfè, 2016, Marfè, 2017, Ai et al., 2018, Lopez, 2021, Weber, 2018, Kogan et al., 2020, Bansal et al., 2021, Gormsen, 2021, Li and Xu, 2024, Zeng and Zhao, 2026). While the search for a structural explanation of the positive slope and cyclicality of the term structure of interest rates has a rather long history, the search for a structural explanation for the negative slope of the term structure of equity has only recently received attention (see Binsbergen and Koijen, 2017 for a survey). While a relatively small sample and potential liquidity issues introduce some controversy as to the sign of the average slope, as argued by Bansal et al. (2021), the cyclical properties of the term structure of equity are so far less controversial. These more recent facts add to the more classic facts documenting a large and countercyclical equity premium and a low and stable risk-free rate.Our simple story captures these empirical regularities, which so far only the reduced-form models in Lettau and Wachter (2011) and Gormsen (2021) have tried to capture, although outside a general-equilibrium context that spells out preferences and production choices. An alternative view, such as Li and Xu (2024) and Zeng and Zhao (2026), focuses on departures from standard assumptions in business-cycle analysis, including behavioral expectations and intermediary-based asset pricing, to capture properties of the term structures of equity, thereby offering a complementary view to ours. We focus instead on explaining asset pricing facts through a business-cycle model in a standard production economy without exotic ingredients.We likewise contribute to a growing literature that explores the asset pricing implications of New Keynesian models, including Rudebusch and Swanson, 2008, Rudebusch and Swanson, 2012, Bekaert et al., 2010, Li and Palomino, 2014, Kung, 2015, Campbell et al., 2020, Gourio and Ngo, 2022, Pflueger and Rinaldi, 2022. None of these studies, however, focuses on the joint properties of the term structures of equity and interest rates. Within this literature, Campbell et al. (2020) and Pflueger and Rinaldi (2022) also study the effects of Campbell–Cochrane-type habits in the presence of sticky prices, highlighting how countercyclical risk premia generated by habits interact with inflation and monetary policy. Their analysis, however, relies on a reduced-form specification of the production side of the economy that abstracts from labor supply and capital accumulation decisions, and hence sidesteps the difficulties in reconciling business cycle facts with habit formation in production economies documented by Lettau and Uhlig (2000).In this context, we show how Campbell–Cochrane habits can be incorporated into a full-fledged production economy in a way that avoids these difficulties. By doing so, we not only respond to the critique by Lettau and Uhlig (2000) and Rudebusch and Swanson (2008)—and related work by Jermann (1998), Uhlig (2007), or Jaccard (2014)—but also show how the additional structure that comes from the production side of the economy jointly delivers realistic properties of the three term structures.Organizational accessGet full-text access by signing in with your organisationAccess through your organizationOther access optionsPurchase PDFNeed help with access?Section snippetsPreferencesWhen habit formation is combined with a production economy, their interaction can generate counterfactual implications, as noted by Lettau and Uhlig (2000) and Rudebusch and Swanson (2008). Consequently, short-duration equities (bonds) have more (less) procyclical payoffs than their long-duration counterparts. Slow-moving consumption habits produce large, countercyclical risk prices, yielding realistic asset valuations. Extending Campbell–Cochrane preferences with both market- and home-consumption habits allows them to operate in production economies while preserving realistic macroeconomic dynamics.

A simple production economy with nominal price rigidities explains several key asset pricing facts, including the average slopes and cyclicality of equity and interest rate term structures. Nominal rigidities amplify the procyclicality of dividends after negative productivity shocks and generate countercyclical inflation, as sluggish price adjustment leads to a gradual dividend recovery. Consequently, short-duration equities (bonds) have more (less) procyclical payoffs than their long-duration counterparts. Slow-moving consumption habits produce large, countercyclical risk prices, yielding realistic asset valuations. Extending Campbell–Cochrane preferences with both market- and home-consumption habits allows them to operate in production economies while preserving realistic macroeconomic dynamics.

Extending Campbell–Cochrane preferences with both market- and home-consumption habits allows them to operate in production economies while preserving realistic macroeconomic dynamics.JEL classificationE32; E43; E44; G12.KeywordsEquity and bond yields; Campbell–Cochrane habits; Nominal rigidities; Macro-finance separation; New Keynesian modelPrevious article in this issueNext article in this issueIntroductionRecent evidence shows that discount rates of financial claims differ across maturities and across asset classes. In particular, the maturity structure and time variation of equity and bond risk premia contain rich information to understand investors’ marginal utility of wealth and their expectations about future macroeconomic variables. The empirical literature has documented that the returns of nominal and real bonds increase with maturity on average, while claims to short-term dividends have high average excess returns, comparable in size to the aggregate equity premium (Binsbergen et al., 2012, Binsbergen and Koijen, 2017). During stock market downturns, the slope of the term structure of equity yields decreases (Binsbergen et al., 2013), while the aggregate equity premium increases by more than short-duration equity premia (Gormsen, 2021); thus, equity yield spreads are procyclical, and equity term premia are countercyclical. Finally, at the bottom of stock market downturns, the term structures of bond yields—both real and nominal—become steeper, as they predict higher future growth and rates (an observation that goes back to at least Estrella and Hardouvelis, 1991).Our main contribution is to offer a quantitative and parsimonious general-equilibrium explanation of the macroeconomic forces that drive this set of empirical features in equity and bond markets. This paper offers a structural story that captures several of the empirical properties of equity and bond prices that so far only the reduced-form, no-arbitrage models of Lettau and Wachter (2011) and Gormsen (2021) have tried to capture. Specifically, we present a New Keynesian model with habit formation that relies on two ingredients. The first ingredient, a textbook sticky-price production economy driven by productivity shocks, provides a familiar model of output and inflation that matches standard macroeconomic data while rationalizing dividends as a levered version of consumption and the payoffs of nominal bonds. The second ingredient, slow-moving habits in consumption as in Campbell and Cochrane (1999) generate realistically large and time-varying discount rates.A key theme of our contribution is how to unite nonlinear consumption habits and a production economy without compromising the model’s ability to fit macroeconomic variables—a challenge documented by Lettau and Uhlig (2000) and Rudebusch and Swanson (2008). We avoid that difficulty by including a second habit in effective leisure, or home consumption. Intuitively, after a bad productivity shock, both market and home consumption drop close to their habit levels, with offsetting effects on the labor choice, thereby neutralizing the undesirable effect of persistent consumption habits on production. In fact, we show how one can preserve the model of quantities derived under CRRA preferences, in spite of nonlinear habits that preserve the Campbell and Cochrane (1999) pricing kernel and produce realistic asset prices. This macro-finance separation (MFS) result—whereby the states that drive variation in discount rates beyond the usual CRRA preferences do not drive consumption, hours, and inflation—implies that habits do not affect the well-known properties of quantities in the macro model. It thus extends to the habit formation setting a result analogous to that of Tallarini (2000) for Epstein–Zin preferences. MFS also implies that we can effectively inspect the mechanism by considering in isolation the role of the two ingredients.We first strip down our mechanism to the essential ingredients; we match most asset pricing facts in a simple model without capital accumulation and with only productivity shocks. Our first ingredient, the production economy with sticky prices, provides a macroeconomic model that matches the observed volatility at different horizons of the key cash flows (consumption growth, dividend growth, and inverse inflation). Thanks to MFS, the model’s quantity and inflation implications and responses to a productivity shock are standard. The central mechanism relies on nominal rigidities that produce countercyclical labor shares after a productivity shock, which imply procyclical corporate profits and countercyclical inflation. Because of this cash flow effect, dividend claims and nominal bonds pay off badly in a downturn and are therefore risky investments. Then, as more and more firms are able to adjust their prices to mark them up over marginal costs, corporate profits recover and the price level increases. Thus, the payoff of long-duration dividend strips is less procyclical and the payoff of long-duration nominal bonds is more procyclical.Our second ingredient, slow-moving external habit formation, then magnifies these cash flow risks into realistically large and countercyclical risk premia. Moreover, in the model, the discount rate also makes all long-term claims inherently risky. Specifically, during a downturn, the prices of longer-duration claims drop more than those of shorter ones. This happens because consumers in the model will get accustomed to the lower consumption level, so they are less willing to defer consumption. As a result, they demand more compensation for shifting resources into the long-term future than into the near future. Because of this habit effect, the model produces an average term structure of the equity premium that is U-shaped—with a negative slope in the short to medium run, driven by the cash flow effect, and a positive slope for longer maturities, driven by the habit effect. By the same habit effect, our model produces a positively sloped term structure of real rates, thereby avoiding a real bond premium puzzle (Backus et al., 1989), while the cyclicality of inflation implies a positive inflation risk premium at all horizons and a positively sloped nominal term structure.The nonlinear habits also generate the cyclicality of the term structures observed in the data. In bad times, dividends drop and are expected to recover, so the slope of equity yields for the observable maturities becomes more negative. Consumption also falls close to habits, which raises risk premia through the habit effect, especially at longer horizons; consequently, in the model, aggregate equity premia rise by more than short-run equity premia. At the same time, inflation is expected to increase sluggishly, and hence the slope of bond yields becomes more positive.In the background of these results, our framework preserves the main achievements of Campbell and Cochrane (1999), including a solution to the average equity premium and the risk-free rate puzzles, long-horizon predictability of excess stock returns, and the countercyclical variation of stock market returns and volatility.We then depart from MFS by extending our model to incorporate realistic capital accumulation, which is the most natural first extension of the MFS baseline and allows us to assess whether the main asset-pricing mechanism survives once realistic investment dynamics are included. We find that it preserves the desirable asset pricing implications of the baseline model, while helping match more facts about quantities. In particular, the extended model has similar implications for the average slope and cyclicality of the term structures of equity and bond returns.The choice of external habits to explain the term structure evidence may seem surprising at first, as Binsbergen et al. (2012) and Gormsen (2021) document the challenges of the habit framework in producing negative and procyclical equity yield spreads, even though they are naturally consistent with the countercyclicality of equity term premia due to the habit effect that manifests at long horizons. Those results, however, are typically derived in endowment economies with exogenous random-walk dividend streams. In fact, the endogenous mean-reverting dividend dynamics implied by our production economy avoid the counterfactual result. In particular, by using the model to make the properties of cash flows match their volatility and autocorrelation in the data, we are able to naturally generate a downward and procyclical slope at the observable end of the term structure of equity yields while preserving the property of habits that generates countercyclical equity term premia.Furthermore, the countercyclicality of equity term premia documented in Gormsen (2021), which is naturally generated in our model by the habit effect just described, challenges the use of Epstein–Zin preferences to model jointly the term structures of equities and bonds. Indeed, Gormsen shows how recent examples in Hasler and Marfè (2016) and Ai et al. (2018), who are able to generate a downward-sloping equity term structure by changing the cash flow process, display as a consequence the wrong cyclicality of the term structure of equity premia. Therefore, the use of Epstein–Zin preferences faces a tension between matching the cyclicality of equity term premia and the slope and cyclicality of equity spreads. Moreover, economies with Epstein–Zin preferences tend to produce real term structures that are downward sloping, as shown by Rudebusch and Swanson (2012) and Li and Palomino (2014), rather than upward sloping as in the data.Finally, we inspect how our quantitative results depend on the key ingredients of the baseline model—namely, the two habits and nominal price rigidities. When we deactivate the habit in effective leisure, we confirm the dramatic distortions to the model’s properties that arise when the effect of habits on the consumption–labor tradeoff is left unchecked, echoing Lettau and Uhlig (2000). As we turn off the nominal rigidities, the desirable cyclical properties of cash flows vanish—as we introduce realistic capital accumulation in the flexible-price version of the two-habit model, we even obtain counterfactually countercyclical dividends, echoing Kaltenbrunner and Lochstoer (2010). Indeed, as we increase the degree of nominal rigidity starting from the flexible-price model, the slope of the equity term structure turns negative while the bond term structure flattens, as the stronger countercyclicality of the labor share generates procyclical and mean-reverting dividends alongside countercyclical and sluggish inflation.Our paper subscribes to a recent literature that focuses on risk pricing across maturities (see, for example, Lettau and Wachter, 2007, Lettau and Wachter, 2011, Binsbergen et al., 2012, Binsbergen et al., 2013, Borovicka and Hansen, 2014, Belo et al., 2015, Hasler and Marfè, 2016, Marfè, 2017, Ai et al., 2018, Lopez, 2021, Weber, 2018, Kogan et al., 2020, Bansal et al., 2021, Gormsen, 2021, Li and Xu, 2024, Zeng and Zhao, 2026). While the search for a structural explanation of the positive slope and cyclicality of the term structure of interest rates has a rather long history, the search for a structural explanation for the negative slope of the term structure of equity has only recently received attention (see Binsbergen and Koijen, 2017 for a survey). While a relatively small sample and potential liquidity issues introduce some controversy as to the sign of the average slope, as argued by Bansal et al. (2021), the cyclical properties of the term structure of equity are so far less controversial. These more recent facts add to the more classic facts documenting a large and countercyclical equity premium and a low and stable risk-free rate.Our simple story captures these empirical regularities, which so far only the reduced-form models in Lettau and Wachter (2011) and Gormsen (2021) have tried to capture, although outside a general-equilibrium context that spells out preferences and production choices. An alternative view, such as Li and Xu (2024) and Zeng and Zhao (2026), focuses on departures from standard assumptions in business-cycle analysis, including behavioral expectations and intermediary-based asset pricing, to capture properties of the term structures of equity, thereby offering a complementary view to ours. We focus instead on explaining asset pricing facts through a business-cycle model in a standard production economy without exotic ingredients.We likewise contribute to a growing literature that explores the asset pricing implications of New Keynesian models, including Rudebusch and Swanson, 2008, Rudebusch and Swanson, 2012, Bekaert et al., 2010, Li and Palomino, 2014, Kung, 2015, Campbell et al., 2020, Gourio and Ngo, 2022, Pflueger and Rinaldi, 2022. None of these studies, however, focuses on the joint properties of the term structures of equity and interest rates. Within this literature, Campbell et al. (2020) and Pflueger and Rinaldi (2022) also study the effects of Campbell–Cochrane-type habits in the presence of sticky prices, highlighting how countercyclical risk premia generated by habits interact with inflation and monetary policy. Their analysis, however, relies on a reduced-form specification of the production side of the economy that abstracts from labor supply and capital accumulation decisions, and hence sidesteps the difficulties in reconciling business cycle facts with habit formation in production economies documented by Lettau and Uhlig (2000).In this context, we show how Campbell–Cochrane habits can be incorporated into a full-fledged production economy in a way that avoids these difficulties. By doing so, we not only respond to the critique by Lettau and Uhlig (2000) and Rudebusch and Swanson (2008)—and related work by Jermann (1998), Uhlig (2007), or Jaccard (2014)—but also show how the additional structure that comes from the production side of the economy jointly delivers realistic properties of the three term structures.Organizational accessGet full-text access by signing in with your organisationAccess through your organizationOther access optionsPurchase PDFNeed help with access?Section snippetsPreferencesWhen habit formation is combined with a production economy, their interaction can generate counterfactual implications, as noted by Lettau and Uhlig (2000) and Rudebusch and Swanson (2008). source_records.abstract: Are banks safer when they hold more safe assets? This paper builds a model in which banks supply liquidity services through uninsured deposits. Define a safe asset as an asset with both low payoff risk and high pledgeability. Banks consider equity costly and because of safe assets’ low payoff risk prefer to fund them largely with deposits. High pledgeability makes this feasible. The rise in banks’ deposit supply increases deposit rates and forces banks to deviate from socially desirable levels of capital to meet return-on-equity targets. Regulatory leverage ratios can be tightened to increase welfare.

Macroprudential regulation and banks’ supply of liquidity services

Are banks safer when they hold more safe assets? This paper builds a model in which banks supply liquidity services through uninsured deposits. Define a safe asset as an asset with both low payoff risk and high pledgeability. Banks consider equity costly and because of safe assets’ low payoff risk prefer to fund them largely with deposits. High pledgeability makes this feasible. The rise in banks’ deposit supply increases deposit rates and forces banks to deviate from socially desirable levels of capital to meet return-on-equity targets. Regulatory leverage ratios can be tightened to increase welfare.

Regulatory leverage ratios can be tightened to increase welfare.JEL classificationE44; E60; G21; G28KeywordsFinancial frictions; Financial intermediation; Banks’ liquidity supply; Macroprudential bank regulation; Safe assets; Central bank reservesPrevious article in this issueNext article in this issueIntroduction“Because banks play an essential intermediation role in the Treasury market, we want to ensure that the leverage ratio does not become regularly binding and discourage banks from participating in low-risk activities, such as Treasury market intermediation.” Chair of the Federal Reserve Jerome H. Powell, 25 June 2025Following the 2007–2008 Global Financial Crisis there have been profound changes in the scope and conduct of bank regulation and monetary policy. Banks are now subject to comprehensive liquidity regulations and encouraged to hold significant reserves.2 This paper identifies banks’ role as providers of liquidity services as a novel economic channel that implies that banks’ holdings of safe assets are already excessive. A key policy implication is that regulatory leverage requirements should be binding during normal times.Banks derive significant revenue from providing liquidity services to the economy.3 Specifically, banks provide liquidity services by issuing demandable deposits and investing the proceeds in safe assets. Adapting the Friedman rule to banks’ liquidity provision, it could then be argued that policy makers should enable or even encourage banks toincrease their holdings of safe assets, to provide more liquidity services.4 The difference in the returns between safe assets and deposits, the “liquidity premium on deposits”, would then be reduced and depositor welfare, at least in a narrow sense, increased. Liquidity regulations and central bank asset purchase programs, which push banks to hold more safe assets, could then be seen as having the positive side effect of lowering liquidity premiums. In contrast, regulatory leverage ratios, typically considered a backstop against potential hidden risk-taking, could then be seen as having the very tangible negative side effect of increasing liquidity premiums.However, this view is too narrow because banks not only provide liquidity services, but also supply risky loans. To smooth banks’ loan supply over financial cycles, recently implemented frameworks for macroprudential capital regulation require banks to hold more equity capital (Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, 2010), which is costly for banks. These frameworks often ignore how profits from liquidity premiums help to compensate banks for the cost of holding equity capital.The paper highlights a novel, and surprising, implication for bank regulation stemming from banks’ role as liquidity providers. Bank regulation that smooths out banks’ supply of loans and liquidity over the financial cycle also maximizes banks’ own funding liquidity. Such a policy requires banks to hold fewer, not more, safe assets during normal times.This result arises in a model with features that are standard in the dynamic stochastic general equilibrium literature. The model economy is populated by households, firms and banks. Banks fund loans to firms and holdings of safe assets with retained earnings (equity) and by supplying liquidity services in the form of deposits to households. Banks consider equity capital costly and face elastic demand for deposits.In the model, safe assets are characterized by both low payoff risk and high pledgeability. These properties imply that banks fund safe assets largely with deposits. Therefore, when banks hold more safe assets, they must offer higher deposit rates. But higher deposit funding costs reduce banks’ net return on assets. The paper shows that this creates a negative pecuniary externality as banks, to meet their return-on-equity targets, further deviate from socially desirable levels of equity capital.Banks’ deposit supply therefore ends up being excessive during normal times. While banks provide ample liquidity to the economy during normal times, this comes at the cost of inefficiently low financial stability. In particular, banks’ holdings of safe assets during normal times are excessive and make credit and liquidity crunches more likely by reducing banks’ ability to provide loans and deposits during episodes of financial stress.5 The contribution of the paper is to highlight this novel pecuniary externality and to offer policy implications. Specifically, a binding leverage ratio requirement can be introduced to increase welfare. In practice this implies a tightening of Basel III supplementary leverage ratio (SLR) requirements.Equity capital has an important role in the economy because over time exogenous shocks to firms’ loan repayments may occasionally deplete equity and thereby cause banks’ funding constraints to bind. The motivation for market-imposed equity constraints is that bank shareholder value should be high enough to ensure that banks have sound risk management and do not engage in moral hazard (as in Gertler and Kiyotaki, 2010).6 While these constraints ensure banks’ solvency at all times, they can create severe liquidity problems for banks because depositors refuse to roll over deposits when banks’ shareholder value is too low. When banks’ funding is sufficiently constrained, then banks’ supplies of both loans and liquidity services (deposits) decrease significantly and the economy experiences a financial crisis.The cost of banks’ deposit funding decreases in the liquidity premium on deposits in the model. This premium reflects the value of deposits to households who use them to meet sudden idiosyncratic consumption needs, or liquidity shocks. While households can also use safe assets to pay for consumption goods, they must first sell them which incurs a deadweight transaction cost. In the model this transaction cost is a decreasing function of the share of aggregate household savings held in form of deposits. This feature captures the intuition that when households can meet more of their liquidity shocks with deposits, then there are fewer sellers in the secondary market for safe assets at a given point in time so that it is easier for each seller to find a buyer. When households allocate their savings optimally, the liquidity premium of deposits is increasing in the transaction cost that households face when selling safe assets at the times of their respective consumption needs. It follows that liquidity premiums on deposits are decreasing in the aggregate amount of deposits in the model.The paper characterizes optimal policy by studying the constrained-efficient allocation, or second best, of the model. Policy implications are derived by comparing the second best and the laissez-faire competitive equilibrium. The focus on constrained-efficiency is motivated by the discretion that financial regulators have in practice. In particular, despite the expanding macroprudential tool kit of regulators, no clear rules regarding its usage have been formulated (there is no “Taylor rule” for macroprudential bank regulation).7 While it is difficult to predict new policy tools or kinds of regulatory forbearance during times of financial stress, it is possible to identify regulators’ objectives (to maximize some measure of welfare) and the important constraints they are facing (debt funding and capital market pressure for banks). Useful policy implications can therefore be derived by comparing constrained-efficient and competitive-equilibrium allocations.The novel, and surprising, insight of the paper is that banks hold fewer safe assets during normal times in the second best than in the competitive equilibrium. Lower safe-asset holdings reduce the need for deposit funding and allow banks to offer lower deposit rates in the second best allocation. This results in higher liquidity premiums, and thus higher interest rate spreads, which enables banks to hold more costly capital during normal times.8 Moreover, while banks’ second-best safe asset holdings are smaller during normal times, compared with the competitive equilibrium, they are larger during financial crises. During normal times, the liquidity premium is higher in second best, compared with the competitive equilibrium, but it is more stable during financial crises. Banks have smaller balance sheets but larger market capitalizations in the second-best allocation.A key policy implication in this paper is that regulatory tools should be coordinated to avoid undermining the effectiveness of recently introduced macroprudential capital buffer frameworks. The analysis implies that banks should reduce the size of their balance sheets by reducing safe asset holdings and should hold more equity. In other words, banks should have smaller balance sheets and focus on funding riskier assets with more stable funding. A tighter SLR requirement would work in support of this implication. Therefore, there is a complementarity, during normal times, between tightening the SLR and requiring banks to build up larger capital buffers.The analysis strengthens the rationale for the SLR, from acting as a backstop against potential hidden buildup of leverage driven by risky lending to preventing the very visible increase in leverage driven by accumulation of safe assets. The reason is that banks’ participation in low-risk activities, paradoxically, reduces financial stability. Introducing a binding SLR-style requirement in the competitive equilibrium of the model strengthens banks’ deposit franchise value and increases banks’ loan supply rather than crowding it out. A policy experiment shows that a combination of SLR and capital buffer requirements delivers welfare gains that are higher compared to the cases where only one of these requirements is imposed. Banks’ balance sheets then look similar as in the second-best allocation during normal times. While capital buffer requirements induce banks to hold more equity, SLR-type requirements make sure that this does not excessively hurt lending.In addition, the analysis suggests that liquidity regulations such as the liquidity coverage ratio (LCR) may not be necessary as banks already over-accumulate safe assets in the model. Banks’ actions display a “paradox of thrift” wherein each bank’s accumulation of safe assets ends up making other banks’ liabilities less stable. In the model, bank funding market participants are wary of the potential for bank moral hazard. Specifically, deposit “run-off rates” adjust endogenously ex ante to mitigate banks’ ex-post incentives to engage in moral hazard. Banks with more equity capital are able to roll over more of their deposit funding each period (Holmstrom and Tirole, 1997, Gertler and Kiyotaki, 2010), consistent with empirical evidence that deteriorations in banks’ funding access are driven by fundamentals (Correia et al., 2024). Excessive safe asset holdings of banks create upward pressure on the deposit funding costs of banks and undermine their ability to maintain high levels of costly equity. This has implications not only for the liquidity of banks themselves but also for banks’ ability to provide loans and liquidity to the economy during times of financial stress. Any positive direct welfare effect of higher safe asset holdings of banks on their supply of liquidity during normal times is more than offset by the general-equilibrium effect of stronger deleveraging during times of financial stress. In the model, welfare is higher over financial cycles when banks hold fewer safe financial assets, and more equity, during normal times.9An extension of the model, in Appendix A, introduces nominal wage rigidity to study the coordination of monetary policy and bank regulation during financial crises. Monetary policies that narrowly focus on closing the labor gap are not constrained-efficient. The reason is that expansionary monetary policy decreases, by assumption, the spread between safe assets and deposits (liquidity premium of deposits) in the model.10 This channel gives rise to an unintended side effect of monetary policy that matters especially during financial crises. While expansive monetary policy operations can avoid inefficiently low employment in the model, they may not actually succeed in stabilizing economic output during times when banks have low equity. Specifically, a more expansive monetary policy reduces banks’ lending by reducing profitability of banks at a time when they are already capital constrained. Constrained-efficient monetary policy is therefore less expansionary, relative to what would be required to close the labor gap, during financial crises. For this reason, there is a complementarity during financial crises between a less expansive monetary policy stance and releasing banks’ regulatory capital buffers.The importance of banks’ deposit spreads on credit supply has also been stressed in Drechsler et al. (2017), Abadi et al. (2023), Eggertsson et al. (2024), and Wang (2025). Deposit spreads are driven by the monetary policy stance in those papers, while in this paper spreads are also affected by bank regulation. My paper complements this literature by showing that a bank regulator that is concerned about financial stability would like to do two things simultaneously during normal times: (i) to induce banks to hold fewer safe assets to reduce deposit supply, and (ii) to require banks to hold more equity capital. The rationale is that higher deposit spreads compensate bank shareholders for retaining more earnings. Financial stability is increased through higher deposit spreads during normal times not by granting rents to banks but by making it feasible to require banks to hold more capital.Begenau (2020) finds that a higher capital requirement reduces the funding cost of banks by reducing deposit supply if the elasticity of deposit demand is sufficiently low. Banks’ holdings of safe assets are exogenous in her model and the optimal capital requirement implies a larger banking sector. In contrast, in this paper the decrease in banks’ funding costs in the constrained-efficient allocation is driven by a smaller banking sector, achieved by a decrease in banks’ safe asset holdings. The rationale for increasing banks’ equity capital in this paper is not to decrease funding costs further (deposit demand is too elastic for that in this paper) but to make banks more resilient. Specifically, banks pay lower deposit rates not because of alternative funding sources (equity) but because they have fewer safe assets to fund. The channel in Begenau (2020) operates within the liability side of banks’ balance sheets, but the channel in this paper operates from the asset to the liability side.Diamond and Rajan (2001) emphasize that demandable deposits are an important disciplining device in the hands of bank creditors. As in this paper, creditors are atomistic and not able to commit among themselves to renegotiating the face value of bank deposits ex post. They simply demand their deposits back (via a “bank run” as in Diamond and Dybvig, 1983), or refuse to roll over in the case of banks’ wholesale or interbank funding sources, if they are concerned about bank moral hazard. In this paper deposits, in addition, play a role in recapitalizing banks after they experience loan losses. A decrease in deposit rates when banks are forced to reduce the size of their balance sheets allows banks to rebuild equity faster. A policy implication is that banks should rely less on demandable deposits, and more on equity, during normal times such that they are forced to reduce deposit supply less during financial crises.Gatev and Strahan (2006) document empirical support for banks benefiting from procyclical funding costs, i.e., from a countercyclical liquidity premium. They argue that higher liquidity premiums during episodes of financial stress enable banks to provide a more stable supply of loans. In contrast, this paper argues that higher liquidity premiums during normal times would enable banks to hold more equity capital which would make their loan supply more resilient during episodes of financial stress.Diamond et al. (2024) find that when banks cannot freely adjust their holdings of highly pledgeable risk-free assets (in aggregate), for example, due to quantitative easing, regulations such as the SLR can hurt lending. Define a safe asset as an asset with both low payoff risk and high pledgeability. Banks consider equity costly and because of safe assets’ low payoff risk prefer to fund them largely with deposits. High pledgeability makes this feasible. The rise in banks’ deposit supply increases deposit rates and forces banks to deviate from socially desirable levels of capital to meet return-on-equity targets. Regulatory leverage ratios can be tightened to increase welfare.

Macroprudential regulation and banks’ supply of liquidity services
Macroprudential regulation and banks’ supply of liquidity services

Are banks safer when they hold more safe assets? This paper builds a model in which banks supply liquidity services through uninsured deposits. Define a safe asset as an asset with both low payoff risk and high pledgeability. Banks consider equity costly and because of safe assets’ low payoff risk prefer to fund them largely with deposits. High pledgeability makes this feasible. The rise in banks’ deposit supply increases deposit rates and forces banks to deviate from socially desirable levels of capital to meet return-on-equity targets. Regulatory leverage ratios can be tightened to increase welfare.

Banks consider equity costly and because of safe assets’ low payoff risk prefer to fund them largely with deposits. High pledgeability makes this feasible. Regulatory leverage ratios can be tightened to increase welfare.JEL classificationE44; E60; G21; G28KeywordsFinancial frictions; Financial intermediation; Banks’ liquidity supply; Macroprudential bank regulation; Safe assets; Central bank reservesPrevious article in this issueNext article in this issueIntroduction“Because banks play an essential intermediation role in the Treasury market, we want to ensure that the leverage ratio does not become regularly binding and discourage banks from participating in low-risk activities, such as Treasury market intermediation.” Chair of the Federal Reserve Jerome H. Powell, 25 June 2025Following the 2007–2008 Global Financial Crisis there have been profound changes in the scope and conduct of bank regulation and monetary policy. Banks are now subject to comprehensive liquidity regulations and encouraged to hold significant reserves.2 This paper identifies banks’ role as providers of liquidity services as a novel economic channel that implies that banks’ holdings of safe assets are already excessive. A key policy implication is that regulatory leverage requirements should be binding during normal times.Banks derive significant revenue from providing liquidity services to the economy.3 Specifically, banks provide liquidity services by issuing demandable deposits and investing the proceeds in safe assets. Adapting the Friedman rule to banks’ liquidity provision, it could then be argued that policy makers should enable or even encourage banks toincrease their holdings of safe assets, to provide more liquidity services.4 The difference in the returns between safe assets and deposits, the “liquidity premium on deposits”, would then be reduced and depositor welfare, at least in a narrow sense, increased. Liquidity regulations and central bank asset purchase programs, which push banks to hold more safe assets, could then be seen as having the positive side effect of lowering liquidity premiums. In contrast, regulatory leverage ratios, typically considered a backstop against potential hidden risk-taking, could then be seen as having the very tangible negative side effect of increasing liquidity premiums.However, this view is too narrow because banks not only provide liquidity services, but also supply risky loans. To smooth banks’ loan supply over financial cycles, recently implemented frameworks for macroprudential capital regulation require banks to hold more equity capital (Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, 2010), which is costly for banks. These frameworks often ignore how profits from liquidity premiums help to compensate banks for the cost of holding equity capital.The paper highlights a novel, and surprising, implication for bank regulation stemming from banks’ role as liquidity providers. Bank regulation that smooths out banks’ supply of loans and liquidity over the financial cycle also maximizes banks’ own funding liquidity. Such a policy requires banks to hold fewer, not more, safe assets during normal times.This result arises in a model with features that are standard in the dynamic stochastic general equilibrium literature. The model economy is populated by households, firms and banks. Banks fund loans to firms and holdings of safe assets with retained earnings (equity) and by supplying liquidity services in the form of deposits to households. Banks consider equity capital costly and face elastic demand for deposits.In the model, safe assets are characterized by both low payoff risk and high pledgeability. These properties imply that banks fund safe assets largely with deposits. Therefore, when banks hold more safe assets, they must offer higher deposit rates. But higher deposit funding costs reduce banks’ net return on assets. The paper shows that this creates a negative pecuniary externality as banks, to meet their return-on-equity targets, further deviate from socially desirable levels of equity capital.Banks’ deposit supply therefore ends up being excessive during normal times. While banks provide ample liquidity to the economy during normal times, this comes at the cost of inefficiently low financial stability. In particular, banks’ holdings of safe assets during normal times are excessive and make credit and liquidity crunches more likely by reducing banks’ ability to provide loans and deposits during episodes of financial stress.5 The contribution of the paper is to highlight this novel pecuniary externality and to offer policy implications. Specifically, a binding leverage ratio requirement can be introduced to increase welfare. In practice this implies a tightening of Basel III supplementary leverage ratio (SLR) requirements.Equity capital has an important role in the economy because over time exogenous shocks to firms’ loan repayments may occasionally deplete equity and thereby cause banks’ funding constraints to bind. The motivation for market-imposed equity constraints is that bank shareholder value should be high enough to ensure that banks have sound risk management and do not engage in moral hazard (as in Gertler and Kiyotaki, 2010).6 While these constraints ensure banks’ solvency at all times, they can create severe liquidity problems for banks because depositors refuse to roll over deposits when banks’ shareholder value is too low. When banks’ funding is sufficiently constrained, then banks’ supplies of both loans and liquidity services (deposits) decrease significantly and the economy experiences a financial crisis.The cost of banks’ deposit funding decreases in the liquidity premium on deposits in the model. This premium reflects the value of deposits to households who use them to meet sudden idiosyncratic consumption needs, or liquidity shocks. While households can also use safe assets to pay for consumption goods, they must first sell them which incurs a deadweight transaction cost. In the model this transaction cost is a decreasing function of the share of aggregate household savings held in form of deposits. This feature captures the intuition that when households can meet more of their liquidity shocks with deposits, then there are fewer sellers in the secondary market for safe assets at a given point in time so that it is easier for each seller to find a buyer. When households allocate their savings optimally, the liquidity premium of deposits is increasing in the transaction cost that households face when selling safe assets at the times of their respective consumption needs. It follows that liquidity premiums on deposits are decreasing in the aggregate amount of deposits in the model.The paper characterizes optimal policy by studying the constrained-efficient allocation, or second best, of the model. Policy implications are derived by comparing the second best and the laissez-faire competitive equilibrium. The focus on constrained-efficiency is motivated by the discretion that financial regulators have in practice. In particular, despite the expanding macroprudential tool kit of regulators, no clear rules regarding its usage have been formulated (there is no “Taylor rule” for macroprudential bank regulation).7 While it is difficult to predict new policy tools or kinds of regulatory forbearance during times of financial stress, it is possible to identify regulators’ objectives (to maximize some measure of welfare) and the important constraints they are facing (debt funding and capital market pressure for banks). Useful policy implications can therefore be derived by comparing constrained-efficient and competitive-equilibrium allocations.The novel, and surprising, insight of the paper is that banks hold fewer safe assets during normal times in the second best than in the competitive equilibrium. Lower safe-asset holdings reduce the need for deposit funding and allow banks to offer lower deposit rates in the second best allocation. This results in higher liquidity premiums, and thus higher interest rate spreads, which enables banks to hold more costly capital during normal times.8 Moreover, while banks’ second-best safe asset holdings are smaller during normal times, compared with the competitive equilibrium, they are larger during financial crises. During normal times, the liquidity premium is higher in second best, compared with the competitive equilibrium, but it is more stable during financial crises. Banks have smaller balance sheets but larger market capitalizations in the second-best allocation.A key policy implication in this paper is that regulatory tools should be coordinated to avoid undermining the effectiveness of recently introduced macroprudential capital buffer frameworks. The analysis implies that banks should reduce the size of their balance sheets by reducing safe asset holdings and should hold more equity. In other words, banks should have smaller balance sheets and focus on funding riskier assets with more stable funding. A tighter SLR requirement would work in support of this implication. Therefore, there is a complementarity, during normal times, between tightening the SLR and requiring banks to build up larger capital buffers.The analysis strengthens the rationale for the SLR, from acting as a backstop against potential hidden buildup of leverage driven by risky lending to preventing the very visible increase in leverage driven by accumulation of safe assets. The reason is that banks’ participation in low-risk activities, paradoxically, reduces financial stability. Introducing a binding SLR-style requirement in the competitive equilibrium of the model strengthens banks’ deposit franchise value and increases banks’ loan supply rather than crowding it out. A policy experiment shows that a combination of SLR and capital buffer requirements delivers welfare gains that are higher compared to the cases where only one of these requirements is imposed. Banks’ balance sheets then look similar as in the second-best allocation during normal times. While capital buffer requirements induce banks to hold more equity, SLR-type requirements make sure that this does not excessively hurt lending.In addition, the analysis suggests that liquidity regulations such as the liquidity coverage ratio (LCR) may not be necessary as banks already over-accumulate safe assets in the model. Banks’ actions display a “paradox of thrift” wherein each bank’s accumulation of safe assets ends up making other banks’ liabilities less stable. In the model, bank funding market participants are wary of the potential for bank moral hazard. Specifically, deposit “run-off rates” adjust endogenously ex ante to mitigate banks’ ex-post incentives to engage in moral hazard. Banks with more equity capital are able to roll over more of their deposit funding each period (Holmstrom and Tirole, 1997, Gertler and Kiyotaki, 2010), consistent with empirical evidence that deteriorations in banks’ funding access are driven by fundamentals (Correia et al., 2024). Excessive safe asset holdings of banks create upward pressure on the deposit funding costs of banks and undermine their ability to maintain high levels of costly equity. This has implications not only for the liquidity of banks themselves but also for banks’ ability to provide loans and liquidity to the economy during times of financial stress. Any positive direct welfare effect of higher safe asset holdings of banks on their supply of liquidity during normal times is more than offset by the general-equilibrium effect of stronger deleveraging during times of financial stress. In the model, welfare is higher over financial cycles when banks hold fewer safe financial assets, and more equity, during normal times.9An extension of the model, in Appendix A, introduces nominal wage rigidity to study the coordination of monetary policy and bank regulation during financial crises. Monetary policies that narrowly focus on closing the labor gap are not constrained-efficient. The reason is that expansionary monetary policy decreases, by assumption, the spread between safe assets and deposits (liquidity premium of deposits) in the model.10 This channel gives rise to an unintended side effect of monetary policy that matters especially during financial crises. While expansive monetary policy operations can avoid inefficiently low employment in the model, they may not actually succeed in stabilizing economic output during times when banks have low equity. Specifically, a more expansive monetary policy reduces banks’ lending by reducing profitability of banks at a time when they are already capital constrained. Constrained-efficient monetary policy is therefore less expansionary, relative to what would be required to close the labor gap, during financial crises. For this reason, there is a complementarity during financial crises between a less expansive monetary policy stance and releasing banks’ regulatory capital buffers.The importance of banks’ deposit spreads on credit supply has also been stressed in Drechsler et al. (2017), Abadi et al. (2023), Eggertsson et al. (2024), and Wang (2025). Deposit spreads are driven by the monetary policy stance in those papers, while in this paper spreads are also affected by bank regulation. My paper complements this literature by showing that a bank regulator that is concerned about financial stability would like to do two things simultaneously during normal times: (i) to induce banks to hold fewer safe assets to reduce deposit supply, and (ii) to require banks to hold more equity capital. The rationale is that higher deposit spreads compensate bank shareholders for retaining more earnings. Financial stability is increased through higher deposit spreads during normal times not by granting rents to banks but by making it feasible to require banks to hold more capital.Begenau (2020) finds that a higher capital requirement reduces the funding cost of banks by reducing deposit supply if the elasticity of deposit demand is sufficiently low. Banks’ holdings of safe assets are exogenous in her model and the optimal capital requirement implies a larger banking sector. In contrast, in this paper the decrease in banks’ funding costs in the constrained-efficient allocation is driven by a smaller banking sector, achieved by a decrease in banks’ safe asset holdings. The rationale for increasing banks’ equity capital in this paper is not to decrease funding costs further (deposit demand is too elastic for that in this paper) but to make banks more resilient. Specifically, banks pay lower deposit rates not because of alternative funding sources (equity) but because they have fewer safe assets to fund. The channel in Begenau (2020) operates within the liability side of banks’ balance sheets, but the channel in this paper operates from the asset to the liability side.Diamond and Rajan (2001) emphasize that demandable deposits are an important disciplining device in the hands of bank creditors. As in this paper, creditors are atomistic and not able to commit among themselves to renegotiating the face value of bank deposits ex post. They simply demand their deposits back (via a “bank run” as in Diamond and Dybvig, 1983), or refuse to roll over in the case of banks’ wholesale or interbank funding sources, if they are concerned about bank moral hazard. In this paper deposits, in addition, play a role in recapitalizing banks after they experience loan losses. A decrease in deposit rates when banks are forced to reduce the size of their balance sheets allows banks to rebuild equity faster. A policy implication is that banks should rely less on demandable deposits, and more on equity, during normal times such that they are forced to reduce deposit supply less during financial crises.Gatev and Strahan (2006) document empirical support for banks benefiting from procyclical funding costs, i.e., from a countercyclical liquidity premium. They argue that higher liquidity premiums during episodes of financial stress enable banks to provide a more stable supply of loans. In contrast, this paper argues that higher liquidity premiums during normal times would enable banks to hold more equity capital which would make their loan supply more resilient during episodes of financial stress.Diamond et al. (2024) find that when banks cannot freely adjust their holdings of highly pledgeable risk-free assets (in aggregate), for example, due to quantitative easing, regulations such as the SLR can hurt lending. In contrast, this paper finds that SLR-type policies increase lending when banks can adjust the amount of safe assets they hold.Organizational accessGet full-text access by signing in with your organisationAccess through your organizationOther access optionsPurchase PDFNeed help with access?Section snippetsModelThis section presents the model economy in which banks lend to firms and provide liquidity services in the form of (uninsured) deposits to households.11Competitive equilibriumDefinition 1A competitive equilibrium is characterized by (i) bank lending returns {Rt+1}, prices for bank deposits {qt+1} and bonds {qt+1b}, household bond transaction costs {gt+1}, wages {wt+1} and bank share prices {pt}; (ii) long-term investor choices for bonds and bank stock holdings {Bt+1i,ςt+1}; (iii) household choices for bonds and bank deposit holdings {Bt+1h,χt+1h} and (iv) bank choices for dividends, deposits, bonds and loans {Dt,χt+1,Bt+1,Kt+1} such that given initial bank equity a0 andOptimal macroprudential policiesThe analysis in this paper has implications for how prudential policy should treat safe assets. The reason is that the pecuniary externality highlighted in Section 3.1 is driven by banks’ holdings of bonds—banks that hold more bonds also issue more deposits and this in turn increases the interest rate 1q they must offer on deposits. Recall that bonds yield 1β>1q, but bank shareholders require a return on equity of at least 1γ>1β. Banks’ ability to provide liquidity services in the form of deposits backed by holdings of safe (risk-free and highly pledgeable) assets is key for this result. From the viewpoint of a macroprudential bank regulator, higher effective risk weights on safe assets, or tighter leverage ratios, and additional capital buffers are complements during normal times. source_records.title: Tax loss carryforwards and firms’ risk
source_records.abstract: Tax loss carryforwards (TLCF) — accumulated losses that reduce taxable income — are an important and risky corporate asset. We show theoretically how TLCF affect equity risk: If TLCF are low and used with certainty, equity risk decreases in TLCF because TLCF represent a safe cash flow; if TLCF are high, equity risk increases in TLCF because TLCF increase after-tax cash flows in good times but may expire unused or be deferred in bad times. In a calibrated model the latter effect dominates and risk increases in TLCF on average. Empirically, TLCF positively forecast firms’ volatility, beta, and return.

•
Firms with high tend to have higher and more volatile equity returns and higher market betas.

These results are consistent with a quantitatively calibrated dynamic model of firm behavior.

In a calibrated model the latter effect dominates and risk increases in TLCF on average. Empirically, TLCF positively forecast firms’ volatility, beta, and return.

IntroductionHow do taxes affect a firm’s risk and cost of capital? The notion that taxes facilitate risk sharing between investors and the government has a long history in economics. Domar and Musgrave (1944) recognized that taxation implies that individual investors share both risk and return with the government. They also, however, point out that the degree of risk sharing depends on the extent to which the government shares symmetrically in both gains and losses.Majd and Myers (1985) and Green and Talmor (1985) examine asymmetric risk sharing in the specific context of tax loss carryforwards (TLCF). TLCF arise because tax codes do not generally allow firms to realize negative taxes, i.e., net operating losses (NOLs) do not automatically generate payments from the government to the firm. Subsequent positive taxable income can be reduced by applying some or all of the TLCF as an offset.1 Both studies argue that TLCF reduce a firm’s risk by reducing its tax liability, creating a safer after-tax cash flow. Specifically, they recognize that a taxable corporation with a TLCF is equivalent to the firm being short a call option held by the government. The call option arises because the government does not collect taxes on taxable income below the level of the TLCF. This is equivalent to the government having the option to collect taxes on all income if it is willing to pay the firm the taxes on the TLCF. Hence, collecting taxes is exercising an option with a strike price of the taxes on the TLCF. Since a firm that is short a call option is safer than a firm without the short position, TLCF reduce firm risk.In this paper we show that this line of thinking is incomplete: Additional TLCF decrease risk if TLCF are likely to be used with certainty in the near term, but additional TLCF increase risk if TLCF are sufficiently likely to be unused in the near term or if they can expire.2 Our contribution is to show that, in theory, it is possible for the relationship between TLCF and risk to be decreasing, increasing, or non-monotonic, depending on a firm’s situation. Furthermore, we find that risk is increasing in TLCF for the typical firm in a calibrated model, and that it is increasing in TLCF for the typical firm in the data. This reflects the fact that as TLCF increases, the strike price of the government’s option increases, thereby reducing the option’s value. As the option value falls, the degree of risk sharing falls, and hence the risk of the firm increases. The non-monotonicity comes from the identification of conditions under which the option will likely not be exercised. In other words, because TLCF is likely to increase after-tax cash flows in good times, but are likely to be unused or even expire in bad times, TLCF are a risky asset.We begin by theoretically deriving our basic results in a simple two period setting. Our task of deriving a general understanding of how TLCF, risk, and return are related is made difficult by the fact that a firm’s TLCF results from complex, path dependent tax minimization decisions. For instance, Cooper and Franks (1983) show how operating decisions, asset allocations, lease or buy decisions and NOLs interact to determine value. Moreover, in any one year, non-operating deductions such as depreciation and interest payments, both of which are the result of endogenous decisions, affect a firm’s NOLs. To show that the insights of our simple model carry over to more complex settings, we then solve and calibrate a dynamic corporate finance model in which firms make investment and capital structure decisions while facing a realistic tax code.Our theoretical models provide a number of empirical implications. First, for firms that are highly likely to use at least some of their TLCF, there should be a U-shaped association between TLCF and risk, shown by the solid black line in Fig. 1. Risk falls as TLCF grows, as long as TLCF is low enough that it will be used in all states of the world. This is because TLCF increases the firm’s after-tax cash flows in times of high and low cash flows, making its after-tax cash flow safer. Once TLCF becomes sufficiently large so that there is a risk of it being unused or deferred, the TLCF–risk relationship switches from negative to positive, with risk rising as TLCF grows. This is because additional TLCF will be used and will increase after-tax cash flow only in times of high cash flows, but will be unused or deferred and will leave the after-tax cash flow unchanged in times of low cash flows.Second, even though the relationship between TLCF and risk is U-shaped when some TLCF are sure to be used, the relationship may be J-shaped – mostly increasing – or even strictly increasing in TLCF if the firm has additional non-TLCF tax shields, shown by the dashed blue and dotted red lines in Fig. 1. This is because when firms have other tax shields, even the first dollar of TLCF has a risk of being unused in bad states of the world. Because TLCF amplify the firm’s exposure to market risk rather than introducing an independent source of risk, firms with higher TLCF should have higher market betas and higher expected returns as compensation.Download: Download high-res image (171KB)Download: Download full-size imageFig. 1. Expected return as a function of TLCF.This figure plots the market beta on the -axis, against the amount of tax loss carryforwards (TLCF) on the -axis from the simple model. We compare (a) a firm with no other tax shields (solid black line), to (b) a firm with existing non-TLCF tax shields (dashed blue line), and (c) a firm with existing non-TLCF tax shields and higher cash flow volatility (dotted red line). To draw these figures, we assume the following parameter values. source_records.abstract: We examine the dramatic collapse of the Terra blockchain in May 2022. Using granular blockchain data, we show that the run resulted from the interaction of three economic forces: subsidized money creation, real-time observability of transactions, and investor concentration. The early success of Terra’s algorithmic stablecoin, UST, was fueled by highly subsidized deposit rates, which attracted many investors but failed to engage them meaningfully with other services. Blockchain transparency allowed investors to observe Terra’s worsening fundamentals and monitor each other’s exits in real time. Larger and sophisticated investors reacted faster to adverse signals and served as catalysts for the run. These findings challenge the idea that blockchain transparency levels the playing field and highlight how greater observability and concentration can amplify financial fragility. Our results contribute to the understanding of the limits of private money creation and the dynamics of runs in fully digital financial systems.

Larger and sophisticated investors reacted faster to adverse signals and served as catalysts for the run. These findings challenge the idea that blockchain transparency levels the playing field and highlight how greater observability and concentration can amplify financial fragility. Our results contribute to the understanding of the limits of private money creation and the dynamics of runs in fully digital financial systems.
