From bank runs in the Free Banking era of 19th-century United States to runs on money market funds during the 2008 Financial Crisis, privately issued money-like instruments have been prone to runs when investor confidence falters, see for example Gorton and Zhang (2021). More recently, cryptocurrency platforms have begun issuing a new generation of private money in the form of stablecoins — cryptocurrencies pegged to a reference fiat currency — which raises familiar questions in a new technological environment: What determines their stability? Which design choices mitigate or exacerbate fragility? How do runs begin and unfold in this context? This paper uses the 2022 collapse of Terra as a natural laboratory to study these fundamental questions. Blockchain data offers detailed information on both network structure and participant behavior allowing us to examine the dynamics of the run at the individual investor level. We show that the economics of the Terra network shared several important parallels with traditional financial systems and collateralized stablecoins. Therefore, our results have implications not only for cryptocurrency runs but also for our understanding of runs more broadly.A defining feature of the Terra ecosystem was its algorithmic stablecoin, UST. UST aimed to function as a money-like asset and to facilitate transactions on the Terra blockchain. Rather than rely on external collateral or government backing, UST maintained its peg through an algorithmic arbitrage mechanism backed solely by Terra’s native cryptocurrency, LUNA. Therefore, the system’s solvency depended entirely on the market capitalization of LUNA. This self-referential design proved vulnerable to runs. Three economic forces contributed to the run and shaped its dynamics: subsidized deposit and lending rates on UST, real-time observability of transactions, and the presence of large and concentrated investors.We document our findings in three main steps. First, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the economic forces driving the Terra network prior to the run. Abstracting from operational details, Terra can be conceptualized as a bank. In this analogy, LUNA represents an equity claim on the bank’s franchise, while UST is akin to private money issued by the bank. We show that Terra’s initial success was fueled by highly subsidized deposit and lending rates on UST, which attracted users to the platform and led to large issuance of UST and a run-up in the price of LUNA. But this dynamic ultimately proved unsustainable because the subsidies failed to engage users with other services on the platform.Second, we provide micro-evidence on the connection between informational transparency and coordination. We show that blockchain transparency enabled investors to track deteriorating fundamentals and to monitor each other’s actions in real time. The presence of large investors, whose actions were observable and could affect prices, reduced the need for coordination typical for canonical models of runs. Once a few large UST holders began unwinding their positions, their sales triggered a cascade where other traders quickly followed suit.Finally, by leveraging wallet-level data, we examine how different investors behaved and reacted to information during the run. The run on Terra displayed clear cross-sectional differences: larger and more sophisticated investors ran faster and reacted more quickly to adverse signals, acting as catalysts for the run and underscoring their superior ability to process and act on information. As a result, smaller investors suffered larger losses. Our results demonstrate that transparency alone is insufficient to level the playing field in financial markets, and in fact, it may exacerbate heterogeneous outcomes across investors.To understand the context of the collapse, we first describe the design of the Terra network and its underlying economics. Terra was developed by TerraForm Labs (TFL), founded in 2018 by Do Kwon and Daniel Shin. Like other smart contract platforms such as Ethereum, Terra aimed to host a range of applications and services on the blockchain to attract users and generate fees for cryptocurrency holders. Starting in March 2020, Terra introduced a suite of algorithmic stablecoins pegged to different fiat currencies, the most prominent being UST pegged to the US dollar.Unlike collateralized stablecoins such as Tether and USDC, which are backed by off-chain assets, UST was backed by Terra’s native cryptocurrency, LUNA, via a pegging mechanism designed to incentivize traders to engage in arbitrage whenever the stablecoin deviated from the peg. Specifically, one UST could always be exchanged for $1 worth of LUNA, and vice versa. If UST traded below $1, arbitrageurs could buy it at a discount and redeem it for $1 worth of LUNA, shrinking UST’s supply. Conversely, if UST traded above $1, they could issue new UST in exchange for LUNA, expanding UST supply until peg was restored. Like other smart contract platforms such as Ethereum, Terra aimed to host a range of applications and services on the blockchain to attract users and generate fees for cryptocurrency holders. Specifically, one UST could always be exchanged for $1 worth of LUNA, and vice versa. If UST traded below $1, arbitrageurs could buy it at a discount and redeem it for $1 worth of LUNA, shrinking UST’s supply. Conversely, if UST traded above $1, they could issue new UST in exchange for LUNA, expanding UST supply until peg was restored. proposed.title: Anatomy of a run: The Terra Luna crash
proposed.abstract: We examine the dramatic collapse of the Terra blockchain in May 2022. Using granular blockchain data, we show that the run resulted from the interaction of three economic forces: subsidized money creation, real-time observability of transactions, and investor concentration. The early success of Terra’s algorithmic stablecoin, UST, was fueled by highly subsidized deposit rates, which attracted many investors but failed to engage them meaningfully with other services. Blockchain transparency allowed investors to observe Terra’s worsening fundamentals and monitor each other’s exits in real time. Larger and sophisticated investors reacted faster to adverse signals and served as catalysts for the run. These findings challenge the idea that blockchain transparency levels the playing field and highlight how greater observability and concentration can amplify financial fragility. Our results contribute to the understanding of the limits of private money creation and the dynamics of runs in fully digital financial systems.

source_records.title: From pitch to progress: The interplay of team reputation and governance in crowdfunded innovation
source_records.abstract: This study examines how team reputation affects both the funding success and the subsequent innovation progress in early-stage crowdfunded projects, with a comparative focus on blockchain-based and conventional crowdfunding platforms. Using development progress data for blockchain projects from the open-source platform GitHub, we find that while teams with stronger reputations raise more funds, their subsequent innovation productivity, measured by development activity, tends to lag. Further analysis reveals an association between higher team reputation and increased turnover of tokens post-fundraising, suggesting team members may strategically exercise exit options soon after securing financing. In contrast, analysis of Kickstarter campaigns reveals a more consistent alignment between team reputation, funding success, and project delivery. Specifically, highly reputable teams are more likely to meet not only their fundraising goal but also delivery commitments. We attribute this contrast to differences in platform governance; Kickstarter’s structured oversight appears to mitigate early team disengagement and enhance project delivery compared to the blockchain context. These findings underscore the importance of effective governance mechanisms in crowdfunding platforms to ensure that team reputation signals translate into sustained innovation outcomes.

Team reputation positively predicts fundraising success in both ICO and Kickstarter.
•
Higher team reputation is negatively associated with post-ICO development progress.
•
Reputable ICO teams exhibit higher early token liquidation rates post-fundraising.
•
Platform governance moderates whether reputation translates into follow-through.

This study examines how team reputation affects both the funding success and the subsequent innovation progress in early-stage crowdfunded projects, with a comparative focus on blockchain-based and conventional crowdfunding platforms. Using development progress data for blockchain projects from the open-source platform GitHub, we find that while teams with stronger reputations raise more funds, their subsequent innovation productivity, measured by development activity, tends to lag. Further analysis reveals an association between higher team reputation and increased turnover of tokens post-fundraising, suggesting team members may strategically exercise exit options soon after securing financing. In contrast, analysis of Kickstarter campaigns reveals a more consistent alignment between team reputation, funding success, and project delivery. Specifically, highly reputable teams are more likely to meet not only their fundraising goal but also delivery commitments. We attribute this contrast to differences in platform governance; Kickstarter’s structured oversight appears to mitigate early team disengagement and enhance project delivery compared to the blockchain context. These findings underscore the importance of effective governance mechanisms in crowdfunding platforms to ensure that team reputation signals translate into sustained innovation outcomes.

These findings underscore the importance of effective governance mechanisms in crowdfunding platforms to ensure that team reputation signals translate into sustained innovation outcomes.JEL classificationD82; G24; G32; G34; L26KeywordsTeam reputation; Governance mechanism; Innovation productivity; Crowdfunding; Blockchain; Token financingPrevious article in this issueNext article in this issueIntroductionInnovation within high-tech ventures has long been regarded as a prominent catalyst for economic growth. However, radical innovation inherently involves a high risk of failure due to pervasive uncertainties surrounding nascent technologies and business models (Holmstrom, 1989). In particular, CB Insights shows that the odds of becoming a unicorn are merely 1%.1 Furthermore, unlike publicly traded firms, small ventures typically lack mandatory performance disclosure requirements, making the evaluation of entrepreneurial effort exceptionally challenging. The lack of transparency gives rise to moral hazard in that entrepreneurs may not exert the desired level of effort. Understanding how to simultaneously foster innovation productivity and mitigate opportunistic behavior among entrepreneurs in these ventures is crucial.Reputation, as an informal enforcement mechanism for incomplete contracts, exerts an important disciplinary influence by mitigating opportunistic behaviors among various market participants, such as managers, product sellers, financial institutions, independent directors, andanalysts (Cabral, 2005, MacLeod, 2007, Karpoff et al., 2008b).2 In particular, entrepreneurial reputation is documented to be positively associated with funding results in crowdfunding (Li and Martin, 2019). However, limited research exists on the relationship between an entrepreneurial team’s reputation and its subsequent innovation productivity. This could be due to the difficulty of observing the progress of tech ventures in development.This paper addresses this gap by employing granular data tracking the development trajectory of blockchain projects from the leading open-source platform, GitHub. Using GitHub data offers two primary advantages in this context. First, as a public repository, GitHub potentially offers transparency into development progress, unlike less observable internal efforts.3 Second, compared to metrics like successful exits or patent registrations used in prior studies, which often involve significant time lags, GitHub activity provides development data at a daily granularity.Furthermore, blockchain project crowdfunding offers an ideal setting to examine reputation’s significance, given the pronounced moral hazard stemming from minimal regulatory oversight and limited legal recourse upon project failure. Cabral (2005) defines reputation as the perception held by others regarding a specific agent, noting that it functions as a deterrent against moral hazard. Within the crowdfunding context, an entrepreneur’s reputation can instil trust in potential investors, assuring the likelihood of successful project execution. This trust, in turn, influences the investors’ willingness to provide financial support for the project (Ahlers et al., 2015). However, many blockchain projects exhibit substantial moral hazard vulnerabilities, primarily stemming from the limited legal recourse or economic penalties associated with project failure (Gan et al., 2021). This allows us to test whether the reputation is sufficient to discipline and motivate entrepreneurs in an unregulated environment.Our initial ICO sample consists of 8132 ended and ongoing blockchain fundraising events, including initial coin offerings (ICOs), security token offerings (STOs), and initial exchanger offerings (IEOs), from 2016 to 2022. Building on Paul P. Momtaz’s Token Offering Research Database (TORD), we first supplement the sample with ICOmarks deals and scrape deal characteristics and team member information from the website. We also download available whitepapers to complement additional information on deal characteristics. Many blockchain projects post their code on GitHub, the largest open-source software platform. We obtain daily development progress data for blockchain projects from GHTorrent, which mirrors GitHub developer activity. Applying filtering criteria, excluding ongoing or planned deals and those lacking necessary characteristics, yields a final sample of 4014 completed ICOs from 2016–2020 that possess available team information and basic deal characteristics. To measure entrepreneurial team reputation within the blockchain community network, we adapt the methodologies of Atanasov et al. (2012), Hochberg et al. (2007), and Larcker et al. (2013) to calculate the centrality measure Degree by constructing an undirected graph with each team as a vertex and with each association of a team member through ICO transactions as an edge.We find a positive correlation between team reputation and fundraising success; specifically, a one-standard-deviation increase in team reputation corresponds to a 3.4 percentage point increase in the probability of fundraising success. In opaque information environments, team reputation can serve as a crucial signal of project quality and certification (Shane and Cable, 2002). Furthermore, small crowdfunding investors, often characterized by limited attention, may gravitate towards more salient, attention-grabbing investment opportunities (Barber et al., 2008). Consequently, reputable entrepreneurial teams likely attract greater investor attention, leading to increased investment and higher fundraising success.However, successful fundraising by reputable entrepreneurial teams does not necessarily translate into greater post-fundraising development progress. Instead, our findings indicate a negative association between team reputation and GitHub development activity across various post-fundraising windows. This suggests that team reputation alone is insufficient to fully mitigate moral hazard in this unregulated market. The economic magnitude of this effect is non-trivial: one-standard-deviation increase in team reputation corresponds to an approximate 12.2% decrease in the development progress during the first three months post-ICO.Further supporting this interpretation, analysis of on-chain transaction data (for a subsample of Ethereum ERC-20 ICOs) reveals that more reputable teams are indeed more likely to liquidate token holdings shortly after fundraising, exercising early exit options. This suggests the previously observed slower development progress may stem from governance weaknesses inherent in blockchain projects; specifically, the readily available option for immediate exit. Consequently, these findings underscore the importance of implementing governance mechanisms designed to prevent teams from prematurely liquidating their stakes before achieving key project milestones.4To contrast with the ICO findings, we analyze crowdfunding on Kickstarter, a platform characterized by stronger governance structures and accountability mechanisms. We select 747 successful projects from the “Apps” subcategory (under “Technology”) for comparability. Data collected includes project basics (e.g., launch/deadline dates, location, pledged amount, backers), creator/collaborator details for centrality measures, and project updates for measuring progress (using post-campaign updates). Unlike the ICO context, on Kickstarter, higher team reputation predicts not only greater fundraising success (a one-standard-deviation increase in degree is associated with a 9.6% increase in pledged amount) but also more subsequent progress (associated with a 4.5% increase in post-fundraising updates). This divergence highlights the crucial role of platform governance in mitigating moral hazard and aligning reputation with project execution commitments.To formalize the mechanism behind these empirical patterns, we develop a stylized model in Appendix A.5 Reputation plays a dual role: it boosts token demand and fundraising success, but also raises the token price, making early liquidation more profitable. A governance parameter controls how much of the founder’s stake can be sold early. When governance is weak, high-reputation founders face a strong temptation to cash out rather than invest in development, and the optimal response is all-or-nothing—either retain all tokens and work, or sell the maximum permissible stake and reduce effort. A reputation threshold separates the two regimes: below it, the future payoff from successful development outweighs the liquidation gain, so founders stay and work; above it, the token price makes cashing out irresistible. Stronger governance raises this threshold by limiting how much can be sold early, shrinking the liquidation payoff and restoring the incentive to develop.The model yields three predictions. First, higher reputation raises token demand and fundraising, consistent with the positive reputation–fundraising relationship in both ICOs and Kickstarter. Second, under weak governance the threshold is low, so a disproportionate share of high-reputation founders falls into the liquidation regime—consistent with the negative association between team degree and post-ICO GitHub activity and with higher early exit rates among well-connected ICOs. Within each regime, effort increases with reputation; the aggregate negative relationship arises from a composition effect. Third, stronger governance raises the threshold, keeping more founders in the effort regime where reputation and development are positively related—consistent with the Kickstarter evidence.Our paper contributes to the fast-growing literature on blockchain technology, a field often associated with the potential to enhance trust and transparency, reduce transaction costs, and foster more efficient and inclusive economies.6 Recent theoretical work demonstrates that tokens can mitigate frictions between platforms and users, often arising from monopoly pricing power or data exploitation (Goldstein et al., 2019, Sockin and Xiong, 2023). Furthermore, tokens provide an effective mechanism for fundraising and for incentivizing platform participants (Cong et al., 2022, Gryglewicz et al., 2021, Lee and Parlour, 2022).7 Beyond these structural advantages, a rapidly expanding behavioral literature highlights how sentiment and online attention shape ICO outcomes and cryptocurrency valuations. Social-media engagement and tone — across platforms such as Twitter, Telegram, and Medium — are robust predictors of fundraising success (Huang et al., 2024, Safi Eljil et al., 2025, Gartner et al., 2025, Sapkota and Grobys, 2023).8 Parallel work on cryptocurrency markets and digital-asset pricing situates these dynamics within a broader framework of investor behavior. Studies document that investor attention and sentiment drive return co-movements (Aslanidis et al., 2024), price jumps (Aysan et al., 2024), and cross-sectional pricing patterns (Borri and Shakhnov, 2022, Fieberg et al., 2025, Lan and Frömmel, 2025).9 Finally, by tracking post-fundraising technological development, our study extends this literature to the innovation phase of blockchain ventures. Development milestones provide a direct measure of project effort and credibility (Lyandres et al., 2022), while governance quality and team reputation act as informal enforcement mechanisms. In this way, our paper bridges the literatures on blockchain governance, behavioral finance, and digital-asset pricing, clarifying both the promises and the vulnerabilities of token-based financing ecosystems.Furthermore, our paper is related to crowdfunding literature. Crowdfunding enables creators to raise capital directly from distributed backers, with Kickstarter being the largest such platform. In this context, particularly given the typical absence of formal due diligence, crowdfunding backers often rely on observable signals (e.g., prior founding success, educational background, and social network size) to assess creator competence and credibility (Hsu, 2007, Mollick, 2014, Colombo et al., 2015, Courtney et al., 2017, Agrawal et al., 2010, Shane and Cable, 2002, Sørensen and Fassiotto, 2011, Stam and Elfring, 2008). Team reputation established through prior campaigns, executive recruitment capabilities, or a strong social media presence attracts early contributions and increases fundraising success. Furthermore, team reputation has implications beyond the fundraising phase, influencing subsequent delivery outcomes and helping to maintain trust within the crowdfunding ecosystem. Approximately 75% of successful Kickstarter projects experience delays (Mollick, 2014), yet teams with stronger reputations are often granted more leniency by backers (Stanko and Henard, 2017).Additionally, our paper contributes to understanding the impact of team reputation. Recognizing that tokens are frequently treated as commodities, marketing scholars have long studied how endorsements by influential figures, such as celebrities, heighten product or service credibility and stimulate consumers’ purchase intentions (Erdogan, 1999, Pringle and Binet, 2005). However, our findings show that team reputation alone does not ensure successful project development, particularly in unregulated markets where early exit is possible. Without complementary governance mechanisms to enforce accountability, team reputation cannot fully serve its disciplinary function. This underscores the necessity of governance structures that reinforce reputational signals with accountability, thereby ensuring that early trust translates into sustained project commitment.The paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 focuses on sample and variable construction. Section 3 shows the impact of team reputation on fundraising success and post-fundraising development progress in ICO projects. Section 4 discusses the relationship between team reputation, fundraising success, and post-campaign development on Kickstarter. Section 5 conducts several additional analyses and robustness checks. What explains the apparent failure of reputation to discipline entrepreneurs and ensure development follow-through after successful fundraising? In this section, we explore the underlying mechanism that drives the aforementioned phenomena and report results from robustness checks.ConclusionBlockchain proponents argue that the technology democratizes investing through ICOs by enabling individual investors to participate in the early stages of startups. fields.title: From pitch to progress: The interplay of team reputation and governance in crowdfunded innovation
fields.authors: Xin Deng a, Yen Teik Lee b, Qi Sun c, Yu Yan d
fields.abstract: This study examines how team reputation affects both the funding success and the subsequent innovation progress in early-stage crowdfunded projects, with a comparative focus on blockchain-based and conventional crowdfunding platforms. Using development progress data for blockchain projects from the open-source platform GitHub, we find that while teams with stronger reputations raise more funds, their subsequent innovation productivity, measured by development activity, tends to lag. Further analysis reveals an association between higher team reputation and increased turnover of tokens post-fundraising, suggesting team members may strategically exercise exit options soon after securing financing. In contrast, analysis of Kickstarter campaigns reveals a more consistent alignment between team reputation, funding success, and project delivery. Specifically, highly reputable teams are more likely to meet not only their fundraising goal but also delivery commitments. We attribute this contrast to differences in platform governance; Kickstarter’s structured oversight appears to mitigate early team disengagement and enhance project delivery compared to the blockchain context. These findings underscore the importance of effective governance mechanisms in crowdfunding platforms to ensure that team reputation signals translate into sustained innovation outcomes.

This study examines how team reputation affects both the funding success and the subsequent innovation progress in early-stage crowdfunded projects, with a comparative focus on blockchain-based and conventional crowdfunding platforms. Using development progress data for blockchain projects from the open-source platform GitHub, we find that while teams with stronger reputations raise more funds, their subsequent innovation productivity, measured by development activity, tends to lag. Further analysis reveals an association between higher team reputation and increased turnover of tokens post-fundraising, suggesting team members may strategically exercise exit options soon after securing financing. In contrast, analysis of Kickstarter campaigns reveals a more consistent alignment between team reputation, funding success, and project delivery. Specifically, highly reputable teams are more likely to meet not only their fundraising goal but also delivery commitments. We attribute this contrast to differences in platform governance; Kickstarter’s structured oversight appears to mitigate early team disengagement and enhance project delivery compared to the blockchain context. These findings underscore the importance of effective governance mechanisms in crowdfunding platforms to ensure that team reputation signals translate into sustained innovation outcomes.

These findings underscore the importance of effective governance mechanisms in crowdfunding platforms to ensure that team reputation signals translate into sustained innovation outcomes.JEL classificationD82; G24; G32; G34; L26KeywordsTeam reputation; Governance mechanism; Innovation productivity; Crowdfunding; Blockchain; Token financingPrevious article in this issueNext article in this issueIntroductionInnovation within high-tech ventures has long been regarded as a prominent catalyst for economic growth. However, radical innovation inherently involves a high risk of failure due to pervasive uncertainties surrounding nascent technologies and business models (Holmstrom, 1989). In particular, CB Insights shows that the odds of becoming a unicorn are merely 1%.1 Furthermore, unlike publicly traded firms, small ventures typically lack mandatory performance disclosure requirements, making the evaluation of entrepreneurial effort exceptionally challenging. The lack of transparency gives rise to moral hazard in that entrepreneurs may not exert the desired level of effort. Understanding how to simultaneously foster innovation productivity and mitigate opportunistic behavior among entrepreneurs in these ventures is crucial.Reputation, as an informal enforcement mechanism for incomplete contracts, exerts an important disciplinary influence by mitigating opportunistic behaviors among various market participants, such as managers, product sellers, financial institutions, independent directors, andanalysts (Cabral, 2005, MacLeod, 2007, Karpoff et al., 2008b).2 In particular, entrepreneurial reputation is documented to be positively associated with funding results in crowdfunding (Li and Martin, 2019). However, limited research exists on the relationship between an entrepreneurial team’s reputation and its subsequent innovation productivity. This could be due to the difficulty of observing the progress of tech ventures in development.This paper addresses this gap by employing granular data tracking the development trajectory of blockchain projects from the leading open-source platform, GitHub. Using GitHub data offers two primary advantages in this context. First, as a public repository, GitHub potentially offers transparency into development progress, unlike less observable internal efforts.3 Second, compared to metrics like successful exits or patent registrations used in prior studies, which often involve significant time lags, GitHub activity provides development data at a daily granularity.Furthermore, blockchain project crowdfunding offers an ideal setting to examine reputation’s significance, given the pronounced moral hazard stemming from minimal regulatory oversight and limited legal recourse upon project failure. Cabral (2005) defines reputation as the perception held by others regarding a specific agent, noting that it functions as a deterrent against moral hazard. Within the crowdfunding context, an entrepreneur’s reputation can instil trust in potential investors, assuring the likelihood of successful project execution. This trust, in turn, influences the investors’ willingness to provide financial support for the project (Ahlers et al., 2015). However, many blockchain projects exhibit substantial moral hazard vulnerabilities, primarily stemming from the limited legal recourse or economic penalties associated with project failure (Gan et al., 2021). This allows us to test whether the reputation is sufficient to discipline and motivate entrepreneurs in an unregulated environment.Our initial ICO sample consists of 8132 ended and ongoing blockchain fundraising events, including initial coin offerings (ICOs), security token offerings (STOs), and initial exchanger offerings (IEOs), from 2016 to 2022. Building on Paul P. Momtaz’s Token Offering Research Database (TORD), we first supplement the sample with ICOmarks deals and scrape deal characteristics and team member information from the website. We also download available whitepapers to complement additional information on deal characteristics. Many blockchain projects post their code on GitHub, the largest open-source software platform. We obtain daily development progress data for blockchain projects from GHTorrent, which mirrors GitHub developer activity. Applying filtering criteria, excluding ongoing or planned deals and those lacking necessary characteristics, yields a final sample of 4014 completed ICOs from 2016–2020 that possess available team information and basic deal characteristics. To measure entrepreneurial team reputation within the blockchain community network, we adapt the methodologies of Atanasov et al. (2012), Hochberg et al. (2007), and Larcker et al. (2013) to calculate the centrality measure Degree by constructing an undirected graph with each team as a vertex and with each association of a team member through ICO transactions as an edge.We find a positive correlation between team reputation and fundraising success; specifically, a one-standard-deviation increase in team reputation corresponds to a 3.4 percentage point increase in the probability of fundraising success. In opaque information environments, team reputation can serve as a crucial signal of project quality and certification (Shane and Cable, 2002). Furthermore, small crowdfunding investors, often characterized by limited attention, may gravitate towards more salient, attention-grabbing investment opportunities (Barber et al., 2008). Consequently, reputable entrepreneurial teams likely attract greater investor attention, leading to increased investment and higher fundraising success.However, successful fundraising by reputable entrepreneurial teams does not necessarily translate into greater post-fundraising development progress. Instead, our findings indicate a negative association between team reputation and GitHub development activity across various post-fundraising windows. This suggests that team reputation alone is insufficient to fully mitigate moral hazard in this unregulated market. The economic magnitude of this effect is non-trivial: one-standard-deviation increase in team reputation corresponds to an approximate 12.2% decrease in the development progress during the first three months post-ICO.Further supporting this interpretation, analysis of on-chain transaction data (for a subsample of Ethereum ERC-20 ICOs) reveals that more reputable teams are indeed more likely to liquidate token holdings shortly after fundraising, exercising early exit options. This suggests the previously observed slower development progress may stem from governance weaknesses inherent in blockchain projects; specifically, the readily available option for immediate exit. Consequently, these findings underscore the importance of implementing governance mechanisms designed to prevent teams from prematurely liquidating their stakes before achieving key project milestones.4To contrast with the ICO findings, we analyze crowdfunding on Kickstarter, a platform characterized by stronger governance structures and accountability mechanisms. We select 747 successful projects from the “Apps” subcategory (under “Technology”) for comparability. Data collected includes project basics (e.g., launch/deadline dates, location, pledged amount, backers), creator/collaborator details for centrality measures, and project updates for measuring progress (using post-campaign updates). Unlike the ICO context, on Kickstarter, higher team reputation predicts not only greater fundraising success (a one-standard-deviation increase in degree is associated with a 9.6% increase in pledged amount) but also more subsequent progress (associated with a 4.5% increase in post-fundraising updates). This divergence highlights the crucial role of platform governance in mitigating moral hazard and aligning reputation with project execution commitments.To formalize the mechanism behind these empirical patterns, we develop a stylized model in Appendix A.5 Reputation plays a dual role: it boosts token demand and fundraising success, but also raises the token price, making early liquidation more profitable. A governance parameter controls how much of the founder’s stake can be sold early. When governance is weak, high-reputation founders face a strong temptation to cash out rather than invest in development, and the optimal response is all-or-nothing—either retain all tokens and work, or sell the maximum permissible stake and reduce effort. A reputation threshold separates the two regimes: below it, the future payoff from successful development outweighs the liquidation gain, so founders stay and work; above it, the token price makes cashing out irresistible. Stronger governance raises this threshold by limiting how much can be sold early, shrinking the liquidation payoff and restoring the incentive to develop.The model yields three predictions. First, higher reputation raises token demand and fundraising, consistent with the positive reputation–fundraising relationship in both ICOs and Kickstarter. Second, under weak governance the threshold is low, so a disproportionate share of high-reputation founders falls into the liquidation regime—consistent with the negative association between team degree and post-ICO GitHub activity and with higher early exit rates among well-connected ICOs. Within each regime, effort increases with reputation; the aggregate negative relationship arises from a composition effect. Third, stronger governance raises the threshold, keeping more founders in the effort regime where reputation and development are positively related—consistent with the Kickstarter evidence.Our paper contributes to the fast-growing literature on blockchain technology, a field often associated with the potential to enhance trust and transparency, reduce transaction costs, and foster more efficient and inclusive economies.6 Recent theoretical work demonstrates that tokens can mitigate frictions between platforms and users, often arising from monopoly pricing power or data exploitation (Goldstein et al., 2019, Sockin and Xiong, 2023). Furthermore, tokens provide an effective mechanism for fundraising and for incentivizing platform participants (Cong et al., 2022, Gryglewicz et al., 2021, Lee and Parlour, 2022).7 Beyond these structural advantages, a rapidly expanding behavioral literature highlights how sentiment and online attention shape ICO outcomes and cryptocurrency valuations. Social-media engagement and tone — across platforms such as Twitter, Telegram, and Medium — are robust predictors of fundraising success (Huang et al., 2024, Safi Eljil et al., 2025, Gartner et al., 2025, Sapkota and Grobys, 2023).8 Parallel work on cryptocurrency markets and digital-asset pricing situates these dynamics within a broader framework of investor behavior. Studies document that investor attention and sentiment drive return co-movements (Aslanidis et al., 2024), price jumps (Aysan et al., 2024), and cross-sectional pricing patterns (Borri and Shakhnov, 2022, Fieberg et al., 2025, Lan and Frömmel, 2025).9 Finally, by tracking post-fundraising technological development, our study extends this literature to the innovation phase of blockchain ventures. Development milestones provide a direct measure of project effort and credibility (Lyandres et al., 2022), while governance quality and team reputation act as informal enforcement mechanisms. In this way, our paper bridges the literatures on blockchain governance, behavioral finance, and digital-asset pricing, clarifying both the promises and the vulnerabilities of token-based financing ecosystems.Furthermore, our paper is related to crowdfunding literature. Crowdfunding enables creators to raise capital directly from distributed backers, with Kickstarter being the largest such platform. In this context, particularly given the typical absence of formal due diligence, crowdfunding backers often rely on observable signals (e.g., prior founding success, educational background, and social network size) to assess creator competence and credibility (Hsu, 2007, Mollick, 2014, Colombo et al., 2015, Courtney et al., 2017, Agrawal et al., 2010, Shane and Cable, 2002, Sørensen and Fassiotto, 2011, Stam and Elfring, 2008). Team reputation established through prior campaigns, executive recruitment capabilities, or a strong social media presence attracts early contributions and increases fundraising success. Furthermore, team reputation has implications beyond the fundraising phase, influencing subsequent delivery outcomes and helping to maintain trust within the crowdfunding ecosystem. Approximately 75% of successful Kickstarter projects experience delays (Mollick, 2014), yet teams with stronger reputations are often granted more leniency by backers (Stanko and Henard, 2017).Additionally, our paper contributes to understanding the impact of team reputation. Recognizing that tokens are frequently treated as commodities, marketing scholars have long studied how endorsements by influential figures, such as celebrities, heighten product or service credibility and stimulate consumers’ purchase intentions (Erdogan, 1999, Pringle and Binet, 2005). However, our findings show that team reputation alone does not ensure successful project development, particularly in unregulated markets where early exit is possible. Without complementary governance mechanisms to enforce accountability, team reputation cannot fully serve its disciplinary function. This underscores the necessity of governance structures that reinforce reputational signals with accountability, thereby ensuring that early trust translates into sustained project commitment.The paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 focuses on sample and variable construction. Section 3 shows the impact of team reputation on fundraising success and post-fundraising development progress in ICO projects. Section 4 discusses the relationship between team reputation, fundraising success, and post-campaign development on Kickstarter. Section 5 conducts several additional analyses and robustness checks. proposed.title: From pitch to progress: The interplay of team reputation and governance in crowdfunded innovation
proposed.abstract:
•
Team reputation positively predicts fundraising success in both ICO and Kickstarter.
•
Higher team reputation is negatively associated with post-ICO development progress.
•
Reputable ICO teams exhibit higher early token liquidation rates post-fundraising.
•
Platform governance moderates whether reputation translates into follow-through.
•
A stylized model formalizes reputation’s dual role under weak and strong governance.

fields.authors: Xin Deng a, Yen Teik Lee b, Qi Sun c, Yu Yan d
fields.abstract: This study examines how team reputation affects both the funding success and the subsequent innovation progress in early-stage crowdfunded projects, with a comparative focus on blockchain-based and conventional crowdfunding platforms. Using development progress data for blockchain projects from the open-source platform GitHub, we find that while teams with stronger reputations raise more funds, their subsequent innovation productivity, measured by development activity, tends to lag. Further analysis reveals an association between higher team reputation and increased turnover of tokens post-fundraising, suggesting team members may strategically exercise exit options soon after securing financing. In contrast, analysis of Kickstarter campaigns reveals a more consistent alignment between team reputation, funding success, and project delivery. Specifically, highly reputable teams are more likely to meet not only their fundraising goal but also delivery commitments. We attribute this contrast to differences in platform governance; Kickstarter’s structured oversight appears to mitigate early team disengagement and enhance project delivery compared to the blockchain context. These findings underscore the importance of effective governance mechanisms in crowdfunding platforms to ensure that team reputation signals translate into sustained innovation outcomes.

source_records.abstract: While public credit guarantees (PCGs) have been around for a long time, their use expanded significantly during the global financial crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic to support the corporate sector and facilitate economic recovery. Given the scale of these programmes and their potential fiscal implications, much of the existing literature has focused on whether PCGs improve credit allocation and financial outcomes. In contrast, this paper examines whether PCGs impact firms' R&D and innovation efforts, utilizing a rich data set from Turkey's Credit Guarantee Fund—one of the largest schemes of this kind—and employing a staggered difference-in-differences (DiD) approach preceded by a comprehensive matching procedure. We find that firms receiving guaranteed loans exhibit significantly greater improvements in both innovation inputs, such as R&D expenditure, and innovation outcomes, such as high-tech exports, compared to non-recipient firms. We also observe a substantially larger beneficial impact for firms already engaged in innovation activities and those facing financial constraints. Our findings have important implications for regulatory authorities in their design of credit support programmes.

IntroductionInvestment in research and development (R&D) and innovation is widely recognized as a central driver of long-term economic growth (Griliches, 1992; Stokey, 1995; Ulku, 2004; Chu and Cozzi, 2014; Liu, 2016). R&D enables firms to develop new products, advance technological progress, and remain competitive in dynamic global markets (Griffith et al., 2004). In emerging economies, R&D plays a particularly transformative role, enabling firms to transition from low-cost, labour-intensive activities toward higher value-added, technology-based production (Felipe et al., 2014). Strong R&D performance in these countries also helps attract high-technology FDI, thereby preparing the foundation for innovation-driven growth and capacity to benefit from external knowledge and technologies (Nelson and Rosenberg, 1993).Despite its importance, R&D investment remains constrained by substantial market and institutional frictions. R&D projects are inherently risky and subject to highly uncertain returns, which makes them particularly prone to underinvestment in the absence of public intervention (Shi, 2003; Hall and Lerner, 2010; Hou et al., 2022). Financial constraints further limit firms' capacity to innovate, with restricted access to external finance emerging as a key obstacle to R&D investment (Aghion et al., 2005a; Aghion et al., 2012). These challenges are especially severe for young and small firms, which often lack collateral, credit history, and scale - factors that significantly increase vulnerability to credit constraints (Beck et al., 2005; Beck and Demirgüç-Kunt, 2006; Beck et al., 2008; Hall and Lerner, 2010; De la Torre et al., 2010).In response, governments have deployed a broad range of policy instruments aimed explicitly at stimulating private R&D. These include direct measures such as R&D grants and subsidies that reduce the cost and risk of innovation activities, particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises, as well as indirect instruments such as R&D tax credits, preferential tax treatment, and accelerated depreciation schemes designed to promote sustained R&D investment across a wider set of firms (David et al., 2000; Bloom et al., 2002).Beyond R&D support programmes, several credit guarantee schemes have been introduced that offer partial government guarantees for loans granted by financial institutions, attempting to overcome market failures and alleviate firms' financing problems (Beck et al., 2010; Cowling, 2010; Uesugi et al., 2010; Bachas et al., 2021b; Horvath and Lang, 2021; Hong and Lucas, 2023).2,3 The success of such initiatives in advanced economies has prompted emerging economies to design similar programmes. Turkey has implemented one of the largest public credit guarantee schemes, allocating credit approaching 16.6% of annual GDP between 2017 and 2020.Although enhancing R&D investment and innovation outcomes has not been the primary motivation for public credit guarantees (PCGs), the alleviation in credit constraints provided by guaranteed loans is likely to alter firms' incentives for spending on R&D. While a growing empirical literature has examined the effects of PCGs on firm outcomes such as sales, investment and employment (e.g., Hurley et al., 2021; Doniger and Kay, 2021; Autor et al., 2022), their implications for R&D investment remain largely unexplored. Indeed, existing work on the role of public financial support in innovation activities almost exclusively utilizes data from R&D support programmes that are specifically designed to increase firms' R&D outputs, such as subsidies and tax incentives (see, for example, David et al., 2000; Almus and Czarnitzki, 2003; González et al., 2005; Czarnitzki et al., 2011; and Guo et al., 2016; Howell, 2016). As a result, our understanding of whether and how public credit guarantees influence firms' innovation behaviour is limited.Motivated by both the central role of R&D in long-run growth and the widespread use of credit guarantee schemes in recent years, this paper examines the impact of PCGs on firms' R&D efforts and innovation outcomes. We exploit a rich data set from Turkey's Credit Guarantee Fund that offers firm-level granular data from 2009 to 2020, with nearly 8 million firm-year observations. Turkey's credit guarantee scheme offers three unique advantages for studying these effects. First, as noted above, Turkey's PCG fund is very large compared to most other schemes, allowing us to carry out a comprehensive examination of its implications. Given the scale of these programmes and their potential fiscal implications, much of the existing literature has focused on whether PCGs improve credit allocation and financial outcomes. In contrast, this paper examines whether PCGs impact firms' R&D and innovation efforts, utilizing a rich data set from Turkey's Credit Guarantee Fund—one of the largest schemes of this kind—and employing a staggered difference-in-differences (DiD) approach preceded by a comprehensive matching procedure. We find that firms receiving guaranteed loans exhibit significantly greater improvements in both innovation inputs, such as R&D expenditure, and innovation outcomes, such as high-tech exports, compared to non-recipient firms. We also observe a substantially larger beneficial impact for firms already engaged in innovation activities and those facing financial constraints. Our findings have important implications for regulatory authorities in their design of credit support programmes.

IntroductionInvestment in research and development (R&D) and innovation is widely recognized as a central driver of long-term economic growth (Griliches, 1992; Stokey, 1995; Ulku, 2004; Chu and Cozzi, 2014; Liu, 2016). R&D enables firms to develop new products, advance technological progress, and remain competitive in dynamic global markets (Griffith et al., 2004). In emerging economies, R&D plays a particularly transformative role, enabling firms to transition from low-cost, labour-intensive activities toward higher value-added, technology-based production (Felipe et al., 2014). Strong R&D performance in these countries also helps attract high-technology FDI, thereby preparing the foundation for innovation-driven growth and capacity to benefit from external knowledge and technologies (Nelson and Rosenberg, 1993).Despite its importance, R&D investment remains constrained by substantial market and institutional frictions. R&D projects are inherently risky and subject to highly uncertain returns, which makes them particularly prone to underinvestment in the absence of public intervention (Shi, 2003; Hall and Lerner, 2010; Hou et al., 2022). Financial constraints further limit firms' capacity to innovate, with restricted access to external finance emerging as a key obstacle to R&D investment (Aghion et al., 2005a; Aghion et al., 2012). These challenges are especially severe for young and small firms, which often lack collateral, credit history, and scale - factors that significantly increase vulnerability to credit constraints (Beck et al., 2005; Beck and Demirgüç-Kunt, 2006; Beck et al., 2008; Hall and Lerner, 2010; De la Torre et al., 2010).In response, governments have deployed a broad range of policy instruments aimed explicitly at stimulating private R&D. These include direct measures such as R&D grants and subsidies that reduce the cost and risk of innovation activities, particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises, as well as indirect instruments such as R&D tax credits, preferential tax treatment, and accelerated depreciation schemes designed to promote sustained R&D investment across a wider set of firms (David et al., 2000; Bloom et al., 2002).Beyond R&D support programmes, several credit guarantee schemes have been introduced that offer partial government guarantees for loans granted by financial institutions, attempting to overcome market failures and alleviate firms' financing problems (Beck et al., 2010; Cowling, 2010; Uesugi et al., 2010; Bachas et al., 2021b; Horvath and Lang, 2021; Hong and Lucas, 2023).2,3 The success of such initiatives in advanced economies has prompted emerging economies to design similar programmes. Turkey has implemented one of the largest public credit guarantee schemes, allocating credit approaching 16.6% of annual GDP between 2017 and 2020.Although enhancing R&D investment and innovation outcomes has not been the primary motivation for public credit guarantees (PCGs), the alleviation in credit constraints provided by guaranteed loans is likely to alter firms' incentives for spending on R&D. While a growing empirical literature has examined the effects of PCGs on firm outcomes such as sales, investment and employment (e.g., Hurley et al., 2021; Doniger and Kay, 2021; Autor et al., 2022), their implications for R&D investment remain largely unexplored. Indeed, existing work on the role of public financial support in innovation activities almost exclusively utilizes data from R&D support programmes that are specifically designed to increase firms' R&D outputs, such as subsidies and tax incentives (see, for example, David et al., 2000; Almus and Czarnitzki, 2003; González et al., 2005; Czarnitzki et al., 2011; and Guo et al., 2016; Howell, 2016). As a result, our understanding of whether and how public credit guarantees influence firms' innovation behaviour is limited.Motivated by both the central role of R&D in long-run growth and the widespread use of credit guarantee schemes in recent years, this paper examines the impact of PCGs on firms' R&D efforts and innovation outcomes. We exploit a rich data set from Turkey's Credit Guarantee Fund that offers firm-level granular data from 2009 to 2020, with nearly 8 million firm-year observations. Turkey's credit guarantee scheme offers three unique advantages for studying these effects. First, as noted above, Turkey's PCG fund is very large compared to most other schemes, allowing us to carry out a comprehensive examination of its implications. source_records.title: Scaling innovation through public procurement: Market acceleration, building, and transformation
source_records.abstract: Public procurement of innovation (PPI) is increasingly recognised as a powerful demand-side instrument for generating solutions to complex societal challenges. Yet realising this transformative potential requires innovations to scale beyond isolated implementation contexts. We contribute to the literature by bridging innovation scaling and market shaping perspectives to develop a novel conceptual framework for scaling in the context of PPI. We identify three distinct scaling modes: ‘market acceleration’, where buyers stimulate business growth by facilitating innovation development, adoption, and dissemination across contexts, ‘market building’, where buyers aggregate public sector needs and broaden the scope of PPI, and ‘market transformation’, where buyers embed innovations by reshaping socio-technical systems. Through empirical investigation of twelve publicly-funded PPI projects in Finland, we identify scaling practices used by public buyers throughout the procurement lifecycle, spanning information dissemination, demand coordination, and institutional norm-shaping. Our findings advance theoretical understanding of how public procurement shapes innovation scaling, while providing practical insights into mechanisms through which public buyers can strategically influence market development.

IntroductionTransformative innovation policy has emerged to address the limitations of traditional innovation frameworks, emphasising the need to direct policy efforts towards addressing societal needs (Haddad et al., 2022; Schot and Steinmueller, 2018; OECD, 2024). Central to this approach is the recognition that transformation depends not just on generating novel ideas but on their widespread diffusion and scaling across diverse contexts (Schot and Steinmueller, 2018; Sengers et al., 2021; Robinson et al., 2025). Critically, we can distinguish between ‘diffusion’ - the often passive spread of innovations through populations over time - and ‘scaling’ - the deliberate, strategic efforts to increase innovations' transformative impact across different settings (Breaugh et al., 2021). For some, the main limitations lie in scaling and diversifying financial flows and instruments to close the climate funding gap, while for others, green finance is fundamentally flawed as an incumbent-led project that opens new environmental frontiers for accumulation. In response, FinTech has been touted as offering the technological solutions that could both bridge the climate financing gap and disrupt the systemic issues green finance faces. Yet, critical voices question whether FinTech is simply the latest ‘technological turn’ in a long line of socioecological fixes, designed to reintermediate financial activity onto increasingly powerful FinTech platforms. To assess the potential for FinTech to innovate green finance, we explore a suite of FinTech innovations aimed at enticing, incentivising, and thus mobilising retail consumers to fund tree planting for forest restoration as a means of delivering climate, biodiversity, and livelihood outcomes. Rooted in the award-winning Ant Forest innovation by Alibaba, we document eight subsequent variations of the Ant Forest model by different FinTech firms, who share the same focus on enabling consumer-funded tree planting – but modify the initial innovation in various ways. By utilising a ‘platform ecologies’ framework, we reveal that these innovations have delivered significant environmental outputs, with these nine FinTechs collectively financing the planting of over 750 million trees, but that evidence of environmental impact in terms of tree survival and carbon sequestration rates, remains vague. Moreover, whilst these nine FinTechs offer novel green finance solutions, they are also fundamentally driven by platform development to increase users and revenue – rather than environmental concern.

IntroductionGreen finance has garnered much attention over the last three decades because of the urgent need to mobilise and direct funds to mitigate and adapt to anthropogenic environmental destruction and climate change (Climate Policy Initiative, 2023). For many, critiques of green finance centre on its failure to bridge the climate financing gap (Fankhauser et al., 2016), currently estimated to be $1.3 trillion by 2035 (Bhattacharya et al., 2024). To address this, some scholars advocate harnessing financial technology (FinTech) to develop innovative products that engage new stakeholders and disintermediate environmental and climate investments away from inefficient incumbents (Castilla-Rubio et al., 2016; Geetha and Biju, 2024). However, for more critical voices, green finance is fundamentally limited as a project led by incumbent financial actors designed to open environmental ‘frontiers’ that prioritise the pursuit of profit over meaningful green change (Bracking, 2019). Simultaneously, critics suggest FinTech's disruptive potential serves only to reintermediate financial activity onto powerful platforms (Lai, 2020), leading to concerns that FinTech represents a ‘technological turn’ which will replicate and reinforce green finance's structural limitations (Campbell-Verduyn, 2024). Consequently, this paper aims to investigate the emergence of several related FinTech innovations to ascertain their impact on green finance. There are two research objectives designed to ensure a balanced appraisal, given the conflicting positions in the debate on green finance. These objectives are to (1) Evaluate the impacts of emergent FinTech platforms on climate change mitigation solutions for green finance, and (2) scrutinise to what extent these innovations reproduce capitalist circuits of accumulation. Objective 1 thus considers the pragmatic perspectives of industry practitioners or business management scholars as FinTech advocates, while Objective 2 considers critical perspectives from scholars within disciplines such as economic geography (Lai, 2025) and international political economy (Newell and Bray, 2025).To investigate the role of FinTech in innovating green finance, we explore a series of FinTech innovations that provide consumers the opportunity to fund climate change mitigation through tree planting. In 2019, China's Ant Forest rose to international prominence through the receipt of the United Nations Environment Programme's (UNEP, 2019) ‘Champions of the Earth’ award, “for turning the green good deeds of half a billion people into real trees planted in some of China's most arid regions”. Launched in 2016, Ant Forest enables consumers to fund the planting of real trees through gamifying their daily activities undertaken on the Alibaba platform, and has engaged 700 million users in funding the planting of at least 548 million trees, as of November 2024 (BBC, 2024). Ant Forest is considered a leading example of FinTech's potential value for green finance by mobilising retail FinTech users to collectively achieve scalable environmental impact. However, some academics have criticised the mechanisms Ant Forest uses to fund this impact for arbitrarily defining ‘greenness’ according to Alibaba's commercial needs whilst gamifying and thereby trivialising ‘green’ behaviour (see, for example: Loizeaux, 2023) – thus highlighting the contested emerging role of FinTech in green finance.Following Ant Forest's success, we identify eight FinTechs that have developed similar innovations. While Ant Forest has garnered significant industry and academic attention, these other firms have gone largely unexplored. Collectively, we refer to these firms, alongside Ant Forest, as FinTech for Forests (FFFs). These FFFs share a focus on developing FinTech innovations that enable retail consumers to fund tree planting as a central tenet of their innovations; however, we also recognize that there are significant variations in how these FFFs operate to engage consumers in tree planting (D'Orazio et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025). fields.title: Can FinTech innovate green finance? Scrutinising the financial ecologies and innovation dynamics of FinTech for forest restoration
fields.authors: Jack L. Harris a, Felicia Liu b, Benjamin S. Thompson a c
fields.abstract: Green finance has struggled to make a difference in climate change mitigation. For some, the main limitations lie in scaling and diversifying financial flows and instruments to close the climate funding gap, while for others, green finance is fundamentally flawed as an incumbent-led project that opens new environmental frontiers for accumulation. In response, FinTech has been touted as offering the technological solutions that could both bridge the climate financing gap and disrupt the systemic issues green finance faces. Yet, critical voices question whether FinTech is simply the latest ‘technological turn’ in a long line of socioecological fixes, designed to reintermediate financial activity onto increasingly powerful FinTech platforms. To assess the potential for FinTech to innovate green finance, we explore a suite of FinTech innovations aimed at enticing, incentivising, and thus mobilising retail consumers to fund tree planting for forest restoration as a means of delivering climate, biodiversity, and livelihood outcomes. Rooted in the award-winning Ant Forest innovation by Alibaba, we document eight subsequent variations of the Ant Forest model by different FinTech firms, who share the same focus on enabling consumer-funded tree planting – but modify the initial innovation in various ways. By utilising a ‘platform ecologies’ framework, we reveal that these innovations have delivered significant environmental outputs, with these nine FinTechs collectively financing the planting of over 750 million trees, but that evidence of environmental impact in terms of tree survival and carbon sequestration rates, remains vague. Moreover, whilst these nine FinTechs offer novel green finance solutions, they are also fundamentally driven by platform development to increase users and revenue – rather than environmental concern.

source_records.title: Hope, signals, and silicon: A game-theoretic model of the pre-doctoral academic labor market in the age of AI
source_records.abstract: Generative AI can make early research work easier to produce and harder to interpret. This paper develops a compact game-theoretic model of this production–evaluation tension in the pre-doctoral academic labor market. In the model, PIs organize RA labor, allocate AI between routine and novel tasks, and choose mentoring intensity. RAs choose effort, while admissions committees infer research potential from noisy task-level signals under fixed admissions capacity. A mechanism-preserving simulation examines whether the model’s qualitative mechanisms continue to hold when RAs and PIs are heterogeneous, research outcomes partly depend on luck, admissions evaluation is noisy, and elite Ph.D. capacity is fixed. The analysis yields three implications. First, routine-task AI can increase observable routine output while reducing the diagnostic precision of routine evidence. Second, heterogeneous PI objectives and task complementarity can lead laboratories to adopt different AI strategies, with some emphasizing scalable routine production and others emphasizing mentoring and novel-task augmentation. Third, when elite Ph.D. capacity is fixed, broad improvements in visible records can raise admissions cutoffs rather than expand access proportionally. The simulation reinforces these mechanisms by showing that AI can raise routine output while weakening the link between evaluated scores and latent ability, increasing the risk that high-ability or high-realized-merit candidates are missed. The paper suggests that as routine evidence loses diagnostic content, evaluation should place greater weight on less easily automated forms of contribution, including judgment, interpretation, research design, and process-based evidence.

Hope, signals, and silicon: A game-theoretic model of the pre-doctoral academic labor market in the age of AI

•
AI expands routine research output but weakens its value as a signal of talent.
•
Research labs may specialize in scaled routine work or mentor-led novel work.
•
Fixed Ph.D. capacity turns stronger records into higher admission cutoffs.
•
Luck and evaluation noise can cause high-ability applicants to be overlooked.
•
Research-process evidence gains value as routine outputs lose signaling power.

Generative AI can make early research work easier to produce and harder to interpret. This paper develops a compact game-theoretic model of this production–evaluation tension in the pre-doctoral academic labor market. In the model, PIs organize RA labor, allocate AI between routine and novel tasks, and choose mentoring intensity. RAs choose effort, while admissions committees infer research potential from noisy task-level signals under fixed admissions capacity. A mechanism-preserving simulation examines whether the model’s qualitative mechanisms continue to hold when RAs and PIs are heterogeneous, research outcomes partly depend on luck, admissions evaluation is noisy, and elite Ph.D. capacity is fixed. The analysis yields three implications. First, routine-task AI can increase observable routine output while reducing the diagnostic precision of routine evidence. Second, heterogeneous PI objectives and task complementarity can lead laboratories to adopt different AI strategies, with some emphasizing scalable routine production and others emphasizing mentoring and novel-task augmentation. Third, when elite Ph.D. capacity is fixed, broad improvements in visible records can raise admissions cutoffs rather than expand access proportionally. The simulation reinforces these mechanisms by showing that AI can raise routine output while weakening the link between evaluated scores and latent ability, increasing the risk that high-ability or high-realized-merit candidates are missed. The paper suggests that as routine evidence loses diagnostic content, evaluation should place greater weight on less easily automated forms of contribution, including judgment, interpretation, research design, and process-based evidence.

It can make research output easier to produce and harder to interpret. A cleaned dataset, polished table, well-documented script, or clear literature summary may still help a project, but it may reveal less about the researcher’s own effort, judgment, and potential. This matters because early-career research output is also a screening device: it helps supervisors, admissions committees, and hiring institutions decide who has research promise. Evidence that generative AI can raise productivity while compressing performance differences or reducing output diversity makes this concern especially salient (Noy and Zhang, 2023, Doshi and Hauser, 2024, Dell’Acqua et al., 2026). This paper studies this production–screening tension in the pre-doctoral academic labor market.The setting is important because pre-doctoral work has become an increasingly important gateway into elite doctoral training in economics and related quantitative social sciences (Stansbury and Schultz, 2023, Schultz and Stansbury, 2022). Admissions committees allocate scarce training slots under uncertainty about future research ability, while Principal Investigators (PIs) need skilled research labor for data work, coding, literature review, and project development (Conley and Önder, 2014, Card and DellaVigna, 2013, Heckman and Moktan, 2020). Following Mangematin (2000)’s view of doctoral training as both career investment for students and research labor for supervisors, we view pre-doctoral appointments as serving three roles at once: labor input, apprenticeship, and extended signal-generation stage.1Before generative AI, this market already relied on a fragile informational arrangement. Research Assistants (RAs) accepted temporary positions for wages, experience, training, and recommendation capital, while PIs obtained motivated research labor and admissions committees used work records and recommendations to infer latent research potential (Stansbury and Schultz, 2023). Because effort, judgment, mentoring quality, and recommendation credibility are difficult to contract on fully, the PI–RA relationship is not a simple spot-market exchange (Baker et al., 2002, Levin, 2003). These signals matter at the market level because elite opportunities are scarce and candidates compete not only against an absolute standard but also against one another (Lazear and Rosen, 1981, Hopkins, 2012, Hopkins, 2023).This paper develops an analytical model of how generative AI changes this arrangement. PIs take an AI capability frontier as given and choose normalized team intensity, AI allocation between routine and novel tasks, and mentoring intensity. RAs differ in ability and choose effort. Routine and novel task outputs generate noisy task-level signals, and admissions committees use a linear evaluation rule to summarize research potential from those signals. Elite PhD admissions are modeled as a fixed-capacity tournament. The model links three objects that are usually considered separately: laboratory production, evaluation from pre-doctoral output, and capacity-constrained selection.The model yields three main findings. First, routine-task AI can raise observable routine output while reducing the diagnostic precision of routine evidence. Polished routine artifacts become more abundant, but they may reveal less about the RA’s own effort and judgment because the artifact contains a larger AI-generated component that evaluators cannot perfectly separate from human contribution. Second, AI can generate segmented laboratory strategies. Quantity-oriented PIs tilt toward scalable routine production, while quality-oriented PIs place greater value on mentoring and novel-task augmentation. Third, fixed-capacity admissions can convert broad improvements in visible records into a higher cutoff rather than broader access. Together, these findings show that AI can improve research production while changing the informational meaning of pre-doctoral output and intensifying competition for scarce academic opportunities.The analysis distinguishes productivity, learning, and signaling effects. In a bottlenecked research-training market, these effects need not move together. Some AI-enabled gains may increase real research output or human-capital formation; others may mainly raise visible records in a fixed-capacity tournament. The baseline model therefore isolates the production-and-evaluation mechanism, while the mechanism-preserving simulation in Section 5 examines whether the same mechanisms appear when RA talent is distributed, PI orientation is continuous, true merit contains project luck, and admissions scores are noisy. The appendix treats learning, welfare, and project-risk extensions as supporting technical material.The contemporary U.S.-style economics pre-doctoral market provides the institutional template because it is visible, formalized, and well documented (Stansbury and Schultz, 2023, Abramitzky et al., 2024). The mechanism is not meant to describe all academic labor markets. It applies most directly to settings in which prospective doctoral students work as temporary RAs, supervisors mediate evaluation through recommendations, and access to elite doctoral training is bottlenecked (Câmara et al., 2023, Hopkins, 2012, Lazear and Rosen, 1981).Organizational accessGet full-text access by signing in with your organisationAccess through your organizationOther access optionsPurchase PDFNeed help with access?Section snippetsRelated literatureThis section positions the paper at the intersection of four literatures that map onto the model’s main margins: the pre-doctoral labor-market setting, task-based AI in scientific work, the PI–RA training relationship, and evaluation under noisy evidence and fixed capacity. fields.title: Hope, signals, and silicon: A game-theoretic model of the pre-doctoral academic labor market in the age of AI
fields.abstract: Generative AI can make early research work easier to produce and harder to interpret. This paper develops a compact game-theoretic model of this production–evaluation tension in the pre-doctoral academic labor market. In the model, PIs organize RA labor, allocate AI between routine and novel tasks, and choose mentoring intensity. RAs choose effort, while admissions committees infer research potential from noisy task-level signals under fixed admissions capacity. A mechanism-preserving simulation examines whether the model’s qualitative mechanisms continue to hold when RAs and PIs are heterogeneous, research outcomes partly depend on luck, admissions evaluation is noisy, and elite Ph.D. capacity is fixed. The analysis yields three implications. First, routine-task AI can increase observable routine output while reducing the diagnostic precision of routine evidence. Second, heterogeneous PI objectives and task complementarity can lead laboratories to adopt different AI strategies, with some emphasizing scalable routine production and others emphasizing mentoring and novel-task augmentation. Third, when elite Ph.D. capacity is fixed, broad improvements in visible records can raise admissions cutoffs rather than expand access proportionally. The simulation reinforces these mechanisms by showing that AI can raise routine output while weakening the link between evaluated scores and latent ability, increasing the risk that high-ability or high-realized-merit candidates are missed. The paper suggests that as routine evidence loses diagnostic content, evaluation should place greater weight on less easily automated forms of contribution, including judgment, interpretation, research design, and process-based evidence.

Generative AI can make early research work easier to produce and harder to interpret. This paper develops a compact game-theoretic model of this production–evaluation tension in the pre-doctoral academic labor market. In the model, PIs organize RA labor, allocate AI between routine and novel tasks, and choose mentoring intensity. RAs choose effort, while admissions committees infer research potential from noisy task-level signals under fixed admissions capacity. A mechanism-preserving simulation examines whether the model’s qualitative mechanisms continue to hold when RAs and PIs are heterogeneous, research outcomes partly depend on luck, admissions evaluation is noisy, and elite Ph.D. capacity is fixed. The analysis yields three implications. First, routine-task AI can increase observable routine output while reducing the diagnostic precision of routine evidence. Second, heterogeneous PI objectives and task complementarity can lead laboratories to adopt different AI strategies, with some emphasizing scalable routine production and others emphasizing mentoring and novel-task augmentation. Third, when elite Ph.D. capacity is fixed, broad improvements in visible records can raise admissions cutoffs rather than expand access proportionally. The simulation reinforces these mechanisms by showing that AI can raise routine output while weakening the link between evaluated scores and latent ability, increasing the risk that high-ability or high-realized-merit candidates are missed. The paper suggests that as routine evidence loses diagnostic content, evaluation should place greater weight on less easily automated forms of contribution, including judgment, interpretation, research design, and process-based evidence.
