It can make research output easier to produce and harder to interpret. A cleaned dataset, polished table, well-documented script, or clear literature summary may still help a project, but it may reveal less about the researcher’s own effort, judgment, and potential. This matters because early-career research output is also a screening device: it helps supervisors, admissions committees, and hiring institutions decide who has research promise. Evidence that generative AI can raise productivity while compressing performance differences or reducing output diversity makes this concern especially salient (Noy and Zhang, 2023, Doshi and Hauser, 2024, Dell’Acqua et al., 2026). This paper studies this production–screening tension in the pre-doctoral academic labor market.The setting is important because pre-doctoral work has become an increasingly important gateway into elite doctoral training in economics and related quantitative social sciences (Stansbury and Schultz, 2023, Schultz and Stansbury, 2022). Admissions committees allocate scarce training slots under uncertainty about future research ability, while Principal Investigators (PIs) need skilled research labor for data work, coding, literature review, and project development (Conley and Önder, 2014, Card and DellaVigna, 2013, Heckman and Moktan, 2020). Following Mangematin (2000)’s view of doctoral training as both career investment for students and research labor for supervisors, we view pre-doctoral appointments as serving three roles at once: labor input, apprenticeship, and extended signal-generation stage.1Before generative AI, this market already relied on a fragile informational arrangement. Research Assistants (RAs) accepted temporary positions for wages, experience, training, and recommendation capital, while PIs obtained motivated research labor and admissions committees used work records and recommendations to infer latent research potential (Stansbury and Schultz, 2023). Because effort, judgment, mentoring quality, and recommendation credibility are difficult to contract on fully, the PI–RA relationship is not a simple spot-market exchange (Baker et al., 2002, Levin, 2003). These signals matter at the market level because elite opportunities are scarce and candidates compete not only against an absolute standard but also against one another (Lazear and Rosen, 1981, Hopkins, 2012, Hopkins, 2023).This paper develops an analytical model of how generative AI changes this arrangement. PIs take an AI capability frontier as given and choose normalized team intensity, AI allocation between routine and novel tasks, and mentoring intensity. RAs differ in ability and choose effort. Routine and novel task outputs generate noisy task-level signals, and admissions committees use a linear evaluation rule to summarize research potential from those signals. Elite PhD admissions are modeled as a fixed-capacity tournament. The model links three objects that are usually considered separately: laboratory production, evaluation from pre-doctoral output, and capacity-constrained selection.The model yields three main findings. First, routine-task AI can raise observable routine output while reducing the diagnostic precision of routine evidence. Polished routine artifacts become more abundant, but they may reveal less about the RA’s own effort and judgment because the artifact contains a larger AI-generated component that evaluators cannot perfectly separate from human contribution. Second, AI can generate segmented laboratory strategies. Quantity-oriented PIs tilt toward scalable routine production, while quality-oriented PIs place greater value on mentoring and novel-task augmentation. Third, fixed-capacity admissions can convert broad improvements in visible records into a higher cutoff rather than broader access. Together, these findings show that AI can improve research production while changing the informational meaning of pre-doctoral output and intensifying competition for scarce academic opportunities.The analysis distinguishes productivity, learning, and signaling effects. In a bottlenecked research-training market, these effects need not move together. Some AI-enabled gains may increase real research output or human-capital formation; others may mainly raise visible records in a fixed-capacity tournament. The baseline model therefore isolates the production-and-evaluation mechanism, while the mechanism-preserving simulation in Section 5 examines whether the same mechanisms appear when RA talent is distributed, PI orientation is continuous, true merit contains project luck, and admissions scores are noisy. The appendix treats learning, welfare, and project-risk extensions as supporting technical material.The contemporary U.S.-style economics pre-doctoral market provides the institutional template because it is visible, formalized, and well documented (Stansbury and Schultz, 2023, Abramitzky et al., 2024). The mechanism is not meant to describe all academic labor markets. It applies most directly to settings in which prospective doctoral students work as temporary RAs, supervisors mediate evaluation through recommendations, and access to elite doctoral training is bottlenecked (Câmara et al., 2023, Hopkins, 2012, Lazear and Rosen, 1981).Organizational accessGet full-text access by signing in with your organisationAccess through your organizationOther access optionsPurchase PDFNeed help with access?Section snippetsRelated literatureThis section positions the paper at the intersection of four literatures that map onto the model’s main margins: the pre-doctoral labor-market setting, task-based AI in scientific work, the PI–RA training relationship, and evaluation under noisy evidence and fixed capacity. We focus on a stylized version of the contemporary U.S.-style pre-doctoral academic labor market, where temporary RA appointments, recommendation-based evaluation, and competition for a fixed number of elite PhD positions are especially salient (Stansbury and Schultz, 2023). It examines whether the model’s qualitative mechanisms continue to hold in a richer setting with heterogeneous RAs and PIs, luck in research outcomes, noisy admissions evaluation, and a fixed number of elite PhD slots. fields.title: Hope, signals, and silicon: A game-theoretic model of the pre-doctoral academic labor market in the age of AI
fields.abstract: Generative AI can make early research work easier to produce and harder to interpret. This paper develops a compact game-theoretic model of this production–evaluation tension in the pre-doctoral academic labor market. In the model, PIs organize RA labor, allocate AI between routine and novel tasks, and choose mentoring intensity. RAs choose effort, while admissions committees infer research potential from noisy task-level signals under fixed admissions capacity. A mechanism-preserving simulation examines whether the model’s qualitative mechanisms continue to hold when RAs and PIs are heterogeneous, research outcomes partly depend on luck, admissions evaluation is noisy, and elite Ph.D. capacity is fixed. The analysis yields three implications. First, routine-task AI can increase observable routine output while reducing the diagnostic precision of routine evidence. Second, heterogeneous PI objectives and task complementarity can lead laboratories to adopt different AI strategies, with some emphasizing scalable routine production and others emphasizing mentoring and novel-task augmentation. Third, when elite Ph.D. capacity is fixed, broad improvements in visible records can raise admissions cutoffs rather than expand access proportionally. The simulation reinforces these mechanisms by showing that AI can raise routine output while weakening the link between evaluated scores and latent ability, increasing the risk that high-ability or high-realized-merit candidates are missed. The paper suggests that as routine evidence loses diagnostic content, evaluation should place greater weight on less easily automated forms of contribution, including judgment, interpretation, research design, and process-based evidence.

Short communication
Complexity and the uncertain impact of novel science☆

•
Novel research addressing complex problems is more likely to become highly cited.
•
Problem complexity reduces the likelihood that novel papers receive minimal recognition.
•
Novel work on complex problems is recognized earlier, avoiding delayed recognition.
•
High novelty combined with high complexity generates broader interdisciplinary impact.
•
Problem structure helps explain why equally novel papers have different outcomes.

Novel scientific ideas drive progress, yet their outcomes are highly uneven. This paper examines whether problem complexity — the degree of interdependence among elements a study must coordinate — shapes the impact of novel research. I introduce a measure of complexity based on the NK framework and find that novel work addressing more complex problems is substantially more likely to achieve high impact, less likely to receive minimal citations, recognized earlier, and cited more broadly across fields. These patterns can be interpreted through the problem-solving view of science, the topology of search landscapes, and characteristics of the combinations themselves. The findings suggest that variation in the outcomes of novel research depends critically on the structure of the problems to which novelty is applied. Data on the complexity of papers are released at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20813592.

IntroductionNovel scientific ideas are widely recognized as a central engine of economic progress (Bush, 1945). A large body of empirical work shows that more novel scientific papers tend, on average, to receive more citations and are disproportionately associated with major breakthroughs (Uzzi et al., 2013, Arts et al., 2025, Azoulay et al., 2011). In this sense, novelty plays a central role in advancing scientific knowledge (Mokyr, 2002). At the same time, the realized impact of novel research is highly uneven. While some novel papers become highly influential, many other novel papers receive little recognition, particularly in the years immediately following publication1 (Wang et al., 2017).Prior research has documented a range of factors that help explain heterogeneity in scientific impact, including author reputation and institutional prestige (Merton, 1968, Azoulay et al., 2014), team size and composition (Wuchty et al., 2007, Singh and Fleming, 2010), journal placement and visibility (Wang et al., 2017), and timing relative to field trajectories (Van Raan, 2004). These explanations have substantially improved our understanding of why some contributions diffuse more widely than others. However, they share a common feature: they are largely external to the scientific content itself. They characterize who produces the research, where it appears, and when it is published, rather than the nature of the scientific problem the research attempts to solve.What remains poorly understood is how the structure of the scientific problems to which novelty is applied shapes with the impact of novel research. In other words, while novelty has been studied extensively as a property of ideas and their recombination, existing work offers limited insight into how differences in the problems being addressed condition the returns to novelty. This gap is striking given a long-standing view, rooted in the philosophy of science, that science is fundamentally a problem-solving activity (Laudan, 1978, Simon, 1977, Kuhn, 1970). From this perspective, scientific progress is not only about introducing new ideas, but about resolving problems that vary in their underlying structure and difficulty.In a recombinatorial perspective, problems differ in the degree to which their constituent elements are interdependent. Some problems can be addressed by combining components that operate largely independently, whereas others require the coordinated alignment of multiple interacting elements. Work in combinatorial search and innovation formalizes this distinction through the concept of complexity, modeled as the degree of interdependence among elements in a solution space (Kauffman, 1993, Levinthal, 1997, Fleming, 2001). Taken together, the problem-solving view of science and the complexity literature suggest that novelty may not have uniform consequences across problems: introducing a novel solution to a simple problem may yield modest advances, while introducing novelty to a complex problem may be associated with resolving constraints that previously limited progress and with greater scientific value.23 Despite these theoretical insights, we lack empirical evidence on whether and how problem complexity shapes the impact of scientific research, and in particular whether novel work is more influential when it tackles more complex problems.Addressing this gap requires a setting in which both novelty and problem complexity are observable. Biomedical research is well suited for this purpose because papers combine identifiable chemical and biological substances—for example, compounds used to inhibit a disease pathway. These substances are the discrete components researchers use and report in their studies, making it possible to observe new combinations and to characterize how interdependent the components are.4 To measure novelty, I follow the well-established principle that novelty arises from new combinations of knowledge elements (Weitzman, 1998, Nelson and Winter, 1985, Schumpeter, 1964). Here, new combinations of substances capture the introduction of a novel idea. To measure complexity, I leverage the NK framework, a widely used model of combinatorial search (Kauffman, 1993, Sorenson et al., 2006, Fleming and Sorenson, 2001, Ganco, 2017, Zhang and Yang, 2022, Frenken, 2006, Levinthal, 1997, Billinger et al., 2014). In this framework, the substances used in a study represent the elements (N), and their documented interactions represent the degree of interdependence (K), where interdependence reflects the extent to which a change in one element requires coordinated changes in others. This approach allows me to quantify the complexity of the problem a paper addresses through the N and K values of the substances it employs. When a paper successfully uses a particular set of interdependent substances, it indicates — among published papers — that researchers have addressed a problem with the specific level of complexity defined by those interactions. Thus, a paper that introduces a new combination of substances contributes novelty to a problem whose complexity can be estimated through the interdependences among the substances involved.5In this work, I analyze 9.6 million biomedical papers published between 1950 and 2023, measuring each paper’s novelty and complexity, and examine how these dimensions relate to three established aspects of scientific impact: citation magnitude, the timing of recognition, and the breadth of diffusion across fields (Wang et al., 2017). These substances are the discrete components researchers use and report in their studies, making it possible to observe new combinations and to characterize how interdependent the components are.4 To measure novelty, I follow the well-established principle that novelty arises from new combinations of knowledge elements (Weitzman, 1998, Nelson and Winter, 1985, Schumpeter, 1964). Here, new combinations of substances capture the introduction of a novel idea. To measure complexity, I leverage the NK framework, a widely used model of combinatorial search (Kauffman, 1993, Sorenson et al., 2006, Fleming and Sorenson, 2001, Ganco, 2017, Zhang and Yang, 2022, Frenken, 2006, Levinthal, 1997, Billinger et al., 2014). In this framework, the substances used in a study represent the elements (N), and their documented interactions represent the degree of interdependence (K), where interdependence reflects the extent to which a change in one element requires coordinated changes in others. This approach allows me to quantify the complexity of the problem a paper addresses through the N and K values of the substances it employs. When a paper successfully uses a particular set of interdependent substances, it indicates — among published papers — that researchers have addressed a problem with the specific level of complexity defined by those interactions. Thus, a paper that introduces a new combination of substances contributes novelty to a problem whose complexity can be estimated through the interdependences among the substances involved.5In this work, I analyze 9.6 million biomedical papers published between 1950 and 2023, measuring each paper’s novelty and complexity, and examine how these dimensions relate to three established aspects of scientific impact: citation magnitude, the timing of recognition, and the breadth of diffusion across fields (Wang et al., 2017). Novel research addressing complex problems is more likely to become highly cited.

fields.abstract: Novel scientific ideas drive progress, yet their outcomes are highly uneven. This paper examines whether problem complexity — the degree of interdependence among elements a study must coordinate — shapes the impact of novel research. I introduce a measure of complexity based on the NK framework and find that novel work addressing more complex problems is substantially more likely to achieve high impact, less likely to receive minimal citations, recognized earlier, and cited more broadly across fields. These patterns can be interpreted through the problem-solving view of science, the topology of search landscapes, and characteristics of the combinations themselves. The findings suggest that variation in the outcomes of novel research depends critically on the structure of the problems to which novelty is applied. Data on the complexity of papers are released at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20813592.

These results suggest that restrictions on software patentability had little effect on venture-backed software startups.

Our empirical approach exploits the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2014 decision in Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank Int’l, which restricted the patentability of many software inventions. Using detailed data on venture capital financing and startup outcomes, we estimate difference-in-differences models comparing firms with greater and lesser exposure to the decision. We find no evidence that startups more exposed to Alice experienced worse financing outcomes, growth, or exit probabilities. These results suggest that restrictions on software patentability had little effect on venture-backed software startups.JEL classificationG24; L86; K40; M13; O30KeywordsVenture capital; Startups; Software; PatentsPrevious article in this issueNext article in this issueIntroductionPatent rights are widely believed to enhance innovators’ ability to attract the funding required to develop and commercialize new ideas. In addition to increasing the expected profitability of an invention by shielding the patent holder from infringing competition, patents may also serve as informational signals of technological quality to early-stage investors (e.g., Conti et al., 2013). Consistent with this view, a large empirical literature finds a positive association between patenting and various measures of startup success (see Hall, 2019 for a review). At the same time, recent evidence suggests that reductions in patent protection need not reduce entrepreneurial activity or venture capital investment and may even increase them (Guler et al., 2026, Feng and Williams, 2026). These findings raise an important question: how does the strength of patent protection affect the financing and performance of startups?We examine how the strength of patent protection affects software startup financing and performance by studying the U.S. Supreme Court’s June 2014 decision in Alice v. CLS Bank,1 which substantially restricted the patentability of many software-related inventions. The Alice decision provides a useful setting for empirical analysis because it generated a sharp and plausibly exogenous change in the availability of patent protection for certain types of software innovations. Our empirical approach combines detailed data on venture-backed software startups with information on firms’ patent portfolios. Using data from PitchBook,2 we construct a range of measures capturing startup financing, growth, and exit outcomes. We then measure firms’ exposure to the Alice decision based on the technological characteristics of their patent portfolios and estimate cross-sectional and difference-in-differences regressions that compare outcomes across firms with different levels of exposure to the decision. Our design allows us to compare outcomes both within the set of patenting startups and across firms that did and did not file patents, thereby isolating the relationship between startup performance and the impact of Alice from the broader relationship between patenting and firm success.To measure Alice’s effect on patent protection, we exploit two well-documented consequences of the decision. First, subject-matter eligibility rejections increased sharply in certain software-related technology areas at the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) after the Alice decision (Chien and Wu, 2018, Kesan and Wang, 2020, Frumkin et al., 2024, Feng and Williams, 2026). Second, courts increasingly invalidated asserted software patents on subject-matter eligibility grounds (Lemley and Zyontz, 2021). We use these changes to identify technology areas most affected by the decision and measure the extent to which startups sought patent protection in those areas prior to Alice.Our regression results focus on software firms founded in the five years prior to the Alice decision. Across a wide range of specifications, we find that startups with greater exposure to Alice experienced investment opportunities, growth trajectories, and exit outcomes that were largely indistinguishable from those of other software startups. In particular, we find no evidence that pre-Alice patenting in Alice-affected technology areas reduced the probability of successful exits (IPOs or acquisitions), increased the likelihood of failure, or decreased firms’ ability to secure venture capital funding in subsequent years. Similarly, our difference-in-differences estimates indicate no significant post-Alice changes in investment size, firm valuation, or employment growth among more exposed startups relative to less exposed firms.While these results are largely null, they are robust across numerous alternative measures of startup performance and multiple definitions of treatment. Our findings are unchanged when we define treatment using either prosecution outcomes or litigation outcomes, and when we measure technological exposure using art units or patent classes. The results are also robust to alternative approaches for assigning firms to treatment and control groups based on their patenting behavior, including binary and continuous treatment definitions and approaches that incorporate predicted examination outcomes based on patent examiner leniency.We additionally assess the precision and statistical power of our estimates by reporting confidence intervals and calculating the ex post Minimal Detectable Effect (MDE) associated with our main regressions. These analyses indicate that our estimates are sufficiently precise to rule out large negative effects of Alice on startup performance. Across specifications, the estimated coefficients are generally small and often positive. Following Abadie (2020), we view these results as informative because they allow us to reject a range of economically important negative effects that have figured prominently in debates over software patent eligibility.Our study contributes to two strands of the literature. First, it contributes to research on startup financing and outcomes by examining how restrictions on patent protection affect venture-backed startups. While previous work documents a positive effect of patenting on startup success (Helmers and Rogers, 2011, Gaule, 2018, Farre-Mensa et al., 2020), our analysis exploits an exogenous legal change to examine the causal relationship between patent protection and startup performance. In doing so, we construct a broad set of performance metrics derived from highly granular firm-level and firm-investment-level data.Second, our analysis contributes to the literature on the social value of software patents. While patent systems are designed to promote innovation by increasing firms’ ability to appropriate returns to R&D investment, many scholars argue that this mechanism may function poorly in the software industry (Bessen et al., 2012, Bessen and Meurer, 2009, Bessen, 2012). Existing empirical studies of publicly traded firms generally find little evidence that the narrowing of software patent protection following Alice harmed innovation or firm performance (Lin and Rai, 2023, Acikalin et al., 2023, Helmers and Love, 2024). Our analysis extends this literature by examining the effects of software patentability on venture-backed startups, including both patenting and non-patenting firms (see also Mann and Sager, 2007, Hicks, 2024, Feng and Williams, 2026).Finally, our findings inform ongoing policy debates regarding the future of the Alice decision and potential reforms to U.S. patent eligibility law. Since Alice was decided, litigants and policymakers have repeatedly called for judicial clarification or legislative reform (e.g., Iancu, 2024, McDermott, 2024, Michel and O’Malley, 2024, Craig, 2024, Pronk, 2023, Hu, 2020, Davis, 2020). Congress has also considered legislation that would expand the scope of patent-eligible subject matter, most recently the Patent Eligibility Restoration Act.3 Because our results suggest that Alice did not significantly affect the financing or performance of software startups, our analysis provides evidence relevant to these debates.The remainder of the paper proceeds as follows. Patent protection and software firm financing☆

•
Court decision restricting software patentability did not affect VC financing.
•
Startups exposed to Alice v. CLS Bank (2014) performed similarly in funding, growth, and exits.
•
Difference-in-differences design using granular deal-level data.
•
Novel exposure measures based on USPTO art units and eligibility rejection rates.
•
Results robust across multiple treatments, outcomes, and power analyses.

We study the relationship between patent protection and the performance of software startups. Our empirical approach exploits the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2014 decision in Alice Corp. v. CLS Bank Int’l, which restricted the patentability of many software inventions. Using detailed data on venture capital financing and startup outcomes, we estimate difference-in-differences models comparing firms with greater and lesser exposure to the decision. We find no evidence that startups more exposed to Alice experienced worse financing outcomes, growth, or exit probabilities. These results suggest that restrictions on software patentability had little effect on venture-backed software startups.

These results suggest that restrictions on software patentability had little effect on venture-backed software startups.JEL classificationG24; L86; K40; M13; O30KeywordsVenture capital; Startups; Software; PatentsPrevious article in this issueNext article in this issueIntroductionPatent rights are widely believed to enhance innovators’ ability to attract the funding required to develop and commercialize new ideas. In addition to increasing the expected profitability of an invention by shielding the patent holder from infringing competition, patents may also serve as informational signals of technological quality to early-stage investors (e.g., Conti et al., 2013). Consistent with this view, a large empirical literature finds a positive association between patenting and various measures of startup success (see Hall, 2019 for a review). At the same time, recent evidence suggests that reductions in patent protection need not reduce entrepreneurial activity or venture capital investment and may even increase them (Guler et al., 2026, Feng and Williams, 2026). These findings raise an important question: how does the strength of patent protection affect the financing and performance of startups?We examine how the strength of patent protection affects software startup financing and performance by studying the U.S. Supreme Court’s June 2014 decision in Alice v. CLS Bank,1 which substantially restricted the patentability of many software-related inventions. The Alice decision provides a useful setting for empirical analysis because it generated a sharp and plausibly exogenous change in the availability of patent protection for certain types of software innovations. Our empirical approach combines detailed data on venture-backed software startups with information on firms’ patent portfolios. Using data from PitchBook,2 we construct a range of measures capturing startup financing, growth, and exit outcomes. We then measure firms’ exposure to the Alice decision based on the technological characteristics of their patent portfolios and estimate cross-sectional and difference-in-differences regressions that compare outcomes across firms with different levels of exposure to the decision. Our design allows us to compare outcomes both within the set of patenting startups and across firms that did and did not file patents, thereby isolating the relationship between startup performance and the impact of Alice from the broader relationship between patenting and firm success.To measure Alice’s effect on patent protection, we exploit two well-documented consequences of the decision. First, subject-matter eligibility rejections increased sharply in certain software-related technology areas at the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) after the Alice decision (Chien and Wu, 2018, Kesan and Wang, 2020, Frumkin et al., 2024, Feng and Williams, 2026). Second, courts increasingly invalidated asserted software patents on subject-matter eligibility grounds (Lemley and Zyontz, 2021). We use these changes to identify technology areas most affected by the decision and measure the extent to which startups sought patent protection in those areas prior to Alice.Our regression results focus on software firms founded in the five years prior to the Alice decision. Across a wide range of specifications, we find that startups with greater exposure to Alice experienced investment opportunities, growth trajectories, and exit outcomes that were largely indistinguishable from those of other software startups. In particular, we find no evidence that pre-Alice patenting in Alice-affected technology areas reduced the probability of successful exits (IPOs or acquisitions), increased the likelihood of failure, or decreased firms’ ability to secure venture capital funding in subsequent years. Similarly, our difference-in-differences estimates indicate no significant post-Alice changes in investment size, firm valuation, or employment growth among more exposed startups relative to less exposed firms.While these results are largely null, they are robust across numerous alternative measures of startup performance and multiple definitions of treatment. Our findings are unchanged when we define treatment using either prosecution outcomes or litigation outcomes, and when we measure technological exposure using art units or patent classes. The results are also robust to alternative approaches for assigning firms to treatment and control groups based on their patenting behavior, including binary and continuous treatment definitions and approaches that incorporate predicted examination outcomes based on patent examiner leniency.We additionally assess the precision and statistical power of our estimates by reporting confidence intervals and calculating the ex post Minimal Detectable Effect (MDE) associated with our main regressions. These analyses indicate that our estimates are sufficiently precise to rule out large negative effects of Alice on startup performance. Across specifications, the estimated coefficients are generally small and often positive. Following Abadie (2020), we view these results as informative because they allow us to reject a range of economically important negative effects that have figured prominently in debates over software patent eligibility.Our study contributes to two strands of the literature. First, it contributes to research on startup financing and outcomes by examining how restrictions on patent protection affect venture-backed startups. While previous work documents a positive effect of patenting on startup success (Helmers and Rogers, 2011, Gaule, 2018, Farre-Mensa et al., 2020), our analysis exploits an exogenous legal change to examine the causal relationship between patent protection and startup performance. In doing so, we construct a broad set of performance metrics derived from highly granular firm-level and firm-investment-level data.Second, our analysis contributes to the literature on the social value of software patents. While patent systems are designed to promote innovation by increasing firms’ ability to appropriate returns to R&D investment, many scholars argue that this mechanism may function poorly in the software industry (Bessen et al., 2012, Bessen and Meurer, 2009, Bessen, 2012). Existing empirical studies of publicly traded firms generally find little evidence that the narrowing of software patent protection following Alice harmed innovation or firm performance (Lin and Rai, 2023, Acikalin et al., 2023, Helmers and Love, 2024). Our analysis extends this literature by examining the effects of software patentability on venture-backed startups, including both patenting and non-patenting firms (see also Mann and Sager, 2007, Hicks, 2024, Feng and Williams, 2026).Finally, our findings inform ongoing policy debates regarding the future of the Alice decision and potential reforms to U.S. patent eligibility law. Since Alice was decided, litigants and policymakers have repeatedly called for judicial clarification or legislative reform (e.g., Iancu, 2024, McDermott, 2024, Michel and O’Malley, 2024, Craig, 2024, Pronk, 2023, Hu, 2020, Davis, 2020). Congress has also considered legislation that would expand the scope of patent-eligible subject matter, most recently the Patent Eligibility Restoration Act.3 Because our results suggest that Alice did not significantly affect the financing or performance of software startups, our analysis provides evidence relevant to these debates.The remainder of the paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 provides institutional background on software patentability and the Alice decision. Section 3 describes the data. Section 4 outlines the empirical strategy. source_records.title: When government shuts down science: Evidence from U.S. Antarctic research
source_records.abstract: We study the 2013 U.S. federal government shutdown and its impact on federally funded research in Antarctica. Although the shutdown lasted only 16 days, it coincided with the start of the Antarctic summer field season, a narrow window for data collection that relies on geographically unique, time-sensitive, and difficult-to-substitute research inputs. Using scientist-level data with a difference-in-differences design and exploiting the timing of the shutdown, we document an 11% decline in the number of byline-weighted publications among affected researchers, as well as altered collaboration patterns, which we corroborate with qualitative survey evidence. These findings show that even brief disruptions can have lasting effects on science when they block access to specialized, time-sensitive, and hard-to-replace research inputs.

We study the 2013 U.S. federal government shutdown and its impact on federally funded research in Antarctica. Although the shutdown lasted only 16 days, it coincided with the start of the Antarctic summer field season, a narrow window for data collection that relies on geographically unique, time-sensitive, and difficult-to-substitute research inputs. Using scientist-level data with a difference-in-differences design and exploiting the timing of the shutdown, we document an 11% decline in the number of byline-weighted publications among affected researchers, as well as altered collaboration patterns, which we corroborate with qualitative survey evidence. These findings show that even brief disruptions can have lasting effects on science when they block access to specialized, time-sensitive, and hard-to-replace research inputs.

We study the 2013 U.S. federal government shutdown and its impact on federally funded research in Antarctica. Although the shutdown lasted only 16 days, it coincided with the start of the Antarctic summer field season, a narrow window for data collection that relies on geographically unique, time-sensitive, and difficult-to-substitute research inputs. Using scientist-level data with a difference-in-differences design and exploiting the timing of the shutdown, we document an 11% decline in the number of byline-weighted publications among affected researchers, as well as altered collaboration patterns, which we corroborate with qualitative survey evidence. These findings show that even brief disruptions can have lasting effects on science when they block access to specialized, time-sensitive, and hard-to-replace research inputs.

fields.authors: Kris Gulati a, Christian Helmers b c
fields.abstract: We study the 2013 U.S. federal government shutdown and its impact on federally funded research in Antarctica. Although the shutdown lasted only 16 days, it coincided with the start of the Antarctic summer field season, a narrow window for data collection that relies on geographically unique, time-sensitive, and difficult-to-substitute research inputs. Using scientist-level data with a difference-in-differences design and exploiting the timing of the shutdown, we document an 11% decline in the number of byline-weighted publications among affected researchers, as well as altered collaboration patterns, which we corroborate with qualitative survey evidence. These findings show that even brief disruptions can have lasting effects on science when they block access to specialized, time-sensitive, and hard-to-replace research inputs.

source_records.abstract: This paper analyzes the association between geopolitical alignment and international research and innovation collaborations using data spanning 2000–2023. Using ideal point distance measures derived from UN General Assembly voting patterns, we find that increases in geopolitical distance are associated with reductions in international collaborations. A one-unit increase in geopolitical distance (roughly the distance between a median country pair) over three years is associated with a 3.1% reduction in collaborations in scientific publications (0.8% per standard deviation). We also find that this relationship is asymmetric: worsening geopolitical relations are associated with reductions in collaborations in scientific publications that are roughly three times larger than the gains associated with equivalent improvements, suggesting that international research partnerships are easier to damage than to build. At the technology level, critical technologies exhibit approximately three times the expected level of international collaboration compared to other fields (conditional on country-pair effects), yet are also more sensitive to shifts in geopolitical alignment, raising concerns about technology sovereignty. At the same time, despite ongoing geopolitical tensions, overall collaboration patterns have not undergone substantial changes in recent years, suggesting resilience in international research and innovation networks.

•
Geopolitical divergence is associated with fewer international research collaborations.
•
Science collaboration is three times more sensitive to worsening than improving ties.
•
Critical technologies are more collaborative but also more geopolitically sensitive.
•
Overall collaboration patterns appear resilient despite geopolitical tensions.
•

This paper analyzes the association between geopolitical alignment and international research and innovation collaborations using data spanning 2000–2023. Using ideal point distance measures derived from UN General Assembly voting patterns, we find that increases in geopolitical distance are associated with reductions in international collaborations. A one-unit increase in geopolitical distance (roughly the distance between a median country pair) over three years is associated with a 3.1% reduction in collaborations in scientific publications (0.8% per standard deviation). We also find that this relationship is asymmetric: worsening geopolitical relations are associated with reductions in collaborations in scientific publications that are roughly three times larger than the gains associated with equivalent improvements, suggesting that international research partnerships are easier to damage than to build. At the technology level, critical technologies exhibit approximately three times the expected level of international collaboration compared to other fields (conditional on country-pair effects), yet are also more sensitive to shifts in geopolitical alignment, raising concerns about technology sovereignty. At the same time, despite ongoing geopolitical tensions, overall collaboration patterns have not undergone substantial changes in recent years, suggesting resilience in international research and innovation networks.

This era has fostered unprecedented number of collaborations (Hou et al., 2021) and reduced the role of distance in the exchange of ideas (Griffith et al., 2011, Li, 2014, Head et al., 2019). These developments have substantially contributed to global economic growth, scientific progress, and innovation. However, the landscape of globalization is shifting. Rising protectionism, geopolitical tensions, and fragmented supply chains threaten the free flow of goods and investment, and increasingly restrict the movement of individuals. These challenges risk hampering scientific and technological progress, particularly by fragmenting global research and innovation networks.Despite extensive research on the determinants of inter-country collaborations (e.g., Picci, 2010), a significant gap remains in understanding how geopolitical alignment relates to collaborations. In this paper, we aim to fill this gap by examining how changes in geopolitical alignment are associated with international research and innovation collaboration patterns. Building on recent research examining political divergence and international collaborations (Charpin et al., 2024), as well as the economic costs of fragmentation (Javorcik et al., 2024, Gopinath et al., 2024, Aiyar et al., 2024, Bosone and Stamato, 2024), we use ideal point estimates from UN General Assembly voting data (Bailey et al., 2017, Voeten et al., 2009) to construct continuous measures of geopolitical distance between countries.Using gravity models following the literature on international trade (reviewed in Head and Mayer, 2014) and innovation (Picci, 2010), we find that increases in geopolitical distance over three-year periods are negatively associated with scientific collaborations, with a 3.1% reduction per unit increase in ideal point distance (IPD) changes over a 3-year horizon. A one-unit change is roughly the same magnitude as the ideal point distance between a median country pair. The standard deviation of IPD change is approximately 0.25, implying that a one-standard-deviation increase in geopolitical divergence is associated with a 0.8% reduction in collaboration. We also find that this association is asymmetric: worsening geopolitical relations are associated with reductions in scientific collaborations that are roughly three times larger than the gains from equivalent improvements, consistent with the idea that collaborative relationships are easier to break than to build (Baldwin and Krugman, 1989, Dixit, 1989). However, despite recent geopolitical rifts, we do not observe a significant shift in overall collaboration patterns.Global collaborations are particularly important in what we define as “critical technologies”, referring to technologies with strategic geopolitical importance. Conditional on country-pair and year effects, our estimates imply that these technologies exhibit approximately three times the number of collaborations compared to non-critical fields. We find that collaborations in these fields show a stronger association with changes in geopolitical alignment, particularly for collaborations involving the United States and China, raising important concerns about technological sovereignty and political risk.As such, while collaboration patterns have remained relatively stable in recent years, emerging geopolitical tensions pose risks to scientific and technological partnerships. Collaborations are particularly prevalent in critical technologies, making these fields especially vulnerable. Given global challenges that rely on these critical technologies, this raises the question of how necessary science and technology can be advanced in spite of geopolitical rifts.The paper is structured as follows. In Section 5, we examine the association between geopolitical distance and overall collaboration patterns, test for directional asymmetry in worsening versus improving geopolitical relations, and analyze collaborations in critical technologies. fields.abstract: This paper analyzes the association between geopolitical alignment and international research and innovation collaborations using data spanning 2000–2023. Using ideal point distance measures derived from UN General Assembly voting patterns, we find that increases in geopolitical distance are associated with reductions in international collaborations. A one-unit increase in geopolitical distance (roughly the distance between a median country pair) over three years is associated with a 3.1% reduction in collaborations in scientific publications (0.8% per standard deviation). We also find that this relationship is asymmetric: worsening geopolitical relations are associated with reductions in collaborations in scientific publications that are roughly three times larger than the gains associated with equivalent improvements, suggesting that international research partnerships are easier to damage than to build. At the technology level, critical technologies exhibit approximately three times the expected level of international collaboration compared to other fields (conditional on country-pair effects), yet are also more sensitive to shifts in geopolitical alignment, raising concerns about technology sovereignty. At the same time, despite ongoing geopolitical tensions, overall collaboration patterns have not undergone substantial changes in recent years, suggesting resilience in international research and innovation networks.

This paper analyzes the association between geopolitical alignment and international research and innovation collaborations using data spanning 2000–2023. Using ideal point distance measures derived from UN General Assembly voting patterns, we find that increases in geopolitical distance are associated with reductions in international collaborations. A one-unit increase in geopolitical distance (roughly the distance between a median country pair) over three years is associated with a 3.1% reduction in collaborations in scientific publications (0.8% per standard deviation). We also find that this relationship is asymmetric: worsening geopolitical relations are associated with reductions in collaborations in scientific publications that are roughly three times larger than the gains associated with equivalent improvements, suggesting that international research partnerships are easier to damage than to build. At the technology level, critical technologies exhibit approximately three times the expected level of international collaboration compared to other fields (conditional on country-pair effects), yet are also more sensitive to shifts in geopolitical alignment, raising concerns about technology sovereignty. At the same time, despite ongoing geopolitical tensions, overall collaboration patterns have not undergone substantial changes in recent years, suggesting resilience in international research and innovation networks.

This era has fostered unprecedented number of collaborations (Hou et al., 2021) and reduced the role of distance in the exchange of ideas (Griffith et al., 2011, Li, 2014, Head et al., 2019). These developments have substantially contributed to global economic growth, scientific progress, and innovation. However, the landscape of globalization is shifting. Rising protectionism, geopolitical tensions, and fragmented supply chains threaten the free flow of goods and investment, and increasingly restrict the movement of individuals. These challenges risk hampering scientific and technological progress, particularly by fragmenting global research and innovation networks.Despite extensive research on the determinants of inter-country collaborations (e.g., Picci, 2010), a significant gap remains in understanding how geopolitical alignment relates to collaborations. In this paper, we aim to fill this gap by examining how changes in geopolitical alignment are associated with international research and innovation collaboration patterns. Building on recent research examining political divergence and international collaborations (Charpin et al., 2024), as well as the economic costs of fragmentation (Javorcik et al., 2024, Gopinath et al., 2024, Aiyar et al., 2024, Bosone and Stamato, 2024), we use ideal point estimates from UN General Assembly voting data (Bailey et al., 2017, Voeten et al., 2009) to construct continuous measures of geopolitical distance between countries.Using gravity models following the literature on international trade (reviewed in Head and Mayer, 2014) and innovation (Picci, 2010), we find that increases in geopolitical distance over three-year periods are negatively associated with scientific collaborations, with a 3.1% reduction per unit increase in ideal point distance (IPD) changes over a 3-year horizon. A one-unit change is roughly the same magnitude as the ideal point distance between a median country pair. The standard deviation of IPD change is approximately 0.25, implying that a one-standard-deviation increase in geopolitical divergence is associated with a 0.8% reduction in collaboration. We also find that this association is asymmetric: worsening geopolitical relations are associated with reductions in scientific collaborations that are roughly three times larger than the gains from equivalent improvements, consistent with the idea that collaborative relationships are easier to break than to build (Baldwin and Krugman, 1989, Dixit, 1989). However, despite recent geopolitical rifts, we do not observe a significant shift in overall collaboration patterns.Global collaborations are particularly important in what we define as “critical technologies”, referring to technologies with strategic geopolitical importance. Conditional on country-pair and year effects, our estimates imply that these technologies exhibit approximately three times the number of collaborations compared to non-critical fields. We find that collaborations in these fields show a stronger association with changes in geopolitical alignment, particularly for collaborations involving the United States and China, raising important concerns about technological sovereignty and political risk.As such, while collaboration patterns have remained relatively stable in recent years, emerging geopolitical tensions pose risks to scientific and technological partnerships. Collaborations are particularly prevalent in critical technologies, making these fields especially vulnerable. Given global challenges that rely on these critical technologies, this raises the question of how necessary science and technology can be advanced in spite of geopolitical rifts.The paper is structured as follows. In Section 4, we analyze collaboration patterns in science and technology. In Section 5, we examine the association between geopolitical distance and overall collaboration patterns, test for directional asymmetry in worsening versus improving geopolitical relations, and analyze collaborations in critical technologies. proposed.title: Burning bridges or bridging divides: Geopolitics and collaboration in research and innovation
proposed.abstract:
•
Geopolitical divergence is associated with fewer international research collaborations.
•
Science collaboration is three times more sensitive to worsening than improving ties.
•
Critical technologies are more collaborative but also more geopolitically sensitive.
•
Overall collaboration patterns appear resilient despite geopolitical tensions.
•
US–China dynamics drive heightened geopolitical sensitivity in critical technologies.

fields.authors: Shreyas Gadgin Matha a, Matte Hartog a, Christian Chacua a, Pierre-Alexandre Balland a b, Ricardo Hausmann a, Muhammed Ali Yıldırım a c d
fields.abstract: This paper analyzes the association between geopolitical alignment and international research and innovation collaborations using data spanning 2000–2023. Using ideal point distance measures derived from UN General Assembly voting patterns, we find that increases in geopolitical distance are associated with reductions in international collaborations. A one-unit increase in geopolitical distance (roughly the distance between a median country pair) over three years is associated with a 3.1% reduction in collaborations in scientific publications (0.8% per standard deviation). We also find that this relationship is asymmetric: worsening geopolitical relations are associated with reductions in collaborations in scientific publications that are roughly three times larger than the gains associated with equivalent improvements, suggesting that international research partnerships are easier to damage than to build. At the technology level, critical technologies exhibit approximately three times the expected level of international collaboration compared to other fields (conditional on country-pair effects), yet are also more sensitive to shifts in geopolitical alignment, raising concerns about technology sovereignty. At the same time, despite ongoing geopolitical tensions, overall collaboration patterns have not undergone substantial changes in recent years, suggesting resilience in international research and innovation networks.

We address this question by leveraging the staggered adoption of Twitter by three top economics journals: the Journal of Political Economy, the Quarterly Journal of Economics, and the Review of Economics and Statistics, to compare citation counts for promoted versus non-promoted articles. We find that institutional promotion increases citations, primarily by exposing research to audiences beyond economics and thereby fostering interdisciplinarity. The effect is larger for high-status authors, and we find suggestive evidence that it operates partly through authors' own networks. At the same time, because the gains accrue disproportionately to already-visible authors, they raise concerns about inequities in scholarly recognition.

Citations in 280 characters: Is social media presence worth it for elite journals?

•
Elite journals gain citations from institutional Twitter promotion.
•
Articles promoted on social media attract more citations beyond their focal discipline.
•
High-status authors receive larger citation gains from journal promotion.
•
Promotion effects build over time, accelerating scholarly recognition.
•
Social media promotion may reinforce unequal scholarly visibility.

Is it worthwhile for elite journals to actively promote their articles through an official social media account? We address this question by leveraging the staggered adoption of Twitter by three top economics journals: the Journal of Political Economy, the Quarterly Journal of Economics, and the Review of Economics and Statistics, to compare citation counts for promoted versus non-promoted articles. We find that institutional promotion increases citations, primarily by exposing research to audiences beyond economics and thereby fostering interdisciplinarity. The effect is larger for high-status authors, and we find suggestive evidence that it operates partly through authors' own networks. The way articles are presented, such as through visual aids, may further amplify their impact. These results show that active institutional promotion can enhance research dissemination even for journals that already command the lion's share of academic attention. At the same time, because the gains accrue disproportionately to already-visible authors, they raise concerns about inequities in scholarly recognition.

Sixteen months later, on May 23, 2023, the account became inactive until August 25, 2025, when it was reactivated.1 Did that temporary closure have an effect on the scholarly impact of SMJ articles that were not promoted on Twitter?This example of SMJ's interrupted foray into social media motivates the central question of this paper: is it worthwhile for elite journals to actively promote their articles through an official social media account? Or is non-engagement, as seen in some top journals like Research Policy, a more efficient approach?On the one hand, in an era of information overload and high search costs for scientists, social media has emerged as an essential tool for researchers for filtering and discovering relevant articles (Anderson and de Palma, 2012; Aridor et al., 2024; Boudreau et al., 2017; Catalini et al., 2020; Mohammadi et al., 2018; Osterloh and Frey, 2020; Starbuck, 2005). This suggests that a social media presence for leading journals might be valuable. Such a social media presence could enhance dissemination by drawing additional attention to articles, or, in a competitive academic landscape, mitigate the risk of losing visibility to other elite journals with active social media engagement.On the other hand, maintaining an active social media presence is costly as it requires material resources, such as hiring social media managers or expanding editorial duties (costs we confirmed, as presented below, through outreach to top journals). Social media exposure may be particularly redundant for elite journals, as researchers already prioritize and frequently cite articles from prestigious outlets (Drivas and Kremmydas, 2020; Heckman and Moktan, 2020; Rubin and Rubin, 2021). As such, traditional channels, such as mailing lists, academic databases, and search engines may be sufficient to ensure that articles in the top journals receive enough attention and are disseminated broadly (Feenberg et al., 2017; McCabe and Snyder, 2015).Extant research has not resolved this puzzle. First, prior work examining tweets from non-journal accounts reports mixed evidence regarding elite journals; Finch et al. (2017) show that articles tweeted by non-journal accounts (mostly users) associate with more citations, but this effect weakens or disappears for papers in high-impact journals. In contrast, Cao et al. (2023) find that articles in elite journals tweeted by non-journal accounts diffuse faster and more broadly on social media than those from non-elite journals. Second, more recent studies employing experimental or quasi-experimental approaches yielding causal estimates have not distinguished between elite and non-elite journals. Chan et al. (2023) use an instrumental variable approach to analyze columns published on VoxEU and find that the presence of at least one tweet increased citations by 16–25%. Similarly, Sofer (2024) reports positive citation effects using NBER working papers published between 2015 and 2018. While informative for forming priors as they both refer to elite settings, these cases differ fundamentally from elite journals. For working-paper platforms (e.g., NBER) and policy-diffusion outlets (e.g., VoxEU), broad dissemination and visibility are core institutional objectives. Put simply, they exist to disseminate and social media promotion is closely aligned with their primary function of maximizing research exposure. In contrast, elite journals, primarily, certify and select rather than maximize reach. The articles they publish are already indexed, circulated through institutional channels, flagged by alert systems, and monitored by the researchers most likely to cite them. For these articles, the audiences a tweet would reach are more likely to have encountered the work through other channels. The marginal informational value of social media promotion is therefore unclear ex ante, which is what makes elite journals a distinct and arguably “least-likely” setting for additional dissemination effects.2 Moreover, because the importance of the elite-journal setting lies precisely in helping identify the margins along which institutional social media promotion can still matter, we also do not know whether active institutional promotion shapes who discovers and amplifies research even in environments where baseline visibility is already strong.3 As we elaborate later, we identify several margins along which promotion matters.Against this background, we build on the recent quasi-experimental approaches to assess whether active official journal accounts enhance the scholarly influence of articles published in those journals. To do that, we exploit the staggered adoption of Twitter (now X) accounts by three leading economics journals: Journal of Political Economy (JPE); Quarterly Journal of Economics (QJE); and Review of Economics and Statistics (ReStat), between 2012 and 2019. Prior to the launch of their Twitter accounts, articles from these journals were not shared on social media (though we account for articles exposed by non-journal accounts). We leverage this timeline to compare the accumulation of citations for articles exposed to Twitter shortly after the account launch (the treatment group) with those published just before the launch (the control group). To account for potential journal-specific effects, we form three additional control groups from articles published in comparable journals without a Twitter account.To examine whether our results extend beyond economics, we also conducted a structured review of 55 journals across management, finance, sociology, political science, public policy, and related fields, drawn primarily from the FT50 and UT Dallas lists. We identified six journals with article promotion practices similar to those in our main study: Journal of Marketing, Journal of Marketing Research, American Sociological Review, Journal of Politics, Journal of Management, and International Organization. For each journal, we compared articles published immediately before the launch of the journal's Twitter account with articles promoted immediately after the launch. The results are consistent with our main findings.Our research design offers three main empirical advantages that address associated endogeneity concerns. First, if higher-quality articles attract more citations, testing the impact of their presence on social media requires comparing articles of similar intrinsic quality. We build the baseline within-journal comparison for that reason, ensuring constant editorial standards, author quality, topic selection, reviewer pool, and overall article quality since articles published just before and after the cut-off are likely similar along these dimensions. Moreover, we rule out journal-specific effects through a complementary between-journal comparison that examines articles published in journals of comparable prestige and quality.Second, identifying the effect of social media presence requires overcoming selection bias, which could arise if (top) journals selectively promote articles based on content, topic, or author prominence. Our design mitigates this concern, as the treated journals tweet all of the articles they publish following the creation of their account (with one exception discussed below), ensuring exposure is not driven by editorial or social media account manager choice.Third, a potential confound is that authors might have strategically timed submissions to coincide with the Twitter account launch, resulting in a non-representative subset of articles receiving exposure. Our design minimizes this source of endogeneity because the launches were unannounced, making such strategic timing highly unlikely.Based on our preferred specification, we find that articles shared by top economics journals on Twitter receive, on average, 0.142 additional citations per month compared to similar articles without such exposure. Given that most citations occur within a 10-year window following publication (Ke et al., 2015), under a constant monthly effect consistent with the citation patterns of these journals, this Twitter exposure translates into a citation premium of 17 citations per article. This premium is significant as it represents around 20% of the total citations accumulated by the average article in these journals before the launch of their Twitter accounts.4Building on this baseline estimate, we first reinforce our findings via a number of robustness checks. Then, aligned with the notion that existing works have not zoomed in identifying the margins along which institutional social media promotion can still matter for elite journals we a) test the empirical grounding of potential theoretical mechanisms driving the results, b) explore heterogeneity in the average treatment effect and c) analyze the temporal dynamics of the main effect. These analyses reveal four main results. First, the main effect arises from exposing research to authors outside economics, who then cite the work, thereby fostering interdisciplinarity — defined here as the exchange and integration of ideas and methods across disciplinary boundaries, as reflected in citation patterns (Uzzi et al., 2013). Second, the main effect is amplified when the articles are authored by high-status researchers, indicating an additive effect of journal and author status. Third, with the caveat of limited sample size for the corresponding analysis, we reveal suggestive evidence that articles promoted with images related to article content or graphs receive additional citations. Fourth, the citation boost emerges gradually, with little effect immediately after publication, with a clear and sustained increase from approximately months 9 to 12 after publication. This pattern indicates that promotion of articles on social media accelerates knowledge diffusion and shortens the lag time between publication and scholarly recognition, highlighting the dynamic timing of the Twitter effect (Eysenbach, 2011; Shuai et al., 2012; Thelwall et al., 2013).Our findings contribute to three streams of literature within the broader theme of how effective knowledge dissemination underpins scientific progress (Furman and Stern, 2011; Mokyr, 2011). First, we add to research on knowledge dissemination in the sciences (Drivas and Kremmydas, 2020; Feenberg et al., 2017; Reschke et al., 2018) by identifying the role of social media in amplifying academic influence through citation counts. Within this stream, our study is novel in focusing on top-tier journals, where the impact of social media is ex-ante ambiguous and prior work has been limited and descriptive (Cao et al., 2023; Finch et al., 2017). Instead, we build a quasi-experimental research design to estimate the effect of exposure on social media, extending recent efforts that have examined dissemination dynamics outside elite journals (Branch et al., 2024; Chan et al., 2023; Sofer, 2024).Second, we address previously unexplored questions including whether social media affects interdisciplinarity, how these effects evolve over time, and how the choice architecture of dissemination platforms conditions the ability of leading journals to harness the potential of social media. We also contribute to the literature on cumulative advantage and the Matthew effect in science (Merton, 1968; Azoulay et al., 2014; Bol et al., 2018) by showing that high-status authors receive a larger citation boost than low status authors when their work is promoted on journals' Twitter accounts.Third, we add to the body of work in management, economics, and marketing, that analyzes the outcomes of social media adoption, such as its effects on public figures' financial gains, work performance, and employee cognition (Leonardi, 2018; Petrova et al., 2021; Wu and Kane, 2021). We contribute to this body of research by showing that institutional social media accounts of top academic journals can similarly enhance the visibility and scholarly impact of published research. Our findings provide evidence that even in academic publishing, where multiple routes can generate impact, including network activities and author status, social media can play a pivotal role in boosting citation accumulation.On a practical level, the immediate takeaway of our estimates is that top journals benefit from social media engagement as it significantly enhances the scholarly impact of the articles they publish. More generally, our findings are relevant given that approximately 90% of journals in the humanities and social sciences have yet to adopt social media (Raamkumar et al., 2019). The results imply that despite the financial and administrative challenges of maintaining a social media presence, journals and their authors may face disadvantages without it. Competition for attention and search costs in the sciences are high and tenure and promotion decisions are often contingent on citation records (Anderson and de Palma, 2012; Boudreau et al., 2017; Catalini et al., 2020; Moher et al., 2018). In such an environment, journals without a social media strategy risk being overshadowed by those that actively embrace online platforms, ultimately diminishing their academic influence.Organizational accessGet full-text access by signing in with your organisationAccess through your organizationOther access optionsPurchase PDFNeed help with access?Section snippetsLiterature reviewThe search for knowledge and information shapes the nature and direction of scientific progress (Simon, 1977; Simon and Simon, 1962). Long-standing theories of scientific communication emphasize that visibility and reputation underpin cumulative advantage in citations, where early attention compounds over time through processes of preferential attachment (Merton, 1968; Price, 1976). In today's research environment, these same dynamics unfold within a far more complex and rapidly expandingEmpirical specificationTo study the potential effects of journal social media account use on citation rates, we use Twitter, which offers a consistent and measurable channel of institutional promotion across journals. This focus implies that journals without Twitter accounts may still maintain other forms of online or social media presence; our design isolates the marginal effect of visibility generated through Twitter activity.Our empirical design compares citation counts for articles showcased online by journalMain resultsTable 3 presents the baseline estimates, sequentially comparing treatment group articles to each of the four control groups.19 For reference, column 5 (Model 5) pools articles from all control groups. Across the board, we can conclude that there is a citation premium for articles promoted by top journal officialRobustness checksGiven the consistent rigor in the peer review process applied to all articles in top journals (Severin et al., 2023), we expect minimal heterogeneity in terms of quality, potential impact and related factors among articles published in the same or similar top journals. proposed.title: Citations in 280 characters: Is social media presence worth it for elite journals?
proposed.abstract: Is it worthwhile for elite journals to actively promote their articles through an official social media account? We address this question by leveraging the staggered adoption of Twitter by three top economics journals: the Journal of Political Economy, the Quarterly Journal of Economics, and the Review of Economics and Statistics, to compare citation counts for promoted versus non-promoted articles. We find that institutional promotion increases citations, primarily by exposing research to audiences beyond economics and thereby fostering interdisciplinarity. The effect is larger for high-status authors, and we find suggestive evidence that it operates partly through authors' own networks. The way articles are presented, such as through visual aids, may further amplify their impact. These results show that active institutional promotion can enhance research dissemination even for journals that already command the lion's share of academic attention. At the same time, because the gains accrue disproportionately to already-visible authors, they raise concerns about inequities in scholarly recognition.

Citations in 280 characters: Is social media presence worth it for elite journals?

•
Elite journals gain citations from institutional Twitter promotion.
•
Articles promoted on social media attract more citations beyond their focal discipline.
•
High-status authors receive larger citation gains from journal promotion.
•
Promotion effects build over time, accelerating scholarly recognition.
•
Social media promotion may reinforce unequal scholarly visibility.

Is it worthwhile for elite journals to actively promote their articles through an official social media account? We address this question by leveraging the staggered adoption of Twitter by three top economics journals: the Journal of Political Economy, the Quarterly Journal of Economics, and the Review of Economics and Statistics, to compare citation counts for promoted versus non-promoted articles. We find that institutional promotion increases citations, primarily by exposing research to audiences beyond economics and thereby fostering interdisciplinarity. The effect is larger for high-status authors, and we find suggestive evidence that it operates partly through authors' own networks. The way articles are presented, such as through visual aids, may further amplify their impact. These results show that active institutional promotion can enhance research dissemination even for journals that already command the lion's share of academic attention. At the same time, because the gains accrue disproportionately to already-visible authors, they raise concerns about inequities in scholarly recognition.
