Sixteen months later, on May 23, 2023, the account became inactive until August 25, 2025, when it was reactivated.1 Did that temporary closure have an effect on the scholarly impact of SMJ articles that were not promoted on Twitter?This example of SMJ's interrupted foray into social media motivates the central question of this paper: is it worthwhile for elite journals to actively promote their articles through an official social media account? Or is non-engagement, as seen in some top journals like Research Policy, a more efficient approach?On the one hand, in an era of information overload and high search costs for scientists, social media has emerged as an essential tool for researchers for filtering and discovering relevant articles (Anderson and de Palma, 2012; Aridor et al., 2024; Boudreau et al., 2017; Catalini et al., 2020; Mohammadi et al., 2018; Osterloh and Frey, 2020; Starbuck, 2005). This suggests that a social media presence for leading journals might be valuable. Such a social media presence could enhance dissemination by drawing additional attention to articles, or, in a competitive academic landscape, mitigate the risk of losing visibility to other elite journals with active social media engagement.On the other hand, maintaining an active social media presence is costly as it requires material resources, such as hiring social media managers or expanding editorial duties (costs we confirmed, as presented below, through outreach to top journals). Social media exposure may be particularly redundant for elite journals, as researchers already prioritize and frequently cite articles from prestigious outlets (Drivas and Kremmydas, 2020; Heckman and Moktan, 2020; Rubin and Rubin, 2021). As such, traditional channels, such as mailing lists, academic databases, and search engines may be sufficient to ensure that articles in the top journals receive enough attention and are disseminated broadly (Feenberg et al., 2017; McCabe and Snyder, 2015).Extant research has not resolved this puzzle. First, prior work examining tweets from non-journal accounts reports mixed evidence regarding elite journals; Finch et al. (2017) show that articles tweeted by non-journal accounts (mostly users) associate with more citations, but this effect weakens or disappears for papers in high-impact journals. In contrast, Cao et al. (2023) find that articles in elite journals tweeted by non-journal accounts diffuse faster and more broadly on social media than those from non-elite journals. Second, more recent studies employing experimental or quasi-experimental approaches yielding causal estimates have not distinguished between elite and non-elite journals. Chan et al. (2023) use an instrumental variable approach to analyze columns published on VoxEU and find that the presence of at least one tweet increased citations by 16–25%. Similarly, Sofer (2024) reports positive citation effects using NBER working papers published between 2015 and 2018. While informative for forming priors as they both refer to elite settings, these cases differ fundamentally from elite journals. For working-paper platforms (e.g., NBER) and policy-diffusion outlets (e.g., VoxEU), broad dissemination and visibility are core institutional objectives. Put simply, they exist to disseminate and social media promotion is closely aligned with their primary function of maximizing research exposure. In contrast, elite journals, primarily, certify and select rather than maximize reach. The articles they publish are already indexed, circulated through institutional channels, flagged by alert systems, and monitored by the researchers most likely to cite them. For these articles, the audiences a tweet would reach are more likely to have encountered the work through other channels. The marginal informational value of social media promotion is therefore unclear ex ante, which is what makes elite journals a distinct and arguably “least-likely” setting for additional dissemination effects.2 Moreover, because the importance of the elite-journal setting lies precisely in helping identify the margins along which institutional social media promotion can still matter, we also do not know whether active institutional promotion shapes who discovers and amplifies research even in environments where baseline visibility is already strong.3 As we elaborate later, we identify several margins along which promotion matters.Against this background, we build on the recent quasi-experimental approaches to assess whether active official journal accounts enhance the scholarly influence of articles published in those journals. To do that, we exploit the staggered adoption of Twitter (now X) accounts by three leading economics journals: Journal of Political Economy (JPE); Quarterly Journal of Economics (QJE); and Review of Economics and Statistics (ReStat), between 2012 and 2019. Prior to the launch of their Twitter accounts, articles from these journals were not shared on social media (though we account for articles exposed by non-journal accounts). We leverage this timeline to compare the accumulation of citations for articles exposed to Twitter shortly after the account launch (the treatment group) with those published just before the launch (the control group). To account for potential journal-specific effects, we form three additional control groups from articles published in comparable journals without a Twitter account.To examine whether our results extend beyond economics, we also conducted a structured review of 55 journals across management, finance, sociology, political science, public policy, and related fields, drawn primarily from the FT50 and UT Dallas lists. We identified six journals with article promotion practices similar to those in our main study: Journal of Marketing, Journal of Marketing Research, American Sociological Review, Journal of Politics, Journal of Management, and International Organization. For each journal, we compared articles published immediately before the launch of the journal's Twitter account with articles promoted immediately after the launch. The results are consistent with our main findings.Our research design offers three main empirical advantages that address associated endogeneity concerns. First, if higher-quality articles attract more citations, testing the impact of their presence on social media requires comparing articles of similar intrinsic quality. We build the baseline within-journal comparison for that reason, ensuring constant editorial standards, author quality, topic selection, reviewer pool, and overall article quality since articles published just before and after the cut-off are likely similar along these dimensions. Moreover, we rule out journal-specific effects through a complementary between-journal comparison that examines articles published in journals of comparable prestige and quality.Second, identifying the effect of social media presence requires overcoming selection bias, which could arise if (top) journals selectively promote articles based on content, topic, or author prominence. Our design mitigates this concern, as the treated journals tweet all of the articles they publish following the creation of their account (with one exception discussed below), ensuring exposure is not driven by editorial or social media account manager choice.Third, a potential confound is that authors might have strategically timed submissions to coincide with the Twitter account launch, resulting in a non-representative subset of articles receiving exposure. Our design minimizes this source of endogeneity because the launches were unannounced, making such strategic timing highly unlikely.Based on our preferred specification, we find that articles shared by top economics journals on Twitter receive, on average, 0.142 additional citations per month compared to similar articles without such exposure. Given that most citations occur within a 10-year window following publication (Ke et al., 2015), under a constant monthly effect consistent with the citation patterns of these journals, this Twitter exposure translates into a citation premium of 17 citations per article. This premium is significant as it represents around 20% of the total citations accumulated by the average article in these journals before the launch of their Twitter accounts.4Building on this baseline estimate, we first reinforce our findings via a number of robustness checks. Then, aligned with the notion that existing works have not zoomed in identifying the margins along which institutional social media promotion can still matter for elite journals we a) test the empirical grounding of potential theoretical mechanisms driving the results, b) explore heterogeneity in the average treatment effect and c) analyze the temporal dynamics of the main effect. These analyses reveal four main results. First, the main effect arises from exposing research to authors outside economics, who then cite the work, thereby fostering interdisciplinarity — defined here as the exchange and integration of ideas and methods across disciplinary boundaries, as reflected in citation patterns (Uzzi et al., 2013). Second, the main effect is amplified when the articles are authored by high-status researchers, indicating an additive effect of journal and author status. Third, with the caveat of limited sample size for the corresponding analysis, we reveal suggestive evidence that articles promoted with images related to article content or graphs receive additional citations. Fourth, the citation boost emerges gradually, with little effect immediately after publication, with a clear and sustained increase from approximately months 9 to 12 after publication. This pattern indicates that promotion of articles on social media accelerates knowledge diffusion and shortens the lag time between publication and scholarly recognition, highlighting the dynamic timing of the Twitter effect (Eysenbach, 2011; Shuai et al., 2012; Thelwall et al., 2013).Our findings contribute to three streams of literature within the broader theme of how effective knowledge dissemination underpins scientific progress (Furman and Stern, 2011; Mokyr, 2011). First, we add to research on knowledge dissemination in the sciences (Drivas and Kremmydas, 2020; Feenberg et al., 2017; Reschke et al., 2018) by identifying the role of social media in amplifying academic influence through citation counts. Within this stream, our study is novel in focusing on top-tier journals, where the impact of social media is ex-ante ambiguous and prior work has been limited and descriptive (Cao et al., 2023; Finch et al., 2017). Instead, we build a quasi-experimental research design to estimate the effect of exposure on social media, extending recent efforts that have examined dissemination dynamics outside elite journals (Branch et al., 2024; Chan et al., 2023; Sofer, 2024).Second, we address previously unexplored questions including whether social media affects interdisciplinarity, how these effects evolve over time, and how the choice architecture of dissemination platforms conditions the ability of leading journals to harness the potential of social media. We also contribute to the literature on cumulative advantage and the Matthew effect in science (Merton, 1968; Azoulay et al., 2014; Bol et al., 2018) by showing that high-status authors receive a larger citation boost than low status authors when their work is promoted on journals' Twitter accounts.Third, we add to the body of work in management, economics, and marketing, that analyzes the outcomes of social media adoption, such as its effects on public figures' financial gains, work performance, and employee cognition (Leonardi, 2018; Petrova et al., 2021; Wu and Kane, 2021). We contribute to this body of research by showing that institutional social media accounts of top academic journals can similarly enhance the visibility and scholarly impact of published research. Our findings provide evidence that even in academic publishing, where multiple routes can generate impact, including network activities and author status, social media can play a pivotal role in boosting citation accumulation.On a practical level, the immediate takeaway of our estimates is that top journals benefit from social media engagement as it significantly enhances the scholarly impact of the articles they publish. More generally, our findings are relevant given that approximately 90% of journals in the humanities and social sciences have yet to adopt social media (Raamkumar et al., 2019). The results imply that despite the financial and administrative challenges of maintaining a social media presence, journals and their authors may face disadvantages without it. Competition for attention and search costs in the sciences are high and tenure and promotion decisions are often contingent on citation records (Anderson and de Palma, 2012; Boudreau et al., 2017; Catalini et al., 2020; Moher et al., 2018). In such an environment, journals without a social media strategy risk being overshadowed by those that actively embrace online platforms, ultimately diminishing their academic influence.Organizational accessGet full-text access by signing in with your organisationAccess through your organizationOther access optionsPurchase PDFNeed help with access?Section snippetsLiterature reviewThe search for knowledge and information shapes the nature and direction of scientific progress (Simon, 1977; Simon and Simon, 1962). proposed.title: Citations in 280 characters: Is social media presence worth it for elite journals?
proposed.abstract: Is it worthwhile for elite journals to actively promote their articles through an official social media account? We address this question by leveraging the staggered adoption of Twitter by three top economics journals: the Journal of Political Economy, the Quarterly Journal of Economics, and the Review of Economics and Statistics, to compare citation counts for promoted versus non-promoted articles. We find that institutional promotion increases citations, primarily by exposing research to audiences beyond economics and thereby fostering interdisciplinarity. The effect is larger for high-status authors, and we find suggestive evidence that it operates partly through authors' own networks. The way articles are presented, such as through visual aids, may further amplify their impact. These results show that active institutional promotion can enhance research dissemination even for journals that already command the lion's share of academic attention. At the same time, because the gains accrue disproportionately to already-visible authors, they raise concerns about inequities in scholarly recognition.

source_records.abstract: We investigate how the global market integration of a firm's home country and the security salience of specific projects shape firms' propensity to form alliances during new product development. The Resource-Based View suggests that the development of technologically complex products often requires unique resources that may be unavailable domestically, driving firms to seek international partnerships. However, we propose that, in high-technology industries where national interests are at stake, alliances in the product development phase face unique constraints. They involve partner firms committing non-redeployable resources to a specific, well-defined product and to new assets and processes to manufacture it. Moreover, because this phase determines which specific features become available for commercial or military deployment, these alliances attract heightened scrutiny from governments, especially in security-sensitive projects. We thus propose that the well-established relationship between product complexity and alliance formation is negatively moderated by two major geopolitical factors: (i) the global market integration of the firm's home country and (ii) the national security salience of the project. Both conditions enable or enhance alternative pathways to resource access that reduce dependence on alliances. Using data on new aircraft development projects, we find support for our predictions. Our findings contribute to the understanding of how home-country global market integration and project national security salience shape firms' innovation strategies by affecting alliance formation decisions during product development.

According to the Resource-Based View, alliances allow firms to obtain difficult-to-trade resources, especially when developing technologically complex products that require substantial external resources (Das and Teng, 2000; Garrette et al., 2009; Rothaermel and Boeker, 2008). Such alliances can facilitate the acquisition of external knowledge in the research phase of the innovation process (Du et al., 2014; Kok et al., 2020; Rothaermel and Deeds, 2006) and support access to complementary assets in manufacturing and marketing during commercialization (Cunningham et al., 2021; Moeen and Mitchell, 2020; Rothaermel, 2001; Rothaermel and Deeds, 2006; Teece, 1986). Research on technology alliances has traditionally examined the research and commercialization phases, focusing on organizational and market-level conditions.However, many technological products have implications that extend beyond the firms producing them or the markets in which they are traded, also affecting their home country's national interests. Firms in high-technology industries such as aerospace, automotive, pharmaceuticals, electronics, and especially defense, regularly develop products with significant implications for national security, technology sovereignty, and economic competitiveness. The development of penicillin during World War II illustrates this phenomenon—a medical breakthrough that became crucial for military effectiveness (Klepper, 2015). Similarly, industries such as semiconductors, telecoms, and advanced materials also often involve dual-use applications, and spillovers between commercial and military projects in such industries happen routinely (Kotha, 2010). This dual-use potential creates a core tension for many firms in high-technology sectors: while they increasingly draw on global partners and resources to innovate and compete (Oxley and Sampson, 2004; Park, 1995), their home country governments may view such international collaborations with concern. As a result, while resource requirements may drive firms toward international collaboration, geopolitical and national security considerations may constrain these opportunities.Our study focuses on horizontal alliances during the product development phase in high-technology manufacturing industries with national security salience. The development phase—where firms transform proven concepts into manufacturable products—is distinct from both upstream research activities, which generate knowledge applicable across multiple products, and from downstream commercialization efforts, which leverage existing production capabilities (Arora et al., 2016; Chesbrough, 2003). Development phase alliances (or simply development alliances) have received relatively limited scholarly attention despite involving unique characteristics: they require product-specific and non-redeployable investments in tooling and specialized assets that often represent a large share of total R&D costs (Fleming, 2002; Vinokurova and Kapoor, 2020) and they determine which specific features become available for commercial or military deployment. These characteristics make development partnerships particularly visible to governments and subject to geopolitical and national security considerations, as international alliances in this phase directly shape national technological capabilities and security interests (Bonardi, 2004; Petricevic and Teece, 2019).While government involvement typically constrains market mechanisms, it may also provide privileged access to resources unavailable through markets, including public funding, infrastructure, and procurement commitments. Firms operating in security-sensitive sectors must therefore manage both market-based resource limitations and government oversight. Although national interests encompass many factors, in industries where alliances are international, government involvement is often influenced by geopolitical factors. These geopolitical factors are central to understanding how national interests affect the tension between market constraints and privileged resource access, ultimately influencing alliance formation and dynamics. Our study focuses on this tension and examines the following research question: under what conditions are firms' decisions to engage in international development alliances shaped not only by resource requirements but also by national interests? We argue that resource-based drivers of alliance formation interact with geopolitical considerations, creating a distinctive environment in which firms consider both market opportunities and political constraints.We directly build on prior research grounded in the Resource-Based View that has established that technologically complex product development projects—those requiring diverse, interdependent technologies and specialized knowledge that must be integrated in non-trivial ways to achieve demanding performance specifications (Ethiraj and Levinthal, 2004; Ethiraj and Posen, 2013)—are associated with higher resource requirements, prompting firms to form alliances (Garrette et al., 2009; Rothaermel and Boeker, 2008). Taking this established finding as a baseline, we examine how this relationship is moderated by two geopolitical factors: (i) the global market integration of the firm's home country, and (ii) the project's national security salience. We argue that both factors create alternative means of accessing key resources, thus reducing firms' reliance on alliances.A firm's home country global market integration—the extent to which a country is integrated into international economic institutions, trade agreements, and cooperative frameworks—can facilitate access to foreign markets, technologies, and components through market channels, reducing the relative advantage of alliances for resource acquisition (Jandhyala and Phene, 2015; Soule et al., 2014). In parallel, projects with high national security salience may receive direct government support, including funding, access to infrastructure, and procurement guarantees, reducing the need for resource-sharing through alliances. Governments may also discourage foreign partnerships to limit knowledge leakage (Devarakonda and Reuer, 2018; Gomes-Casseres et al., 2006).We test our theoretical model in the global aircraft manufacturing industry, which is characterized by high fixed costs concentrated in the development phase (Dussauge and Garrette, 1995). Aircraft manufacturing has both a commercial and a defense component and requires access to global markets, making it an ideal context to examine the interplay between technological complexity, national interests, and alliance formation (Boubakri et al., 2009; Teece, 1991; Yoshitomi, 1991). According to the Resource-Based View, alliances allow firms to obtain difficult-to-trade resources, especially when developing technologically complex products that require substantial external resources (Das and Teng, 2000; Garrette et al., 2009; Rothaermel and Boeker, 2008). Such alliances can facilitate the acquisition of external knowledge in the research phase of the innovation process (Du et al., 2014; Kok et al., 2020; Rothaermel and Deeds, 2006) and support access to complementary assets in manufacturing and marketing during commercialization (Cunningham et al., 2021; Moeen and Mitchell, 2020; Rothaermel, 2001; Rothaermel and Deeds, 2006; Teece, 1986). Research on technology alliances has traditionally examined the research and commercialization phases, focusing on organizational and market-level conditions.However, many technological products have implications that extend beyond the firms producing them or the markets in which they are traded, also affecting their home country's national interests. Firms in high-technology industries such as aerospace, automotive, pharmaceuticals, electronics, and especially defense, regularly develop products with significant implications for national security, technology sovereignty, and economic competitiveness. The development of penicillin during World War II illustrates this phenomenon—a medical breakthrough that became crucial for military effectiveness (Klepper, 2015). Similarly, industries such as semiconductors, telecoms, and advanced materials also often involve dual-use applications, and spillovers between commercial and military projects in such industries happen routinely (Kotha, 2010). This dual-use potential creates a core tension for many firms in high-technology sectors: while they increasingly draw on global partners and resources to innovate and compete (Oxley and Sampson, 2004; Park, 1995), their home country governments may view such international collaborations with concern. As a result, while resource requirements may drive firms toward international collaboration, geopolitical and national security considerations may constrain these opportunities.Our study focuses on horizontal alliances during the product development phase in high-technology manufacturing industries with national security salience. The development phase—where firms transform proven concepts into manufacturable products—is distinct from both upstream research activities, which generate knowledge applicable across multiple products, and from downstream commercialization efforts, which leverage existing production capabilities (Arora et al., 2016; Chesbrough, 2003). Development phase alliances (or simply development alliances) have received relatively limited scholarly attention despite involving unique characteristics: they require product-specific and non-redeployable investments in tooling and specialized assets that often represent a large share of total R&D costs (Fleming, 2002; Vinokurova and Kapoor, 2020) and they determine which specific features become available for commercial or military deployment. These characteristics make development partnerships particularly visible to governments and subject to geopolitical and national security considerations, as international alliances in this phase directly shape national technological capabilities and security interests (Bonardi, 2004; Petricevic and Teece, 2019).While government involvement typically constrains market mechanisms, it may also provide privileged access to resources unavailable through markets, including public funding, infrastructure, and procurement commitments. Firms operating in security-sensitive sectors must therefore manage both market-based resource limitations and government oversight. Although national interests encompass many factors, in industries where alliances are international, government involvement is often influenced by geopolitical factors. These geopolitical factors are central to understanding how national interests affect the tension between market constraints and privileged resource access, ultimately influencing alliance formation and dynamics. Our study focuses on this tension and examines the following research question: under what conditions are firms' decisions to engage in international development alliances shaped not only by resource requirements but also by national interests? We argue that resource-based drivers of alliance formation interact with geopolitical considerations, creating a distinctive environment in which firms consider both market opportunities and political constraints.We directly build on prior research grounded in the Resource-Based View that has established that technologically complex product development projects—those requiring diverse, interdependent technologies and specialized knowledge that must be integrated in non-trivial ways to achieve demanding performance specifications (Ethiraj and Levinthal, 2004; Ethiraj and Posen, 2013)—are associated with higher resource requirements, prompting firms to form alliances (Garrette et al., 2009; Rothaermel and Boeker, 2008). Taking this established finding as a baseline, we examine how this relationship is moderated by two geopolitical factors: (i) the global market integration of the firm's home country, and (ii) the project's national security salience. We argue that both factors create alternative means of accessing key resources, thus reducing firms' reliance on alliances.A firm's home country global market integration—the extent to which a country is integrated into international economic institutions, trade agreements, and cooperative frameworks—can facilitate access to foreign markets, technologies, and components through market channels, reducing the relative advantage of alliances for resource acquisition (Jandhyala and Phene, 2015; Soule et al., 2014). In parallel, projects with high national security salience may receive direct government support, including funding, access to infrastructure, and procurement guarantees, reducing the need for resource-sharing through alliances. Governments may also discourage foreign partnerships to limit knowledge leakage (Devarakonda and Reuer, 2018; Gomes-Casseres et al., 2006).We test our theoretical model in the global aircraft manufacturing industry, which is characterized by high fixed costs concentrated in the development phase (Dussauge and Garrette, 1995). Aircraft manufacturing has both a commercial and a defense component and requires access to global markets, making it an ideal context to examine the interplay between technological complexity, national interests, and alliance formation (Boubakri et al., 2009; Teece, 1991; Yoshitomi, 1991). We examine whether a firm developing a new aircraft project does so through a horizontal alliance (i.e., two or more firms sharing prime-contractorship, excluding public-private partnerships) or on a solo firm basis (i.e., one firm taking on the full prime-contractor responsibility).Our data include the whole population of 334 new aircraft projects developed in non-communist countries during the 1944–2000 period. We capture a project's technological complexity based on its technical features (Castañer et al., 2014; Garrette et al., 2009). To capture geopolitical factors, we follow prior research in operationalizing (i) home country global market integration through the firm's home country memberships in intergovernmental organizations (IGOs) (Jandhyala and Phene, 2015; Soule et al., 2014), and (ii) national security salience as the extent to which an aircraft project is developed for military purposes (Dussauge and Garrette, 1995). We find support for our predictions.Our study contributes to three literatures. First, we advance research on innovation and technological change by focusing on the use of alliances in the underexplored development phase. Second, we extend theories on alliance formation by showing that geopolitical factors may shape firms' resource-seeking strategies. Third, we provide evidence that the global market integration of a firm's home country can affect alliance formation, contributing to international business research on home-country advantages.Organizational accessGet full-text access by signing in with your organisationAccess through your organizationOther access optionsPurchase PDFNeed help with access?Section snippetsThe development phase in innovationThe development phase of the innovation process represents a distinct stage that bridges upstream research and downstream commercialization. We investigate how geopolitical factors influence co-development alliances.

fields.title: Global market integration, national security salience, and new product development alliances in aircraft manufacturing
fields.authors: João Albino-Pimentel a b, Pierre Dussauge c, Louis Mulotte d, Elie Sung c, Stephen Tallman e
fields.abstract: We investigate how the global market integration of a firm's home country and the security salience of specific projects shape firms' propensity to form alliances during new product development. The Resource-Based View suggests that the development of technologically complex products often requires unique resources that may be unavailable domestically, driving firms to seek international partnerships. However, we propose that, in high-technology industries where national interests are at stake, alliances in the product development phase face unique constraints. They involve partner firms committing non-redeployable resources to a specific, well-defined product and to new assets and processes to manufacture it. Moreover, because this phase determines which specific features become available for commercial or military deployment, these alliances attract heightened scrutiny from governments, especially in security-sensitive projects. We thus propose that the well-established relationship between product complexity and alliance formation is negatively moderated by two major geopolitical factors: (i) the global market integration of the firm's home country and (ii) the national security salience of the project. Both conditions enable or enhance alternative pathways to resource access that reduce dependence on alliances. Using data on new aircraft development projects, we find support for our predictions. Our findings contribute to the understanding of how home-country global market integration and project national security salience shape firms' innovation strategies by affecting alliance formation decisions during product development.

source_records.abstract: In the pursuit of innovation, diverse actors engage in frequent interactions. Although Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming an active participant in innovation search, less is understood about how its distinct search capabilities complement those of human actors. We explore the complementarities that emerge in human–AI search and identify three relational dialectics that arise in these interactions. The first contrasts human-centered search, which draws on internal organizational knowledge and relational networks, with AI's boundary-spanning search across distant and unfamiliar domains and its ability to synthesize dispersed internal knowledge. The second juxtaposes human contextualizing, which brings relevance and situational meaning, with AI de-contextualizing, which removes assumptions and exposes abstract, pattern-based connections. The third contrasts human judging, involving evaluation and persuasion, with AI envisaging, which generates and visualizes alternative possibilities. We argue that these dialectical complementarities bring about expanded rationality and mitigate biases in the search process, thereby enhancing the potential for innovation.

IntroductionInnovation search is a collaborative and uncertain process of new combinations and novel solutions surfacing along the interactions of multiple actors, where external search often runs in parallel with internal search (Monteiro and Birkinshaw, 2017; Fabrizio, 2009; Lopez-Vega et al., 2016). The innovativeness lies in the ability of the problem solver to explore optimal solutions to specific problems effectively (Cyert and March, 1963; Nelson and Winter, 1982) or to serendipitously arrive at solutions to previously unknown problems (Hippel and Von Krogh, 2016). Innovation search enables organizations to solve problems beyond the resolution capabilities of their existing routines to address challenges in uncertain environments (Huber, 1991). Organizations can enhance their knowledge base through local search within their boundaries; however, fostering innovation requires expanding this knowledge base (Katila and Ahuja, 2002). External and broader knowledge search offer increased opportunities for identifying viable solutions (Ehls et al., 2020; Reinsberger et al., 2026).The search literature often overlooks the fact that the search for new information and knowledge is a human capability; it is managers who search, not the organization itself (Li et al., 2013), which brings forth the role of cognition in the search process (Posen et al., 2018). Search is therefore a behavioral process that depends on the actors' beliefs, which derive from their mental models of the world. This also brings to the fore the limitations of managers in the search process, such as bounded rationality manifested in limited or imperfect cognitive representations of their environments (Gavetti and Levinthal, 2000) and biases originating from past experience (Cabral et al., 2024).Advancements in machine learning and the pursuit of artificial general intelligence, potentially surpassing human capabilities, necessitate a reevaluation of how AI is redefining creativity and work organization (Goos and Savona, 2024). Alongside these advancements, the rapidly evolving role of artificial actors in innovation search, relying on diverse cognitive processes, continues to grow (Just, 2024; Ramoglou et al., 2026). The representations of the world encoded by these AI models are fundamentally different from human mental models or from the representations traditionally used in computing. For instance, generative AI might not even ‘encode any kind of representations of our world’ (Riemer et al., 2023, 2). It lacks an objective ontology and doesn't learn about object properties, relationships, or their existence in our world. Instead, it encodes patterns in training data and thus focuses on relationships between patterns and words, forming a purely relational representational body of patterns (Riemer et al., 2023). Such distinct learning and understanding of the world would strip words and objects of their context (Choudhury et al., 2020), thus having profound implications for innovation. For instance, when instructing AI to find solutions to a particular problem, it may yield seemingly irrelevant answers, or, at times, hallucinated responses. However, within these seemingly unrelated responses, unexpected solutions to unknown problems may emerge. Even these seemingly irrelevant responses can spark new ideas and reveal new opportunities akin to serendipitous discovery of solutions to previously unexplored challenges (Hippel and Von Krogh, 2016). In this regard, the current assumptions about AI being an extension of human capabilities through mere emulation of cognitive processes (von Krogh, 2018) might be flawed. source_records.abstract: Firm productivity dispersion has widened across many OECD countries and is often interpreted as evidence of persistent divergence between frontier and laggard firms, reflecting weakened technology diffusion and growing structural rigidities. This study revisits that narrative using comprehensive Canadian microdata and shows that conclusions about productivity divergence depend on how frontier and laggard firms are defined. Consistent with the existing literature, annually selected frontier and laggard firms exhibit a widening productivity gap over time. However, when the same firms are followed as fixed cohorts, the analysis reveals substantial productivity convergence rather than divergence. This contrast reflects the highly dynamic nature of firm productivity: approximately 15% of lagging firms move into the middle or frontier groups within three years, while 37% of frontier firms no longer remain at the frontier over the same period. The study demonstrates that the widely documented productivity gap between frontier and laggard firms partly reflects changes in firm composition rather than persistent differences among fixed groups of firms. A growing literature documents a widening productivity gap between frontier and laggard firms across many OECD countries and links this trend to the broader slowdown in productivity growth (Andrews et al., 2016; Gu, 2019; Berlingieri et al., 2020). This widening gap has often been interpreted as evidence of weakened technology diffusion, increasing market concentration, and structural barriers that prevent lagging firms from catching up to frontier firms.However, the evidence for persistent productivity divergence depends critically on how frontier and laggard firms are defined. Most existing studies identify frontier firms as the top-performing firms in each year and laggards as the remaining or bottom-performing firms.1 Because these groups are redefined annually, firms frequently enter and exit frontier and laggard status over time. This raises an important question: does the widening productivity gap reflect persistent divergence between the same firms, or does it partly reflect changing group composition within the productivity distribution?This distinction is important both conceptually and from a policy perspective. If frontier firms consistently maintain productivity leadership over time, they may provide reliable benchmarks for laggard firms to emulate. However, if frontier membership is highly dynamic, then annually redefined frontiers may overstate the persistence of productivity leadership and provide a misleading picture of firm-level productivity dynamics. The distinction also matters for interpreting the extent to which widening productivity gaps reflect persistent structural barriers versus ongoing firm mobility and upgrading.This paper revisits the productivity divergence narrative by comparing two alternative approaches to defining frontier and laggard firms. The first follows the standard approach in the literature, where frontier and laggard firms are identified annually according to their productivity rankings. The second tracks fixed cohorts of firms that were initially classified as frontier or laggard firms at the beginning of the sample period. Using comprehensive Canadian firm-level microdata from 2005 to 2021, the analysis shows that the two approaches lead to substantially different conclusions.Consistent with the existing literature, annually selected frontier and laggard firms exhibit a widening productivity gap over time. However, when the same frontier and laggard firms are tracked as fixed cohorts, the analysis reveals substantial productivity convergence rather than divergence. This contrast reflects the dynamic nature of firm productivity performance. Some initially frontier firms lose frontier status and move toward the middle or the bottom of the productivity distribution, while some laggard firms improve sufficiently to become mid-performing or frontier firms. The results therefore suggest that the widely documented productivity divergence between frontier and laggard firms partly reflects changing group composition rather than persistent divergence among fixed groups of firms.The findings also have important implications for interpreting the knowledge-diffusion narrative in the productivity literature. The convergence observed among fixed frontier and laggard cohorts suggests that productivity leadership among incumbent firms is not permanently fixed and that some laggard firms are able to improve productivity performance over time. At the same time, the continued divergence between annually selected frontier and laggard firms and the persistence of low-productivity firms indicate that important frictions and structural barriers remain.Several explanations have been proposed for the widening productivity gap between frontier and laggard firms, including slower technology diffusion (Andrews et al., 2016; Akcigit and Ates, 2021),2 differences in technology adoption and management practices (Bloom and van Reenen, 2007; Brynjolfsson and McAfee, 2014; Bartelsman E. et al., 2013), and increasing market concentration associated with “superstar” firms (Autor et al., 2020). While these explanations provide important insights into productivity dispersion, they focus primarily on broad industry-level patterns and provide limited evidence on the firm-level dynamics underlying productivity mobility. In particular, existing studies provide relatively little evidence on why some laggard firms successfully improve productivity performance while others remain stagnant, or why some frontier firms fail to sustain productivity leadership over time.To better understand firm-level productivity dynamics, this study combines firm production data with information on productivity-enhancing activities, including investments in R&D, technology adoption, exporting, and foreign direct investment (FDI). The first follows the standard approach in the literature, where frontier and laggard firms are identified annually according to their productivity rankings. The second tracks fixed cohorts of firms that were initially classified as frontier or laggard firms at the beginning of the sample period. Using comprehensive Canadian firm-level microdata from 2005 to 2021, the analysis shows that the two approaches lead to substantially different conclusions.Consistent with the existing literature, annually selected frontier and laggard firms exhibit a widening productivity gap over time. However, when the same frontier and laggard firms are tracked as fixed cohorts, the analysis reveals substantial productivity convergence rather than divergence. This contrast reflects the dynamic nature of firm productivity performance. Some initially frontier firms lose frontier status and move toward the middle or the bottom of the productivity distribution, while some laggard firms improve sufficiently to become mid-performing or frontier firms. The results therefore suggest that the widely documented productivity divergence between frontier and laggard firms partly reflects changing group composition rather than persistent divergence among fixed groups of firms.The findings also have important implications for interpreting the knowledge-diffusion narrative in the productivity literature. The convergence observed among fixed frontier and laggard cohorts suggests that productivity leadership among incumbent firms is not permanently fixed and that some laggard firms are able to improve productivity performance over time. At the same time, the continued divergence between annually selected frontier and laggard firms and the persistence of low-productivity firms indicate that important frictions and structural barriers remain.Several explanations have been proposed for the widening productivity gap between frontier and laggard firms, including slower technology diffusion (Andrews et al., 2016; Akcigit and Ates, 2021),2 differences in technology adoption and management practices (Bloom and van Reenen, 2007; Brynjolfsson and McAfee, 2014; Bartelsman E. et al., 2013), and increasing market concentration associated with “superstar” firms (Autor et al., 2020). While these explanations provide important insights into productivity dispersion, they focus primarily on broad industry-level patterns and provide limited evidence on the firm-level dynamics underlying productivity mobility. In particular, existing studies provide relatively little evidence on why some laggard firms successfully improve productivity performance while others remain stagnant, or why some frontier firms fail to sustain productivity leadership over time.To better understand firm-level productivity dynamics, this study combines firm production data with information on productivity-enhancing activities, including investments in R&D, technology adoption, exporting, and foreign direct investment (FDI). The analysis shows that firms with stronger investment performance in R&D and technology adoption are more likely to improve productivity rankings or maintain frontier status over time. While these relationships are descriptive rather than causal, they suggest that sustained investment in innovation and technology upgrading is closely associated with long-term productivity performance and firm productivity mobility.This study contributes to the literature in two main ways. First, it demonstrates that conclusions regarding productivity divergence are highly sensitive to how frontier and laggard firms are defined. Second, it provides new evidence on the relationship between firm investment behavior and productivity mobility.The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 5 analyzes productivity dynamics between frontier and laggard firms. Section 6 investigates the determinants of productivity differences and mobility. Section 7 examines the relationship between firm investment behavior and productivity dynamics. proposed.abstract:
•
Frontier and laggard firms are not fixed groups: some laggards improve productivity rapidly, while some frontier firms fall behind.
•
Annual frontier–laggard comparisons show a widening gap, while fixed-cohort analysis shows productivity convergence.
•
R&D investment and technology adoption are common factors among firms with higher productivity growth or that sustain frontier status.

fields.authors: Jianmin Tang a, Weimin Wang b, Sadaf Yalinejad a
fields.abstract: Firm productivity dispersion has widened across many OECD countries and is often interpreted as evidence of persistent divergence between frontier and laggard firms, reflecting weakened technology diffusion and growing structural rigidities. This study revisits that narrative using comprehensive Canadian microdata and shows that conclusions about productivity divergence depend on how frontier and laggard firms are defined. Consistent with the existing literature, annually selected frontier and laggard firms exhibit a widening productivity gap over time. However, when the same firms are followed as fixed cohorts, the analysis reveals substantial productivity convergence rather than divergence. This contrast reflects the highly dynamic nature of firm productivity: approximately 15% of lagging firms move into the middle or frontier groups within three years, while 37% of frontier firms no longer remain at the frontier over the same period. The study demonstrates that the widely documented productivity gap between frontier and laggard firms partly reflects changes in firm composition rather than persistent differences among fixed groups of firms. The study further shows that sustained investments in R&D and technology are consistently associated with productivity mobility and the ability to maintain frontier status, with such investments being more prevalent among firms that improve their productivity performance or remain at the productivity frontier. These findings have important implications for interpreting productivity dispersion and for designing policies aimed at fostering productivity growth.

source_records.abstract: While technological advancements have reduced barriers to remote collaboration, the extent to which geographical proximity still shapes research outcomes remains a critical yet underexplored question. This study examines how geographical separation, defined as the loss of city-level co-location following collaborator mobility, affects the performance of established research collaborations. Using a quasi-experimental design, we analyze changes in research outcomes among 16,505 scientist pairs following inter-city relocation (treatment group) relative to intra-city relocation (control group). Our findings reveal that geographical separation leads to significant declines in both collaborative productivity (co-authored publications) and scientific impact (citation counts), underscoring the persistent role of proximity in sustaining effective collaboration. We further document important heterogeneity: interdisciplinary collaborations are more resilient in maintaining publication output but experience larger declines in scientific impact; same-stage collaborations are more vulnerable than cross-stage collaborations; and the negative effect is stronger in geographically larger countries. These findings highlight the enduring importance of geographical proximity in maintaining effective research collaboration.

These findings highlight the enduring importance of geographical proximity in maintaining effective research collaboration.KeywordsGeographical separation; Proximity; Distance; Research collaboration; Mobility; RelocationPrevious article in this issueNext article in this issueIntroductionResearch collaboration has emerged as the dominant approach to knowledge production, driven by increasing specialization and the growing complexity of scientific problems (Wuchty et al., 2007). Collaboration enables knowledge to flow across individual, organizational and regional levels, facilitating the exchange of ideas and the integration of complementary expertise and resources (Jones, 2009; Milojević, 2014). It has been demonstrated to yield substantial advantages, such as enhancing knowledge flow and producing high-quality, innovative research (Ding, 2011; Wuchty et al., 2007). However, collaboration also involves certain costs. The formation and maintenance of effective collaborations require substantial investments in social capital and coordination, including establishing new workflows, monitoring work progress, managing schedules and allocating tasks (Bikard et al., 2015; Boschma, 2005; Petersen, 2015). Thus, scientists strategically evaluate the costs and benefits of collaboration when deciding whom to collaborate with and how to sustain these relationships (Wu et al., 2024).Research collaboration is a dynamic system, evolving through stages of formation, development, and termination. Over the course of a partnership, events such as career progression, institutional relocation, or major disruptions like the COVID-19 pandemic can alter the geographic distance between established collaborators. For instance, collaborators who were once co-located in the same region may become dispersed across different cities or even countries. This geographical separation poses a challenge to maintaining collaboration, as a foundational tenet in economic geographics is that geographical proximity is crucial for knowledge spillovers and innovation (Feldman and Kogler, 2010; Jaffe et al., 1993; Ponds et al., 2007). However, the proliferation of advanced information and communication technologies (ICTs) has sparked a debate regarding whether distance still matters. On the one hand, these technologies have significantly lowered the barriers to remote communication, leading to a marked increase in remote scientific collaboration (Hoekman et al., 2010; Luo et al., 2018; Yao et al., 2020). The “death of distance” hypothesis has thus been proposed, suggesting that distance no longer significantly affects remote collaboration (Cairncross, 2001; Grözinger et al., 2020; Werker and Ooms, 2020).On the other hand, a substantial body of recent studies contends that geographic proximity remains a significant factor. Indeed, numerous studies have demonstrated the significant benefits of geographical proximity in reducing communication and coordination costs (Katz, 1994; Rosenkopf and Almeida, 2003; Storper and Venables, 2004; Yang et al., 2022). Geographical proximity can facilitate communication, trust and the transfer of tacit knowledge through frequent face-to-face interaction (Collins et al., 2022; Ganesan et al., 2005; Lin et al., 2023). Although beneficial, digital communication cannot fully replace in-person interaction, and the challenges of remote collaboration still exist (Yang et al., 2022). Yet, these studies have primarily focused on static comparisons between geographically proximate and remote collaborations (Kabo et al., 2014; Ponds et al., 2007; Roche et al., 2024). While numerous studies have highlighted the advantages of proximity in promoting the search for new collaborators and fostering more collaboration, the longitudinal impact of geographical separation on research collaboration is less understood.This study is motivated by the need to understand how the transition from co-location to separation impacts the performance of research collaborations. Established trust and shared working experience within existing partnerships can enhance communication and coordination effectiveness, rendering such ties more resilient than newly formed collaborations (Dahlander and McFarland, 2013; Nilsson and Mattes, 2015). Furthermore, remote collaborators with prior co-located experience may anticipate potential difficulties and proactively make greater efforts to overcome the challenges (Mors and Waguespack, 2021). Thus, it remains uncertain whether the advantages of these pre-existing strong ties or the new benefits afforded by remote collaboration, such as obtaining and integrating diverse knowledge, can compensate for the challenges posed by geographical separation.This study investigates the impact of geographical separation on research collaboration by comparing performance changes following collaborator mobility. We focus on the discrete transition from co-located collaboration to geographically separated collaboration. We operationalize this transition at the city level, defining co-located pairs as those located in the same city and geographically separated pairs as those located in different cities. Collaboration performance is measured through changes in collaborative productivity and scientific impact. We systematically track scientists' education and employment histories from ORCID records to identify institutional mobility events. By integrating mobility data with publication data from OpenAlex, we construct a scientist-pair-year panel comprising 16,505 scientist pairs and their publication histories. Using a difference-in-differences framework, we compare changes in collaboration performance between pairs in which one collaborator moves to a different city and matched pairs in which one collaborator changes institutions but remains in the same city. First, we examine boundary-spanning heterogeneity by comparing interdisciplinary collaborations with monodisciplinary ones, as these two types exhibit distinct communication and coordination modes. Second, we investigate hierarchical heterogeneity by distinguishing between peer collaborations and cross-stage collaborations. This distinction is important because these collaboration types differ in their core functions of peer communication versus guidance, which may be differentially affected by geographical separation. Third, we examine geographic-context heterogeneity by assessing whether the effect differs between pairs located in larger versus smaller countries, where inter-city separation may imply different levels of travel and coordination costs.The results show that geographical separation significantly reduces both the productivity and scientific impact of established scientific collaborations. Scientist pairs publish fewer co-publications after separation, and the citation impact of their joint publications also declines. The average effect, however, masks important heterogeneity. Interdisciplinary collaborations appear more resilient in maintaining publication output after separation, but their scientific impact is more adversely affected. Same-stage collaborations experience larger declines than cross-stage collaborations, suggesting that peer collaborations may be particularly vulnerable to the loss of routine interaction. The negative effect of geographical separation is also more pronounced in larger countries, consistent with the idea that inter-city separation imposes greater travel and coordination costs in larger geographic contexts.Our findings contribute to the literature in several ways. Specifically, the findings highlight the advantages of proximate collaboration over remote collaboration. Rather than focusing on collaborative initiation, we shift the analytical lens to collaborative resilience by examining how collaboration performance changes when collaborators become geographically separated after a period of co-location. This study examines how geographical separation, defined as the loss of city-level co-location following collaborator mobility, affects the performance of established research collaborations. proposed.title: Farther apart, faltering partnerships? The impact of geographical separation on research collaboration
proposed.abstract:
•
Geographical separation of city-level co-location significantly reduces collaborative productivity and scientific impact in established research pairs.
•
Interdisciplinary collaborations show resilience in publication output but suffer greater declines in scientific impact after separation.
•
Same-stage collaborations are more vulnerable to geographical separation, with stronger negative effects observed in larger countries.

fields.title: Farther apart, faltering partnerships? The impact of geographical separation on research collaboration
fields.authors: Xin Liu a b, Ka Lok Pang c, Yiwei Li c, Zhiya Zuo d, Dan Tian e, Jiang Li a
fields.abstract: While technological advancements have reduced barriers to remote collaboration, the extent to which geographical proximity still shapes research outcomes remains a critical yet underexplored question. This study examines how geographical separation, defined as the loss of city-level co-location following collaborator mobility, affects the performance of established research collaborations. Using a quasi-experimental design, we analyze changes in research outcomes among 16,505 scientist pairs following inter-city relocation (treatment group) relative to intra-city relocation (control group). Our findings reveal that geographical separation leads to significant declines in both collaborative productivity (co-authored publications) and scientific impact (citation counts), underscoring the persistent role of proximity in sustaining effective collaboration. We further document important heterogeneity: interdisciplinary collaborations are more resilient in maintaining publication output but experience larger declines in scientific impact; same-stage collaborations are more vulnerable than cross-stage collaborations; and the negative effect is stronger in geographically larger countries. These findings highlight the enduring importance of geographical proximity in maintaining effective research collaboration.

source_records.title: Rent Guarantee Insurance
source_records.abstract: A rent guarantee insurance (RGI) policy makes a limited number of rent payments to the landlord on behalf of an insured tenant unable to pay rent due to a negative income or health expenditure shock. We introduce RGI in a rich quantitative equilibrium model of housing insecurity and show it increases welfare by improving risk sharing across idiosyncratic and aggregate states of the world, reducing the need for a large security deposits, and reducing homelessness which imposes large costs on society. While unrestricted access to RGI is not financially viable due to moral hazard and adverse selection, restricting access can restore viability. Private insurers target better off renters to break even, while public insurers focus on households most at-risk of homelessness. Stronger tenant protections increase the effectiveness of RGI.

before.title_zh: 租金担保保险
before.abstract_zh: 租金保证保险（RGI）保单代表因收入或健康支出负向冲击而无力支付租金的参保租户，向房东支付有限次数的租金。我们将RGI引入一个关于住房不安全的丰富定量均衡模型，并表明它通过改善对异质性和总体世界状态的风险分担、减少对大额押金的需求，以及减少给社会带来巨大成本的无家可归现象，提高了福利。虽然由于道德风险和逆向选择，无限制地获得RGI在财务上不可行，但限制获得可以恢复可行性。私人保险公司以状况较好的租户为目标以实现收支平衡，而公共保险公司则关注最有可能无家可归的家庭。更强的租户保护提高了RGI的有效性。

source_records.title: The Effect of Education Policy on Crime: An Intergenerational Perspective
source_records.abstract: We examine the intergenerational effect of education policy on crime. Using administrative data that link outcomes across generations with crime records, we show that the Swedish comprehensive school reform, gradually implemented between 1949 and 1962, reduced conviction rates both for the generation directly affected and for their sons. The reduction occurred across several types of crime. Mediation analysis suggests that the key channels include increased parental educational attainment and household income, as well as reduced criminal behavior among fathers.

before.abstract_original: We examine the intergenerational effect of education policy on crime. Using administrative data that link outcomes across generations with crime records, we show that the Swedish comprehensive school reform, gradually implemented between 1949 and 1962, reduced conviction rates both for the generation directly affected and for their sons. The reduction occurred across several types of crime. Mediation analysis suggests that the key channels include increased parental educational attainment and household income, as well as reduced criminal behavior among fathers.
before.title_zh: 教育政策对犯罪的影响：代际视角
before.abstract_zh: 我们考察教育政策对犯罪的代际效应。利用将各代人的结果与犯罪记录相链接的行政数据，我们表明，在1949年至1962年间逐步实施的瑞典综合学校改革，既降低了直接受影响那一代人的定罪率，也降低了其儿子的定罪率。这一下降出现在若干犯罪类型中。中介分析表明，关键渠道包括父母受教育程度提高和家庭收入增加，以及父亲犯罪行为减少。

source_records.abstract: Using novel survey data from 1426 firms in Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador, we examine the voluntary adoption of accounting systems by microenterprises operating in the informal economy and its association with access to credit and business growth. Despite the absence of regulatory mandates, 44 percent of informal microbusinesses maintain systematic financial records, with roughly three-quarters of those using notebooks and one-quarter using digital records. Accounting quality is closely linked to the owner’s startup motivation, financial stake, and management capabilities. Informal firms that rely on larger suppliers, extend customer installment credit, engage in marketing promotions, or employ more formal organizational structures are also more likely to adopt structured recordkeeping systems, highlighting accounting’s role as a managerial tool rather than as a compliance function or as a precursor to entering the formal economy. Informal firms that maintain notebooks separating business and personal accounts are significantly more likely to apply for and obtain bank loans. Our inferences for access to credit also extend to microenterprises in the Dominican Republic. In addition, accounting quality appears to support lender due diligence even among informal firms, particularly when lenders are more sophisticated. Using a broader measure of credit market status, we find that accounting quality rises monotonically across credit tiers. Finally, we find that entrepreneurs with higher-quality accounting systems are more likely to plan for business expansion. By illuminating the motivations behind accounting choices in low-enforcement settings, this study deepens our understanding of the foundational role accounting plays in early-stage business development in emerging markets.

The role of accounting in the informal economy

Conference Manuscript
The role of accounting in the informal economy☆

•
Cost–benefit drives formalization and accounting decisions of microenterprises.
•
Owners with personal capital at stake voluntarily adopt higher-quality accounting.
•
Personal motivation, management skills, and customer relations also play a role.
•
Accounting quality improves credit access for informal microenterprises.
•
Informal firms with better records are 9% more likely to apply and 14% to obtain loans.

Using novel survey data from 1426 firms in Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador, we examine the voluntary adoption of accounting systems by microenterprises operating in the informal economy and its association with access to credit and business growth. Despite the absence of regulatory mandates, 44 percent of informal microbusinesses maintain systematic financial records, with roughly three-quarters of those using notebooks and one-quarter using digital records. Accounting quality is closely linked to the owner’s startup motivation, financial stake, and management capabilities. Informal firms that rely on larger suppliers, extend customer installment credit, engage in marketing promotions, or employ more formal organizational structures are also more likely to adopt structured recordkeeping systems, highlighting accounting’s role as a managerial tool rather than as a compliance function or as a precursor to entering the formal economy. Informal firms that maintain notebooks separating business and personal accounts are significantly more likely to apply for and obtain bank loans. Our inferences for access to credit also extend to microenterprises in the Dominican Republic. In addition, accounting quality appears to support lender due diligence even among informal firms, particularly when lenders are more sophisticated. Using a broader measure of credit market status, we find that accounting quality rises monotonically across credit tiers. Finally, we find that entrepreneurs with higher-quality accounting systems are more likely to plan for business expansion. By illuminating the motivations behind accounting choices in low-enforcement settings, this study deepens our understanding of the foundational role accounting plays in early-stage business development in emerging markets.
