We focus on informal microenterprises, defined as those that are not registered with the national tax authority, that are not in compliance with business registration requirements (ILO, 2020), and that employ fewer than ten persons (see European Union, ILO, IDB). Using cross-sectional data from a 2019 survey by the International Labour Organization (ILO) on 1426 microenterprises in Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador, we document the economic trade-offs associated with recordkeeping practices in informal firms and how these practices relate to access to credit and business growth.1Despite accounting for approximately 30 percent of global GDP and 50 percent of employment, the informal economy, where micro and small enterprises are dominant, remains underexplored in the accounting literature (ILO, 2020, Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2024, Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2025). Their business practices are typically rudimentary (Buehn and Schneider, 2012, Halvorson-Quevedo, 1991, IFC, 2010, Ulyssea, 2020) and their financial transactions are often governed by social capital and trust-based relationships (Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2024, Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2025).Prior research on private firms shows that even absent public disclosure mandates, their accounting choices are typically shaped by tax rules, loan covenants, and statutory reporting thresholds (e.g., Bernard and Sutherland, 2025, Allee and Yohn, 2009, Ball, 2024, Beuselinck et al., 2023, Lisowsky and Minnis, 2020, Minnis, 2011). In contrast, entrepreneurs in the informal economy face no such mandates, so even maintaining rudimentary records reflects a direct cost-benefit trade-off. The contrast between formal and informal firms in our data underscores this point: nearly all formal microenterprises maintain systematic, often digitized records, whereas informal firms display wide heterogeneity.2 The informal economy thus provides a distinctive lens through which to observe the foundational, emergent role of accounting, which is not readily visible in more developed and institutionally mature markets (Ball, 2024, Ball, 2025b).3Our survey-based measures capture both whether systematic records are kept and gradations in their level of sophistication, providing direct descriptive evidence on accounting adoption in the informal sector absent regulatory mandates. We first focus on a binary outcome, the voluntary decision of informal microbusinesses to adopt a systematic recordkeeping system (Systematic Recordkeeping). We later exploit the survey’s granularity to develop a four-level ordinal measure of Accounting Quality: (1) No systematic recordkeeping; (2) Commingled NB, where business and personal financial records are combined in a single physical, paper-based notebook; (3) Separate NB, where business records are maintained separately in a dedicated, paper-based notebook; and (4) Digitized, representing a more sophisticated accounting system (see Fig. 1). A distinctive feature of our setting is the commingled category (Jayachandran, 2020) because most microenterprise training programs emphasize separating business and personal finances (Dyer et al., 2016, McKenzie and Woodruff, 2014). While such separation may facilitate business sustainability and serve as a behavioral commitment device (Drexler et al., 2014), whether it has real effects is an open question.In our sample of informal firms, 44 percent maintain systematic records, with nearly three-quarters relying on a paper-based notebook. Notably, more than one-quarter of these notebook users do not separate business and personal finances. In our setting, there is no separation of ownership and control, which implies that accounting system choices are less likely to reflect classic agency conflicts. Instead, these choices primarily reflect entrepreneurs’ trade-offs between the costs and benefits of systematic recordkeeping. Using a reduced-form probit (ordered probit) model, we examine the association between Systematic Recordkeeping (Accounting Quality) and the determinants that shape these trade-offs.We find that entrepreneurs with stronger business orientation (Calderon et al., 2017), but not those motivated by family considerations, and those with greater managerial human capital (Bloom et al., 2010, Bloom et al., 2013, Bloom and Van Reenen, 2007, Karlan and Valdivia, 2011) are more likely to adopt systematic recordkeeping. Entrepreneurs who view their own equity capital or banks as desirable funding sources or who are saving toward a future capital infusion are more likely to have systematic financial records (Cassar, 2009, Dupas and Robinson, 2013). The observed association between accounting choices and owner characteristics provides novel descriptive evidence that broadens our understanding of the role of accounting in evolving business organizations (Sunder, 1997).Among operational factors, firms that extend installment credit or engage in marketing promotion activities are more likely to rely on systematic financial records, with accounting plausibly serving as a managerial tool for customer acquisition and retention. Consistent with the informational demands of supply-chain relationships, informal firms that rely on large suppliers are more likely to have systematic records. Reflecting the level of informality in organizational design (Brickley et al., 2003), businesses that rely more heavily on family members or temporary workers tend to use more rudimentary records, whereas those with more full-time employees opt for higher-quality accounting.Turning to Accounting Quality, we report the marginal effects from the ordered probit model for each outcome category. We find that these marginal effects indicate a shift in probability away from no systematic financial records toward higher-quality systems, with commingled notebooks playing only a limited role. For example, at the margin, firms that extend installment credit are 33 percentage points less likely to have no systematic records, and about 16 percentage points more likely to adopt either separate notebooks or digitized systems, relative to firms that do not extend installment credit. Robustness analyses show that accounting choices are not associated with anticipated formalization and are not merely proxies for general business sophistication. Taken together, our results align with historical evidence that merchants and money changers created accounting systems to support the efficient management of their businesses rather than as a compliance mechanism (Ball, 2025b, Basu et al., 2009).We next examine the role of accounting in microenterprises’ access to credit, a key indicator of financial development (Guiso et al., 2004). Prior research highlights the importance of social capital and trust in facilitating supplier credit in informal economies (Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2024). By contrast, we find that firms that prefer bank financing are more likely to maintain systematic financial records, raising the empirical question of whether accounting quality is associated with access to bank credit in the informal economy. For this analysis, we use the microenterprises in the formal economy as a comparison group (footnote 2).Roughly 40 percent of the microenterprises in our sample have ever applied for a bank loan, with 34 percent of informal firms and 52 percent of formal firms doing so. Among applicants, 77 percent of informal firms and 93 percent of formal firms reported receiving the loan. To model both the decision to apply and the likelihood of approval, we estimate separate Heckman selection models for informal firms and for the benchmark sample of formal firms. Our specifications include controls for collateral, contracting reputation, customer and supplier credits, and business age (Berger and Udell, 1995, Petersen and Rajan, 1994, Banerjee et al., 2017).For informal firms, only the coefficient on notebooks with separate accounts (Separate NB) is statistically significant for both loan applications and approvals, suggesting that separating business and personal financial records may be particularly relevant for credit access. For formal firms, digitized records are associated with a higher likelihood of loan applications and approvals, consistent with lenders placing greater weight on more sophisticated accounting systems. We draw similar inferences when using a broader measure of credit market status beyond mere access to bank loans, and these patterns remain robust to copula-based selection models that relax the joint normality assumption. Taken together, the results point to a positive relationship between accounting quality and credit access among microenterprises.4 However, we acknowledge that our cross-sectional data limit our ability to make causal inferences about the relationships we observe.To mitigate concerns about generalizability, we replicate our findings from the credit access analysis using data from a similar ILO survey in the Dominican Republic (DR) conducted in 2023. The results also highlight the role of social capital (Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2024): small banks appear less likely to demand systematic financial records when providing small loans to informal firms, consistent with trust-based lending. For large loan requests, systematic recordkeeping is common regardless of bank type, suggesting that traditional financial due diligence becomes more important when financial stakes are larger.Lastly, using the CA sample and controlling for the entrepreneur’s human capital, firm size, and country/sector fixed effects, we find that firms with higher-quality accounting systems are more likely to report business expansion plans, particularly along the extensive margin. We also find that higher-quality accounting is associated with greater productivity (monthly sales per employee) among informal firms. Taken together, these findings shed light on the managerial role of accounting in informal firms (Datar et al., 2009).Because accounting evolves in parallel with broader institutional transformations, establishing causation in this setting is inherently difficult and may be unproductive in assessing its social value (Ball, 2024, Ball, 2025a, Ball, 2025b). Using rich survey data from Central America, we provide descriptive evidence on the role of accounting outside the shadow of regulatory mandates, where adoption reflects a direct cost-benefit trade-off. This unique setting allows us to observe accounting in its foundational role as a managerial tool rather than as a compliance mechanism.5The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 examines when and why informal firms voluntarily keep systematic accounting records. Next, Section 3 explores how accounting quality relates to access to credit. Finally, Section 4 examines how accounting quality is associated with managerial decisions regarding microenterprise growth plans and productivity. title.text: The role of accounting in the informal economy

authors.text: Marcela Aguilar a, Gary Lind b, K. Ramesh c

abstract.text: Using novel survey data from 1426 firms in Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador, we examine the voluntary adoption of accounting systems by microenterprises operating in the informal economy and its association with access to credit and business growth. Despite the absence of regulatory mandates, 44 percent of informal microbusinesses maintain systematic financial records, with roughly three-quarters of those using notebooks and one-quarter using digital records. Accounting quality is closely linked to the owner’s startup motivation, financial stake, and management capabilities. Informal firms that rely on larger suppliers, extend customer installment credit, engage in marketing promotions, or employ more formal organizational structures are also more likely to adopt structured recordkeeping systems, highlighting accounting’s role as a managerial tool rather than as a compliance function or as a precursor to entering the formal economy. Informal firms that maintain notebooks separating business and personal accounts are significantly more likely to apply for and obtain bank loans. Our inferences for access to credit also extend to microenterprises in the Dominican Republic. In addition, accounting quality appears to support lender due diligence even among informal firms, particularly when lenders are more sophisticated. Using a broader measure of credit market status, we find that accounting quality rises monotonically across credit tiers. Finally, we find that entrepreneurs with higher-quality accounting systems are more likely to plan for business expansion. By illuminating the motivations behind accounting choices in low-enforcement settings, this study deepens our understanding of the foundational role accounting plays in early-stage business development in emerging markets.

The role of accounting in the informal economy☆

•
Cost–benefit drives formalization and accounting decisions of microenterprises.
•
Owners with personal capital at stake voluntarily adopt higher-quality accounting.
•
Personal motivation, management skills, and customer relations also play a role.
•
Accounting quality improves credit access for informal microenterprises.
•
Informal firms with better records are 9% more likely to apply and 14% to obtain loans.

Using novel survey data from 1426 firms in Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador, we examine the voluntary adoption of accounting systems by microenterprises operating in the informal economy and its association with access to credit and business growth. Despite the absence of regulatory mandates, 44 percent of informal microbusinesses maintain systematic financial records, with roughly three-quarters of those using notebooks and one-quarter using digital records. Accounting quality is closely linked to the owner’s startup motivation, financial stake, and management capabilities. Informal firms that rely on larger suppliers, extend customer installment credit, engage in marketing promotions, or employ more formal organizational structures are also more likely to adopt structured recordkeeping systems, highlighting accounting’s role as a managerial tool rather than as a compliance function or as a precursor to entering the formal economy. Informal firms that maintain notebooks separating business and personal accounts are significantly more likely to apply for and obtain bank loans. Our inferences for access to credit also extend to microenterprises in the Dominican Republic. In addition, accounting quality appears to support lender due diligence even among informal firms, particularly when lenders are more sophisticated. Using a broader measure of credit market status, we find that accounting quality rises monotonically across credit tiers. Finally, we find that entrepreneurs with higher-quality accounting systems are more likely to plan for business expansion. By illuminating the motivations behind accounting choices in low-enforcement settings, this study deepens our understanding of the foundational role accounting plays in early-stage business development in emerging markets.

By illuminating the motivations behind accounting choices in low-enforcement settings, this study deepens our understanding of the foundational role accounting plays in early-stage business development in emerging markets.JEL classificationG21; M13; M4; O17KeywordsInformal economy; Developing economies; Microenterprises; Recordkeeping; Accounting quality; Financial inclusion; Access to creditIntroductionThis study examines the relationship between voluntary accounting practices and the informal economy in developing countries, where firms largely operate outside tax and business registrations, and beyond government enforcement (Ulyssea, 2020). We focus on informal microenterprises, defined as those that are not registered with the national tax authority, that are not in compliance with business registration requirements (ILO, 2020), and that employ fewer than ten persons (see European Union, ILO, IDB). Using cross-sectional data from a 2019 survey by the International Labour Organization (ILO) on 1426 microenterprises in Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador, we document the economic trade-offs associated with recordkeeping practices in informal firms and how these practices relate to access to credit and business growth.1Despite accounting for approximately 30 percent of global GDP and 50 percent of employment, the informal economy, where micro and small enterprises are dominant, remains underexplored in the accounting literature (ILO, 2020, Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2024, Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2025). Their business practices are typically rudimentary (Buehn and Schneider, 2012, Halvorson-Quevedo, 1991, IFC, 2010, Ulyssea, 2020) and their financial transactions are often governed by social capital and trust-based relationships (Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2024, Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2025).Prior research on private firms shows that even absent public disclosure mandates, their accounting choices are typically shaped by tax rules, loan covenants, and statutory reporting thresholds (e.g., Bernard and Sutherland, 2025, Allee and Yohn, 2009, Ball, 2024, Beuselinck et al., 2023, Lisowsky and Minnis, 2020, Minnis, 2011). In contrast, entrepreneurs in the informal economy face no such mandates, so even maintaining rudimentary records reflects a direct cost-benefit trade-off. The contrast between formal and informal firms in our data underscores this point: nearly all formal microenterprises maintain systematic, often digitized records, whereas informal firms display wide heterogeneity.2 The informal economy thus provides a distinctive lens through which to observe the foundational, emergent role of accounting, which is not readily visible in more developed and institutionally mature markets (Ball, 2024, Ball, 2025b).3Our survey-based measures capture both whether systematic records are kept and gradations in their level of sophistication, providing direct descriptive evidence on accounting adoption in the informal sector absent regulatory mandates. We first focus on a binary outcome, the voluntary decision of informal microbusinesses to adopt a systematic recordkeeping system (Systematic Recordkeeping). We later exploit the survey’s granularity to develop a four-level ordinal measure of Accounting Quality: (1) No systematic recordkeeping; (2) Commingled NB, where business and personal financial records are combined in a single physical, paper-based notebook; (3) Separate NB, where business records are maintained separately in a dedicated, paper-based notebook; and (4) Digitized, representing a more sophisticated accounting system (see Fig. 1). A distinctive feature of our setting is the commingled category (Jayachandran, 2020) because most microenterprise training programs emphasize separating business and personal finances (Dyer et al., 2016, McKenzie and Woodruff, 2014). While such separation may facilitate business sustainability and serve as a behavioral commitment device (Drexler et al., 2014), whether it has real effects is an open question.In our sample of informal firms, 44 percent maintain systematic records, with nearly three-quarters relying on a paper-based notebook. Notably, more than one-quarter of these notebook users do not separate business and personal finances. In our setting, there is no separation of ownership and control, which implies that accounting system choices are less likely to reflect classic agency conflicts. Instead, these choices primarily reflect entrepreneurs’ trade-offs between the costs and benefits of systematic recordkeeping. Using a reduced-form probit (ordered probit) model, we examine the association between Systematic Recordkeeping (Accounting Quality) and the determinants that shape these trade-offs.We find that entrepreneurs with stronger business orientation (Calderon et al., 2017), but not those motivated by family considerations, and those with greater managerial human capital (Bloom et al., 2010, Bloom et al., 2013, Bloom and Van Reenen, 2007, Karlan and Valdivia, 2011) are more likely to adopt systematic recordkeeping. Entrepreneurs who view their own equity capital or banks as desirable funding sources or who are saving toward a future capital infusion are more likely to have systematic financial records (Cassar, 2009, Dupas and Robinson, 2013). The observed association between accounting choices and owner characteristics provides novel descriptive evidence that broadens our understanding of the role of accounting in evolving business organizations (Sunder, 1997).Among operational factors, firms that extend installment credit or engage in marketing promotion activities are more likely to rely on systematic financial records, with accounting plausibly serving as a managerial tool for customer acquisition and retention. Consistent with the informational demands of supply-chain relationships, informal firms that rely on large suppliers are more likely to have systematic records. Reflecting the level of informality in organizational design (Brickley et al., 2003), businesses that rely more heavily on family members or temporary workers tend to use more rudimentary records, whereas those with more full-time employees opt for higher-quality accounting.Turning to Accounting Quality, we report the marginal effects from the ordered probit model for each outcome category. We find that these marginal effects indicate a shift in probability away from no systematic financial records toward higher-quality systems, with commingled notebooks playing only a limited role. For example, at the margin, firms that extend installment credit are 33 percentage points less likely to have no systematic records, and about 16 percentage points more likely to adopt either separate notebooks or digitized systems, relative to firms that do not extend installment credit. Robustness analyses show that accounting choices are not associated with anticipated formalization and are not merely proxies for general business sophistication. Taken together, our results align with historical evidence that merchants and money changers created accounting systems to support the efficient management of their businesses rather than as a compliance mechanism (Ball, 2025b, Basu et al., 2009).We next examine the role of accounting in microenterprises’ access to credit, a key indicator of financial development (Guiso et al., 2004). Prior research highlights the importance of social capital and trust in facilitating supplier credit in informal economies (Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2024). By contrast, we find that firms that prefer bank financing are more likely to maintain systematic financial records, raising the empirical question of whether accounting quality is associated with access to bank credit in the informal economy. For this analysis, we use the microenterprises in the formal economy as a comparison group (footnote 2).Roughly 40 percent of the microenterprises in our sample have ever applied for a bank loan, with 34 percent of informal firms and 52 percent of formal firms doing so. Among applicants, 77 percent of informal firms and 93 percent of formal firms reported receiving the loan. To model both the decision to apply and the likelihood of approval, we estimate separate Heckman selection models for informal firms and for the benchmark sample of formal firms. Our specifications include controls for collateral, contracting reputation, customer and supplier credits, and business age (Berger and Udell, 1995, Petersen and Rajan, 1994, Banerjee et al., 2017).For informal firms, only the coefficient on notebooks with separate accounts (Separate NB) is statistically significant for both loan applications and approvals, suggesting that separating business and personal financial records may be particularly relevant for credit access. For formal firms, digitized records are associated with a higher likelihood of loan applications and approvals, consistent with lenders placing greater weight on more sophisticated accounting systems. We draw similar inferences when using a broader measure of credit market status beyond mere access to bank loans, and these patterns remain robust to copula-based selection models that relax the joint normality assumption. Taken together, the results point to a positive relationship between accounting quality and credit access among microenterprises.4 However, we acknowledge that our cross-sectional data limit our ability to make causal inferences about the relationships we observe.To mitigate concerns about generalizability, we replicate our findings from the credit access analysis using data from a similar ILO survey in the Dominican Republic (DR) conducted in 2023. The results also highlight the role of social capital (Tomy and Wittenberg-Moerman, 2024): small banks appear less likely to demand systematic financial records when providing small loans to informal firms, consistent with trust-based lending. For large loan requests, systematic recordkeeping is common regardless of bank type, suggesting that traditional financial due diligence becomes more important when financial stakes are larger.Lastly, using the CA sample and controlling for the entrepreneur’s human capital, firm size, and country/sector fixed effects, we find that firms with higher-quality accounting systems are more likely to report business expansion plans, particularly along the extensive margin. We also find that higher-quality accounting is associated with greater productivity (monthly sales per employee) among informal firms. Taken together, these findings shed light on the managerial role of accounting in informal firms (Datar et al., 2009).Because accounting evolves in parallel with broader institutional transformations, establishing causation in this setting is inherently difficult and may be unproductive in assessing its social value (Ball, 2024, Ball, 2025a, Ball, 2025b). Using rich survey data from Central America, we provide descriptive evidence on the role of accounting outside the shadow of regulatory mandates, where adoption reflects a direct cost-benefit trade-off. This unique setting allows us to observe accounting in its foundational role as a managerial tool rather than as a compliance mechanism.5The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 examines when and why informal firms voluntarily keep systematic accounting records. Next, Section 3 explores how accounting quality relates to access to credit. Finally, Section 4 examines how accounting quality is associated with managerial decisions regarding microenterprise growth plans and productivity. proposed.title: The role of accounting in the informal economy
proposed.abstract:
•
Cost–benefit drives formalization and accounting decisions of microenterprises.
•
Owners with personal capital at stake voluntarily adopt higher-quality accounting.
•
Personal motivation, management skills, and customer relations also play a role.
•
Accounting quality improves credit access for informal microenterprises.
•
Informal firms with better records are 9% more likely to apply and 14% to obtain loans.

fields.abstract: Using novel survey data from 1426 firms in Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador, we examine the voluntary adoption of accounting systems by microenterprises operating in the informal economy and its association with access to credit and business growth. Despite the absence of regulatory mandates, 44 percent of informal microbusinesses maintain systematic financial records, with roughly three-quarters of those using notebooks and one-quarter using digital records. Accounting quality is closely linked to the owner’s startup motivation, financial stake, and management capabilities. Informal firms that rely on larger suppliers, extend customer installment credit, engage in marketing promotions, or employ more formal organizational structures are also more likely to adopt structured recordkeeping systems, highlighting accounting’s role as a managerial tool rather than as a compliance function or as a precursor to entering the formal economy. Informal firms that maintain notebooks separating business and personal accounts are significantly more likely to apply for and obtain bank loans. Our inferences for access to credit also extend to microenterprises in the Dominican Republic. In addition, accounting quality appears to support lender due diligence even among informal firms, particularly when lenders are more sophisticated. Using a broader measure of credit market status, we find that accounting quality rises monotonically across credit tiers. Finally, we find that entrepreneurs with higher-quality accounting systems are more likely to plan for business expansion. By illuminating the motivations behind accounting choices in low-enforcement settings, this study deepens our understanding of the foundational role accounting plays in early-stage business development in emerging markets.

Leveraging a specially designed investor education website, we conduct a field experiment, sharing insights on the pricing of accounting accruals with investors across China and the US on social media. We find that the treatment stocks experience a reduction in accrual mispricing relative to the control stocks. This effect is particularly pronounced when knowledge that enhances the conceptual understanding of accruals is paired with knowledge that aids in the quantitative application of accruals. Furthermore, the treatment effect is strengthened among stocks with investors who engage more deeply with the educational content yet possess lower financial sophistication.

Furthermore, the treatment effect is strengthened among stocks with investors who engage more deeply with the educational content yet possess lower financial sophistication.KeywordsFinancial knowledge; Accrual mispricing; Investor education; Field experiment; Social mediaJEL classificationG14; G41; G53; C93IntroductionHaving knowledge of financial concepts and skills is crucial for making sound financial decisions. Research indicates that financial knowledge influences individuals’ financial behavior in various aspects, such as market participation and asset allocation.1 Given that financial behavior drives asset prices, it is surprising that the literature does not directly assess the effects of financial knowledge on asset prices. This study aims to fill this gap by examining whether financial knowledge affects asset pricing. Education can empower investors with the knowledge and skills needed to process and interpret public information (e.g., corporate disclosures). This, in turn, supplies the market with more informed investors, improving the efficiency of stock prices.This topic poses both conceptual and empirical challenges. First, in perfect market conditions, where investors possess comprehensive knowledge and the full capacity to process information, additional education should not influence their decisions and, consequently, stock prices (Simon, 1987). Although, in reality, investors have imperfect knowledge and limited cognitive resources (Simon, 1955; Kahneman and Tversky, 1973), education may still prove ineffective if investors lack motivation and the requisite expertise to comprehend the educational materials (Piaget, 2003; Fernandes et al., 2014), or cannot apply their newfound knowledge to real-world decisions (Merkoulova and Veld, 2022).2Empirically, it is hard to establish a causal link between financial knowledge and asset pricing. One primary hurdle is the potential endogeneity between financial knowledge and stock prices (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014; Bianchi, 2018). For instance, financial knowledge and market outcomes can be simultaneously shaped by less observable factors such as individuals’ time preferences and wealth endowment (Jappelli and Padula, 2013; Meier and Sprenger, 2013). Moreover, there is a possibility of a feedback loop: when investors gain experience and learn from past stock prices, their financial knowledge deepens, which in turn could influence prices.To tackle these challenges and investigate our research question, we conduct a field experiment that involves educating investors about accounting accruals, a concrete type of financial knowledge. Accruals represent the difference between a firm's reported earnings and its underlying cash flows, reflecting the firm's estimates of future benefits and obligations. In essence, the accrual component of earnings is less persistent than the cash flow component in predicting future earnings. However, numerous studies show that, due to cognitive limitations, investors often overlook the transient nature of accruals and overprice stocks with high accruals, a phenomenon known as the “accrual anomaly” (or “accrual mispricing”) (Sloan, 1996; Xie, 2001; Richardson et al., 2005; Chan et al., 2006; Allen et al., 2013). Our study investigates whether investor education can address the anomaly.We choose to focus on accruals for three reasons. First, the literature identifies accrual mispricing as one of the most pervasive and robust financial anomalies (Fama and French, 2008; Hirshleifer et al., 2012; Avramov et al., 2013). While extensive efforts are made to explain this phenomenon (Mashruwala et al., 2006; Khan, 2008), the mechanisms underlying accrual mispricing remain unclear (Richardson et al., 2010). Second, unlike basic financial concepts such as compounding, inflation, interest rates, and diversification (Van Rooij et al., 2011; Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014), accruals represent a more intricate concept. Gaining proficiency in this area can notably enhance an individual's financial acumen (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014). Third, given that grasping the economic implications of accruals demands a sophisticated cognitive aptitude (Collins et al., 2003), accruals present an ideal base to test the efficacy of investor education.We implement randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to examine whether providing accrual knowledge to investors reduces accrual mispricing. Our experiment has two distinctive features. First, we convey this specialized knowledge to investors via social media platforms. Evidence indicates that social media, serving as vital conduits of information for investors, play a significant role in influencing investor behaviors and stock market outcomes (Miller and Skinner, 2015). A testament to this is the stock price rebound for GameStop and AMC in January 2021, highlighting the growing sway of social media in the investment community.3Second, we conduct the experiment to across firms listed in both the Chinese and US markets. Nobel laureate Abhijit Banerjee posits that “a very simple approach to generalization … is to implement the same concept in multiple locations to build confidence in its impact” (Banerjee, 2020, p.1938). As the leading developed market, the US operates under rigorous securities regulations and features significant participation of institutional investors. Conversely, China, while being the world's largest emerging market and second-largest stock market by capitalization, has a more relaxed regulatory environment and tends to be dominated by retail investors (Titman et al., 2022). Given the large institutional differences between the two countries, any consistent findings from our study would support the generalizability of our conclusion.Our experiment ran from January to December 2020, covering all publicly listed firms in China and the US. We develop two distinct educational modules on the concepts and pricing implications of accruals. The first module offers a conceptual introduction of accruals, detailing their definition, properties, and implications for future earnings (conceptual knowledge). The second module introduces methodologies for estimating accruals, detailing specific models, key variables, data sources, and tools (methodological knowledge). The materials are made available in Chinese and English for the respective markets.We disseminate these materials using social media platforms in each country, namely Weibo, Xueqiu, and Guba EastMoney in China and Twitter and StockTwits in the US. Over a 19-day window around firms’ earnings announcement (EA) days in 2020, we share the two sets of knowledge, along with the upcoming EA news, on the designated tag pages for the treatment group of stocks. For a subset of stocks, only the conceptual knowledge and EA news are shared. Each of these posts contains a hyperlink to a custom webpage we built for the relevant stock, ensuring easy access to the complete educational materials.We create a control group of stocks by merely sharing the upcoming EA news as a placebo. In theory, any observed difference in accrual pricing between the treatment and control groups should reflect the effect of accrual education. For a robustness check, we establish an alternative benchmark by creating a comparison group of stocks for which we did not share any information. Our final dataset comprises 2284 stocks from the Chinese market and 2387 stocks from the US market. Our educational materials garnered a total of 26,834,089 views in China and 3,397,437 views in the US, tallied one day after posting on platforms that provide such data. Diagnostic tests confirm no significant differences in firm characteristics between the treatment and control groups, and the stock price movements prior to the experiment are parallel across groups.In line with prior studies (Sloan, 1996; Xie, 2001), high-accrual stocks in the control group earn positive abnormal returns around the EAs that subsequently reverse over the following year. The evidence confirms the presence of accrual mispricing in our setting and echoes recent findings that the anomaly persists when measured with true release dates and as-filed data (Du et al., 2023; Bowles et al., 2024).Next, we examine whether accrual education reduces this mispricing, which can be broken down into two components: overvaluation of accruals during EAs and subsequent price correction in the post-EA phase. First, using a difference-in-differences (DID) analysis, we find that EA returns for high-accrual stocks are lower in the treatment group than in the control group across both markets, suggesting that the education treatment results in a price discount for high-accrual stocks at the announcement. When separating the treatments, we find that the effect is driven by the treatment of combined conceptual and methodological knowledge; the conceptual-only treatment has the expected sign but lacks statistical significance. proposed.title: Knowledge is power: A field experiment in the Chinese and US stock markets
proposed.abstract: This study examines the causal effect of financial knowledge on stock pricing efficiency. Leveraging a specially designed investor education website, we conduct a field experiment, sharing insights on the pricing of accounting accruals with investors across China and the US on social media. We find that the treatment stocks experience a reduction in accrual mispricing relative to the control stocks. This effect is particularly pronounced when knowledge that enhances the conceptual understanding of accruals is paired with knowledge that aids in the quantitative application of accruals. Furthermore, the treatment effect is strengthened among stocks with investors who engage more deeply with the educational content yet possess lower financial sophistication.

Research indicates that financial knowledge influences individuals’ financial behavior in various aspects, such as market participation and asset allocation.1 Given that financial behavior drives asset prices, it is surprising that the literature does not directly assess the effects of financial knowledge on asset prices. This study aims to fill this gap by examining whether financial knowledge affects asset pricing. Education can empower investors with the knowledge and skills needed to process and interpret public information (e.g., corporate disclosures). This, in turn, supplies the market with more informed investors, improving the efficiency of stock prices.This topic poses both conceptual and empirical challenges. First, in perfect market conditions, where investors possess comprehensive knowledge and the full capacity to process information, additional education should not influence their decisions and, consequently, stock prices (Simon, 1987). Although, in reality, investors have imperfect knowledge and limited cognitive resources (Simon, 1955; Kahneman and Tversky, 1973), education may still prove ineffective if investors lack motivation and the requisite expertise to comprehend the educational materials (Piaget, 2003; Fernandes et al., 2014), or cannot apply their newfound knowledge to real-world decisions (Merkoulova and Veld, 2022).2Empirically, it is hard to establish a causal link between financial knowledge and asset pricing. One primary hurdle is the potential endogeneity between financial knowledge and stock prices (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014; Bianchi, 2018). For instance, financial knowledge and market outcomes can be simultaneously shaped by less observable factors such as individuals’ time preferences and wealth endowment (Jappelli and Padula, 2013; Meier and Sprenger, 2013). Moreover, there is a possibility of a feedback loop: when investors gain experience and learn from past stock prices, their financial knowledge deepens, which in turn could influence prices.To tackle these challenges and investigate our research question, we conduct a field experiment that involves educating investors about accounting accruals, a concrete type of financial knowledge. Accruals represent the difference between a firm's reported earnings and its underlying cash flows, reflecting the firm's estimates of future benefits and obligations. In essence, the accrual component of earnings is less persistent than the cash flow component in predicting future earnings. First, the literature identifies accrual mispricing as one of the most pervasive and robust financial anomalies (Fama and French, 2008; Hirshleifer et al., 2012; Avramov et al., 2013). While extensive efforts are made to explain this phenomenon (Mashruwala et al., 2006; Khan, 2008), the mechanisms underlying accrual mispricing remain unclear (Richardson et al., 2010). Second, unlike basic financial concepts such as compounding, inflation, interest rates, and diversification (Van Rooij et al., 2011; Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014), accruals represent a more intricate concept. Gaining proficiency in this area can notably enhance an individual's financial acumen (Lusardi and Mitchell, 2014). proposed.title: Knowledge is power: A field experiment in the Chinese and US stock markets
proposed.abstract: This study examines the causal effect of financial knowledge on stock pricing efficiency. Leveraging a specially designed investor education website, we conduct a field experiment, sharing insights on the pricing of accounting accruals with investors across China and the US on social media. We find that the treatment stocks experience a reduction in accrual mispricing relative to the control stocks. This effect is particularly pronounced when knowledge that enhances the conceptual understanding of accruals is paired with knowledge that aids in the quantitative application of accruals. Furthermore, the treatment effect is strengthened among stocks with investors who engage more deeply with the educational content yet possess lower financial sophistication.

Do proprietary traders provide liquidity?
Do proprietary traders provide liquidity?✰

Whether proprietary traders provide or take liquidity, and how their behavior evolves over the business cycle and across stocks, remains at the center of an ongoing debate. Using a unique dataset from the NYSE, we document that proprietary traders act as net liquidity providers, buying after price declines in a contrarian pattern. Proprietary trader liquidity provision is concentrated in large, liquid, low-volatility stocks and diminishes significantly when intermediary balance sheets are weak. Liquidity provision is stronger when price movements are plausibly not driven by information. Our findings highlight both the role and the limits of proprietary traders in supporting market liquidity across time and market segments.

Moulton dShow moreCiteAdd to MendeleyShare10.1016/j.jfineco.2026.104325Access through your organizationPurchase PDFMore actionsArticle previewAbstractIntroductionSection snippetsReferences (31)AbstractWhether proprietary traders provide or take liquidity, and how their behavior evolves over the business cycle and across stocks, remains at the center of an ongoing debate. Using a unique dataset from the NYSE, we document that proprietary traders act as net liquidity providers, buying after price declines in a contrarian pattern. Proprietary trader liquidity provision is concentrated in large, liquid, low-volatility stocks and diminishes significantly when intermediary balance sheets are weak. Liquidity provision is stronger when price movements are plausibly not driven by information. Our findings highlight both the role and the limits of proprietary traders in supporting market liquidity across time and market segments.KeywordsProprietary traders; Liquidity; Bank capitalJEL classificationG12; G20; G28Previous article in this issueNext article in this issueIntroductionThe role of proprietary trading in capital markets has received heightened attention since the 2008 financial crisis. On one hand, proprietary trading – the practice of financial institutions trading for their own accounts – is generally considered riskier and more speculative than traditional banking activities such as taking deposits and granting loans, facilitating corporate finance transactions, or trading on behalf of clients.1 On the other hand, it is argued that proprietary traders provide liquidity in markets especially when it is most needed, thereby reducing systemic risk. Using unique data, this paper documents a number of key facts about proprietary trading activity and analyzes whether, under what circumstances, and in which stocks proprietary traders provide liquidity.Proprietary (prop) trading grew in popularity during the 1990s and early 2000s, with proprietary trading desks effectively functioning as internal hedge funds within their institutions. In the aftermath of the financial crisis, the Volcker Rule limited financial institutions’ speculative activity by prohibiting proprietary trading. Much of the public debate over the Volcker Rule revolves around the role of proprietary trading in providing liquidity in financial markets. A key argument put forth by opponents of the rule is that no clear-cut distinction exists between liquidity provision and speculation, and so curbing proprietary trading would hinder liquidity provision by financial institutions. For example, a report issued by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce (see Thakor, 2012) argues that “the Volcker Rule will have a negative effect on market making and liquidity provision for many securities.” Given this debate on the merits of the Volcker Rule, policy is still in flux. In 2018, Congress passed the EGRRCP Act, which exempted smaller banks from the Volcker Rule (see, e.g., Erkens and Gan, 2022), and in 2019 and 2022, financial regulatory agencies responsible for enforcing the Volcker Rule relaxed constraints on banks’ ability to engage in proprietary trading and invest in hedge funds and private equity funds.2Despite the continued debate on the effects of proprietary trading, evidence on the trading practices of proprietary traders is scarce, as is evidence of whether proprietary traders do indeed provide liquidity in security markets. This fact may not be surprising given that data on the trades of proprietary traders are not broadly and publicly available. In this paper, we fill this gap by using a unique dataset from the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) that allows us to track, for each stock, the aggregate trading activity of proprietary traders on a daily basis between 1999 and 2010 (the last year of available data). This time period precedes the Volcker Rule and therefore captures a period during which proprietary trading was not constrained. We use these data to gain insight into the following fundamental questions:(i)Do proprietary traders provide liquidity in equity markets?(ii)In which stocks do proprietary traders play a more dominant role in liquidity provision?(iii)How does liquidity provision in equity markets by proprietary traders vary over time and how does it relate to the strength of financial institutions’ balance sheets?We begin our analysis by providing a set of basic, yet novel, stylized facts on proprietary trading activity. We document that proprietary trading is concentrated in large, liquid, and less volatile stocks. For example, in 1999, 80% of average daily proprietary trading volume occurred in 216 stocks on the NYSE, with these stocks representing 76% of total NYSE market capitalization. In 2010, the last year of our sample, the equivalent statistics are 276 stocks and 80% of total NYSE market capitalization. Examining the subset of stocks in which proprietary traders focus their activity, our results further indicate that the percentage of trading volume accounted for by proprietary traders increases markedly with firm size and stock liquidity and decreases with stock volatility. Across the stocks in which proprietary traders are active, proprietary traders account for approximately one-quarter of trading volume.Trading, however, is not equivalent to liquidity provision. We thus continue by constructing a daily measure of aggregate proprietary trade imbalance for each stock on the NYSE and use it to analyze whether, and to what extent, proprietary traders provide or demand liquidity. A positive proprietary trade imbalance for a stock on a given day indicates that proprietary traders are net buyers, whereas a negative imbalance indicates they are net sellers for the day. Following Lehmann (1990), Lo and MacKinlay (1990), and Nagel (2012), which identify liquidity provision with short-term reversal strategies, these imbalances allow us to examine whether proprietary traders provide liquidity or take liquidity in a given stock on a given day. The underlying idea is that traders who buy stocks whose price decreased in recent days, or sell stocks whose price increased during prior days, provide liquidity to other market participants.3Due to data availability limitations, much of the prior research on liquidity provision does not examine actual trading activity of market participants and the extent to which these participants provide liquidity. Instead, in the absence of data on actual trades, much of this literature has focused on the returns to liquidity provision, as proxied by the returns to contrarian strategies (see, e.g., Nagel, 2012). In contrast, our data allow us to observe the aggregate trading activity of proprietary traders at the stock-day level, with which we can create a direct proxy for liquidity provision using trading behavior.Using these unique data, our analysis shows that, on average, proprietary traders do provide liquidity: a one-standard-deviation decline in daily market-adjusted stock returns is associated with an increase of following-day proprietary trade imbalance of 0.7% of the stock’s average daily trading volume. This baseline result is robust to the inclusion of dynamic effects in an autoregressive structure in which lagged returns may influence current flows and, conversely, trading activity may impact subsequent returns. We study the dynamic effects using a local projection analysis (as in Jordà, 2005, Ramey and Zubairy, 2018; and Gorodnichenko et al., 2023) as well as a panel vector autoregression (VAR) framework.We next examine how liquidity provision by proprietary traders varies over time and across stocks. By definition, proprietary trading requires risking the financial institution’s own capital. Garleanu and Pedersen (2007) and Brunnermeier and Pedersen (2009) show that internal funding and risk management considerations constrain the ability of financial intermediaries to provide liquidity in financial markets. We thus hypothesize that proprietary trader liquidity provision varies positively with the strength of financial institutions’ balance sheets.4 Further, we hypothesize that, cross-sectionally, liquidity provision by proprietary traders varies negatively with the riskiness of stocks being traded.We employ two measures to proxy for the strength of banks’ balance sheets. The first is the intermediary capital risk factor (ICRF) proposed in He, Kelly, and Manela (2017).5 A high ICRF corresponds to periods in which bank capital is relatively abundant. The second measure is the Treasury over Eurodollar (TED) spread. A high TED spread reflects periods in which bank capital is scarce as indicated by a relatively high price of credit. We find that proprietary traders provide liquidity during periods in which bank balance sheets are relatively strong as measured by the ICRF or the TED spread. In contrast, during periods when intermediary capital is weak, liquidity provision by proprietary traders is sharply reduced.Next, we consider the characteristics of the stocks for which proprietary traders provide liquidity. We hypothesize that proprietary trading is negatively related to the risk of the stock being traded, as liquidity provision requires risking financial institutions’ own capital. Consistent with this hypothesis, we find that proprietary traders concentrate their liquidity provision in large and medium-sized firms, and among more liquid, less volatile, and higher-volume stocks.We continue by studying non-linearities in proprietary traders’ liquidity provision. There are two main reasons to expect a non-linear relation. First, liquidity provision may be limited following large returns due to capital constraints or balance sheet stress (Comerton-Forde, Hendershott, Jones, Moulton, and Seasholes, 2010). Second, we expect more liquidity provision following non-information-driven shocks to prices, because such price shocks are expected to revert (e.g., Campbell, Grossman, and Wang, 1993). Since extreme price movements are more likely to be information-driven (see, e.g., Jylhä et al., 2014), we hypothesize that information considerations are also expected to drive a non-linear relation between liquidity provision and returns – with less extreme returns being associated with more liquidity provision.To test for non-linearity, we employ two approaches. In the first, we consider a winsorized sample of returns. Consistent with our hypothesis, we find that liquidity provision by proprietary traders is indeed stronger when large price movements are winsorized. For example, proprietary trader liquidity provision increases by approximately 30% in the 1% winsorized sample relative to the baseline. For our second approach, we compare liquidity provision following prior-day returns within one-half standard deviation of the mean market-adjusted return to liquidity provision following prior-day returns outside one-half standard deviation of the mean market-adjusted return. Consistent with non-linear liquidity provision due to capital constraints or information concerns, we find that proprietary trader liquidity provision is three times larger within one-half standard deviation than outside one-half standard deviation of returns.To further examine the role of information in liquidity provision, we analyze trading activity on stock ex-dividend dates. proposed.title: Do proprietary traders provide liquidity?
proposed.abstract: Whether proprietary traders provide or take liquidity, and how their behavior evolves over the business cycle and across stocks, remains at the center of an ongoing debate. Using a unique dataset from the NYSE, we document that proprietary traders act as net liquidity providers, buying after price declines in a contrarian pattern. Proprietary trader liquidity provision is concentrated in large, liquid, low-volatility stocks and diminishes significantly when intermediary balance sheets are weak. Liquidity provision is stronger when price movements are plausibly not driven by information. Our findings highlight both the role and the limits of proprietary traders in supporting market liquidity across time and market segments.

On one hand, proprietary trading – the practice of financial institutions trading for their own accounts – is generally considered riskier and more speculative than traditional banking activities such as taking deposits and granting loans, facilitating corporate finance transactions, or trading on behalf of clients.1 On the other hand, it is argued that proprietary traders provide liquidity in markets especially when it is most needed, thereby reducing systemic risk. Using unique data, this paper documents a number of key facts about proprietary trading activity and analyzes whether, under what circumstances, and in which stocks proprietary traders provide liquidity.Proprietary (prop) trading grew in popularity during the 1990s and early 2000s, with proprietary trading desks effectively functioning as internal hedge funds within their institutions. In the aftermath of the financial crisis, the Volcker Rule limited financial institutions’ speculative activity by prohibiting proprietary trading. Much of the public debate over the Volcker Rule revolves around the role of proprietary trading in providing liquidity in financial markets. A key argument put forth by opponents of the rule is that no clear-cut distinction exists between liquidity provision and speculation, and so curbing proprietary trading would hinder liquidity provision by financial institutions. For example, a report issued by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce (see Thakor, 2012) argues that “the Volcker Rule will have a negative effect on market making and liquidity provision for many securities.” Given this debate on the merits of the Volcker Rule, policy is still in flux. In 2018, Congress passed the EGRRCP Act, which exempted smaller banks from the Volcker Rule (see, e.g., Erkens and Gan, 2022), and in 2019 and 2022, financial regulatory agencies responsible for enforcing the Volcker Rule relaxed constraints on banks’ ability to engage in proprietary trading and invest in hedge funds and private equity funds.2Despite the continued debate on the effects of proprietary trading, evidence on the trading practices of proprietary traders is scarce, as is evidence of whether proprietary traders do indeed provide liquidity in security markets. This fact may not be surprising given that data on the trades of proprietary traders are not broadly and publicly available. In this paper, we fill this gap by using a unique dataset from the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) that allows us to track, for each stock, the aggregate trading activity of proprietary traders on a daily basis between 1999 and 2010 (the last year of available data). This time period precedes the Volcker Rule and therefore captures a period during which proprietary trading was not constrained. We document that proprietary trading is concentrated in large, liquid, and less volatile stocks. For example, in 1999, 80% of average daily proprietary trading volume occurred in 216 stocks on the NYSE, with these stocks representing 76% of total NYSE market capitalization. In 2010, the last year of our sample, the equivalent statistics are 276 stocks and 80% of total NYSE market capitalization. Examining the subset of stocks in which proprietary traders focus their activity, our results further indicate that the percentage of trading volume accounted for by proprietary traders increases markedly with firm size and stock liquidity and decreases with stock volatility. Across the stocks in which proprietary traders are active, proprietary traders account for approximately one-quarter of trading volume.Trading, however, is not equivalent to liquidity provision. We thus continue by constructing a daily measure of aggregate proprietary trade imbalance for each stock on the NYSE and use it to analyze whether, and to what extent, proprietary traders provide or demand liquidity. A positive proprietary trade imbalance for a stock on a given day indicates that proprietary traders are net buyers, whereas a negative imbalance indicates they are net sellers for the day. Following Lehmann (1990), Lo and MacKinlay (1990), and Nagel (2012), which identify liquidity provision with short-term reversal strategies, these imbalances allow us to examine whether proprietary traders provide liquidity or take liquidity in a given stock on a given day. proposed.title: Do proprietary traders provide liquidity?
proposed.abstract: Whether proprietary traders provide or take liquidity, and how their behavior evolves over the business cycle and across stocks, remains at the center of an ongoing debate. Using a unique dataset from the NYSE, we document that proprietary traders act as net liquidity providers, buying after price declines in a contrarian pattern. Proprietary trader liquidity provision is concentrated in large, liquid, low-volatility stocks and diminishes significantly when intermediary balance sheets are weak. Liquidity provision is stronger when price movements are plausibly not driven by information. Our findings highlight both the role and the limits of proprietary traders in supporting market liquidity across time and market segments.

We demonstrate the passthrough of Treasury supply to bank deposits through bank market power. We show that a larger Treasury supply crowds out deposits with disproportionate effects in more competitive deposit markets. A larger Treasury supply further curtails bank lending and affects bank funding structure. The explanatory power of Treasury supply is not driven by other shocks to deposit demand and supply. In comparison, monetary policy rate hikes have a larger impact on deposit funding in more concentrated markets, consistent with the deposits channel of monetary policy. Our empirical findings are rationalized in a model of imperfect deposit competition.

We show that a larger Treasury supply crowds out deposits with disproportionate effects in more competitive deposit markets. A larger Treasury supply further curtails bank lending and affects bank funding structure. The explanatory power of Treasury supply is not driven by other shocks to deposit demand and supply. In comparison, monetary policy rate hikes have a larger impact on deposit funding in more concentrated markets, consistent with the deposits channel of monetary policy. Our empirical findings are rationalized in a model of imperfect deposit competition.KeywordsTreasuries; Bank deposits; Safe assets; Financial intermediation; Monetary policyPrevious article in this issueNext article in this issueIntroductionFrom February 2007 to February 2020, the volume of marketable Treasuries almost quadrupled, followed by an additional $4.2 trillion increase during the Covid-19 pandemic. One important question arising from this rapid expansion of Treasury supply is its effect on the funding and lending capacity of the commercial banking sector. After all, one of the central roles of the banking sector is to provide liquidity (Diamond and Dybvig, 1983). Treasury securities that satisfy the demand for liquidity may thus reduce investors’ demand for bank deposits. At the same time, individual banks compete with each other in local deposit markets by supplying differentiated deposit products (Drechsler et al., 2017). Such differentiation across banks gives rise to bank market power and influences the rate sensitivity of banks’ aggregate deposit supply. As a result, deposit competition is a crucial determinant of the extent to which Treasury supply affects bank deposit funding.In this paper, we examine the effect of Treasury supply on the banking sector in the presence of bank market power. We show that higher deposit competition renders the aggregate deposit supply more rate-sensitive. Thus, when an increase in Treasury supply reduces the demand for deposits, its substitute good, the contraction in deposit funding is amplified by deposit competition.The impact of Treasury supply on bank funding is especially important to understand because surges in Treasury growth often occur during economic downturns, when investors and banks are more constrained. Empirically tracing out the impact of Treasury supply on the banking sector is challenging precisely for the same reason: Treasury supply varies with the business cycle along with other shocks to investors’ demand for deposits and banks’ supply of deposits. While the literature has mostly focused on time-series variation, we identify the impact of Treasury supply using cross-sectional variation in deposit rates and volumes.Our results have several important implications. First, we demonstrate that Treasury supply affects financial stability by altering the composition of bank funding. Wholesale deposit markets are more competitive than retail deposit markets, so a larger Treasury supply disproportionately crowds out wholesale deposits. The reduced reliance on wholesale funding may, in turn, lower the likelihood of bank default because wholesale funding is more runnable than retail deposits.Second, because deposits are an important and irreplaceable funding source for banks, Treasury growth contracts bank lending to the real economy and alters the distribution of loan supply in different geographical areas. For a one-standard-deviation increase in Treasury growth, banks at the third quartile of deposit competition experience a 159.4bps larger drop in new small business lending and a 233.3bps larger drop in on-balance-sheet new mortgage loans relative to banks at the first quartile of deposit competition.Finally, we contrast the transmission of Treasury supply with that of monetary policy as in Drechsler et al. (2017). Our analysis jointly considers both policies and shows that more competitive deposit markets experience the most pronounced crowding out of deposits following Treasury growth while benefiting the least from the deposit expansion following policy rate cuts. These results arise because Treasury supply primarily affects investors’ demand for deposits, while the policy rate primarily shifts banks’ supply of deposits. We thus confirm the deposits channel of monetary policy and establish the different passthrough of Treasury supply to bank deposit funding.We first build a simple model to shed light on the mechanisms at play. In the model, deposits are supplied by differentiated banks. When there are more banks or when deposits appear less differentiated to investors, deposit competition is stronger so that the aggregate deposit supply is more rate sensitive. Investors choose a portfolio of deposits, cash, Treasuries, and a benchmark capital market bond that is available at the monetary policy rate, i.e., the Fed funds rate. Cash earns zero interest, and therefore, the Fed funds rate is the opportunity cost of holding cash. Similarly, the opportunity cost of holding Treasuries and deposits are reflected by the Fed funds-Treasury spread and the Fed funds-deposit spread, respectively. Banks raise deposit funding to invest in loans and face a downward-sloping loan demand with respect to the loan spread.When Treasury supply increases, the demand for deposits drops because Treasuries and deposits are substitutes in providing liquidity to investors. The drop in demand makes both the quantity and price of deposits, i.e., the deposit spread, fall. The relative impact on price versus quantity depends on the slope of the deposit supply curve, which depends on the level of deposit competition between banks. If competition is high, the deposit supply curve is relatively rate sensitive and the impact is primarily on deposit quantities. If competition is low, the deposit supply curve is relatively less rate sensitive and the impact is mainly on deposit spreads.In contrast, increases in the Fed funds rate primarily contract the aggregate deposit supply curve. A higher Fed funds rate increases the cost of holding cash and thereby reduces the substitution away from deposits, consistent with the deposits channel of monetary policy (Drechsler et al., 2017). Therefore, banks have more deposit market power when the Fed funds rate is high, which reduces the aggregate supply of deposits and increases the Fed funds-deposit spread. When deposit competition is high, the aggregate deposit supply is relatively more rate sensitive, so the Fed funds-deposit spread increases by less.Our model also provides insights into the effect of Treasury supply on banks’ wholesale funding ratio. Institutional investors tend to be more active in searching for better deposit rates than retail investors. This renders wholesale deposits at different banks better substitutes and leads to a more rate-sensitive supply for wholesale deposits. Since a more rate-sensitive deposit supply magnifies the crowding-out effect of Treasury supply, government-supplied liquidity curbs the reliance on wholesale funding.The aggregate time series provides preliminary evidence for our model predictions. We find that Treasury growth is negatively correlated with total deposit growth, with the negative correlation being stronger for wholesale deposits. These results are robust to controlling for Fed funds rate changes, but it could be that other macroeconomic variables comove with Treasury supply and deposit volume in the time series. For example, economic downturns may drive both an increase in Treasury issuance and a decline in firms’ demand for bank loans, which reduces banks’ funding needs and their supply of deposits. Further, Treasury issuance may comove with economic conditions that influence investors’ demand for deposits.To avoid the confounding effect of comoving investment opportunities, we use within-bank, across-branch variation in deposit volumes and rates to verify our model predictions. The identification assumption is that funds can be freely transferred within branches of the same bank. Hence, the remaining variation observed across branches of the same bank should be due to banks’ deposit pricing strategies under different levels of local deposit competition. In the baseline specification, we use a standard Herfindahl Index (HHI) to measure deposit competition at the county level. We also control for Fed funds rate changes to clearly distinguish between the effects of monetary policy and Treasury supply.Further, to ensure that our results are not driven by deposit demand shocks correlated with Treasury supply, we control for time-varying county-level conditions and use an instrumented specification. Our results remain robust when we control for observable county-level economic characteristics, including the percentage change in income per capita, population growth, and the change in unemployment rate. We further instrument for Treasury growth to account for unobservable deposit demand shocks. Our first instrument is based on shocks to military expenditure, where positive shocks to military expenditure increase the issuance of Treasuries but are plausibly exogenous to local economic conditions that affect county-level deposit demand. Our second instrument is based on high-frequency variation in Treasury supply associated with seasonal tax deadlines following Greenwood et al. (2015). Finally, we show that our estimates are robust to a number of alternative specifications.Taken together, our estimation results confirm the model predictions. When Treasury supply increases, banks widen their Treasury-deposit spreads by more and experience more substantial outflows at branches located in more competitive areas. For a one-standard-deviation increase in Treasury growth, branches at the third quartile of deposit competition, i.e., the 25th percentile of HHI, experience a 43.3bps larger drop in deposit growth compared to branches of the same bank at the first quartile of deposit competition, i.e., the 75th percentile of HHI. These magnitudes are economically significant. Applying our estimates to project the overall effect of Treasury growth, we find a 140.9bps drop in deposit growth for a one-standard-deviation increase in Treasury growth.1The distributional effect of Fed funds rate changes is opposite to that of Treasury growth. For a one-standard-deviation increase (decrease) in the Fed funds rate, branches at the third quartile of deposit competition experience a 32.0bps smaller decrease (increase) in deposit growth than branches of the same bank at the first quartile of deposit competition.We find that both short-term and long-term Treasuries play a role in the crowding out of deposits. While Treasuries with less than one-year maturity, including Treasury Bills, command a higher liquidity premium than Treasuries with more than one-year maturity, the much larger volume of Treasuries with more than one-year maturity partially offsets their lower liquidity premium compared to short-term Treasuries.Treasury supply also affects the structure of bank funding. Quantitatively, we find that the wholesale funding ratio decreases by 23.0bps following a one-standard-deviation increase in Treasury growth. At the same time, we find that a one-standard-deviation cut in the Fed funds rate lowers the wholesale funding ratio by 26.6bps. This implies that monetary easing and increased Treasury issuance during a financial downturn may jointly reduce the dependence on wholesale funding and improve the funding stability of the banking sector.Finally, the crowding out of deposits by Treasury supply spills over to contract bank lending to the real economy and affects the distribution of loan supply. Because money is fungible across branches of the same bank, we evaluate the effect of deposit competition at the bank level, where the bank-level exposure to deposit competition is the weighted average of branch-level deposit competition. Comparing loans to borrowers in the same county, we find that the effect of deposit competition on bank lending is economically significant and consistent with our findings on deposits. For a one-standard-deviation increase in Treasury growth, banks at the third quartile of deposit competition experience a 159.4bps larger drop in new small business lending and a 233.3bps larger drop in on-balance-sheet new mortgage loans relative to banks at the first quartile of deposit competition.Literature ReviewOur paper contributes to several strands of research. First, we build on the safe assets literature that has demonstrated an aggregate demand for money-like convenience services by Treasuries and its effect on the financial sector (Krishnamurthy and Vissing-Jorgensen, 2012, Krishnamurthy and Vissing-Jorgensen, 2015, Greenwood et al., 2010, Greenwood et al., 2015). Several papers have zoomed in on demand for shorter-term debt like Treasury bills and repos (d’Avernas and Vandeweyer, 2024, Infante, 2020, d’Avernas et al., 2025), while Krishnamurthy and Li (2023) incorporate Treasuries of all maturities and shadow bank liabilities. We show that an important determinant in the crowding out of deposits by Treasuries is deposit competition between differentiated banks. Heterogeneity in deposit competition across markets and deposit types also leads to distributional effects in the cross-section of banks and influences bank funding structure.We also contribute to a growing banking literature on deposit competition. Several papers analyze the effect of deposit competition in the transmission of conventional monetary policy (Drechsler et al., 2017, Wang et al., 2022, Whited et al., 2021) and unconventional monetary policy (Diamond et al., 2024, Albertazzi et al., 2022). We are the first to show how deposit competition affects the transmission of Treasury supply to bank funding and lending. We also confirm the effect of monetary policy on bank deposits as in Drechsler et al. (2017) while establishing the distinct and different passthrough of Treasury supply.Finally, our findings provide insights into the effect of publicly supplied safe assets on financial stability. Gorton and Metrick, 2012, Carlson et al., 2016, Sunderam, 2015, and Kacperczyk et al. (2021) illustrate how the demand for safe and liquid assets fueled the expansion of shadow banks. We show that increases in the supply of Treasuries reduce banks’ wholesale funding ratio. This reduced reliance on wholesale funding contributes to the funding stability of banks, consistent with the evidence from Egan et al. (2017) that uninsured wholesale deposits are subject to runs.This paper is organized as follows: Section 2 examines the aggregate time series. Section 3 develops a model of imperfect deposit competition to rationalize the observed trends and guide the subsequent empirical strategy. Section 4 explains the data sources used in estimating the crowding out of deposits in Section 5. In Sections 6 Impact on bank lending, 7 Impact on bank funding structure, we estimate the effect of Treasury supply on bank lending and wholesale funding, respectively. Section 8 concludes.Organizational accessGet full-text access by signing in with your organisationAccess through your organizationOther access optionsPurchase PDFNeed help with access?Section snippetsAggregate trendsWe begin by examining the aggregate relationship between Treasury supply and deposit funding. Fig. 4 shows the overall composition of US commercial bank assets from 1980 to 2018, illustrating that loans and securities, including Treasuries, are the two dominant asset categories on bank balance sheets. Fig. 1(a) plots the year-over-year deposit growth and the year-over-year Treasury growth from 1973 to 2019.2ModelWe develop a model to understand the impact of Treasury supply on bank deposits in the presence of deposit competition. We first explain our identification strategy and then present the estimation results.Impact on bank lendingThis section examines the effect of Treasury supply on bank lending to firms and mortgage borrowers. Wholesale investors respond more to changes in Treasury supply relative to retail investors. A larger Treasury supply further curtails bank lending and affects bank funding structure. The explanatory power of Treasury supply is not driven by other shocks to deposit demand and supply. In comparison, monetary policy rate hikes have a larger impact on deposit funding in more concentrated markets, consistent with the deposits channel of monetary policy. Our empirical findings are rationalized in a model of imperfect deposit competition.

The passthrough of treasury supply to bank deposit funding

We demonstrate the passthrough of Treasury supply to bank deposits through bank market power. We show that a larger Treasury supply crowds out deposits with disproportionate effects in more competitive deposit markets. A larger Treasury supply further curtails bank lending and affects bank funding structure. The explanatory power of Treasury supply is not driven by other shocks to deposit demand and supply. In comparison, monetary policy rate hikes have a larger impact on deposit funding in more concentrated markets, consistent with the deposits channel of monetary policy. Our empirical findings are rationalized in a model of imperfect deposit competition.
