Extending Campbell–Cochrane preferences with both market- and home-consumption habits allows them to operate in production economies while preserving realistic macroeconomic dynamics.JEL classificationE32; E43; E44; G12.KeywordsEquity and bond yields; Campbell–Cochrane habits; Nominal rigidities; Macro-finance separation; New Keynesian modelPrevious article in this issueNext article in this issueIntroductionRecent evidence shows that discount rates of financial claims differ across maturities and across asset classes. In particular, the maturity structure and time variation of equity and bond risk premia contain rich information to understand investors’ marginal utility of wealth and their expectations about future macroeconomic variables. The empirical literature has documented that the returns of nominal and real bonds increase with maturity on average, while claims to short-term dividends have high average excess returns, comparable in size to the aggregate equity premium (Binsbergen et al., 2012, Binsbergen and Koijen, 2017). During stock market downturns, the slope of the term structure of equity yields decreases (Binsbergen et al., 2013), while the aggregate equity premium increases by more than short-duration equity premia (Gormsen, 2021); thus, equity yield spreads are procyclical, and equity term premia are countercyclical. Finally, at the bottom of stock market downturns, the term structures of bond yields—both real and nominal—become steeper, as they predict higher future growth and rates (an observation that goes back to at least Estrella and Hardouvelis, 1991).Our main contribution is to offer a quantitative and parsimonious general-equilibrium explanation of the macroeconomic forces that drive this set of empirical features in equity and bond markets. This paper offers a structural story that captures several of the empirical properties of equity and bond prices that so far only the reduced-form, no-arbitrage models of Lettau and Wachter (2011) and Gormsen (2021) have tried to capture. Specifically, we present a New Keynesian model with habit formation that relies on two ingredients. The first ingredient, a textbook sticky-price production economy driven by productivity shocks, provides a familiar model of output and inflation that matches standard macroeconomic data while rationalizing dividends as a levered version of consumption and the payoffs of nominal bonds. The second ingredient, slow-moving habits in consumption as in Campbell and Cochrane (1999) generate realistically large and time-varying discount rates.A key theme of our contribution is how to unite nonlinear consumption habits and a production economy without compromising the model’s ability to fit macroeconomic variables—a challenge documented by Lettau and Uhlig (2000) and Rudebusch and Swanson (2008). We avoid that difficulty by including a second habit in effective leisure, or home consumption. Intuitively, after a bad productivity shock, both market and home consumption drop close to their habit levels, with offsetting effects on the labor choice, thereby neutralizing the undesirable effect of persistent consumption habits on production. In fact, we show how one can preserve the model of quantities derived under CRRA preferences, in spite of nonlinear habits that preserve the Campbell and Cochrane (1999) pricing kernel and produce realistic asset prices. This macro-finance separation (MFS) result—whereby the states that drive variation in discount rates beyond the usual CRRA preferences do not drive consumption, hours, and inflation—implies that habits do not affect the well-known properties of quantities in the macro model. It thus extends to the habit formation setting a result analogous to that of Tallarini (2000) for Epstein–Zin preferences. MFS also implies that we can effectively inspect the mechanism by considering in isolation the role of the two ingredients.We first strip down our mechanism to the essential ingredients; we match most asset pricing facts in a simple model without capital accumulation and with only productivity shocks. Our first ingredient, the production economy with sticky prices, provides a macroeconomic model that matches the observed volatility at different horizons of the key cash flows (consumption growth, dividend growth, and inverse inflation). Thanks to MFS, the model’s quantity and inflation implications and responses to a productivity shock are standard. The central mechanism relies on nominal rigidities that produce countercyclical labor shares after a productivity shock, which imply procyclical corporate profits and countercyclical inflation. Because of this cash flow effect, dividend claims and nominal bonds pay off badly in a downturn and are therefore risky investments. Then, as more and more firms are able to adjust their prices to mark them up over marginal costs, corporate profits recover and the price level increases. Thus, the payoff of long-duration dividend strips is less procyclical and the payoff of long-duration nominal bonds is more procyclical.Our second ingredient, slow-moving external habit formation, then magnifies these cash flow risks into realistically large and countercyclical risk premia. Moreover, in the model, the discount rate also makes all long-term claims inherently risky. Specifically, during a downturn, the prices of longer-duration claims drop more than those of shorter ones. This happens because consumers in the model will get accustomed to the lower consumption level, so they are less willing to defer consumption. As a result, they demand more compensation for shifting resources into the long-term future than into the near future. Because of this habit effect, the model produces an average term structure of the equity premium that is U-shaped—with a negative slope in the short to medium run, driven by the cash flow effect, and a positive slope for longer maturities, driven by the habit effect. By the same habit effect, our model produces a positively sloped term structure of real rates, thereby avoiding a real bond premium puzzle (Backus et al., 1989), while the cyclicality of inflation implies a positive inflation risk premium at all horizons and a positively sloped nominal term structure.The nonlinear habits also generate the cyclicality of the term structures observed in the data. In bad times, dividends drop and are expected to recover, so the slope of equity yields for the observable maturities becomes more negative. Consumption also falls close to habits, which raises risk premia through the habit effect, especially at longer horizons; consequently, in the model, aggregate equity premia rise by more than short-run equity premia. At the same time, inflation is expected to increase sluggishly, and hence the slope of bond yields becomes more positive.In the background of these results, our framework preserves the main achievements of Campbell and Cochrane (1999), including a solution to the average equity premium and the risk-free rate puzzles, long-horizon predictability of excess stock returns, and the countercyclical variation of stock market returns and volatility.We then depart from MFS by extending our model to incorporate realistic capital accumulation, which is the most natural first extension of the MFS baseline and allows us to assess whether the main asset-pricing mechanism survives once realistic investment dynamics are included. We find that it preserves the desirable asset pricing implications of the baseline model, while helping match more facts about quantities. In particular, the extended model has similar implications for the average slope and cyclicality of the term structures of equity and bond returns.The choice of external habits to explain the term structure evidence may seem surprising at first, as Binsbergen et al. proposed.title: A New Keynesian model of the term structures of equity and bond returns
proposed.abstract: A simple production economy with nominal price rigidities explains several key asset pricing facts, including the average slopes and cyclicality of equity and interest rate term structures. Nominal rigidities amplify the procyclicality of dividends after negative productivity shocks and generate countercyclical inflation, as sluggish price adjustment leads to a gradual dividend recovery. Consequently, short-duration equities (bonds) have more (less) procyclical payoffs than their long-duration counterparts. Slow-moving consumption habits produce large, countercyclical risk prices, yielding realistic asset valuations. Extending Campbell–Cochrane preferences with both market- and home-consumption habits allows them to operate in production economies while preserving realistic macroeconomic dynamics.

proposed.title: A New Keynesian model of the term structures of equity and bond returns
proposed.abstract: A simple production economy with nominal price rigidities explains several key asset pricing facts, including the average slopes and cyclicality of equity and interest rate term structures. Nominal rigidities amplify the procyclicality of dividends after negative productivity shocks and generate countercyclical inflation, as sluggish price adjustment leads to a gradual dividend recovery. Consequently, short-duration equities (bonds) have more (less) procyclical payoffs than their long-duration counterparts. Slow-moving consumption habits produce large, countercyclical risk prices, yielding realistic asset valuations. Extending Campbell–Cochrane preferences with both market- and home-consumption habits allows them to operate in production economies while preserving realistic macroeconomic dynamics.

Regulatory leverage ratios can be tightened to increase welfare.

Regulatory leverage ratios can be tightened to increase welfare.JEL classificationE44; E60; G21; G28KeywordsFinancial frictions; Financial intermediation; Banks’ liquidity supply; Macroprudential bank regulation; Safe assets; Central bank reservesPrevious article in this issueNext article in this issueIntroduction“Because banks play an essential intermediation role in the Treasury market, we want to ensure that the leverage ratio does not become regularly binding and discourage banks from participating in low-risk activities, such as Treasury market intermediation.” Chair of the Federal Reserve Jerome H. Powell, 25 June 2025Following the 2007–2008 Global Financial Crisis there have been profound changes in the scope and conduct of bank regulation and monetary policy. Banks are now subject to comprehensive liquidity regulations and encouraged to hold significant reserves.2 This paper identifies banks’ role as providers of liquidity services as a novel economic channel that implies that banks’ holdings of safe assets are already excessive. A key policy implication is that regulatory leverage requirements should be binding during normal times.Banks derive significant revenue from providing liquidity services to the economy.3 Specifically, banks provide liquidity services by issuing demandable deposits and investing the proceeds in safe assets. Adapting the Friedman rule to banks’ liquidity provision, it could then be argued that policy makers should enable or even encourage banks toincrease their holdings of safe assets, to provide more liquidity services.4 The difference in the returns between safe assets and deposits, the “liquidity premium on deposits”, would then be reduced and depositor welfare, at least in a narrow sense, increased. Liquidity regulations and central bank asset purchase programs, which push banks to hold more safe assets, could then be seen as having the positive side effect of lowering liquidity premiums. In contrast, regulatory leverage ratios, typically considered a backstop against potential hidden risk-taking, could then be seen as having the very tangible negative side effect of increasing liquidity premiums.However, this view is too narrow because banks not only provide liquidity services, but also supply risky loans. To smooth banks’ loan supply over financial cycles, recently implemented frameworks for macroprudential capital regulation require banks to hold more equity capital (Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, 2010), which is costly for banks. These frameworks often ignore how profits from liquidity premiums help to compensate banks for the cost of holding equity capital.The paper highlights a novel, and surprising, implication for bank regulation stemming from banks’ role as liquidity providers. Bank regulation that smooths out banks’ supply of loans and liquidity over the financial cycle also maximizes banks’ own funding liquidity. Such a policy requires banks to hold fewer, not more, safe assets during normal times.This result arises in a model with features that are standard in the dynamic stochastic general equilibrium literature. The model economy is populated by households, firms and banks. Banks fund loans to firms and holdings of safe assets with retained earnings (equity) and by supplying liquidity services in the form of deposits to households. Banks consider equity capital costly and face elastic demand for deposits.In the model, safe assets are characterized by both low payoff risk and high pledgeability. These properties imply that banks fund safe assets largely with deposits. Therefore, when banks hold more safe assets, they must offer higher deposit rates. But higher deposit funding costs reduce banks’ net return on assets. The paper shows that this creates a negative pecuniary externality as banks, to meet their return-on-equity targets, further deviate from socially desirable levels of equity capital.Banks’ deposit supply therefore ends up being excessive during normal times. While banks provide ample liquidity to the economy during normal times, this comes at the cost of inefficiently low financial stability. In particular, banks’ holdings of safe assets during normal times are excessive and make credit and liquidity crunches more likely by reducing banks’ ability to provide loans and deposits during episodes of financial stress.5 The contribution of the paper is to highlight this novel pecuniary externality and to offer policy implications. Specifically, a binding leverage ratio requirement can be introduced to increase welfare. In practice this implies a tightening of Basel III supplementary leverage ratio (SLR) requirements.Equity capital has an important role in the economy because over time exogenous shocks to firms’ loan repayments may occasionally deplete equity and thereby cause banks’ funding constraints to bind. The motivation for market-imposed equity constraints is that bank shareholder value should be high enough to ensure that banks have sound risk management and do not engage in moral hazard (as in Gertler and Kiyotaki, 2010).6 While these constraints ensure banks’ solvency at all times, they can create severe liquidity problems for banks because depositors refuse to roll over deposits when banks’ shareholder value is too low. When banks’ funding is sufficiently constrained, then banks’ supplies of both loans and liquidity services (deposits) decrease significantly and the economy experiences a financial crisis.The cost of banks’ deposit funding decreases in the liquidity premium on deposits in the model. This premium reflects the value of deposits to households who use them to meet sudden idiosyncratic consumption needs, or liquidity shocks. While households can also use safe assets to pay for consumption goods, they must first sell them which incurs a deadweight transaction cost. In the model this transaction cost is a decreasing function of the share of aggregate household savings held in form of deposits. This feature captures the intuition that when households can meet more of their liquidity shocks with deposits, then there are fewer sellers in the secondary market for safe assets at a given point in time so that it is easier for each seller to find a buyer. When households allocate their savings optimally, the liquidity premium of deposits is increasing in the transaction cost that households face when selling safe assets at the times of their respective consumption needs. It follows that liquidity premiums on deposits are decreasing in the aggregate amount of deposits in the model.The paper characterizes optimal policy by studying the constrained-efficient allocation, or second best, of the model. Policy implications are derived by comparing the second best and the laissez-faire competitive equilibrium. The focus on constrained-efficiency is motivated by the discretion that financial regulators have in practice. In particular, despite the expanding macroprudential tool kit of regulators, no clear rules regarding its usage have been formulated (there is no “Taylor rule” for macroprudential bank regulation).7 While it is difficult to predict new policy tools or kinds of regulatory forbearance during times of financial stress, it is possible to identify regulators’ objectives (to maximize some measure of welfare) and the important constraints they are facing (debt funding and capital market pressure for banks). Useful policy implications can therefore be derived by comparing constrained-efficient and competitive-equilibrium allocations.The novel, and surprising, insight of the paper is that banks hold fewer safe assets during normal times in the second best than in the competitive equilibrium. Lower safe-asset holdings reduce the need for deposit funding and allow banks to offer lower deposit rates in the second best allocation. This results in higher liquidity premiums, and thus higher interest rate spreads, which enables banks to hold more costly capital during normal times.8 Moreover, while banks’ second-best safe asset holdings are smaller during normal times, compared with the competitive equilibrium, they are larger during financial crises. During normal times, the liquidity premium is higher in second best, compared with the competitive equilibrium, but it is more stable during financial crises. Banks have smaller balance sheets but larger market capitalizations in the second-best allocation.A key policy implication in this paper is that regulatory tools should be coordinated to avoid undermining the effectiveness of recently introduced macroprudential capital buffer frameworks. The analysis implies that banks should reduce the size of their balance sheets by reducing safe asset holdings and should hold more equity. In other words, banks should have smaller balance sheets and focus on funding riskier assets with more stable funding. A tighter SLR requirement would work in support of this implication. Therefore, there is a complementarity, during normal times, between tightening the SLR and requiring banks to build up larger capital buffers.The analysis strengthens the rationale for the SLR, from acting as a backstop against potential hidden buildup of leverage driven by risky lending to preventing the very visible increase in leverage driven by accumulation of safe assets. The reason is that banks’ participation in low-risk activities, paradoxically, reduces financial stability. proposed.title: Macroprudential regulation and banks’ supply of liquidity services
proposed.abstract: Are banks safer when they hold more safe assets? This paper builds a model in which banks supply liquidity services through uninsured deposits. Define a safe asset as an asset with both low payoff risk and high pledgeability. Banks consider equity costly and because of safe assets’ low payoff risk prefer to fund them largely with deposits. High pledgeability makes this feasible. The rise in banks’ deposit supply increases deposit rates and forces banks to deviate from socially desirable levels of capital to meet return-on-equity targets. Regulatory leverage ratios can be tightened to increase welfare.

The rationale for increasing banks’ equity capital in this paper is not to decrease funding costs further (deposit demand is too elastic for that in this paper) but to make banks more resilient. Specifically, banks pay lower deposit rates not because of alternative funding sources (equity) but because they have fewer safe assets to fund. The channel in Begenau (2020) operates within the liability side of banks’ balance sheets, but the channel in this paper operates from the asset to the liability side.Diamond and Rajan (2001) emphasize that demandable deposits are an important disciplining device in the hands of bank creditors. As in this paper, creditors are atomistic and not able to commit among themselves to renegotiating the face value of bank deposits ex post. They simply demand their deposits back (via a “bank run” as in Diamond and Dybvig, 1983), or refuse to roll over in the case of banks’ wholesale or interbank funding sources, if they are concerned about bank moral hazard. In this paper deposits, in addition, play a role in recapitalizing banks after they experience loan losses. A decrease in deposit rates when banks are forced to reduce the size of their balance sheets allows banks to rebuild equity faster. A policy implication is that banks should rely less on demandable deposits, and more on equity, during normal times such that they are forced to reduce deposit supply less during financial crises.Gatev and Strahan (2006) document empirical support for banks benefiting from procyclical funding costs, i.e., from a countercyclical liquidity premium. They argue that higher liquidity premiums during episodes of financial stress enable banks to provide a more stable supply of loans. proposed.title: Macroprudential regulation and banks’ supply of liquidity services
proposed.abstract: Are banks safer when they hold more safe assets? This paper builds a model in which banks supply liquidity services through uninsured deposits. Define a safe asset as an asset with both low payoff risk and high pledgeability. Banks consider equity costly and because of safe assets’ low payoff risk prefer to fund them largely with deposits. High pledgeability makes this feasible. The rise in banks’ deposit supply increases deposit rates and forces banks to deviate from socially desirable levels of capital to meet return-on-equity targets. Regulatory leverage ratios can be tightened to increase welfare.

Tax loss carryforwards and firms’ risk☆

•
Tax loss carry forwards (TLCF) are an important and risky corporate asset.
•
Firms with high tend to have higher and more volatile equity returns and higher market betas.
•
These results are consistent with a quantitatively calibrated dynamic model of firm behavior.

Tax loss carryforwards (TLCF) — accumulated losses that reduce taxable income — are an important and risky corporate asset. We show theoretically how TLCF affect equity risk: If TLCF are low and used with certainty, equity risk decreases in TLCF because TLCF represent a safe cash flow; if TLCF are high, equity risk increases in TLCF because TLCF increase after-tax cash flows in good times but may expire unused or be deferred in bad times. In a calibrated model the latter effect dominates and risk increases in TLCF on average. Empirically, TLCF positively forecast firms’ volatility, beta, and return.

IntroductionHow do taxes affect a firm’s risk and cost of capital? The notion that taxes facilitate risk sharing between investors and the government has a long history in economics. Domar and Musgrave (1944) recognized that taxation implies that individual investors share both risk and return with the government. They also, however, point out that the degree of risk sharing depends on the extent to which the government shares symmetrically in both gains and losses.Majd and Myers (1985) and Green and Talmor (1985) examine asymmetric risk sharing in the specific context of tax loss carryforwards (TLCF). TLCF arise because tax codes do not generally allow firms to realize negative taxes, i.e., net operating losses (NOLs) do not automatically generate payments from the government to the firm. Subsequent positive taxable income can be reduced by applying some or all of the TLCF as an offset.1 Both studies argue that TLCF reduce a firm’s risk by reducing its tax liability, creating a safer after-tax cash flow. Specifically, they recognize that a taxable corporation with a TLCF is equivalent to the firm being short a call option held by the government. The call option arises because the government does not collect taxes on taxable income below the level of the TLCF. This is equivalent to the government having the option to collect taxes on all income if it is willing to pay the firm the taxes on the TLCF. Hence, collecting taxes is exercising an option with a strike price of the taxes on the TLCF. Since a firm that is short a call option is safer than a firm without the short position, TLCF reduce firm risk.In this paper we show that this line of thinking is incomplete: Additional TLCF decrease risk if TLCF are likely to be used with certainty in the near term, but additional TLCF increase risk if TLCF are sufficiently likely to be unused in the near term or if they can expire.2 Our contribution is to show that, in theory, it is possible for the relationship between TLCF and risk to be decreasing, increasing, or non-monotonic, depending on a firm’s situation. Furthermore, we find that risk is increasing in TLCF for the typical firm in a calibrated model, and that it is increasing in TLCF for the typical firm in the data. This reflects the fact that as TLCF increases, the strike price of the government’s option increases, thereby reducing the option’s value. As the option value falls, the degree of risk sharing falls, and hence the risk of the firm increases. The non-monotonicity comes from the identification of conditions under which the option will likely not be exercised. In other words, because TLCF is likely to increase after-tax cash flows in good times, but are likely to be unused or even expire in bad times, TLCF are a risky asset.We begin by theoretically deriving our basic results in a simple two period setting. Our task of deriving a general understanding of how TLCF, risk, and return are related is made difficult by the fact that a firm’s TLCF results from complex, path dependent tax minimization decisions. For instance, Cooper and Franks (1983) show how operating decisions, asset allocations, lease or buy decisions and NOLs interact to determine value. Moreover, in any one year, non-operating deductions such as depreciation and interest payments, both of which are the result of endogenous decisions, affect a firm’s NOLs. To show that the insights of our simple model carry over to more complex settings, we then solve and calibrate a dynamic corporate finance model in which firms make investment and capital structure decisions while facing a realistic tax code.Our theoretical models provide a number of empirical implications. First, for firms that are highly likely to use at least some of their TLCF, there should be a U-shaped association between TLCF and risk, shown by the solid black line in Fig. 1. Risk falls as TLCF grows, as long as TLCF is low enough that it will be used in all states of the world. This is because TLCF increases the firm’s after-tax cash flows in times of high and low cash flows, making its after-tax cash flow safer. Once TLCF becomes sufficiently large so that there is a risk of it being unused or deferred, the TLCF–risk relationship switches from negative to positive, with risk rising as TLCF grows. This is because additional TLCF will be used and will increase after-tax cash flow only in times of high cash flows, but will be unused or deferred and will leave the after-tax cash flow unchanged in times of low cash flows.Second, even though the relationship between TLCF and risk is U-shaped when some TLCF are sure to be used, the relationship may be J-shaped – mostly increasing – or even strictly increasing in TLCF if the firm has additional non-TLCF tax shields, shown by the dashed blue and dotted red lines in Fig. 1. This is because when firms have other tax shields, even the first dollar of TLCF has a risk of being unused in bad states of the world. Because TLCF amplify the firm’s exposure to market risk rather than introducing an independent source of risk, firms with higher TLCF should have higher market betas and higher expected returns as compensation.Download: Download high-res image (171KB)Download: Download full-size imageFig. 1. We compare (a) a firm with no other tax shields (solid black line), to (b) a firm with existing non-TLCF tax shields (dashed blue line), and (c) a firm with existing non-TLCF tax shields and higher cash flow volatility (dotted red line). IntroductionHow do taxes affect a firm’s risk and cost of capital? The notion that taxes facilitate risk sharing between investors and the government has a long history in economics. Domar and Musgrave (1944) recognized that taxation implies that individual investors share both risk and return with the government. They also, however, point out that the degree of risk sharing depends on the extent to which the government shares symmetrically in both gains and losses.Majd and Myers (1985) and Green and Talmor (1985) examine asymmetric risk sharing in the specific context of tax loss carryforwards (TLCF). TLCF arise because tax codes do not generally allow firms to realize negative taxes, i.e., net operating losses (NOLs) do not automatically generate payments from the government to the firm. Subsequent positive taxable income can be reduced by applying some or all of the TLCF as an offset.1 Both studies argue that TLCF reduce a firm’s risk by reducing its tax liability, creating a safer after-tax cash flow. Specifically, they recognize that a taxable corporation with a TLCF is equivalent to the firm being short a call option held by the government. The call option arises because the government does not collect taxes on taxable income below the level of the TLCF. This is equivalent to the government having the option to collect taxes on all income if it is willing to pay the firm the taxes on the TLCF. Hence, collecting taxes is exercising an option with a strike price of the taxes on the TLCF. Since a firm that is short a call option is safer than a firm without the short position, TLCF reduce firm risk.In this paper we show that this line of thinking is incomplete: Additional TLCF decrease risk if TLCF are likely to be used with certainty in the near term, but additional TLCF increase risk if TLCF are sufficiently likely to be unused in the near term or if they can expire.2 Our contribution is to show that, in theory, it is possible for the relationship between TLCF and risk to be decreasing, increasing, or non-monotonic, depending on a firm’s situation. Furthermore, we find that risk is increasing in TLCF for the typical firm in a calibrated model, and that it is increasing in TLCF for the typical firm in the data. This reflects the fact that as TLCF increases, the strike price of the government’s option increases, thereby reducing the option’s value. As the option value falls, the degree of risk sharing falls, and hence the risk of the firm increases. The non-monotonicity comes from the identification of conditions under which the option will likely not be exercised. In other words, because TLCF is likely to increase after-tax cash flows in good times, but are likely to be unused or even expire in bad times, TLCF are a risky asset.We begin by theoretically deriving our basic results in a simple two period setting. Our task of deriving a general understanding of how TLCF, risk, and return are related is made difficult by the fact that a firm’s TLCF results from complex, path dependent tax minimization decisions. For instance, Cooper and Franks (1983) show how operating decisions, asset allocations, lease or buy decisions and NOLs interact to determine value. Moreover, in any one year, non-operating deductions such as depreciation and interest payments, both of which are the result of endogenous decisions, affect a firm’s NOLs. To show that the insights of our simple model carry over to more complex settings, we then solve and calibrate a dynamic corporate finance model in which firms make investment and capital structure decisions while facing a realistic tax code.Our theoretical models provide a number of empirical implications. First, for firms that are highly likely to use at least some of their TLCF, there should be a U-shaped association between TLCF and risk, shown by the solid black line in Fig. 1. Risk falls as TLCF grows, as long as TLCF is low enough that it will be used in all states of the world. This is because TLCF increases the firm’s after-tax cash flows in times of high and low cash flows, making its after-tax cash flow safer. Once TLCF becomes sufficiently large so that there is a risk of it being unused or deferred, the TLCF–risk relationship switches from negative to positive, with risk rising as TLCF grows. This is because additional TLCF will be used and will increase after-tax cash flow only in times of high cash flows, but will be unused or deferred and will leave the after-tax cash flow unchanged in times of low cash flows.Second, even though the relationship between TLCF and risk is U-shaped when some TLCF are sure to be used, the relationship may be J-shaped – mostly increasing – or even strictly increasing in TLCF if the firm has additional non-TLCF tax shields, shown by the dashed blue and dotted red lines in Fig. 1. This is because when firms have other tax shields, even the first dollar of TLCF has a risk of being unused in bad states of the world. source_records.title: Anatomy of a run: The Terra Luna crash
source_records.abstract: We examine the dramatic collapse of the Terra blockchain in May 2022. Using granular blockchain data, we show that the run resulted from the interaction of three economic forces: subsidized money creation, real-time observability of transactions, and investor concentration. The early success of Terra’s algorithmic stablecoin, UST, was fueled by highly subsidized deposit rates, which attracted many investors but failed to engage them meaningfully with other services. Blockchain transparency allowed investors to observe Terra’s worsening fundamentals and monitor each other’s exits in real time. Larger and sophisticated investors reacted faster to adverse signals and served as catalysts for the run. These findings challenge the idea that blockchain transparency levels the playing field and highlight how greater observability and concentration can amplify financial fragility. Our results contribute to the understanding of the limits of private money creation and the dynamics of runs in fully digital financial systems.

From bank runs in the Free Banking era of 19th-century United States to runs on money market funds during the 2008 Financial Crisis, privately issued money-like instruments have been prone to runs when investor confidence falters, see for example Gorton and Zhang (2021). More recently, cryptocurrency platforms have begun issuing a new generation of private money in the form of stablecoins — cryptocurrencies pegged to a reference fiat currency — which raises familiar questions in a new technological environment: What determines their stability? Which design choices mitigate or exacerbate fragility? How do runs begin and unfold in this context? This paper uses the 2022 collapse of Terra as a natural laboratory to study these fundamental questions. Blockchain data offers detailed information on both network structure and participant behavior allowing us to examine the dynamics of the run at the individual investor level. We show that the economics of the Terra network shared several important parallels with traditional financial systems and collateralized stablecoins. Therefore, our results have implications not only for cryptocurrency runs but also for our understanding of runs more broadly.A defining feature of the Terra ecosystem was its algorithmic stablecoin, UST. UST aimed to function as a money-like asset and to facilitate transactions on the Terra blockchain. Rather than rely on external collateral or government backing, UST maintained its peg through an algorithmic arbitrage mechanism backed solely by Terra’s native cryptocurrency, LUNA. Therefore, the system’s solvency depended entirely on the market capitalization of LUNA. This self-referential design proved vulnerable to runs. source_records.title: From pitch to progress: The interplay of team reputation and governance in crowdfunded innovation
source_records.abstract: This study examines how team reputation affects both the funding success and the subsequent innovation progress in early-stage crowdfunded projects, with a comparative focus on blockchain-based and conventional crowdfunding platforms. Using development progress data for blockchain projects from the open-source platform GitHub, we find that while teams with stronger reputations raise more funds, their subsequent innovation productivity, measured by development activity, tends to lag. Further analysis reveals an association between higher team reputation and increased turnover of tokens post-fundraising, suggesting team members may strategically exercise exit options soon after securing financing. In contrast, analysis of Kickstarter campaigns reveals a more consistent alignment between team reputation, funding success, and project delivery. Specifically, highly reputable teams are more likely to meet not only their fundraising goal but also delivery commitments. We attribute this contrast to differences in platform governance; Kickstarter’s structured oversight appears to mitigate early team disengagement and enhance project delivery compared to the blockchain context. These findings underscore the importance of effective governance mechanisms in crowdfunding platforms to ensure that team reputation signals translate into sustained innovation outcomes.

This study examines how team reputation affects both the funding success and the subsequent innovation progress in early-stage crowdfunded projects, with a comparative focus on blockchain-based and conventional crowdfunding platforms. Further analysis reveals an association between higher team reputation and increased turnover of tokens post-fundraising, suggesting team members may strategically exercise exit options soon after securing financing. However, radical innovation inherently involves a high risk of failure due to pervasive uncertainties surrounding nascent technologies and business models (Holmstrom, 1989). In particular, CB Insights shows that the odds of becoming a unicorn are merely 1%.1 Furthermore, unlike publicly traded firms, small ventures typically lack mandatory performance disclosure requirements, making the evaluation of entrepreneurial effort exceptionally challenging. The lack of transparency gives rise to moral hazard in that entrepreneurs may not exert the desired level of effort. Understanding how to simultaneously foster innovation productivity and mitigate opportunistic behavior among entrepreneurs in these ventures is crucial.Reputation, as an informal enforcement mechanism for incomplete contracts, exerts an important disciplinary influence by mitigating opportunistic behaviors among various market participants, such as managers, product sellers, financial institutions, independent directors, andanalysts (Cabral, 2005, MacLeod, 2007, Karpoff et al., 2008b).2 In particular, entrepreneurial reputation is documented to be positively associated with funding results in crowdfunding (Li and Martin, 2019). However, limited research exists on the relationship between an entrepreneurial team’s reputation and its subsequent innovation productivity. This could be due to the difficulty of observing the progress of tech ventures in development.This paper addresses this gap by employing granular data tracking the development trajectory of blockchain projects from the leading open-source platform, GitHub. Using GitHub data offers two primary advantages in this context. First, as a public repository, GitHub potentially offers transparency into development progress, unlike less observable internal efforts.3 Second, compared to metrics like successful exits or patent registrations used in prior studies, which often involve significant time lags, GitHub activity provides development data at a daily granularity.Furthermore, blockchain project crowdfunding offers an ideal setting to examine reputation’s significance, given the pronounced moral hazard stemming from minimal regulatory oversight and limited legal recourse upon project failure. Cabral (2005) defines reputation as the perception held by others regarding a specific agent, noting that it functions as a deterrent against moral hazard. Within the crowdfunding context, an entrepreneur’s reputation can instil trust in potential investors, assuring the likelihood of successful project execution. This trust, in turn, influences the investors’ willingness to provide financial support for the project (Ahlers et al., 2015). However, many blockchain projects exhibit substantial moral hazard vulnerabilities, primarily stemming from the limited legal recourse or economic penalties associated with project failure (Gan et al., 2021). This allows us to test whether the reputation is sufficient to discipline and motivate entrepreneurs in an unregulated environment.Our initial ICO sample consists of 8132 ended and ongoing blockchain fundraising events, including initial coin offerings (ICOs), security token offerings (STOs), and initial exchanger offerings (IEOs), from 2016 to 2022. Building on Paul P. Momtaz’s Token Offering Research Database (TORD), we first supplement the sample with ICOmarks deals and scrape deal characteristics and team member information from the website. We also download available whitepapers to complement additional information on deal characteristics. Many blockchain projects post their code on GitHub, the largest open-source software platform. We obtain daily development progress data for blockchain projects from GHTorrent, which mirrors GitHub developer activity. Applying filtering criteria, excluding ongoing or planned deals and those lacking necessary characteristics, yields a final sample of 4014 completed ICOs from 2016–2020 that possess available team information and basic deal characteristics. To measure entrepreneurial team reputation within the blockchain community network, we adapt the methodologies of Atanasov et al. (2012), Hochberg et al. (2007), and Larcker et al. (2013) to calculate the centrality measure Degree by constructing an undirected graph with each team as a vertex and with each association of a team member through ICO transactions as an edge.We find a positive correlation between team reputation and fundraising success; specifically, a one-standard-deviation increase in team reputation corresponds to a 3.4 percentage point increase in the probability of fundraising success. In opaque information environments, team reputation can serve as a crucial signal of project quality and certification (Shane and Cable, 2002). Furthermore, small crowdfunding investors, often characterized by limited attention, may gravitate towards more salient, attention-grabbing investment opportunities (Barber et al., 2008). Consequently, reputable entrepreneurial teams likely attract greater investor attention, leading to increased investment and higher fundraising success.However, successful fundraising by reputable entrepreneurial teams does not necessarily translate into greater post-fundraising development progress. Instead, our findings indicate a negative association between team reputation and GitHub development activity across various post-fundraising windows. This suggests that team reputation alone is insufficient to fully mitigate moral hazard in this unregulated market. The economic magnitude of this effect is non-trivial: one-standard-deviation increase in team reputation corresponds to an approximate 12.2% decrease in the development progress during the first three months post-ICO.Further supporting this interpretation, analysis of on-chain transaction data (for a subsample of Ethereum ERC-20 ICOs) reveals that more reputable teams are indeed more likely to liquidate token holdings shortly after fundraising, exercising early exit options. This suggests the previously observed slower development progress may stem from governance weaknesses inherent in blockchain projects; specifically, the readily available option for immediate exit. Consequently, these findings underscore the importance of implementing governance mechanisms designed to prevent teams from prematurely liquidating their stakes before achieving key project milestones.4To contrast with the ICO findings, we analyze crowdfunding on Kickstarter, a platform characterized by stronger governance structures and accountability mechanisms. We select 747 successful projects from the “Apps” subcategory (under “Technology”) for comparability. Data collected includes project basics (e.g., launch/deadline dates, location, pledged amount, backers), creator/collaborator details for centrality measures, and project updates for measuring progress (using post-campaign updates). Unlike the ICO context, on Kickstarter, higher team reputation predicts not only greater fundraising success (a one-standard-deviation increase in degree is associated with a 9.6% increase in pledged amount) but also more subsequent progress (associated with a 4.5% increase in post-fundraising updates). This divergence highlights the crucial role of platform governance in mitigating moral hazard and aligning reputation with project execution commitments.To formalize the mechanism behind these empirical patterns, we develop a stylized model in Appendix A.5 Reputation plays a dual role: it boosts token demand and fundraising success, but also raises the token price, making early liquidation more profitable. A governance parameter controls how much of the founder’s stake can be sold early. When governance is weak, high-reputation founders face a strong temptation to cash out rather than invest in development, and the optimal response is all-or-nothing—either retain all tokens and work, or sell the maximum permissible stake and reduce effort. A reputation threshold separates the two regimes: below it, the future payoff from successful development outweighs the liquidation gain, so founders stay and work; above it, the token price makes cashing out irresistible. Stronger governance raises this threshold by limiting how much can be sold early, shrinking the liquidation payoff and restoring the incentive to develop.The model yields three predictions. First, higher reputation raises token demand and fundraising, consistent with the positive reputation–fundraising relationship in both ICOs and Kickstarter. Second, under weak governance the threshold is low, so a disproportionate share of high-reputation founders falls into the liquidation regime—consistent with the negative association between team degree and post-ICO GitHub activity and with higher early exit rates among well-connected ICOs. Within each regime, effort increases with reputation; the aggregate negative relationship arises from a composition effect. Third, stronger governance raises the threshold, keeping more founders in the effort regime where reputation and development are positively related—consistent with the Kickstarter evidence.Our paper contributes to the fast-growing literature on blockchain technology, a field often associated with the potential to enhance trust and transparency, reduce transaction costs, and foster more efficient and inclusive economies.6 Recent theoretical work demonstrates that tokens can mitigate frictions between platforms and users, often arising from monopoly pricing power or data exploitation (Goldstein et al., 2019, Sockin and Xiong, 2023). Furthermore, tokens provide an effective mechanism for fundraising and for incentivizing platform participants (Cong et al., 2022, Gryglewicz et al., 2021, Lee and Parlour, 2022).7 Beyond these structural advantages, a rapidly expanding behavioral literature highlights how sentiment and online attention shape ICO outcomes and cryptocurrency valuations. Social-media engagement and tone — across platforms such as Twitter, Telegram, and Medium — are robust predictors of fundraising success (Huang et al., 2024, Safi Eljil et al., 2025, Gartner et al., 2025, Sapkota and Grobys, 2023).8 Parallel work on cryptocurrency markets and digital-asset pricing situates these dynamics within a broader framework of investor behavior. Studies document that investor attention and sentiment drive return co-movements (Aslanidis et al., 2024), price jumps (Aysan et al., 2024), and cross-sectional pricing patterns (Borri and Shakhnov, 2022, Fieberg et al., 2025, Lan and Frömmel, 2025).9 Finally, by tracking post-fundraising technological development, our study extends this literature to the innovation phase of blockchain ventures. Development milestones provide a direct measure of project effort and credibility (Lyandres et al., 2022), while governance quality and team reputation act as informal enforcement mechanisms. In this way, our paper bridges the literatures on blockchain governance, behavioral finance, and digital-asset pricing, clarifying both the promises and the vulnerabilities of token-based financing ecosystems.Furthermore, our paper is related to crowdfunding literature. Crowdfunding enables creators to raise capital directly from distributed backers, with Kickstarter being the largest such platform. In this context, particularly given the typical absence of formal due diligence, crowdfunding backers often rely on observable signals (e.g., prior founding success, educational background, and social network size) to assess creator competence and credibility (Hsu, 2007, Mollick, 2014, Colombo et al., 2015, Courtney et al., 2017, Agrawal et al., 2010, Shane and Cable, 2002, Sørensen and Fassiotto, 2011, Stam and Elfring, 2008). Team reputation established through prior campaigns, executive recruitment capabilities, or a strong social media presence attracts early contributions and increases fundraising success. Furthermore, team reputation has implications beyond the fundraising phase, influencing subsequent delivery outcomes and helping to maintain trust within the crowdfunding ecosystem. Approximately 75% of successful Kickstarter projects experience delays (Mollick, 2014), yet teams with stronger reputations are often granted more leniency by backers (Stanko and Henard, 2017).Additionally, our paper contributes to understanding the impact of team reputation. Recognizing that tokens are frequently treated as commodities, marketing scholars have long studied how endorsements by influential figures, such as celebrities, heighten product or service credibility and stimulate consumers’ purchase intentions (Erdogan, 1999, Pringle and Binet, 2005). However, our findings show that team reputation alone does not ensure successful project development, particularly in unregulated markets where early exit is possible. Without complementary governance mechanisms to enforce accountability, team reputation cannot fully serve its disciplinary function. This underscores the necessity of governance structures that reinforce reputational signals with accountability, thereby ensuring that early trust translates into sustained project commitment.The paper proceeds as follows. However, radical innovation inherently involves a high risk of failure due to pervasive uncertainties surrounding nascent technologies and business models (Holmstrom, 1989). In particular, CB Insights shows that the odds of becoming a unicorn are merely 1%.1 Furthermore, unlike publicly traded firms, small ventures typically lack mandatory performance disclosure requirements, making the evaluation of entrepreneurial effort exceptionally challenging. The lack of transparency gives rise to moral hazard in that entrepreneurs may not exert the desired level of effort. Understanding how to simultaneously foster innovation productivity and mitigate opportunistic behavior among entrepreneurs in these ventures is crucial.Reputation, as an informal enforcement mechanism for incomplete contracts, exerts an important disciplinary influence by mitigating opportunistic behaviors among various market participants, such as managers, product sellers, financial institutions, independent directors, andanalysts (Cabral, 2005, MacLeod, 2007, Karpoff et al., 2008b).2 In particular, entrepreneurial reputation is documented to be positively associated with funding results in crowdfunding (Li and Martin, 2019). However, limited research exists on the relationship between an entrepreneurial team’s reputation and its subsequent innovation productivity. This could be due to the difficulty of observing the progress of tech ventures in development.This paper addresses this gap by employing granular data tracking the development trajectory of blockchain projects from the leading open-source platform, GitHub. Using GitHub data offers two primary advantages in this context. First, as a public repository, GitHub potentially offers transparency into development progress, unlike less observable internal efforts.3 Second, compared to metrics like successful exits or patent registrations used in prior studies, which often involve significant time lags, GitHub activity provides development data at a daily granularity.Furthermore, blockchain project crowdfunding offers an ideal setting to examine reputation’s significance, given the pronounced moral hazard stemming from minimal regulatory oversight and limited legal recourse upon project failure. Cabral (2005) defines reputation as the perception held by others regarding a specific agent, noting that it functions as a deterrent against moral hazard. Within the crowdfunding context, an entrepreneur’s reputation can instil trust in potential investors, assuring the likelihood of successful project execution. This trust, in turn, influences the investors’ willingness to provide financial support for the project (Ahlers et al., 2015). However, many blockchain projects exhibit substantial moral hazard vulnerabilities, primarily stemming from the limited legal recourse or economic penalties associated with project failure (Gan et al., 2021). This allows us to test whether the reputation is sufficient to discipline and motivate entrepreneurs in an unregulated environment.Our initial ICO sample consists of 8132 ended and ongoing blockchain fundraising events, including initial coin offerings (ICOs), security token offerings (STOs), and initial exchanger offerings (IEOs), from 2016 to 2022. Building on Paul P. Momtaz’s Token Offering Research Database (TORD), we first supplement the sample with ICOmarks deals and scrape deal characteristics and team member information from the website. We also download available whitepapers to complement additional information on deal characteristics. Many blockchain projects post their code on GitHub, the largest open-source software platform. We obtain daily development progress data for blockchain projects from GHTorrent, which mirrors GitHub developer activity. Applying filtering criteria, excluding ongoing or planned deals and those lacking necessary characteristics, yields a final sample of 4014 completed ICOs from 2016–2020 that possess available team information and basic deal characteristics. To measure entrepreneurial team reputation within the blockchain community network, we adapt the methodologies of Atanasov et al. (2012), Hochberg et al. (2007), and Larcker et al. (2013) to calculate the centrality measure Degree by constructing an undirected graph with each team as a vertex and with each association of a team member through ICO transactions as an edge.We find a positive correlation between team reputation and fundraising success; specifically, a one-standard-deviation increase in team reputation corresponds to a 3.4 percentage point increase in the probability of fundraising success. In opaque information environments, team reputation can serve as a crucial signal of project quality and certification (Shane and Cable, 2002). Furthermore, small crowdfunding investors, often characterized by limited attention, may gravitate towards more salient, attention-grabbing investment opportunities (Barber et al., 2008). Consequently, reputable entrepreneurial teams likely attract greater investor attention, leading to increased investment and higher fundraising success.However, successful fundraising by reputable entrepreneurial teams does not necessarily translate into greater post-fundraising development progress. Instead, our findings indicate a negative association between team reputation and GitHub development activity across various post-fundraising windows. This suggests that team reputation alone is insufficient to fully mitigate moral hazard in this unregulated market. The economic magnitude of this effect is non-trivial: one-standard-deviation increase in team reputation corresponds to an approximate 12.2% decrease in the development progress during the first three months post-ICO.Further supporting this interpretation, analysis of on-chain transaction data (for a subsample of Ethereum ERC-20 ICOs) reveals that more reputable teams are indeed more likely to liquidate token holdings shortly after fundraising, exercising early exit options. This suggests the previously observed slower development progress may stem from governance weaknesses inherent in blockchain projects; specifically, the readily available option for immediate exit. Consequently, these findings underscore the importance of implementing governance mechanisms designed to prevent teams from prematurely liquidating their stakes before achieving key project milestones.4To contrast with the ICO findings, we analyze crowdfunding on Kickstarter, a platform characterized by stronger governance structures and accountability mechanisms. We select 747 successful projects from the “Apps” subcategory (under “Technology”) for comparability. Data collected includes project basics (e.g., launch/deadline dates, location, pledged amount, backers), creator/collaborator details for centrality measures, and project updates for measuring progress (using post-campaign updates). Unlike the ICO context, on Kickstarter, higher team reputation predicts not only greater fundraising success (a one-standard-deviation increase in degree is associated with a 9.6% increase in pledged amount) but also more subsequent progress (associated with a 4.5% increase in post-fundraising updates). This divergence highlights the crucial role of platform governance in mitigating moral hazard and aligning reputation with project execution commitments.To formalize the mechanism behind these empirical patterns, we develop a stylized model in Appendix A.5 Reputation plays a dual role: it boosts token demand and fundraising success, but also raises the token price, making early liquidation more profitable. A governance parameter controls how much of the founder’s stake can be sold early. When governance is weak, high-reputation founders face a strong temptation to cash out rather than invest in development, and the optimal response is all-or-nothing—either retain all tokens and work, or sell the maximum permissible stake and reduce effort. A reputation threshold separates the two regimes: below it, the future payoff from successful development outweighs the liquidation gain, so founders stay and work; above it, the token price makes cashing out irresistible. Stronger governance raises this threshold by limiting how much can be sold early, shrinking the liquidation payoff and restoring the incentive to develop.The model yields three predictions. First, higher reputation raises token demand and fundraising, consistent with the positive reputation–fundraising relationship in both ICOs and Kickstarter. Second, under weak governance the threshold is low, so a disproportionate share of high-reputation founders falls into the liquidation regime—consistent with the negative association between team degree and post-ICO GitHub activity and with higher early exit rates among well-connected ICOs. Within each regime, effort increases with reputation; the aggregate negative relationship arises from a composition effect. Third, stronger governance raises the threshold, keeping more founders in the effort regime where reputation and development are positively related—consistent with the Kickstarter evidence.Our paper contributes to the fast-growing literature on blockchain technology, a field often associated with the potential to enhance trust and transparency, reduce transaction costs, and foster more efficient and inclusive economies.6 Recent theoretical work demonstrates that tokens can mitigate frictions between platforms and users, often arising from monopoly pricing power or data exploitation (Goldstein et al., 2019, Sockin and Xiong, 2023). Furthermore, tokens provide an effective mechanism for fundraising and for incentivizing platform participants (Cong et al., 2022, Gryglewicz et al., 2021, Lee and Parlour, 2022).7 Beyond these structural advantages, a rapidly expanding behavioral literature highlights how sentiment and online attention shape ICO outcomes and cryptocurrency valuations. Social-media engagement and tone — across platforms such as Twitter, Telegram, and Medium — are robust predictors of fundraising success (Huang et al., 2024, Safi Eljil et al., 2025, Gartner et al., 2025, Sapkota and Grobys, 2023).8 Parallel work on cryptocurrency markets and digital-asset pricing situates these dynamics within a broader framework of investor behavior. Studies document that investor attention and sentiment drive return co-movements (Aslanidis et al., 2024), price jumps (Aysan et al., 2024), and cross-sectional pricing patterns (Borri and Shakhnov, 2022, Fieberg et al., 2025, Lan and Frömmel, 2025).9 Finally, by tracking post-fundraising technological development, our study extends this literature to the innovation phase of blockchain ventures. Development milestones provide a direct measure of project effort and credibility (Lyandres et al., 2022), while governance quality and team reputation act as informal enforcement mechanisms. In this way, our paper bridges the literatures on blockchain governance, behavioral finance, and digital-asset pricing, clarifying both the promises and the vulnerabilities of token-based financing ecosystems.Furthermore, our paper is related to crowdfunding literature. Crowdfunding enables creators to raise capital directly from distributed backers, with Kickstarter being the largest such platform. In this context, particularly given the typical absence of formal due diligence, crowdfunding backers often rely on observable signals (e.g., prior founding success, educational background, and social network size) to assess creator competence and credibility (Hsu, 2007, Mollick, 2014, Colombo et al., 2015, Courtney et al., 2017, Agrawal et al., 2010, Shane and Cable, 2002, Sørensen and Fassiotto, 2011, Stam and Elfring, 2008). Team reputation established through prior campaigns, executive recruitment capabilities, or a strong social media presence attracts early contributions and increases fundraising success. Furthermore, team reputation has implications beyond the fundraising phase, influencing subsequent delivery outcomes and helping to maintain trust within the crowdfunding ecosystem. Approximately 75% of successful Kickstarter projects experience delays (Mollick, 2014), yet teams with stronger reputations are often granted more leniency by backers (Stanko and Henard, 2017).Additionally, our paper contributes to understanding the impact of team reputation. Recognizing that tokens are frequently treated as commodities, marketing scholars have long studied how endorsements by influential figures, such as celebrities, heighten product or service credibility and stimulate consumers’ purchase intentions (Erdogan, 1999, Pringle and Binet, 2005). However, our findings show that team reputation alone does not ensure successful project development, particularly in unregulated markets where early exit is possible. Without complementary governance mechanisms to enforce accountability, team reputation cannot fully serve its disciplinary function. This underscores the necessity of governance structures that reinforce reputational signals with accountability, thereby ensuring that early trust translates into sustained project commitment.The paper proceeds as follows. Section 2 focuses on sample and variable construction. Section 3 shows the impact of team reputation on fundraising success and post-fundraising development progress in ICO projects. Section 4 discusses the relationship between team reputation, fundraising success, and post-campaign development on Kickstarter. Section 5 conducts several additional analyses and robustness checks. source_records.title: Do public credit guarantees boost R&D and innovation?
source_records.abstract: While public credit guarantees (PCGs) have been around for a long time, their use expanded significantly during the global financial crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic to support the corporate sector and facilitate economic recovery. Given the scale of these programmes and their potential fiscal implications, much of the existing literature has focused on whether PCGs improve credit allocation and financial outcomes. In contrast, this paper examines whether PCGs impact firms' R&D and innovation efforts, utilizing a rich data set from Turkey's Credit Guarantee Fund—one of the largest schemes of this kind—and employing a staggered difference-in-differences (DiD) approach preceded by a comprehensive matching procedure. We find that firms receiving guaranteed loans exhibit significantly greater improvements in both innovation inputs, such as R&D expenditure, and innovation outcomes, such as high-tech exports, compared to non-recipient firms. We also observe a substantially larger beneficial impact for firms already engaged in innovation activities and those facing financial constraints. Our findings have important implications for regulatory authorities in their design of credit support programmes.

IntroductionInvestment in research and development (R&D) and innovation is widely recognized as a central driver of long-term economic growth (Griliches, 1992; Stokey, 1995; Ulku, 2004; Chu and Cozzi, 2014; Liu, 2016). R&D enables firms to develop new products, advance technological progress, and remain competitive in dynamic global markets (Griffith et al., 2004). In emerging economies, R&D plays a particularly transformative role, enabling firms to transition from low-cost, labour-intensive activities toward higher value-added, technology-based production (Felipe et al., 2014). Strong R&D performance in these countries also helps attract high-technology FDI, thereby preparing the foundation for innovation-driven growth and capacity to benefit from external knowledge and technologies (Nelson and Rosenberg, 1993).Despite its importance, R&D investment remains constrained by substantial market and institutional frictions. R&D projects are inherently risky and subject to highly uncertain returns, which makes them particularly prone to underinvestment in the absence of public intervention (Shi, 2003; Hall and Lerner, 2010; Hou et al., 2022). Financial constraints further limit firms' capacity to innovate, with restricted access to external finance emerging as a key obstacle to R&D investment (Aghion et al., 2005a; Aghion et al., 2012). These challenges are especially severe for young and small firms, which often lack collateral, credit history, and scale - factors that significantly increase vulnerability to credit constraints (Beck et al., 2005; Beck and Demirgüç-Kunt, 2006; Beck et al., 2008; Hall and Lerner, 2010; De la Torre et al., 2010).In response, governments have deployed a broad range of policy instruments aimed explicitly at stimulating private R&D. These include direct measures such as R&D grants and subsidies that reduce the cost and risk of innovation activities, particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises, as well as indirect instruments such as R&D tax credits, preferential tax treatment, and accelerated depreciation schemes designed to promote sustained R&D investment across a wider set of firms (David et al., 2000; Bloom et al., 2002).Beyond R&D support programmes, several credit guarantee schemes have been introduced that offer partial government guarantees for loans granted by financial institutions, attempting to overcome market failures and alleviate firms' financing problems (Beck et al., 2010; Cowling, 2010; Uesugi et al., 2010; Bachas et al., 2021b; Horvath and Lang, 2021; Hong and Lucas, 2023).2,3 The success of such initiatives in advanced economies has prompted emerging economies to design similar programmes. Turkey has implemented one of the largest public credit guarantee schemes, allocating credit approaching 16.6% of annual GDP between 2017 and 2020.Although enhancing R&D investment and innovation outcomes has not been the primary motivation for public credit guarantees (PCGs), the alleviation in credit constraints provided by guaranteed loans is likely to alter firms' incentives for spending on R&D. While a growing empirical literature has examined the effects of PCGs on firm outcomes such as sales, investment and employment (e.g., Hurley et al., 2021; Doniger and Kay, 2021; Autor et al., 2022), their implications for R&D investment remain largely unexplored. Indeed, existing work on the role of public financial support in innovation activities almost exclusively utilizes data from R&D support programmes that are specifically designed to increase firms' R&D outputs, such as subsidies and tax incentives (see, for example, David et al., 2000; Almus and Czarnitzki, 2003; González et al., 2005; Czarnitzki et al., 2011; and Guo et al., 2016; Howell, 2016). As a result, our understanding of whether and how public credit guarantees influence firms' innovation behaviour is limited.Motivated by both the central role of R&D in long-run growth and the widespread use of credit guarantee schemes in recent years, this paper examines the impact of PCGs on firms' R&D efforts and innovation outcomes. We exploit a rich data set from Turkey's Credit Guarantee Fund that offers firm-level granular data from 2009 to 2020, with nearly 8 million firm-year observations. Turkey's credit guarantee scheme offers three unique advantages for studying these effects. First, as noted above, Turkey's PCG fund is very large compared to most other schemes, allowing us to carry out a comprehensive examination of its implications. In contrast, this paper examines whether PCGs impact firms' R&D and innovation efforts, utilizing a rich data set from Turkey's Credit Guarantee Fund—one of the largest schemes of this kind—and employing a staggered difference-in-differences (DiD) approach preceded by a comprehensive matching procedure. We find that firms receiving guaranteed loans exhibit significantly greater improvements in both innovation inputs, such as R&D expenditure, and innovation outcomes, such as high-tech exports, compared to non-recipient firms. We also observe a substantially larger beneficial impact for firms already engaged in innovation activities and those facing financial constraints. Our findings have important implications for regulatory authorities in their design of credit support programmes.

source_records.abstract: Public procurement of innovation (PPI) is increasingly recognised as a powerful demand-side instrument for generating solutions to complex societal challenges. Yet realising this transformative potential requires innovations to scale beyond isolated implementation contexts. We contribute to the literature by bridging innovation scaling and market shaping perspectives to develop a novel conceptual framework for scaling in the context of PPI. We identify three distinct scaling modes: ‘market acceleration’, where buyers stimulate business growth by facilitating innovation development, adoption, and dissemination across contexts, ‘market building’, where buyers aggregate public sector needs and broaden the scope of PPI, and ‘market transformation’, where buyers embed innovations by reshaping socio-technical systems. Our findings advance theoretical understanding of how public procurement shapes innovation scaling, while providing practical insights into mechanisms through which public buyers can strategically influence market development.

IntroductionTransformative innovation policy has emerged to address the limitations of traditional innovation frameworks, emphasising the need to direct policy efforts towards addressing societal needs (Haddad et al., 2022; Schot and Steinmueller, 2018; OECD, 2024). Central to this approach is the recognition that transformation depends not just on generating novel ideas but on their widespread diffusion and scaling across diverse contexts (Schot and Steinmueller, 2018; Sengers et al., 2021; Robinson et al., 2025). Critically, we can distinguish between ‘diffusion’ - the often passive spread of innovations through populations over time - and ‘scaling’ - the deliberate, strategic efforts to increase innovations' transformative impact across different settings (Breaugh et al., 2021). This distinction emphasises agency and intentionality in promoting innovation adoption beyond initial or scattered implementation contexts.Paradoxically, while transformative innovation policy emphasises the need for widespread scaling to address societal challenges, it has focused primarily on supply-side interventions – R&D funding and innovation systems – while neglecting demand-side policy instruments such as public procurement of innovation (PPI) (Edler, 2023), which remains ‘the weakest point’ in mission-oriented innovation policies (OECD, 2023). With public authorities in the EU spending over €2 trillion annually on procuring goods, services, and works (European Commission, 2021), their capacity to stimulate and promote innovations that address societal challenges, such as responding to climate change, is substantial (e.g. Edquist and Zabala-Iturriagagoitia, 2012; Uyarra et al., 2017, Uyarra et al., 2020; Wesseling and Edquist, 2018).To achieve meaningful societal impact, however, innovations resulting from PPI must extend beyond isolated implementation contexts. This is acknowledged, for instance, by the EU directive (2014/24/EU), which explicitly positions demand aggregation through PPI as a key mechanism for achieving economies of scale, and by other policy initiatives like the European Scale-up manifesto (Hofheinz, 2016). While recognising that public demand can catalyse innovation diffusion (Edler and Georghiou, 2007; Uyarra and Flanagan, 2010; Rolfstam et al., 2011), the PPI literature has focused mainly on innovation generation and adoption within individual organisations, paying much less attention to how public buyers actively promote innovation scaling. This represents a critical knowledge gap, as without effective scaling, PPI's potential to address pressing societal challenges remains unfulfilled (Wesseling and Edquist, 2018).Given this, our research addresses two central questions: (1) What types of scaling occur in PPI contexts? and (2) What specific practices do public buyers employ to promote innovation scaling throughout the procurement lifecycle? Building on emerging work that connects innovation scaling with market-shaping perspectives (e.g., Flaig et al., 2021; Nenonen and Storbacka, 2020), we draw on these literatures to inform our conceptual framing. We distinguish three complementary scaling modes in PPI settings – market acceleration, market building, and market transformation – extending existing scaling typologies to the specific dynamics of public procurement. We then examine twelve PPI projects in Finland to identify the practices through which public buyers facilitate these forms of scaling throughout the procurement lifecycle.Our findings contribute to both the theoretical understanding of scaling in PPI and the practical knowledge of how public buyers can effectively support scaling processes. By integrating market-shaping insights, we highlight how public buyers act not only as adopters but as intentional market shapers whose procurement strategies influence innovation trajectories. We show that scaling in PPI is a multifaceted challenge requiring different approaches depending on the innovation characteristics and contexts (Breaugh et al., 2021). Scaling often involves a combination of replicating solutions, aligning with broader societal needs, and addressing systemic barriers (Lam et al., 2020). Our findings reveal that scaling innovation through procurement requires new competences and a more transformative role for procurement officers (Kattel and Mazzucato, 2018), contributing to emerging discussions on the transformative capacity of public sector organisations (Borrás et al., 2024).The remainder of this paper is structured as follows.
