These findings highlight the enduring importance of geographical proximity in maintaining effective research collaboration.KeywordsGeographical separation; Proximity; Distance; Research collaboration; Mobility; RelocationPrevious article in this issueNext article in this issueIntroductionResearch collaboration has emerged as the dominant approach to knowledge production, driven by increasing specialization and the growing complexity of scientific problems (Wuchty et al., 2007). Collaboration enables knowledge to flow across individual, organizational and regional levels, facilitating the exchange of ideas and the integration of complementary expertise and resources (Jones, 2009; Milojević, 2014). It has been demonstrated to yield substantial advantages, such as enhancing knowledge flow and producing high-quality, innovative research (Ding, 2011; Wuchty et al., 2007). However, collaboration also involves certain costs. The formation and maintenance of effective collaborations require substantial investments in social capital and coordination, including establishing new workflows, monitoring work progress, managing schedules and allocating tasks (Bikard et al., 2015; Boschma, 2005; Petersen, 2015). Thus, scientists strategically evaluate the costs and benefits of collaboration when deciding whom to collaborate with and how to sustain these relationships (Wu et al., 2024).Research collaboration is a dynamic system, evolving through stages of formation, development, and termination. Over the course of a partnership, events such as career progression, institutional relocation, or major disruptions like the COVID-19 pandemic can alter the geographic distance between established collaborators. For instance, collaborators who were once co-located in the same region may become dispersed across different cities or even countries. This geographical separation poses a challenge to maintaining collaboration, as a foundational tenet in economic geographics is that geographical proximity is crucial for knowledge spillovers and innovation (Feldman and Kogler, 2010; Jaffe et al., 1993; Ponds et al., 2007). However, the proliferation of advanced information and communication technologies (ICTs) has sparked a debate regarding whether distance still matters. On the one hand, these technologies have significantly lowered the barriers to remote communication, leading to a marked increase in remote scientific collaboration (Hoekman et al., 2010; Luo et al., 2018; Yao et al., 2020). The “death of distance” hypothesis has thus been proposed, suggesting that distance no longer significantly affects remote collaboration (Cairncross, 2001; Grözinger et al., 2020; Werker and Ooms, 2020).On the other hand, a substantial body of recent studies contends that geographic proximity remains a significant factor. Indeed, numerous studies have demonstrated the significant benefits of geographical proximity in reducing communication and coordination costs (Katz, 1994; Rosenkopf and Almeida, 2003; Storper and Venables, 2004; Yang et al., 2022). Geographical proximity can facilitate communication, trust and the transfer of tacit knowledge through frequent face-to-face interaction (Collins et al., 2022; Ganesan et al., 2005; Lin et al., 2023). Although beneficial, digital communication cannot fully replace in-person interaction, and the challenges of remote collaboration still exist (Yang et al., 2022). Yet, these studies have primarily focused on static comparisons between geographically proximate and remote collaborations (Kabo et al., 2014; Ponds et al., 2007; Roche et al., 2024). While numerous studies have highlighted the advantages of proximity in promoting the search for new collaborators and fostering more collaboration, the longitudinal impact of geographical separation on research collaboration is less understood.This study is motivated by the need to understand how the transition from co-location to separation impacts the performance of research collaborations. Established trust and shared working experience within existing partnerships can enhance communication and coordination effectiveness, rendering such ties more resilient than newly formed collaborations (Dahlander and McFarland, 2013; Nilsson and Mattes, 2015). Furthermore, remote collaborators with prior co-located experience may anticipate potential difficulties and proactively make greater efforts to overcome the challenges (Mors and Waguespack, 2021). Thus, it remains uncertain whether the advantages of these pre-existing strong ties or the new benefits afforded by remote collaboration, such as obtaining and integrating diverse knowledge, can compensate for the challenges posed by geographical separation.This study investigates the impact of geographical separation on research collaboration by comparing performance changes following collaborator mobility. We focus on the discrete transition from co-located collaboration to geographically separated collaboration. We operationalize this transition at the city level, defining co-located pairs as those located in the same city and geographically separated pairs as those located in different cities. Collaboration performance is measured through changes in collaborative productivity and scientific impact. We systematically track scientists' education and employment histories from ORCID records to identify institutional mobility events. By integrating mobility data with publication data from OpenAlex, we construct a scientist-pair-year panel comprising 16,505 scientist pairs and their publication histories. Using a difference-in-differences framework, we compare changes in collaboration performance between pairs in which one collaborator moves to a different city and matched pairs in which one collaborator changes institutions but remains in the same city. This design allows us to isolate the effect of geographical separation from the effect of institutional mobility.We further examine whether the effect of geographical separation varies across different collaboration contexts. First, we examine boundary-spanning heterogeneity by comparing interdisciplinary collaborations with monodisciplinary ones, as these two types exhibit distinct communication and coordination modes. Second, we investigate hierarchical heterogeneity by distinguishing between peer collaborations and cross-stage collaborations. This distinction is important because these collaboration types differ in their core functions of peer communication versus guidance, which may be differentially affected by geographical separation. Third, we examine geographic-context heterogeneity by assessing whether the effect differs between pairs located in larger versus smaller countries, where inter-city separation may imply different levels of travel and coordination costs.The results show that geographical separation significantly reduces both the productivity and scientific impact of established scientific collaborations. Scientist pairs publish fewer co-publications after separation, and the citation impact of their joint publications also declines. The average effect, however, masks important heterogeneity. Interdisciplinary collaborations appear more resilient in maintaining publication output after separation, but their scientific impact is more adversely affected. Same-stage collaborations experience larger declines than cross-stage collaborations, suggesting that peer collaborations may be particularly vulnerable to the loss of routine interaction. The negative effect of geographical separation is also more pronounced in larger countries, consistent with the idea that inter-city separation imposes greater travel and coordination costs in larger geographic contexts.Our findings contribute to the literature in several ways. First, this study provides insight into the debate on whether geographical proximity still matters in collaboration. Specifically, the findings highlight the advantages of proximate collaboration over remote collaboration. These benefits primarily stem from the opportunities for face-to-face interaction, which is pivotal for scientific collaboration (Collins et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2023). When collaboration occurs at a distance, these advantages are lost and replaced by the high costs associated with face-to-face interaction, which in turn impedes the development of interpersonal trust and the transfer of tacit knowledge. Second, this study extends the literature on the dynamics of scientific collaboration. Rather than focusing on collaborative initiation, we shift the analytical lens to collaborative resilience by examining how collaboration performance changes when collaborators become geographically separated after a period of co-location. Our findings demonstrate that while pre-existing relational assets are beneficial, they are often insufficient to fully counteract the challenges posed by distance.The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 reviews existing studies and develops hypotheses. Section 3 introduces data construction, descriptive statistics, and empirical strategies. Section 4 reports the main results, along with a series of robustness checks and heterogeneity exploration. Finally, Section 5 discusses the implications of the findings and Section 6 concludes the study.Organizational accessGet full-text access by signing in with your organisationAccess through your organizationOther access optionsPurchase PDFNeed help with access?Section snippetsGeographical proximity and collaborationExisting studies have revealed that geographic distance remains a significant factor in research collaboration (Lin et al., 2023; Vieira et al., 2022). source_records.title: Rent Guarantee Insurance
source_records.abstract: A rent guarantee insurance (RGI) policy makes a limited number of rent payments to the landlord on behalf of an insured tenant unable to pay rent due to a negative income or health expenditure shock. We introduce RGI in a rich quantitative equilibrium model of housing insecurity and show it increases welfare by improving risk sharing across idiosyncratic and aggregate states of the world, reducing the need for a large security deposits, and reducing homelessness which imposes large costs on society. While unrestricted access to RGI is not financially viable due to moral hazard and adverse selection, restricting access can restore viability. Private insurers target better off renters to break even, while public insurers focus on households most at-risk of homelessness. Stronger tenant protections increase the effectiveness of RGI.

before.title_zh: 租金担保保险
before.abstract_zh: 租金保证保险（RGI）保单代表因收入或健康支出负向冲击而无力支付租金的参保租户，向房东支付有限次数的租金。我们将RGI引入一个关于住房不安全的丰富定量均衡模型，并表明它通过改善对异质性和总体世界状态的风险分担、减少对大额押金的需求，以及减少给社会带来巨大成本的无家可归现象，提高了福利。虽然由于道德风险和逆向选择，无限制地获得RGI在财务上不可行，但限制获得可以恢复可行性。私人保险公司以状况较好的租户为目标以实现收支平衡，而公共保险公司则关注最有可能无家可归的家庭。更强的租户保护提高了RGI的有效性。

We introduce RGI in a quantitative equilibrium model of housing insecurity and show it increases welfare by improving risk sharing across idiosyncratic and aggregate states, reducing the need for large security deposits and reducing homelessness that imposes large costs on society. existing_records.title: Rent Guarantee Insurance
existing_records.abstract: A rent guarantee insurance (RGI) policy makes a limited number of rent payments to the landlord on behalf of an insured tenant unable to pay rent due to a negative income or health expenditure shock. We introduce RGI in a rich quantitative equilibrium model of housing insecurity and show it increases welfare by improving risk sharing across idiosyncratic and aggregate states of the world, reducing the need for a large security deposits, and reducing homelessness which imposes large costs on society. While unrestricted access to RGI is not financially viable due to moral hazard and adverse selection, restricting access can restore viability. Private insurers target better off renters to break even, while public insurers focus on households most at-risk of homelessness. Stronger tenant protections increase the effectiveness of RGI.

after.title_zh: 租金担保保险
after.abstract_zh: 租金保证保险（RGI）保单代表因收入或健康支出负向冲击而无力支付租金的参保租户，向房东支付有限次数的租金。我们将RGI引入一个关于住房不安全的丰富定量均衡模型，并表明它通过改善对异质性和总体世界状态的风险分担、减少对大额押金的需求，以及减少给社会带来巨大成本的无家可归现象，提高了福利。虽然由于道德风险和逆向选择，无限制地获得RGI在财务上不可行，但限制获得可以恢复可行性。私人保险公司以状况较好的租户为目标以实现收支平衡，而公共保险公司则关注最有可能无家可归的家庭。更强的租户保护提高了RGI的有效性。

source_records.title: The Effect of Education Policy on Crime: An Intergenerational Perspective
source_records.abstract: We examine the intergenerational effect of education policy on crime. Using administrative data that link outcomes across generations with crime records, we show that the Swedish comprehensive school reform, gradually implemented between 1949 and 1962, reduced conviction rates both for the generation directly affected and for their sons. The reduction occurred across several types of crime. Mediation analysis suggests that the key channels include increased parental educational attainment and household income, as well as reduced criminal behavior among fathers.

before.title_zh: 教育政策对犯罪的影响：代际视角
before.abstract_zh: 我们考察教育政策对犯罪的代际效应。利用将各代人的结果与犯罪记录相链接的行政数据，我们表明，在1949年至1962年间逐步实施的瑞典综合学校改革，既降低了直接受影响那一代人的定罪率，也降低了其儿子的定罪率。这一下降出现在若干犯罪类型中。中介分析表明，关键渠道包括父母受教育程度提高和家庭收入增加，以及父亲犯罪行为减少。
